en: Then, after some time had passed, King Daśaratha, the joy of the Raghus, spoke to his son Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī:
"My dear son, this son of the King of Kekaya is staying here."
"O hero, your maternal uncle Yudhājit has come to take you away.
Upon hearing this from Daśaratha, Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī,
then set out for the journey accompanied by Śatrughna.
Having taken leave of his father, of Rāma who performs deeds without weariness,
and of his mothers as well, that hero, the best among men, departed accompanied by Śatrughna.
Having received Bharata along with Śatrughna, Yudhājit was filled with great joy.

The hero entered his own city, and his father was indeed filled with joy. There he dwelt together with his brother, honored with hospitable reception and cherished by his maternal uncle, Aśvapati, out of affection for his son.
While dwelling there and being gratified according to their desires,
those two heroic brothers remembered King Daśaratha, the aged monarch;
and the king of great splendor also remembered his two sons who were living in exile.
Both Bharata and Śatrughna were like Mahendra and Varuṇa; indeed,
all four of those bulls among men were as dear to him as his own four arms extending from his body.
Among them, Rāma, possessed of great splendor and highly virtuous, became the source of delight for his father, just as the Self-born Creator is for all living beings.
And when Bharata had departed, Rāma and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa—
Then they both honored their father, who was like a god.
Placing his father’s command foremost, the righteous Rāma performed all the affairs of the citizens, doing what was pleasing and beneficial.
Having performed his maternal duties toward his mothers with the utmost self-restraint,
he attended to the weighty affairs of his elders from time to time.
Thus, Daśaratha was pleased, as were the Brahmins and the merchants.
All the inhabitants of the realm [were won over] by Rāma’s character and conduct;
for he was always tranquil in soul and spoke with gentleness,
and even when addressed harshly, he did not offer a retort.
He is satisfied with even a single benefit rendered in some way,
yet by virtue of his self-control, he does not remember even a hundred injuries;
he is honored by virtuous people who are advanced in character, advanced in knowledge, and advanced in age.
He remained constantly engaged in conversation even during intervals between his weapons training;
he was of noble lineage, virtuous, undaunted, truthful, and upright,
and had been thoroughly instructed by elders— twice-born men who perceived the true nature of dharma and artha.
He knows the true nature of dharma, artha, and kāma; he possesses memory and eloquence; he is skilled and confident in worldly conventions and conduct;
he is learned in the scriptures, grateful, and discerning of the differences between men.
He who is discerning in the proper application of restraint and favor,
who knows the means for the work of revenue, and who understands the management of expenditures;
he who has attained preeminence in the collections of scriptures, even those of mixed content.
Gathering both wealth and righteousness, he was devoted to pleasure yet not indolent;
he was an expert in the mechanical arts of recreation and knew the distinctions of meaning; he was skilled in the mounting and training of elephants and horses.
He is the best among those skilled in the science of archery, esteemed in the world as an Atiratha;
he is an assailant and a striker, expert in the leadership of armies,
and invincible in battle even by the enraged gods and asuras.
Free from envy, having conquered anger, neither arrogant nor envious,
he did not despise living beings, nor was he subject to the power of time. Thus endowed with these preeminent virtues was the prince, the protector of his subjects.
He was esteemed in the three worlds for his qualities of forbearance like those of the Earth; he was equal to Bṛhaspati in wisdom and to the Lord of Śacī in valor.
Likewise, through qualities beloved by all subjects that produced joy in his father—
Rāma shone with his virtues like the blazing sun with its rays.
The Earth desired him as her lord— he who was endowed with such conduct, possessed of invincible prowess, and comparable to the guardians of the world.
But seeing his son endowed with these many incomparable virtues, King Daśaratha, the scorcher of enemies, fell into deep reflection;
for this supreme joy revolved within his heart.
When indeed shall I see my beloved son consecrated?
For he desires the prosperity of the world and has compassion for all beings; he is dearer to the world than I am, like a rain-bearing cloud.
Equal to Yama and Śakra in valor, equal to Bṛhaspati in intellect,
and equal to the mountain king in fortitude, he is even more virtuous than I.
[I shall see] my son ruling over this entire earth.
"Having seen him at this age, may I attain heaven.
Having observed that he was endowed with all these combined virtues, the great king,
after deliberating with his ministers, decided upon him as the crown prince.
The lord of the earth also summoned the foremost men of the world, including commoners from various provinces and residents of diverse cities.
Then, they sat upon the various seats provided by the king.

The kings sat down, self-restrained, facing the king himself. Surrounded by those local and provincial men who had received honors and were full of humility as they sat near him, the monarch shone like the thousand-eyed Lord Indra surrounded by the immortals.
Then, having addressed the entire assembly, the lord of the earth spoke these incomparable words, which were beneficial,
heartening, and profound, resonating like the sound of a kettledrum.
With a great voice, making it resound like a thundercloud, the king said:
"I am he who desires to endow with prosperity this entire world, which is worthy of happiness and has been protected by the Ikṣvākus, the former lords of men."
Following the path practiced by my predecessors, I too have always protected my subjects with vigilance to the best of my ability;
for this body has been dedicated to securing the welfare of the entire world.
I have grown old in the shade of this white parasol;
having lived for many thousands of years and reached the end of my lifespan,
I desire rest for this worn-out body.
For, bearing the heavy yoke of dharma for the world— a burden difficult to carry for those who have not conquered their senses and yet graced by royal majesty— I am weary.
Therefore, having appointed my son to the welfare of the subjects, I desire rest.
Having honored all these eminent brahmins gathered here,
[I declare]: for my eldest son Rāma, the conqueror of enemy cities, is my own offspring who is equal to Purandara in valor and is indeed my equal in every virtue.

Just as the moon is joined with the constellation Puṣya, I shall joyfully appoint that best of the upholders of dharma, that bull among men, to the position of crown prince. He, the fortunate elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, is a worthy lord for you all.
By him, our lord, even the three worlds would become more truly possessed of a protector.
By immediately uniting this earth with such a blessing, and having entrusted my daughter to him, I shall indeed be freed from all affliction.
As the king spoke thus, the delighted kings greeted him in return,
like peacocks responding to a great rain-bearing cloud that is thundering.
Having fully understood the disposition of that king, who was learned in dharma and artha, [they acted accordingly].
And having learned of it in their minds, they said to King Daśaratha, who was aged:
"O King, you are advanced in years, having lived for many thousands of years;
therefore, consecrate Rāma as the prince regent."
Having heard those words so pleasing to their hearts, the king, as if not knowing their intent and desiring to learn more, spoke these words:
"How is it that while I am ruling the earth according to dharma..."
"Sirs, you wish to see my son, the crown prince.
They, together with the people of the city and the countryside, said to that high-souled one:
"O King, your son possesses many auspicious virtues."
Equal to Śakra in divine qualities, Rāma, whose prowess is truth,
O lord of the people, is indeed more beloved than all the Ikṣvākus;
Rāma is a virtuous man in this world, devoted to truth and righteousness.
He knows the Dharma, is true to his word, virtuous, and free from envy; he is patient, consoling, gentle, grateful, and has conquered his senses;
he is mild, steady-minded, always auspicious, and free from malice.
Rāghava speaks kindly to all beings and is a speaker of truth;
he is a devoted servant of the learned and aged brahmins.
Because of this, his incomparable fame, glory, and splendor increase in this world.
Skilled in all weapons of the gods, asuras, and humans,
whenever he goes forth to battle for the sake of a village or a city,
he never returns from it without having achieved victory, accompanied by the son of Sumitrā.
Having returned from battle, whether by elephant or chariot,
he constantly inquires after the welfare of the citizens as if they were his own kin,
and likewise among his sons, his sacred fires, his wives, and the groups of his servants and pupils.
"O tiger among men, Rāma always asks us: 'Do your disciples serve you in every way and in due order, like sons born of your own loins? And are they diligent in their duties? (Rāmāyaṇa 2.2.26–27)
He becomes deeply distressed by the misfortunes of men and rejoices at all their festivals like a father;
he is a speaker of truth, a great archer, a servant of the elders, and one who has conquered his senses.
"By good fortune, this Rāghava of yours has been born for your welfare; by good fortune, he is endowed with the virtues of a son, like Kaśyapa’s son Mārīca.
Strength, health, and long life belong to Rāma, who knows his own self."
All the people in the kingdom and in that excellent city—
both those within and those outside, the citizens and the country folk,
women, the elderly, and the young— all with concentrated minds, hope [for his return] morning and evening.
They pay homage to all the gods for the sake of the illustrious Rāma;
O God, may their prayer be fulfilled through your grace.
[They pray for] Rāma, dark as a blue lotus, the destroyer of all enemies.
We behold your son, O best of kings, established in the position of crown prince.

O granter of boons, you ought to joyfully and swiftly consecrate that son of yours— who resembles a god of gods and is intent on the welfare of the entire world— for our own benefit, for he is one who delights in noble deeds.
Having accepted all their lotus-like hands joined in salutation, the king spoke these words, which were both pleasing and beneficial, to them:
"Oh, I am supremely delighted; my power is indeed incomparable!"

"Since you desire my eldest and beloved son, who is established as the heir apparent," having thus honored those brahmins, the king spoke these words to Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva while they were listening.
"This month of Caitra is glorious and auspicious, with its forests in full bloom;
let everything be prepared for Rāma’s consecration as crown prince.
Approaching the lord of the world, they both replied, "It is done."
When the two bulls among the twice-born had heard these words as spoken, they were filled with joy and delight.
Then the radiant king spoke these words to Sumantra:
"Let the self-disciplined Rāma be brought here by you immediately."
Having agreed, saying "So be it," Sumantra, by the king's command,
brought Rāma— the best among chariot-warriors— to that place by means of his chariot.
Then, those who were seated there [beheld] King Daśaratha.
The rulers of the east, the north, the west, and the south— Mlecchas, Aryas, and others who dwell in forests and mountain fastnesses—
all waited upon him as the gods wait upon Vāsava.
In their midst, that royal sage, standing upon his palace like Vāsava among the Maruts, beheld his son approaching on a chariot—
one who resembled the king of the Gandharvas and was renowned in the world for his prowess.
Long-armed, a Great Being with the gait of an elephant in rut,
Rāma had a face as lovely as the moon; exceedingly pleasing to behold, he captivated the eyes and hearts of men with his beauty, nobility, and virtues.
Like creatures scorched by the heat longing for the rain-cloud that brings refreshment,
the lord of men was not satiated as he gazed upon him approaching.
Having helped Raghava down from his excellent chariot, Sumantra [proceeded].

With palms joined in reverence, he followed behind his father as he went toward him. That bull among men, Rāghava, together with his charioteer, ascended the palace which resembled a peak of Mount Kailāsa, in order to see the king.
Approaching with palms joined in reverence and bowing down before his father,
Rāma announced his own name and paid homage at his father's feet.
Seeing him prostrate by his side with hands folded in supplication, the king—
Drawing his beloved son toward him as he held out his joined palms, the king embraced him;
then the illustrious monarch directed a beautiful, supreme seat, adorned with gems and gold, which had been prepared for him, to Rāma.
Having obtained that excellent seat, Rāghava illuminated it with his own radiance, like the stainless sun at its rising illuminating Mount Meru;
and made radiant by him, that assembly hall shone forth brilliantly.
Like the autumnal sky, with its stainless planets and stars, graced by the moon,
the king beheld his beloved son and rejoiced,
as if seeing his own self adorned upon the surface of a mirror.
Addressing his son with a smile, that king, the best among those who possess sons, spoke these words to him, just as Kaśyapa spoke to Devendra:
"You are a worthy son born of my eldest wife, who is herself worthy of you."
"You have been born as the most excellent in virtue, my dear son Rāma. Since these subjects have been won over by you through your own qualities, therefore,
under the conjunction of Puṣya, receive the office of heir apparent."

"By your very nature you are disciplined and possessed of virtue; yet, O son, because of my affection for you who are already virtuous, I shall tell you what is for your benefit. By applying yourself even further to discipline, remain forever one who has conquered his senses."
Abandon those vices that arise from desire and anger. Conducting yourself both through indirect means and through direct observation,
please all the subjects, beginning with the ministers.
The friends of that king who protects the earth with his subjects satisfied and devoted rejoice, like the immortals upon obtaining the nectar of immortality;
therefore, my son, conduct yourself by restraining yourself.
Having heard that, his friends, who were intent on doing what was pleasing to Rāma,
quickly approached and informed Kausalyā.
She [gave] gold, cows, and various kinds of jewels.
Then Kausalyā, the best of women, gave instructions to her dear attendants.
Thereupon, having paid his respects to the king and mounted his chariot, Rāghava departed for his own radiant residence, honored by throngs of people.
And those citizens, having heard those words of the king, felt as if they had attained a desired gain;
having taken leave of the lord of men and gone to their homes, they worshipped the gods with exceeding joy.
Then, when the citizens had departed, the king, together with his ministers, [sat] once more.
Having deliberated, that lord, who knew how to reach a decision, then made his resolution:
"Tomorrow the constellation Puṣya will be in the ascendant; tomorrow my son Rāma, whose eyes are as copper-red as lotuses, shall be consecrated as the heir apparent."
Then, having entered the inner apartments, King Daśaratha commanded the charioteer, "Bring Rāma back here once more.
Accepting those words, the charioteer returned again.
Once again, the gatekeepers were quickly informed to bring Rāma to the palace;
and upon hearing that he had arrived once more, Rāma became filled with apprehension.
Having quickly ushered him in, Rāma spoke these words:
"Tell me in full once more the purpose for which you have come.
Then the charioteer said to him, "The king desires to see you."
"Having heard this, you shall be the authority here regarding whether to go or otherwise.
Having heard these words of the charioteer, Rāma, filled with haste,
then proceeded toward the royal palace to see the lord of men once more.

Hearing that Rāma had arrived, King Daśaratha, desiring to see his most beloved son, ushered him into the palace. And as soon as the illustrious Rāghava entered his father’s residence, he was received with honor.
He saw his father from afar and, bowing down with palms joined in reverence, approached him.
Raising up the prince as he prostrated, the lord of the earth embraced him,
offered him a beautiful seat, and spoke to him again.
"O Rāma, I am old and long-lived; I have enjoyed all the pleasures I desired, and likewise performed hundreds of sacrifices provided with abundant food and profuse sacrificial fees.
Today, you have been born to me as a son, peerless on this earth."
"O best of men, I have given gifts, performed sacrifices, and studied the Vedas. O hero, I have experienced all desired pleasures;
thus, I am free from debt to the gods, the seers, the ancestors, the brahmins, and to myself."
There is nothing whatsoever that I must do for you other than your consecration;
therefore, you ought to do for me what I shall tell you.
Today, all the subjects desire you as their sovereign.
Therefore, my son, I shall consecrate you as the crown prince.
Moreover, O Rāma, today I see inauspicious and terrible dreams;
great meteors, accompanied by thunderclaps, are falling here with a loud roar.
"O Rāma, the astrologers announce that my birth star has been seized by cruel planets— the Sun, Mars, and Rāhu.
Indeed, when such portents as these generally arise,"

"Either the king will meet his death or he will encounter a terrible calamity. Therefore, O Raghava, consecrate yourself while my mind is not yet deluded; for the intellect of living beings is fickle."
"Today the moon has entered Punarvasu, which precedes Puṣya;
tomorrow, the astrologers say, the conjunction with Puṣya is certain.
Therefore, perform the consecration under that Puṣya; my mind seems to urge me on."
"Tomorrow, O scorcher of foes, I shall consecrate you as the crown prince;
therefore, you must spend this night today as one observing a vow, self-restrained,
fasting together with your wife, and sleeping upon a bed of darbha grass."
Let your friends, remaining vigilant, protect you on all sides today;
for such undertakings as these are indeed beset by many obstacles.
Moreover, Bharata has not yet departed from this city.
"In my view, this very moment is the time for your consecration.
Indeed, Bharata, your brother, abides in the conduct of the virtuous; he follows his elder brother, is righteous-souled, compassionate, and has conquered his senses."
"But it is my conviction, O Raghava, that the minds of men are fickle, whereas for the virtuous who are constant in dharma, their conduct is ever beautiful.
Having been addressed thus and granted leave, [he waited] for the consecration to take place on the following day.

Having saluted his father, Rāma departed for his own home. Having entered his own residence at the moment the consecration was announced by the king, he went out from there and proceeded to his mother’s inner apartments.
There, in the temple of the deity, he saw his mother, dressed in linen, restrained in speech, and devotedly praying for Śrī;
Sumitrā and Lakṣmaṇa had already arrived there before him.
And having heard the pleasant news of Rāma’s consecration, Sītā was summoned;
for at that time Kausalyā stood with her eyes closed, attended by Sumitrā, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa.
Having heard that his son’s consecration as crown prince would take place under the asterism Puṣya,
she was meditating upon Janārdana, the Supreme Person, through the practice of breath control (prāṇāyāma). Approaching her while she remained thus restrained by her vows, he saluted her.
Then Rāma spoke these words to her, gladdening her:
"O Mother, I have been appointed by my father to the task of protecting the subjects;
according to my father's command, my consecration shall take place tomorrow."
"Sītā must also fast this night along with me;
thus did my father speak to me together with the officiating priests and preceptors regarding whatever rites are appropriate here for the consecration to take place tomorrow."
"Perform those auspicious rites for me today, and likewise for Vaidehī.
Having heard these words, which she had long desired, Kausalyā addressed Rāma with this speech, choked with tears of joy.
"Child Rāma, live long! Those who stood as your adversaries are slain.
Endowed with glory, you shall bring joy to my kinsmen and to Sumitrā.
Oh, what a fortunate lunar mansion it was when you were born, my son!"
"By you, through your virtues, your father Daśaratha has been propitiated.
Ah, my patient endurance toward that lotus-eyed man has not been in vain,
for this royal fortune of the Ikṣvākus shall now rest upon you, my son."
Having been addressed thus by his mother, Rāma, looking at his brother who sat before him with joined palms and bowed head, spoke as if smiling:
"O Lakṣmaṇa, you must rule this earth together with me."
"This Goddess of Fortune has come to you, my second self.
O Saumitri, enjoy the pleasures you desire and the fruits of sovereignty;
for both life and the kingdom, I desire only for your sake."
Having spoken thus to Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma saluted his two mothers,
took leave of Sītā, and went to his own quarters.
The king, having instructed Rāma regarding the consecration to take place on the following day, [departed].
Having summoned his family priest Vasiṣṭha, he spoke these words:
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, go today and cause the descendant of Kakutstha,
together with his bride, to observe a fast according to his vows for the sake of attaining prosperity, fame, and the kingdom."
Saying "So be it" to the king, the venerable Vasiṣṭha, the best among those who know the Vedas, went himself to Rāma’s residence.
Having reached Rāma’s palace, which shone like a mass of white clouds, he entered.

The best of sages entered through three courtyards as if by means of a chariot. Seeing that the seer had arrived, Rāma, acting with haste and agitation, went out from his residence to honor him who was worthy of honor.
Hurrying toward the vicinity of the wise man's chariot,
he himself took hold of him and helped him descend from the vehicle. Then, seeing him humble, he addressed him and won his favor.
Gladdening Rāma, who was worthy of affection, the family priest spoke thus:
"O Rāma, your father is pleased with you; you shall receive the position of crown prince.
You should observe a fast today together with Sītā."
"Tomorrow morning, King Daśaratha, your father, will joyfully consecrate you as the crown prince, just as Nahuṣa consecrated Yayāti.
Having said this to Rāma, who was observing a fast and restrained by his vows, he then—

The sage had the ceremony performed for him together with Vaidehī according to the sacred mantras. Then, having been duly honored by Rāma, that preceptor of the king took leave of the descendant of Kakutstha and departed from Rāma’s residence.
There, Rāma also took leave of his friends after honoring them in every way; having dismissed them all,
he then entered the residence of Rāma, which shone with joyful men and women.
Like a lake filled with blossoming lotuses and flocks of intoxicated birds,
Vasiṣṭha emerged from that residence of Rāma— which resembled a royal palace— and beheld the road crowded with people.
In Ayodhyā, the royal highways on all sides became congested, crowded by throngs upon throngs of curious people;
at that time, they resounded with the joyful noise of the surging waves of the human multitude.
The sound of the royal highway was like that of the ocean. On that day, the city of Ayodhyā, adorned with forest garlands, had its streets sprinkled and swept, and its house-banners were raised high.
For then the people dwelling in Ayodhyā— including women, children, and the elderly—
longed for Rāma’s consecration, just as they long for the rising of the sun;
he who was the ornament of the subjects and the increaser of the people’s joy.
The people were eager to witness that great festival of Ayodhyā.
Thus, as if parting the flood of the crowd, the family priest proceeded slowly toward the royal palace along that royal highway crowded with people.
Having ascended the palace, which resembled the peak of a white cloud,
he met with the lord of men as Bṛhaspati meets Śakra.
Seeing that he had arrived, the king abandoned his royal throne.
He questioned him, and he reported to him that it had been done.
Having been permitted by his preceptor and having dismissed that multitude of men,
the king entered the inner apartments like a lion entering a mountain cave.

Then the king entered that residence, which was crowded with women in exquisite attire and resembled the palace of Mahendra; illuminating it, he entered as the moon enters the sky filled with hosts of stars.
When the family priest had departed, Rāma, having bathed and composed his mind, [entered].
Together with his large-eyed wife, he approached Nārāyaṇa;
then, holding a vessel of sacrificial oblation to his head,
he duly offered the clarified butter into the blazing fire for the great deity.
Having consumed the remainder of that sacrificial oblation and having invoked blessings for his own welfare,
he meditated upon the god Nārāyaṇa while lying on a well-spread bed of kuśa grass; remaining silent, he stayed there with Vaidehī, his mind firmly restrained.
In the glorious abode of Viṣṇu, the son of the best of men lay down to rest.
When one watch of the night remained, he awoke and had the entire decoration of the palace prepared.
There, listening to the pleasant words of the *sūtas*, *māgadhas*, and bards,
he performed his morning devotions and, with a restrained mind, recited his prayers;
then, bowing with his head, he offered praise to Madhusūdana.
Clad in spotless linen garments, he caused the twice-born to recite the prayers;
then the deep and sweet sound of their proclamation of an auspicious day filled Ayodhyā, resonating with the sound of musical instruments.
When all the people residing in Ayodhyā heard that Rāghava, together with Vaidehī, had then undertaken a fast, they were all filled with joy.
Then, having heard of Rāma’s consecration, all the citizens rejoiced.
Seeing that the night had turned to dawn, he once again created supreme splendor in the temples resembling the peaks of white clouds,
at the crossroads, on the streets, at the shrines, and upon the watchtowers.
In marketplaces abounding with various wares belonging to merchants,
in the prosperous and magnificent mansions of householders,
in all the assembly halls, and even among the visible trees.
Then, variegated banners and flags were raised on high;
and from here and there, the voices of troupes of actors, dancers, and singing minstrels were heard, pleasing to the mind and the ear.
And as the consecration of Rāma drew near, the people conversed with one another about it in the courtyards and in their homes;
even the children, playing in groups at the doorways of their houses, spoke of it.

They engaged in mutual conversation concerning the consecration of Rāma. For the consecration of Rāma, the citizens had prepared the magnificent royal highway, strewn with offerings of flowers and perfumed with the fragrance of incense.
And for the purpose of illumination, fearing the arrival of night,
they likewise set up lamp-trees everywhere along the streets;
having thus performed the adornment of the city, the inhabitants of that town—
Desiring the consecration of Rāma as the crown prince,
they all gathered in groups at the crossroads and in the assembly halls;
conversing with one another there, they praised the lord of men.
"Oh, what a great-souled king is this, the joy of the Ikṣvāku lineage,
who, knowing himself to be old, will consecrate Rāma in the kingdom!
For we have all been truly blessed that Rāma shall be our sovereign."
For a long time he will be our protector, having perceived the higher and lower realms of the world.
Wise, righteous-souled, affectionate toward his brothers, and with a mind free from arrogance,
Raghava is as devoted to us as he is to his brothers.
"May the righteous King Daśaratha live long, O sinless one,
by whose grace we shall behold Rāma consecrated!"—
this was what they heard from the citizens as they were speaking in such a manner.
People from the countryside, having heard the news from all directions,
arrived; those country folk, having reached the city from every quarter to witness Rāma’s consecration, filled the city.
As those surging throngs of people moved along, a roar was heard there like the roar of the ocean when its momentum is unleashed during the change of seasons.
Then, that city, resembling the abode of Indra, was filled with country folk who had arrived, eager to behold it.
On all sides, it appeared tumultuous and filled with noise, like the waters of the ocean teeming with sea-monsters.
Then Jñātidāsī, who had been born a slave and had lived with Kaikeyī,
ascended by chance to the palace that resembled the moon.
From that palace, Mantharā gazed down upon the entire city of Ayodhyā, its main roads sprinkled with water and strewn with lotuses and water-lilies,
and beautifully adorned with banners worthy of the highest honor and various flags.
Seeing her standing nearby— sprinkled with sandalwood water and surrounded by those who had bathed her head— the nurse Maṇtharā,
devoted to her own interests, was filled with supreme joy and questioned her.
"Why is Rāma’s mother bestowing wealth upon the people?
Tell me why this excessive joy has come upon the folk,
and what it is that the delighted lord of the earth intends to have done."
Torn asunder by joy and with supreme delight, the nurse then announced to the hunchback the even greater fortune of Rāghava:
"Tomorrow, under the asterism of Puṣya, they will invest Rāghava, who has conquered his anger, with the office of crown prince."
"King Daśaratha intends to consecrate the sinless Rāma.
Having heard these words of the nurse, the hunchback, suddenly provoked with indignation,
descended from the palace which resembled a peak of Mount Kailāsa.
Burning with rage, the evil-sighted Mantharā approached Kaikeyī as she lay there and spoke these words:
"Arise, you fool! Why do you lie there? A great danger is approaching you."
Why do you not realize that you yourself are being overwhelmed by a great flood? O woman of lovely form, you boast of your good fortune,
yet your good fortune is as fickle as the current of a river during the summer heat.
Thus addressed with harsh words by the angry and evil-minded Kubjā, Kaikeyī fell into a state of extreme despondency.
But Kaikeyī said to the hunchback: "O Mantharā, is all not well?"
"For I perceive you with a dejected countenance, deeply afflicted by sorrow.
Hearing these sweet-syllabled words of Kaikeyī, Mantharā,
skilled in speech, spoke these words filled with anger.
Becoming even more despondent, that hunchback, who desired her welfare,
spoke to her while causing her distress and sowing discord against Rāghava:
"O Queen, a very great misfortune has begun, leading to your destruction."
"King Daśaratha will consecrate Rāma as the heir apparent. Thus,
plunged into bottomless fear and filled with misery and grief, I have come here as if burning with fire for the sake of your welfare."
"O Kaikeyī, through your sorrow my own sorrow shall become great;
and through your prosperity my prosperity shall likewise increase—of this there is no doubt.
Born into a lineage of kings, you are the queen of the lord of the earth."
O Queen, how is it that you do not perceive the ferocity inherent in the duties of kings?
Your husband speaks of righteousness while being deceitful; he speaks with gentleness while being cruel.
O pure-hearted one, you did not know him, and thus you have been deceived by him in this way.
Employing empty conciliation toward you,
your husband will today unite Kausalyā with actual wealth,
having sent that evil-minded Bharata away to your kinsmen.
Having established Rāma on the throne early tomorrow morning, once all thorns have been removed,
you, O young woman, have embraced an enemy under the guise of a husband, out of a desire for his welfare as if he were your own mother, like a venomous serpent held in your lap.
Just as one would treat a snake or an enemy once they have been observed,
so has King Daśaratha treated you today along with your sons— you,
who are young and always accustomed to happiness— by means of wicked and false conciliation.
"By establishing Rāma in the kingdom, you have indeed destroyed yourself along with your kin.
O Kaikeyī, whose appearance is so wondrous, act quickly for your own welfare now that the time has come; save your son, yourself, and me."
Having heard Mantharā’s words, that woman of beautiful countenance rose from her bed and gave those auspicious ornaments to the hunchbacked woman.
Having bestowed the ornaments upon that hunchbacked woman, the most excellent of women—
Delighted, Kaikeyī spoke these words once more to Mantharā: "Mantharā, you have told me this most pleasing news;
what further can I do for you who have brought me such joy?"
"I perceive no difference between Rāma and Bharata;
therefore, I am pleased that the king will consecrate Rāma in the kingdom.
O you who deserve what is dear, there is nothing more dear to me than this, nor could any better word be spoken by you."
"For you have spoken thus; therefore, I shall grant you another supreme boon, even more beloved than this—choose it.

But Mantharā, full of malice toward her, cast off that ornament and, filled with anger and grief, spoke these words: Mantharā, however, having reviled her and cast aside that jewelry, then spoke these words, overcome with anger and sorrow.
"O foolish woman, why have you felt this joy at an inappropriate time?
You do not realize that you yourself are standing in the midst of an ocean of grief.
Truly fortunate is Kausalyā, whose son is to be consecrated."
Tomorrow, under the asterism Puṣya, you shall be installed in the great office of crown prince by the best of the twice-born.
Having slain your enemies, you will behold Kausalyā, who has attained immense joy, with a mind full of confidence; you, however, shall wait upon her with joined palms like a maidservant.
"Rāma’s foremost wives will surely be delighted,
while your daughters-in-law will be despondent at the downfall of Bharata.
Then, seeing Mantharā speaking thus with great joy, [Kaikeyī said:]
Queen Kaikeyī indeed praised the virtues of Rāma alone:
"Rāma, the eldest son of the king, knows the dharma, is self-controlled by his elders, grateful, truthful, and pure; therefore, he deserves the position of heir apparent."
Long-lived as he is, he will protect his brothers and servants like a father;
O hunchback, why do you grieve upon hearing of Rāma’s consecration?
And Bharata, too, will certainly [serve] Rāma for more than a hundred years.
That bull among men shall obtain the kingdom of his father and grandfather;
O Mantharā, why do you grieve when prosperity has arrived, is present, and will continue to be auspicious?
"He indeed serves me even more than he does Kausalyā.
Having heard Kaikeyī's words, Mantharā was deeply distressed;
sighing long and hot, she spoke this to Kaikeyī.
"Out of folly you do not perceive this misfortune, nor do you realize your own situation as you sink into an ocean of suffering, vast with grief and calamity.
Rāghava will become king, and so too shall his son."
"O Kaikeyī, Bharata will be excluded from the royal lineage;
for not all the sons of a king remain in the kingdom, O beautiful lady, for if all were installed, a very great disorder would arise."
Therefore, O Kaikeyī of faultless limbs, kings establish the affairs of state with their eldest son, even if other sons possess superior virtues; thus,
this son of yours will become utterly submissive.
O affectionate one, like one who is helpless, you have been deprived of pleasures and your royal lineage;
yet, for my sake, I have come here, and you do not recognize me—
you who wish to give me away as a prize upon the increase of your co-wife.
Once Rāma has obtained the kingdom free from all obstacles, he will surely cause Bharata to be sent away to another land— or even to the other world—
since you have already sent the child Bharata to his maternal uncle’s house.
"From close proximity, even among stationary things, affection arises.
For Laksmana is the protector of Rama, and Raghava is the protector of Laksmana; their brotherly love is as renowned throughout the worlds as that of the two Ashvins."
Therefore, Rāma will not do anything harmful to Lakṣmaṇa;
however, there is no doubt that Rāma might do harm to Bharata.
For this reason, let your son go from the royal palace itself to the forest.
For this indeed pleases me and is also highly beneficial for you;
in this way, there will be welfare for your side of the kinsmen,
provided that Bharata obtains his father’s kingdom in accordance with dharma.
How will that boy, accustomed to comfort and the natural enemy of Rāma,
survive under your control— he who has lost his wealth while you have attained all your goals,
like a leader of an elephant herd pursued by a lion in the forest?
You ought to protect Bharata, who is being overwhelmed by Rāma.
Having previously been slighted by you because of your own good fortune,
how could your co-wife, the mother of Rāma, not seek to avenge her enmity?
"For when Rāma obtains the earth, Bharata will certainly be ruined;
therefore, consider now how to secure the kingdom for your own son and the cause for the exile of the other.
Thus addressed, Kaikeyī, her face ablaze with anger, spoke.
Sighing long and hot, he spoke these words slowly:
"Today I shall quickly dispatch Rāma from here to the forest; I shall have Bharata consecrated as the heir apparent at once."
"But now, Mantharā, consider this: by what means might Bharata obtain the kingdom, and not Rāma, by any means whatsoever?
Thus addressed by that queen, the evil-minded Mantharā [reflected].
Harassing Kaikeyī for the sake of Rāma, she spoke these words to her:
"Come now, O Kaikeyī, listen to me as I shall explain how your son Bharata will obtain the kingdom exclusively."
Having heard these words of Mantharā, Kaikeyī rose slightly from her well-spread bed and said this:
"Tell me, Mantharā, what means do you have; by what means?"
"Bharata shall obtain the kingdom, and Rama never under any circumstances.
Thus addressed by the queen, the hunchbacked Mantharā, who perceives only evil and seeks to harm Rāma's interests, spoke these words.

O Kaikeyī, during the war between the gods and the asuras, your husband, taking you with him, went toward the southern region of the Daṇḍaka forest to provide assistance to the king of the gods along with the royal sages.
There is a city renowned as Vaijayanta, where the one whose banner bears the sign of a sea-monster resides.
That great Asura, known as Śambara, who possessed a hundred illusions and was unconquered by the hosts of gods, gave battle to Śakra.
In that great battle, O Queen, King Daśaratha was then deprived of consciousness; having been carried away from the fray by you,
your husband, though wounded there by weapons, was protected by you.
"O lady of auspicious appearance, being pleased, he granted you two boons.
You said to your husband, 'O Queen, whenever I desire, I shall take those two boons,' and that was agreed upon as 'so be it' by that high-souled one."
"O Queen, I was indeed unaware; for you yourself told me this long ago:
'Ask these two boons of your husband: the consecration of Bharata and the exile of Rāma for fourteen years.'"
"Having entered the chamber of wrath today like one enraged, O daughter of Aśvapati, lie down on the ground while remaining invisible, wearing soiled garments;
do not look at him, nor speak to him."
"You are always beloved by your husband; of this I have no doubt.
For your sake, the great king would even enter the fire.
He is not able to provoke you to anger, nor can he bear to look upon you when you are angry."
For the sake of pleasing you, the king would indeed renounce even his own life.
Indeed, the lord of the earth is not able to transgress your word;
O woman of gentle nature, recognize the power of your own good fortune.
King Daśaratha may give you jewels, pearls, gold, and various kinds of gems; do not set your mind upon them.
Those two boons which Daśaratha granted during the war between the gods and the asuras— [those he has already fulfilled].
"O highly fortunate lady, remind him of that; let not that purpose elude you.
When Raghava himself rises to grant you a boon, you must first establish the great king in his resolve and then choose this boon."
"Exile Rāma to the forest for nine and five years;
let Bharata, that bull among kings, be made king upon the earth.
For once Rāma has been thus exiled, he will no longer be delightful."
And Bharata, having slain his enemies, shall become your king. By the time that Rama returns from the forest,
your son will have established his firm foundation.
And having won over the people together with his friends, that self-possessed man—
O fearless ones, you should consider this the right time to restrain the king’s intention regarding Rāma’s consecration and turn him back from it.
Having been made to perceive what was harmful as beneficial by her,
Kaikeyī, delighted and convinced, then said this to Mantharā:
"O Kubjā, I did not recognize you as one who is excellent and speaks what is excellent."
"On this earth, you are the best among hunchbacks in the certainty of your intellect.
You alone are ever intent on my welfare and seek my benefit;
O hunchback, I would not have understood what the king intends to do."
There are those who are ill-formed, hunchbacked, crooked, and exceedingly wicked;
you, however, are lovely to behold, bent like a lotus by the wind. Indeed, your chest is broad and rises high up to your shoulders.
And your lower abdomen is tranquil, like a well-formed navel that seems bashful; your hips resound with beauty, adorned by a girdle of bells;
your calves are perfectly set, and both your feet are long and well-proportioned.
O Mantharā, clad in linen, as you walk before me with your long thighs, you shine like a royal swan. This protruding hump of yours is as long and extended as the pole of a chariot.
"Intuitions, the sciences of the Kṣatriyas, and magical powers— all these shall dwell within you here.
O hunchback, once Bharata has been consecrated and Rāghava has gone to the forest, I shall place this golden garland upon you."
And with genuine gold, O beautiful one, well-refined and obtained for its purpose, I shall paint your hump;
and upon your face, I shall place a wonderful, auspicious tilaka made of gold.
"O hunchback, I shall have beautiful ornaments made for you;
having put on two splendid garments, you will move about like a goddess with a peerless face that rivals the moon."
"You shall go to the foremost destination, making your enemies bow down in pride.
O hunchback, all the hunchbacks adorned with every ornament will serve at your feet, just as you always serve mine."
Thus being praised, she spoke these words to Kaikeyī,
who lay upon a bright couch like a flame of fire upon a sacrificial altar:
"O blessed lady, once the water has flowed away, it is not possible to build a dam."
"Arise, perform what is auspicious, and show favor to the king.
Thus encouraged by Mantharā, the large-eyed queen, proud with the intoxication of her own good fortune, went with her to the chamber of wrath.
Then, having removed a pearl necklace worth many hundreds of thousands, as well as beautiful and precious ornaments worthy of a noble woman,
the hunchback there, who resembled gold, fell under the power of his words.
Having lain down upon the ground, Kaikeyī spoke thus to Mantharā:
"O hunchback, you shall report me as dead here to the king;
but when Rāghava has departed for the forest, Bharata shall obtain the earth."
Then, having spoken these most cruel words and casting off all her ornaments, that beautiful woman lay down upon the bare earth, uncovered by any bedding, like a fallen kinnarī;
her face shrouded in the darkness of rising fury, she had likewise cast aside her finest garlands and jewels.
The consort of the lord of men became despondent, like the sky shrouded in darkness with its stars submerged.
(2, 9.47) Having issued the command for Rāghava’s consecration, the self-controlled great king entered the inner apartments to tell the pleasant news to his beloved wife. (2, 10.1)
There the lord of the earth beheld her fallen upon the ground, lying in a state unaccustomed to such suffering, as if scorched by grief;
he was an old man, and she was his young wife, dearer to him than his own life.
On the surface of the earth, the sinless one beheld her who harbored sinful intentions;
like a great elephant in the forest, he stroked her with affection, as she lay there like a female elephant pierced by a hunter’s poisoned arrow in the woods.
Feeling his way with both hands, his mind overcome with terror,
the lover spoke these words to the lotus-eyed woman:
"I did not perceive the anger residing within you."
"O Queen, by whom have you been assailed, or by whom have you been insulted?
Why do you lie here in the dust upon the ground, O auspicious one, causing me such sorrow, when my heart is devoted to your welfare?"
Like one whose mind is possessed by a spirit, you are tormenting my heart.
I have skilled physicians who are well-satisfied in every way; they will restore you to health—tell me your ailment, O beautiful lady.
Whose dear wish must be fulfilled, or by whom has an offense been committed?
Who shall receive favor today, or who shall suffer great displeasure?
Who is there that should not be slain yet must be slain, or who, though deserving death, should be set free?
"Let the poor become wealthy, or let the man possessed of riches become destitute.
I myself and all my followers are subject to your will;
I do not venture to thwart any intention of yours."
"Tell me what you desire in your heart, even at the cost of my own life;
as far as the wheel turns, so far is the earth mine. Thus addressed, she was comforted and desired to speak those unpleasant words.
She proceeded once more to press her husband:
"O Lord, I have not been mistreated by anyone, nor have I been insulted;
however, I have a certain desire that I wish for you to fulfill."
"Make a solemn promise if you wish to do it; then I shall declare that which has been requested by me.
Thus addressed by his beloved wife, the king fell under the sway of woman.
The one of great splendor, smiling slightly, said to Kaikeyī:
"O haughty woman, you do not realize that there is no human being dearer to me than Rāma, that tiger among men; indeed, no other human exists who is more beloved."
"O blessed lady, reflect upon this very heart of mine and extract it;
having considered this, O Kaikeyī, speak what you deem to be right. Seeing the strength within yourself, you ought not to have any doubt regarding me."
"I shall bring you pleasure; I swear it to you by my own good deeds.
At these words, she was thrilled and spoke of her own most terrible intention, which was like the arrival of Death itself.
As you swear by your word in due order and grant me this boon,
let the thirty-three gods, led by Indra, hear it—
the moon, the sun, the sky, the planets, night and day, and the quarters of the earth.
The world and the earth itself, along with the Gandharvas and Rākṣasas;
the night-roaming spirits and the household deities within homes;
and whatever other beings there may be—they shall all know what you have spoken.
"True to his promise, possessed of great splendor, knower of dharma, and perfectly composed, he shall grant me a boon; let the gods hear this of mine!
Having thus addressed the great archer and embraced him, the queen—
Thereafter, he spoke these words to the granter of boons, who was deluded by desire:
"O Lord, O Ruler of the Earth, those two boons which were granted to me by you at that time—those very ones I shall now declare; listen to my words."
"The preparations for Rāghava’s consecration have been made;
let Bharata be consecrated with this very same consecration. As for me, I shall take refuge in the Daṇḍaka forest for nine and five years."
Let Rāma become an ascetic, wearing bark garments, deerskins, and matted hair;
let Bharata enjoy the thornless sovereignty of the heir apparent today,
and may I see the descendant of Raghu departing for the forest this very day.
Then, O Great King, having heard Kaikeyī’s cruel words,
he was distressed and lamented like a deer that has seen a tigress;
sitting upon the bare ground, he sighed deeply.
"Alas! Woe!"—having uttered these words with indignation, the lord of men, his consciousness struck by grief, fell once more into a swoon.
After a long time, however, the king regained his senses, deeply distressed.
Enraged, as if burning her with his eyes, he said to Kaikeyī:
"O cruel woman of wicked conduct, destroyer of this lineage! O sinful woman, what wrong has Rāma ever done to you, or even to me?"
Rāghava always maintains toward you a conduct equal to that shown to his own mother;
for what reason, then, are you prepared here for his ruin?
You were brought by me into this house for my own destruction.
"Because of my ignorance, I am like a sharp-venomed female serpent to the prince.
Since the entire world here sings the praises of Rāma's virtues, for what offense shall I abandon my beloved son? (Rāmāyaṇa 2.10.35–36)
I might abandon Kausalyā or Sumitrā, or even my royal fortune or my own life, but never Rāma, who is so devoted to his father. My joy becomes supreme upon seeing my eldest son.
But for me, not seeing Rāma, my consciousness has perished. The world might endure without the sun, or crops without water,
but my life cannot remain within my body without Rāma.
Therefore, enough! Let this resolve be abandoned; even though you have made a sinful resolve, I touch your feet with my head—be gracious to me.
Thus did that protector of the earth lament like one who is helpless, while his heart was excessively gripped by his wife.
He fell, failing to touch both outstretched feet of the queen, just like a sick man; he lay there, undeserving of such a fate and unaccustomed to it,
like King Yayāti fallen from the world of the gods at the exhaustion of his merit.
Though her purpose was not yet accomplished, the woman— undaunted even while perceiving fear— again requested that very same boon.
"O Great King, you boast that you are a speaker of truth and firm in your vows."
"And why do you wish to withhold this boon from me?
Thus addressed by Kaikeyī, King Daśaratha then replied, enraged and as if distraught for a moment.
"When I am dead and Rāma, that bull among men, has gone to the forest— alas,
my ignoble enemy has caused Rāma to be exiled to the forest!
If I speak this truth, it will become a lie."
"In this world, my infamy will be incomparable, and my humiliation is certain.
As he lamented thus, his mind wandering in distress,
the sun set and night drew on.
Thus, for the king who was thus afflicted and lamenting, that three-watch night, though adorned by the orb of the moon, did not shine;
likewise, King Daśaratha, the elder, sighed hotly.
With eyes fixed upon the sky, he lamented in distress like one afflicted:
"I do not wish for dawn to break while you are here; I offer this salutation with joined palms.
Or rather, depart quickly; I have no desire for a heartless woman."
"Because of whom this great calamity has come upon me, I must see the cruel Kaikeyī.
Having spoken thus, the king, with palms joined in reverence, again sought to appease Kaikeyī and said this to her.
"O Queen, show favor to one of virtuous conduct who is wretched, devoted to you, and whose life is spent; especially for the sake of the king, O blessed lady.
Indeed, O fair-hipped one, these words were spoken by me in my desolation."

"O child, show me favor; you are indeed compassionate. Having heard the varied and piteous lamentation of her husband—the king whose eyes were copper-red and filled with tears—she, being of wicked intent toward one of pure heart, did not heed her lord's words.
Then that king, seeing his beloved wife dissatisfied and speaking contrary words regarding the exile of his son, fell to the ground unconscious and distressed.
The wicked woman saw him fallen on the earth, overcome by grief for his son and deprived of his senses.
Seeing the descendant of Ikṣvāku writhing on the ground, he spoke these words:
"Having made a solemn promise to me, why do you lie prostrate on the surface of the earth as if you had committed a sin? You ought to remain steadfast in your integrity."
Those who know the Dharma say that truth is indeed the supreme Dharma;
for it was by relying on truth that I have exhorted you and you,
O Śaibya, having given your word to the hawk, offered your own body, O lord of the earth.
Having given [the food] to the bird, O King, he went to the supreme goal.
For likewise, when a Brahmin who had mastered the Vedas begged him, the radiant Alarka plucked out his own eyes and gave them away with an undisturbed mind.
The lord of rivers, ever devoted to truth, does not overstep his own boundary at the appointed time out of regard for that truth;
and if you, O noble one, do not fulfill this promise made to me, [the consequences will follow].
"Since you have already abandoned me, I shall abandon my life.
Thus urged by Kaikeyī, who was free from hesitation, the king was unable to release himself from the snare, just as Bali could not escape the one set by Indra.
With his heart bewildered and his face turned pale,
that leader of men, as if struggling between the yoke and the wheels,
seemed to lose sight of the ground with his agitated eyes.
Having steadied himself with great effort and fortitude, he spoke thus to Kaikeyī:
"O sinful woman, that hand which was joined with mine in the presence of the fire according to the sacred mantras—
that I now renounce, as do I my own son, along with you."
Then Kaikeyī, of evil conduct, skilled in speech and overwhelmed with rage, spoke these harsh words again to the king:
"O King, why do you utter such words that are like the pain of poison?"
"You ought to bring my son Rāma here without difficulty;
having installed my son in the kingdom and made Rāma a forest-dweller,
you will have fulfilled your purpose and rendered me free of rivals."
Like a noble horse pricked by a sharp goad,
the king, being repeatedly urged on, spoke thus to Kaikeyī:
"I am bound by the bond of dharma, and my own discernment has perished."
"I wish to see my eldest son, the beloved and righteous Rāma.
Upon hearing these words of the king, Kaikeyī immediately spoke to the charioteer herself: "Go, bring Rāma here."
Then that illustrious and righteous king, his joy vanished regarding his son and his eyes reddened with grief, looked up at the charioteer and spoke.
Having heard his piteous words and seeing the monarch so dejected, Sumantra [responded].
With palms joined in reverence, he stepped back slightly from that spot;
when the lord of the earth was unable to speak himself due to his distress, Kaikeyī, skilled in counsel, then addressed Sumantra.
"Sumantra, bring the handsome Rāma quickly so that I may see him";
thinking thus, he rejoiced in his heart at the auspicious prospect. Thus urged by her, Sumantra reflected with haste.
"Clearly, Rāma, the knower of dharma, will come here for the sake of his consecration.
Having formed this thought, the charioteer, possessed of great luster, went forth again with immense joy, desiring to see the descendant of Raghu.

Then, having suddenly emerged from the front, he beheld various wealthy citizens standing at the gate; looking toward the kings who had arrived there, he saw them stationed before the entrance. Having spent that night there, those brahmins, masters of the Vedas, [prepared for his departure].
Accompanied by the king and the family priest,
the ministers, the military commanders,
and the leading members of the merchant guild gathered together, full of joy, to perform the ceremony for the consecration of Raghava.
When the stainless sun had risen and the day of Puṣya had arrived, the lords of the twice-born prepared the materials for Rāma’s consecration:
golden water-jars and a well-adorned auspicious throne.
And for Rāma, a bed was properly spread with a shining tiger skin;
water was brought from the holy confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā,
as well as from other sacred rivers, lakes, wells, and ponds.
The waters flowing eastward, upward, and across were gathered together;
likewise, water was brought from all the oceans.
There was honey, curd, ghee, parched grain, darbha grass, flowers, and milk.
Golden and silver jars, filled with the finest water and adorned with lotuses and lilies, shone forth; they were covered with sprigs of grain and draped with the bark of milk-exuding trees.
A white canopy, decorated with jewels and radiant as the blossoming rays of the moon, was spread above.
The excellent yak-tail fan stands ready for Rāma;
and the white parasol, resembling the orb of the moon,
radiant, glorious, and prepared for the consecration, stands ready.
A white bull is ready, a white horse stands firm,
and the majestic royal elephant Prasruta awaits you;
furthermore, eight auspicious maidens, adorned with every ornament, are present.
All musical instruments were sounded, and likewise others, the bards,
gathered together all the materials for the consecration of the Ikṣvākus as they had been prepared in the past, for the consecration of the prince.
Gathered there at the king's command, not seeing the lord of the earth, they said, "Who indeed will announce us to the king?
We do not see the king, yet the sun has risen."
"And the consecration for the heir-apparentship of the wise Rāma is ready. While they were speaking thus, Sumantra, honored by the king, addressed all those sovereign monarchs as follows.
"By your word, I ask after the welfare of the venerable ones,
as well as the reason for the arrival of King Saṃpratibuddha.
Having said this, the knower of ancient lore approached the gate of the inner apartments.
He praised Rāghava with blessings endowed with virtuous qualities:
"The blessed night has passed; the auspicious day has arrived. Wake up, O tiger among kings, and perform what must be done next."
"O King, the brahmins, the military leaders, and the merchants have arrived and long to see you; wake up, O Raghava!
Thus did Sumantra, the charioteer skilled in counsel, speak as he praised him at that time.
Then, having awakened, the king spoke these words:
"I have not been asleep at all; bring Rāghava here quickly.
Thus King Daśaratha commanded the charioteer there once again.
Having heard the king's words and honored them by bowing his head, he departed from the royal palace, considering it a great favor;
he then set out upon the royal road, which was adorned with banners and flags.
There, the charioteer heard stories concerning Rāma;
then Sumantra beheld the beautiful residence of Rāma, which possessed a splendor like Mount Kailāsa and a radiance equal to the palace of Śakra.
It was closed with great doors, adorned with hundreds of balconies,
featuring a single golden statue and archways of jewels and coral;
it resembled a dense autumn cloud, radiant like a cave on Mount Meru.
Adorned with great strings of choice garlands, he,
the charioteer, beholding the royal palace crowded with men from his horse-drawn chariot,
approached that great and immensely wealthy place, and his hair stood on end with joy.
Like a sea-monster entering the ocean filled with abundant jewels, the charioteer entered unopposed that supreme palace within the great mansion, which resembled a mountain peak or a mass of clouds.
Having passed through the gate of the inner apartments crowded with people, he proceeded further.
Then, the knower of ancient lore reached a secluded courtyard,
which was guarded by young men who carried spears and bows, wore polished earrings, were vigilant, focused, and deeply devoted.
There he saw elderly women wearing saffron robes, carrying canes in their hands, well-adorned, stationed at the gate as female overseers, and composed in mind;
seeing him approaching, they desired to do what was pleasing to Rāma.
They immediately informed Rāma, who was together with his wife.
Having learned of the report, Rāghava, desiring to please his father, had the charioteer summoned from within his father's quarters to that very place.
The charioteer beheld him, who resembled Vaiśravaṇa, seated upon a golden couch covered with a fine spread, well-adorned,
and anointed with pure, fragrant sandalwood paste that had the hue of boar's blood.
The scorcher of foes was anointed with the most excellent sandalwood paste;
and he was further attended by Sītā standing at his side with a yak-tail fan in her hand, like the moon accompanied by Citrā.
To him who was like the scorching sun, endowed with his own splendor,
the bard— who was well-versed in the rules of conduct— paid homage with humility, as one who bestows boons.
With palms joined in reverence, he inquired after his comfort regarding his recreation, his bed, and his seat.
Sumantra, honored by the king, spoke these words to the prince:
"O Lord, Kausalyā is radiant; your father desires to see you along with Queen Kaikeyī. Go there without delay."
Thus addressed, the immensely radiant Narasiṃha was filled with joy;
he then honored Sītā and spoke these words to her:
"O Queen, both the god and the goddess have come together on my behalf."
They are surely discussing something related to the consecration;
for Sudakṣiṇā, desiring my welfare and possessing intoxicating eyes, has observed the king's intention and is urging him on my behalf.
"Since the assembly there was such as this, a messenger of corresponding character has arrived;
surely the king will consecrate me as crown prince this very day.
Come now, let us go quickly from here and see the lord of the earth."
"Stay here with your attendants and enjoy yourself in happiness. Thus addressed by her husband, the dark-eyed Sītā, honored by him, followed after her lord to the gate, reciting auspicious blessings.
Having seen all those who sought his favor, and having met with them and greeted them,
he then ascended that excellent chariot which resembled fire,
dazzling the eyes with its splendor and possessing the luster of gold.
Yoked with excellent horses resembling young elephants,
Raghava, blazing with splendor, ascended that swift chariot drawn by bay steeds and departed quickly, like the thousand-eyed Indra.
Resounding like a rain-cloud in the sky and making the dwellings echo, the illustrious prince went forth like the moon emerging from a great cloud;
Lakṣmaṇa, the younger brother of Rāghava, followed with parasol and fly-whisk in hand.
The brother, mounting the chariot behind him, protected his brother. Then,
as he was departing, a tumultuous roar arose from the mass of people on all sides.
There Rāghava heard the chatter of the people gathered together— various words concerning himself from the citizens of the city who appeared joyful— as they spoke of his great fortune:
"Today this Rāghava attains prosperity, receiving vast rewards through the king's favor."
"We have all our desires fulfilled, for he who shall be our ruler has appeared; it is the gain of this people that he shall obtain this entire kingdom for a long time.
With horses making a resonant sound, with elephants in the lead, and with heralds, bards, and genealogists [proclaiming his auspiciousness], [he set forth].
Being honored by eminent disputants and praised like Vaiśravaṇa, he proceeded.

Rāma beheld the beautiful main road, crowded with female elephants, male elephants, chariots, and horses; its crossroads filled with throngs of people, abounding in jewels, and stocked with many articles for sale.
Mounting his chariot with his joyful friends, the illustrious Rāma beheld the city crowded with various people,
adorned with white houses resembling clouds.
Rāma proceeded along the royal highway, which was perfumed with the smoke of aloe-wood;
that excellent royal road was beautiful, spacious,
and lined with various wares as well as diverse kinds of foodstuffs.
Hearing many blessings uttered by his friends and honoring all the men according to their merit, he departed,
following the path practiced by his grandfathers and likewise by his great-grandfathers.
"From this day forward, you who have been consecrated shall protect that path. Just as we were cherished by our father and by our ancestors of old,
so shall we all live in even greater happiness under King Rāma."
Enough indeed with food today, and enough for us with all other ultimate goals,
so that we may see Rāma departing and being established once more in his kingdom. For there will be nothing else more dear to us than this.
Just as was the consecration of Rāma of immeasurable splendor to the kingship,
so did Rāma proceed along the great highway, listening to these and other auspicious stories concerning his friends— tales that celebrated his own virtues, while remaining indifferent to them.
For no man was able to withdraw his mind or his eyes from that best of men, even after Rāghava had passed away;
for that righteous-souled one extends compassion to all social classes.

"For those four who are in their prime follow him; thus they are devoted to him. Having reached the royal palace, which resembled the abode of Mahendra, the prince, blazing with splendor, entered his father's residence.

Having passed through all the courtyards, the son of Daśaratha dismissed all his attendants and entered the inner apartments. When the prince had thus entered his father’s presence, all the people were then filled with joy.
He awaited his father's departure, just as the lord of rivers awaits the rising of the moon.
Then Rāma saw his father seated upon a splendid throne together with Kaikeyī, looking dejected with a parched countenance.
Having first saluted his father’s feet with humility, he,
being deeply composed, then paid homage to the feet of Kaikeyī.
And calling out the word "Rāma," his eyes became clouded with tears.
The wretched king was unable to look at him or to speak.
Seeing that unprecedented and terrifying form of the monarch,
Rāma too was seized with fear, as if he had stepped upon a serpent.
With senses uncheered, emaciated by grief and torment,
sighing deeply, that great king— whose mind was pained and agitated—
was like the unshakeable ocean, garlanded with waves, now appearing to be in turmoil.
Like the sun eclipsed, or like a seer who has spoken a falsehood,
he beheld that inconceivable grief of his father and became even more agitated, like the ocean on a full-moon day.
Then Rāma, who was devoted to his father’s welfare, reflected:
"Why is it that today the king does not greet me with joy?
On other occasions, my father would become placid even if he had been angry upon seeing me."
"Seeing me today, why does this distress come upon him? Thus,
like one wretched and afflicted by grief, his face and luster dejected, Rāma saluted Kaikeyī and spoke these words.
"Tell me if I have committed some offense through ignorance for which my father is angry; you yourself must appease him.
For with a pale face and dejected, he does not speak to me."

Does no physical or mental affliction, nor any distress or intense suffering, trouble him? For happiness is indeed always difficult to obtain. Does Bharata not grieve for anything regarding the handsome Kumāra?
Whether it be ill fortune for Śatrughna, that great being, or for my mothers, or for myself—
if I have failed to please the Great King or have not carried out my father’s word,
I would not wish to live even for a moment while the monarch is angry.
Since a man perceives his own origin here to be rooted in that [father], how could he not behave with devotion toward him, who is a deity manifest before one's eyes?
Has my father ever spoken anything harsh to you out of pride?
"You have spoken with anger regarding that which has agitated his mind.
O Queen, tell this to me in truth as I ask you: for what reason does this unprecedented transformation exist in the lord of men?"

if you wish to make your father true to his promise.
And for your own sake, O best of men, listen to these words of mine:
abide by your father’s command just as it was promised by him;

"Abandoning this consecration, dwell for seven times seven years in the Daṇḍaka forest, wearing matted hair and bark garments;

The invincible subduer of enemies does not rejoice as he did before. O Queen, you should not feel anger; speak before me, and I shall go to the forest with matted hair and bark garments, so that you may be well-pleased.
Being confidently commanded by my well-wishing elder, by my father, and by the grateful king, what dear service would I not perform? Yet,
this one falsehood in my mind burns as it were my very heart.
Since the king himself did not tell me of Bharata’s consecration,
I would have gladly given Sītā, the kingdom, my own life, and all my cherished wealth to my brother Bharata of my own accord, even without being prompted.

How much more so, then, when he has been personally urged by his father, the lord of men, and is now fulfilling his promise for the sake of doing what is pleasing to you? Therefore, do you comfort him; why indeed does the lord of the earth act thus?
With his eyes fixed upon the earth, he slowly shed tears.
"Let messengers go this very day on swift horses at the king's command to bring Bharata from his maternal uncle's house."
"I am going from here in haste to the Daṇḍaka forest,
without deliberating on my father's word, to dwell there for fourteen years.
Hearing those words of Rāma, Kaikeyī was delighted.
Full of faith, she urged Raghava toward his departure. "So be it," he replied; "men shall go on swift-footed horses as messengers to bring Bharata back from his maternal uncle's house."
But I consider it appropriate for you, O Rāma, that you do not delay while you are so eager; therefore, you ought to go from here to the forest quickly.
And as for the fact that the king himself does not speak to you out of shame—
"O best of men, this is nothing; let this anger be cast aside.
O Rāma, as long as you have not departed from this city in haste for the forest, your father shall neither bathe nor eat."
"Alas, what misery! sighing thus, the king, overwhelmed by grief, fell unconscious upon that gold-adorned couch.
Rāma, too, having raised the king up, was urged on by Kaikeyī.
Like a stallion struck by a whip, he made haste to go to the forest.
Having heard those unpleasant words of the ignoble woman, which were harsh in their core, Rāma remained free from distress and spoke these words to Kaikeyī.
"O Queen, I do not venture to dwell in this world for the sake of material wealth;
know me to be equal to the seers, established solely in dharma.
Whatever can be done here to please my lord, I shall perform it."
Even at the cost of sacrificing one's own life, that [duty] has indeed been fully accomplished;
for there is no practice of dharma greater than this: namely, service to one's father or the carrying out of his word.
"Even though not told by your honor, at your word I shall dwell here in the lonely forest for fourteen years.
Surely, Kaikeyī, you do not expect any merit from me."
"Since you have said to the King, 'I am your sovereign,' as long as I do not take leave of my mother and persuade Sītā,
I shall depart this very day for the great Daṇḍaka forest."
"Bharata should protect the kingdom and serve his father;
this is how it must be done by you, for that is the eternal dharma.
Having heard Rāma's words, his father was deeply stricken with grief.

Overcome by grief and unable to restrain his tears, he wept aloud with a great sound. Then, having prostrated at the feet of his unconscious father and also at those of the ignoble Kaikeyī, the immensely radiant Rāma departed.
Having circumambulated his father and Kaikeyī, Rāma departed from that inner apartment and beheld his circle of friends.
With eyes overflowing with tears, he followed after them.
Lakṣmaṇa, the enhancer of Sumitrā’s joy, was filled with supreme rage.
Having circumambulated the vessels for the consecration, Rāma walked away slowly, full of longing and not averting his gaze from that spot.
And the loss of his kingdom does not diminish his great splendor, for he is beloved by the world; just as the night does not diminish the loveliness of the cool-rayed moon.
This is true even as he desires to go to the forest and renounces the earth.
As if he were one who has transcended all the worlds, no sign of mental agitation was perceived in him. Holding his sorrow within his mind and restraining his senses,
the self-possessed prince entered his mother’s quarters, though he did not wish to announce the unpleasant news.
Having entered his home, which was filled with extreme joy, and seeing that misfortune regarding his wealth had arrived,
Rāma did not undergo any change of state there, due to his apprehension for the welfare of his kinsmen.
But Rāma, deeply distressed, sighed like an elephant.
Self-controlled, he went with his brother to his mother’s inner apartments. There he saw an elderly man of great honor seated at the door of the house, and many others standing nearby.
Having entered the first courtyard, he beheld in the second elderly brahmins, perfected in the Vedas and honored by the king;
having bowed to those elders, Rāma beheld them in the third courtyard.
The women— both old and young— were intent on guarding the gates;
having increased their joy and entered the house, those women then quickly announced the pleasant news to Rāma’s mother.

Queen Kausalyā also, having remained composed throughout that night, performed worship to Viṣṇu at dawn, desiring the welfare of her son. Clad in linen garments, she was joyful and constantly devoted to her vows.

Then, having performed the auspicious rites, she offered oblations into the fire with sacred mantras. And having entered his mother’s splendid inner apartments, Rāma then beheld his mother there, causing the sacrificial fire to be fed.
Having seen her son, the delighter of his mother, returned after a long time,
she rushed toward him in great joy, like a mare toward her foal.
She spoke to that unassailable Raghava, her own son.
Out of maternal affection for her son, Kausalyā spoke these words, which were both pleasing and beneficial:
"May you attain long life, fame, and the dharma established in your lineage from the aged, virtuous, and high-souled royal sages."
"O Raghava, behold your father, the king, who is true to his promise;
for this very day, that righteous soul shall consecrate you as the crown prince.
Stretching out his joined palms slightly, Raghava addressed his mother.
He is naturally disciplined and bowed down with reverence;
O Queen, you surely do not realize that a great danger has arisen,
which will bring sorrow to you, Vaidehī, and Lakṣmaṇa.
"For fourteen years I shall dwell in the lonely forest,
living on honey, roots, and fruits like a sage, having abandoned meat;
for the Great King is bestowing the status of crown prince upon Bharata."
"But he exiles me, a mere ascetic, to the Daṇḍaka forest.
Seeing her fallen like a plantain tree, unaccustomed to such sorrow and deprived of her senses, Rāma raised his mother up.
Having turned back and risen, like a weary mare that has been driven,
her entire body covered in dust, he stroked her with his hand.
She, accustomed to comfort, was now afflicted by misery as she sat near Rāghava.
He spoke to that tiger among men while Lakṣmaṇa listened:
"O Rāghava, my son, had you not been born to cause me grief,
I would not have experienced such further sorrow as this, being childless."
For a barren woman, O son, there is only one human sorrow:
the anguish that "I am childless"; no other exists. She has never before seen anything auspicious or happiness through the prowess of a husband.
"May I see my son again"— this was the hope I held while Rama remained away.
Yet, though I am the most excellent of women, I shall have to hear many unpleasant words from my inferior co-wives that pierce the heart.
What indeed could be more painful for women than this?
Even while you were present, I was thus rejected;
O father, how much more so when you have departed—certainly, my death is now inevitable.
For anyone who serves me or follows me,
O Rāghava, that person does not speak to me when they look upon the son of Kaikeyī;
seventeen years have passed since you were born.
Desiring the destruction of my suffering, I have longed for the past;
yet through fasts, yogic practices, and many labors,
you have been raised in hardship in vain by me, unfortunate as I am.
I consider this heart of mine to be truly steadfast, since it does not shatter like the bank of a great river struck by the new waters during the rainy season.
Surely death does not exist for me, nor is there any room for me in the abode of Yama.
That Death does not seize me today by force, as a lion might seize a weeping doe—
surely my heart is made of iron, since it remains firm, neither breaking nor rending upon this earth under such sorrow; for indeed, death at an untimely hour does not exist.
But this is my sorrow: that my vows, gifts, restraints, and the asceticism I have practiced for the sake of offspring have been utterly fruitless, like seed sown in barren soil.
For if anyone emaciated by heavy grief could obtain death at will before their time—

"Without you, I shall go this very day to the assembly of the departed, like a cow deprived of her calf. Uttering these words, she then lamented profusely in great distress upon seeing Raghava; she was like a Kinnarī who, perceiving a great calamity, sees her son bound.

I see no offense nor any such fault in him by which Raghava should be exiled from the kingdom to dwell in the forest; indeed,
I do not perceive any man in this world, even one who is out of my sight, who could find such a cause.

What son, mindful of the conduct of kings, would take to heart these words of the king who has returned to childhood? As long as no man knows this matter, [let it remain so].
At that very moment, place the burden of governance within yourself along with me.

"I shall slay them all, for one who is mild is indeed treated with contempt.

who has the power to give the sovereignty to Bharata?"
"O Queen, I am devoted to my brother in truth of heart;
I swear this to you by my sincerity, by my bow, and by the gifts and sacrifices I have offered.

O Goddess, consider that I have already entered there.
Like the risen sun dispelling the darkness, I shall remove your sorrow by my prowess;

Having heard these words of the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa,

Do whatever you deem appropriate hereafter, if it pleases you.
Having heard the unrighteous words spoken by my co-wife,
you ought not to abandon me as I am consumed by grief and depart from this place.
"O knower of dharma, if you are most righteous and wish to practice dharma,
