then while remaining here, serve me and practice the unsurpassed dharma. O son, by serving your mother and living in your own home with self-restraint, you shall do so."
Endowed with supreme ascetic power, Kāśyapa has gone to the third heaven.
Just as the king is worthy of your honor, so indeed am I;
therefore, I do not give you my permission—you must not go from here to the forest.
"Separated from you, I have no need for life or for happiness; it would be better for me to eat even grass than to be without you.
If you go to the forest, abandoning me while I am consumed by grief,"
"I shall sit here awaiting death by fasting, for I shall not be able to live.
Then, O son, you will incur a hell renowned throughout the world,
just as the ocean, the lord of rivers, incurred the sin of killing a Brahmin through unrighteousness."
Then, to his mother Kausalyā, who was thus lamenting in such distress,
the righteous Rāma spoke these words consistent with dharma:
"I do not have the power to transgress my father's command."
I seek to propitiate you with my head bowed; I wish to go to the forest.
Even by the wise seer Kaṇḍu, who was observing his vows and knew the dharma, a cow was killed while carrying out his father's command.
And in our own lineage, in former times, while digging the ocean at the command of their father Sagara,
the sons of Sagara met with a very great slaughter.
Furthermore, by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, his own mother Reṇukā was slain.
"Chopped down with an axe in the forest by one who carries out his father's command—
this father’s decree is certainly not being carried out by me alone; rather, this path intended by my ancestors is being followed."
"This task must indeed be performed by me on this earth and not otherwise;
for by carrying out the word of one's father, no one ever comes to grief.
Having spoken thus to his mother, he spoke again to Lakṣmaṇa.

"O Lakṣmaṇa, I know your unsurpassed affection for me, yet you do not understand my intention regarding truth and tranquility. For dharma is supreme in this world, and truth is established upon dharma."
And this supreme word of my father is rooted in righteousness. O hero, having promised the word of a father, a mother, or a brahmin, one who stands firm in dharma must not let it go in vain.
Therefore, O hero, I shall not be able to transgress my father’s command;
for it was at my father’s word that I was urged by Kaikeyī. Thus, abandon this ignoble resolve which relies upon the dharma of the Kṣatriyas.
"Take refuge in righteousness, not in harshness; let my mind be followed.
Having spoken thus to his brother out of affection, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa spoke again to Kausalyā with joined palms and head bowed low.
"O Goddess, grant me leave as I am about to depart from here for the forest;
you are bound by my life-breaths to perform rites for my welfare.
Having fulfilled my vow, I shall return again from the forest to the city."
"For I am not able to cast aside my great glory for the sake of mere sovereignty; O Queen, I do not choose this inferior earth today through unrighteousness, especially when life is so short.
Thus did that bull among men, seeking to propitiate his mother while desiring to depart for the Daṇḍaka forest by means of his prowess, speak.
Then, having strictly instructed his younger brother, he paid homage to his mother in his heart by circumambulating her.
Then [he beheld] him, dejected with anguish and especially provoked to indignation,
panting like a lordly elephant, his eyes wide with rage.
Having approached his beloved brother Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā and his dear friend, the self-possessed Rāma, maintaining his composure with fortitude, said this:
"O Saumitri, regarding that flurry of preparations for my consecration..."
Let this haste for the gathering of provisions be for the purpose of preventing my consecration.
Act in such a way that our mother, whose mind is tormented on account of my consecration, may be free from apprehension.
O Saumitri, I cannot bear to neglect for even a moment the pain born of her anxiety that has arisen in my mind;
nor do I recall ever having done so here, whether intentionally or unintentionally.
Whether it was toward my mother or my father, whatever slight displeasure I have caused,
may my father— who is truthful, faithful to his word, and ever possessed of true valor— be freed from fear, even though he fears the world beyond.
"For if this ritual act were not withdrawn, he would surely suffer mental anguish, thinking 'it is not true,' and his torment would consume me as well.
Therefore, O Lakṣmaṇa, withdraw the preparations for the consecration."
"I desire to go from here to the forest immediately;
once my son Bharata has been consecrated without distraction, the king's daughter-in-law will have fulfilled her duty today through my departure."
When I have gone to the forest, wearing bark garments and deerskin and bearing a mass of matted hair, Kaikeyī’s mind will find its peace—
she by whom this resolve was formed and whose mind is so well-composed.
But I ought not to be distressed by that; I shall go forth into the forest without delay.
O Saumitri, Fate alone must be seen as the cause of my exile and of the reversal of the kingdom that had already been bestowed.
For how could Kaikeyī’s resolve have been directed toward my suffering, were it not for this divine disposition ordained by Fate?
You know well, O gentle one, that I make no distinction among my mothers.
In the past, was there any distinction between her feelings toward me and toward her son?
With those harsh and terrible words intended to prevent his consecration and to bring about his exile, I can attribute nothing to her other than fate.
"How could a princess, endowed with such noble nature and virtues, speak thus like an ordinary woman of the common folk regarding my suffering in the presence of her husband?
That which is inconceivable is destiny; it cannot be overcome even among living beings."
Clearly, O Saumitri, a reversal of fortune has fallen upon both her and me;
for what man, O gentle one, can venture to fight against destiny,
whose grasp is seen to be nothing other than the result of past actions?

Happiness and sorrow, fear and anger, gain and loss, existence and non-existence— whatever such things as these may be, they are surely the work of destiny. Even though my consecration has been thwarted, I feel no distress.
Therefore, do not grieve; following my lead, you too should quickly withdraw the preparations for the consecration.
O Lakṣmaṇa, my younger mother should not be suspected of plotting against me regarding this obstacle to my kingship.
"For those struck by fate speak what is undesirable; you know both fate and its power.
While Rāma was speaking thus, Lakṣmaṇa, with his head bowed, repeatedly listened and, as it were, entered into the midst of his mind's sorrow and joy.
Then that bull among men, knitting his brow between his eyebrows,
sighed like an enraged great serpent in its hole.
That face of his, accompanied by the knitting of his brows, was then difficult even to look upon.
His face shone like the mouth of an enraged lion.
Shaking him off as an elephant shakes its own trunk,
he threw his neck sideways and upwards against the body.
Glancing askance with the corner of his eye, he said to his brother:
"This very great agitation has indeed arisen in you at an improper time,
due to a concern for a flaw in dharma and out of a lack of confidence in the world."
For how could one such as you, being undeluded, speak thus? O bull among Kshatriyas, you are a hero;
why do you praise that wretched, powerless destiny which is itself devoid of prowess?
But how indeed can there be no suspicion regarding those two evildoers?
O righteous-souled one, do you not perceive that there are subtle pretexts for unrighteousness,
and that the consecration of someone other than you— an act loathed by the world— has been undertaken?
O lord of the earth, that by which your mind has come to this duality is indeed the dharma I detest, for it is through attachment to it that you are deluded—
even though your understanding of those two [options] may be divinely inspired.
Nevertheless, you must disregard it; even that does not please me. He who is despondent and devoid of valor follows fate;
heroes who esteem themselves do not wait upon fate.
He who is capable of counteracting fate through human effort does not perish; that man whose purpose has been thwarted by fate alone is the one who sinks.
Today, however, they shall behold the power of both fate and human exertion.
Today the distinction between fate and human effort will become manifest.
Today people shall indeed behold fate struck down by my manly prowess,
for they have witnessed today your consecration to the kingdom brought about by fate.
Like a wild elephant, unrestrained and arrogant with the strength of rut, rushing forward, I shall turn back fate through human effort.
O guardians of the world, you all must not today [permit] the consecration of Rāma.

Not even all the three worlds together could prevail against you, much less your father. O King, those by whom your exile to the forest was mutually agreed upon shall themselves dwell in the forest for fourteen years.
I shall shatter that hope of your father and of her,
which exists for the sake of your son’s kingdom by obstructing his consecration;
for the power of fate cannot prevail against one who is opposed by my own strength.
It will lead to suffering as severe as my own human effort.
After a thousand years have passed, O noble sons, when you have gone to dwell in the forest, they will thereafter take over the protection of the subjects.

"For it is ordained by the conduct of former royal seers that one should dwell in the forest after entrusting the subjects to one's sons for their protection, as if they were one's own children. If, however, the king is distracted, there may be a risk of confusion in the kingdom."
"O righteous-souled Rāma, you do not desire the kingdom for yourself;
I promise you this, O hero: may I never partake in the world of heroes, and I shall protect your kingdom as the shore protects the ocean."
"Be consecrated with auspicious rites; apply yourself there.
I alone am sufficient to restrain these kings by force. These two arms of mine are not for the sake of ornament, nor is this bow for my decoration."
These are not for the purpose of binding my head with a turban, nor are these arrows intended to prop up a pillar.
This entire fourfold array is for the sake of subduing my enemies;
yet I do not desire anything excessively, even that which might be considered my enemy.
With a sharp-edged sword, possessing the brilliance of flashing lightning,
held firmly in my grasp, I would not consider even an enemy like Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt.
My path is dense and difficult to traverse, strewn with those crushed by the impact of my sword.
The earth shall be covered with the trunks, thighs, heads, and torsos of elephants, horses, and men.
Struck today by the edge of my sword, they will fall upon the ground like blazing mountains, or like clouds accompanied by lightning.
With my finger-guards of iguana-skin bound on and my bow grasped, how could any man consider himself a hero while I stand here— one who,
with many arrows, strikes down a single foe, and with a single arrow, strikes down many men?
I shall discharge my arrows into the vital organs of men, horses, and elephants.
Today, the power of my weapons' majesty shall prevail:
it shall bring about the king's lack of authority and establish your own sovereignty, O Lord.
Today these two arms of Rāma, worthy of the finest sandalwood paste, of never loosening their armlets, of bestowing wealth, and of protecting friends, shall perform their proper task.
"Tell me who among those who have created obstacles to my consecration shall today be deprived by me of their life, their fame, and their kinsmen,
so that this earth may come under your control; command me as I am your servant."

Wiping away his tears and repeatedly consoling Lakṣmaṇa, that enhancer of the Raghava lineage said to him, who was firmly resolved upon his father’s command: "Listen to me, gentle one; this indeed is the path of the righteous.
Having observed him thus intent on carrying out his father's instruction, [he spoke].
Kausalyā, her voice choked with tears, spoke these most righteous words:
"How can he, born of Daśaratha from me— his soul devoted to dharma, never having known sorrow, and always speaking kindly to all beings— how can he subsist on gleaned grains?"
How shall this lord, whose servants and slaves eat choice foods, now eat roots and fruits in the forest?
Who, having heard this, would believe it, or who would not be struck with fear?
Since Raghava, who is virtuous and beloved by the king, is being exiled,
this great and incomparable fire of grief will consume me here when I am deprived of you, just as a blazing fire consumes dry wood at the end of winter.
"For how could a cow not follow her own calf as it departs?
I shall follow you, my son, wherever you go. To these words thus spoken by his mother, that bull among men [replied].
Having heard this, Rāma spoke these words to his mother, who was deeply distressed:
"The king has been deceived by Kaikeyī; now that I have taken refuge in the forest and you have abandoned him, he will surely not survive."

Indeed, the abandonment of a husband is a cruel act for a woman alone; it must not be committed by you even in thought, for it is utterly contemptible. As long as my father, the descendant of Kakutstha and lord of the world, lives, [you must remain faithful].
"Let service be rendered to him for now; for that is the eternal dharma.
Thus addressed by Rāma, the beautiful Kausalyā, being well-pleased, said "So be it" to Rāma, the doer of effortless deeds.
Thus addressed, Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma,
spoke these words once more to his mother, who was deeply distressed:
"Both you and I must carry out the command of our father."
"The king is the sustainer, the preceptor, the most excellent, the lord, and the master of all.
Having wandered through this great forest for these fourteen years— five and nine— I shall abide by your word with the greatest joy."
Having been addressed thus by her dear son, Kausalyā, who was devoted to her son and deeply afflicted, then spoke with a face filled with tears:
"O Rāma, it is not possible for me to live in the midst of these co-wives."
"O descendant of Kakutstha, take me too to the forest, like a wild doe,
if your mind is set on going out of regard for your father.
To her, as she was thus weeping, Rāma, weeping himself, spoke these words:
"For as long as a woman lives, her husband is indeed her deity and her lord; today, the King is the sovereign lord over both you and me.
And Bharata too is righteous-souled and speaks kindly to all beings."
He will surely follow you, for he is always devoted to dharma. Therefore, being vigilant, act in such a way that the king does not suffer any distress upon my departure due to grief for his son.
That most excellent woman who, though devoted to vows and fasting, does not follow her husband, shall meet with a sinful destiny; therefore,
she should perform service alone, delighting in what is pleasing and beneficial to her husband.
This is the dharma seen of old in the world, heard in the Veda, and recorded in the Smṛtis. O Queen, for my sake, these Brāhmaṇas of firm vows must be honored;
thus, wait for the time while longing for my return.
"You shall attain your supreme desire once I have returned,
provided that the best among the upholders of dharma continues to hold onto life.
Thus addressed by Rāma, she, her eyes clouded with tears, [spoke].
Afflicted with grief for her son, Kausalyā spoke these words to Rāma:
"Go, my son, with a focused mind; may it ever be well with you, O lord.
For thus did the queen, having perceived that Rāma was resolved upon dwelling in the forest, address him with her supreme resolve.
She spoke these words to Rāma, who was endowed with auspicious marks, and she became intent upon performing rites for his well-being. Having removed that distress and sipped pure water,
the wise mother performed the auspicious ceremonies for Rāma.
May the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and the Maruts, along with the great seers, grant well-being;
may Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ grant well-being, as well as Pūṣan, Bhaga, and Aryaman.
May the seasons, the fortnights, the months, the years, and the nights likewise grant well-being.
May the days and the moments always grant you well-being.
O son, may mindfulness, fortitude, and righteousness protect you on all sides; and may the blessed Lord Skanda, Soma, and Bṛhaspati protect you as well.
May the seven seers and Nārada protect you on all sides,
as well as all the constellations and the planets together with their presiding deities,
for you who are wise and wander in the guise of a sage through the great forests.
May there be no monkeys, scorpions, stinging insects, or mosquitoes in the forest for you, nor any reptiles or worms in the thicket.
May there be no great elephants, lions, tigers, bears, or fanged beasts.
"O son, let not the fierce horned buffaloes do you harm;
nor let those other fierce species of creatures that feed on human flesh injure you, for they have been propitiated here by me."
"May your paths be auspicious; may your endeavors be successful;
may you possess all prosperity, O Rāma; go forth in well-being, my dear son!
May there be well-being for you from the beings of the atmosphere and from those of the earth, again and again."
May all the gods, as well as those who stand as your adversaries;
may Brahmā, the lord of all worlds and the sustainer of beings, as well as the ṛṣis and whatever other deities remain— may they all protect you while you dwell in the forest.
Thus the illustrious, large-eyed lady honored the hosts of gods with garlands, perfumes, and appropriate hymns of praise;
whatever auspiciousness resides in the thousand-eyed one, who is saluted by all the deities— [may that be mine].
That auspiciousness which arose at the destruction of Vṛtra— may that be your blessing.
That auspiciousness which Vinatā prepared of old for Suparṇa as he sought the nectar of immortality— may that be your blessing.
Kausalyā also prepared the auspicious *oṣadhī* herb known as *siddhārthā*, which removes all pain, and performed protective rites while chanting sacred mantras; then,
the illustrious lady bowed her head, smelled it, and embraced him.
Siddhārtha said, "Go, Rāma, as you please. My son,
I shall see you returned safely to Ayodhyā, free from ailment, having accomplished all your goals, and dwelling happily in the royal palace."
"May the hosts of gods headed by Śiva, the great seers, the spirits, the great asuras, and the serpents— worshipped by me—
desire your welfare as you depart for the forest for a long time, O Rāghava, and may the quarters of the sky do likewise.
Having spoken thus, her eyes filled with tears, she completed the rites for a safe journey according to the prescribed rules.
He performed a circumambulation of Rāghava and, embracing him again and again, pressed him closely.
Having thus been circumambulated by the queen and having repeatedly pressed his mother’s feet,
that highly illustrious Rāghava, blazing with his own splendor, went to Sītā’s dwelling.
Having paid homage to Kausalyā, Rāma set out for the forest;
having received blessings from his mother, he remained steadfast on the path of righteousness,
illuminating the royal highway crowded with men.
By his excellence of character, he seemed to churn the very hearts of the people.
But the ascetic Vaidehī heard none of that; her heart was fixed solely upon his consecration as the crown prince.
Having performed her duty toward the gods, she, grateful and joyful in heart, being well-versed in the duties of kings, awaited the prince. Then Rāma entered his own well-decorated residence.
In that place filled with joyful people, his face slightly cast down in shame,
Sītā then rose up and, trembling, beheld her husband tormented by grief, his senses agitated by anxiety.
Seeing him with a pale face, perspiring and impatient, she, tormented by grief, said: "O Lord, what is this now?
O Raghava, today the auspicious Puṣya constellation is conjoined with Bṛhaspati."
"It is said by wise Brahmins: 'By what means have you become so dejected?
Your lovely face, which was once graced by a parasol with a hundred ribs, resembling the foam of water, does not shine forth today."

And your face, O bull among men, whose eyes resemble the hundred-petaled lotus, is fanned by two principal fans that possess the luster of the moon and the swan. Furthermore, eloquent bards, filled with joy, attend upon you.
Today, the Sūtas and Māgadhas are not seen praising him with auspicious hymns.
Nor do those Brāhmaṇas, masters of the Vedas, according to the prescribed rite, place honey and curd upon the head of the consecrated king.
Neither do all the subjects, nor the adorned leaders of the guilds, nor likewise the citizens and the people of the countryside,
wish to follow you on four swift horses adorned with gold.
Why does your principal state chariot, yoked and ready, not go before you?
O hero, why is your glorious elephant— adorned with auspicious marks and possessing the luster of a dark cloud or a mountain— not seen at your side as you depart?
O Priyadarśana, I do not see you going ahead with the heroic ones, preceded by your auspicious throne adorned with gold;
since the consecration was already prepared, what is this now that has come upon you?
"Your facial complexion is unprecedented, and no joy is to be seen," she said.
To her who was thus lamenting, the joy of the Raghus replied:
"Sītā, our honorable father is sending me away to the forest."
Born into a great lineage, knower of dharma, and practitioner of dharma—
listen, O Jānaki, to how this has come upon me in due course,
through my father, King Daśaratha, who is true to his promise.
In the past, two great boons were granted to Kaikeyī by me with a joyful heart;
today, as this royal consecration of mine is being prepared, she has urged me to fulfill that time-bound promise, which must be discharged according to dharma.
"For fourteen years must I dwell in Daṇḍaka;
meanwhile, my father has appointed Bharata as the heir apparent.
Thus, having come to see you, I am now setting out for the lonely forest."
"You must never speak of me in Bharata's presence;
for men endowed with great prosperity cannot endure the praise of others.
Therefore, my virtues must not be recounted before Bharata."
Nor should you ever be supported by him in any special way; it is impossible to remain in his presence with favorability.
And I too, fulfilling that promise of my elder, [shall depart].
"I shall go to the forest this very day; remain firm, O wise lady.
Once I have departed for the forest frequented by sages, O auspicious and sinless one, you must devote yourself to vows and fasting."
Having risen early and performed the worship of the gods according to the prescribed rites,
my father Daśaratha, the lord of men, must be saluted;
as must my mother Kausalyā, who is aged and emaciated by grief.
Placing dharma alone at the forefront, she deserves honor from you.
Furthermore, my other mothers must always be saluted by you;
for they are equal to my mother in affection, tenderness, and care.
Furthermore, Lakṣmaṇa and Śatrughna, who are dearer to me than my own life, must especially be regarded by you as equal to your own brothers and sons;
you must never do anything displeasing to Bharata.
For that king is indeed the lord of both the country and the family.
Kings are truly gratified when propitiated by good conduct and served with diligent effort; they become enraged in the opposite case.
For kings abandon even their own legitimate sons if they act against their interests, yet they accept even strangers if they are capable.
O beloved, I shall go to the great forest; you, O beautiful lady, must remain right here.
"Just as you do not cause offense to anyone, so must you act upon these words of mine.
Thus addressed, Vaidehī— who was worthy of kindness and spoke kindly—
became angry out of very much affection and said this to her husband:
"Noble son, the father, mother, brother, son, and likewise the daughter-in-law,
each enjoy their own merits and experience their respective fortunes.
But it is the wife alone, O bull among men, who shares in the fortune of her husband."

For this reason, I have been commanded that I must dwell in the forest. For women, neither father, nor son, nor self, nor mother, nor circle of friends is ever their sole refuge—both in this world and after death; the husband alone is always their resort.
"O Raghava, if you are setting out for the impenetrable forest this very day, I shall go before you, treading down the kusha grass and thorns.
Having cast aside envy and anger, I shall follow like water left over after one has drunk."
"Lead me, O hero, with confidence; no evil exists in me.
Whether by means of palace rooftops, celestial chariots, or traveling through the air, the shadow of a husband's feet is superior in every circumstance."
I have been instructed by my mother and father in various matters;
I need not now be told how I must conduct myself.
I shall dwell happily in the forest just as if I were in my father’s palace.
Disregarding the three worlds and thinking only of my devotion to my husband,
I shall serve you constantly, self-restrained and living a life of celibacy; O hero, I shall take delight with you in the forests fragrant with honey.
For you, O Rāma, are capable of providing protection even for other people in the forest, let alone for me, O giver of honor.
I shall always subsist on fruits and roots; of this there is no doubt.
"I shall not cause you any suffering while dwelling with you.
I wish to see rivers, mountains, ponds, and forests everywhere, free from fear, with you as my wise protector."
Surrounded by swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, with lotus ponds in full bloom,
I wish to see them while happy and united with you, O hero.
Together with you, O large-eyed one, I shall sport in supreme delight.
"In this way,
O Raghava, tiger among men, even if I were to dwell with you in heaven for a hundred thousand years, if it were to be without you, I would not find pleasure even in that."
"I shall go to the forest, so difficult to traverse, filled with deer and inhabited by monkeys and elephants;
there I will dwell as if in my father's house, devotedly clinging to your very feet. For I am single-minded, my heart is devoted to you, and separated from you, I am resolved upon death."
"Take me with you; grant my request, for I shall not be a burden to you.
Though she spoke thus, that best of men, who is devoted to righteousness, did not wish to take Sītā away.
Instead, he spoke many words to her, who was distressed at the thought of dwelling in the forest, in order to turn her back.
To Sītā, who was speaking thus, that righteous-souled one, who knows the dharma and is devoted to dharma, spoke these words for the sake of her returning:
"Sītā, you are born of a noble lineage and are always devoted to dharma."

"O Sītā, practice your own dharma here; do not act merely according to the pleasure of your mind. O frail woman, you must do exactly as I tell you, for there are many dangers in the forest. Listen to them as I describe them."
"Sītā, let this intention to dwell in the forest be abandoned;
for the wilderness is called 'forest' because it is full of many dangers.
Indeed, these words are spoken by me with the intent of your welfare."

I never know happiness; the forest is always nothing but suffering. For those dwelling in mountain caves, the roars of lions produced by the mountain torrents are painful to hear; therefore, the forest is misery.

One sleeps upon beds of leaves that have been broken off by oneself on the bare ground during nights exhausted by fatigue; therefore, O Maithilī, the forest is even more painful than that, and one must observe fasts according to one's physical strength.
One must wear a mass of matted hair and dress in garments of bark;
moreover, there is constant wind, darkness, and hunger here,
as well as great terrors— therefore, the forest is even more painful than that.
And many reptiles of various forms roam the earth out of pride, O beautiful lady; therefore, this forest is more painful [than the city].
There are serpents dwelling in rivers, moving as crookedly as the rivers themselves.
They stand blocking the path; therefore, the forest is more painful than this.
Moths, scorpions, insects, gadflies, and mosquitoes constantly harass one, O frail lady; for these reasons, the forest is entirely full of suffering.
O beautiful lady, there are thorny trees as well as kuśa and kāśa grasses in the forest with their branch-tips entangled; therefore, the forest is even more painful for you.
So, enough of your going to the forest, for the forest is not suitable for you.

Reflecting upon this, I see that the forest is full of many greater evils. At that time, when the high-souled Rāma had not yet resolved to lead me to the forest, Sītā did not heed his words; then, deeply distressed, she spoke thus to Rāma.
Having heard these words of Rāma, the sorrowful Sītā,
her face bathed in continuous tears, spoke these words softly:
"As for those faults you have mentioned regarding dwelling in the forest..."
"Know that these virtues of yours have been preceded by my affection for you.
O Rāma, I must go with you at the command of my elders; yet, because of separation from you, I must give up my life here."
Moreover, O Raghava, even Śakra, the lord of the gods, is not able to overcome me by his might while I am in your presence.
But a woman who is deprived of her husband will not be able to live.
"O Rāma, you have indeed shown me such a thing as this;
yet, O man of great wisdom, I have heard from the Brāhmaṇas long ago in my father’s house that I must truly dwell in the forest."
O one of great strength, having heard these words from the twice-born experts in omens while at home, I have always been intent upon dwelling in the forest;
indeed, that command for forest-dwelling must be received by me.
I shall go there with you, my beloved; it cannot be otherwise.
Having received your command, I will go along with you;
for this time has now arrived, and let the word of the twice-born sage be true.
For I know, O hero, that many kinds of sufferings are indeed inevitably encountered by men of undisciplined soul while living in the forest;
and I have heard of this forest-dwelling from my father’s daughter regarding her own stay at her father's house.
O Lord, you were previously propitiated by me, a nun of virtuous conduct, here before my mother; indeed, your departure for residence in the forest was long desired by her along with yours.
"I have made my opportunity for departure, O Raghava—blessings be upon you;
for the life of a hero dwelling in the forest is pleasing to me.
Indeed, through this spirit of love, O pure-souled one, I shall become free from sin."
Following my husband, for my husband is indeed my deity;
even in the state after death, there will be an auspicious union with you.
For such is the sacred Vedic revelation heard from illustrious Brahmins.
"O high-minded one, in this world, whatever woman has been given by her parents to a man according to their own dharma through the pouring of water, she belongs to him even in the state after death.
Thus, from me, take your own wife, who is of virtuous conduct and devoted to her husband."
For what reason here do you not wish to take me with you?
O descendant of Kakutstha, you ought to take me— your devoted and faithful wife, who is now distressed and shares equally in both your joy and your sorrow.
"If you do not wish to take me, who am thus suffering, to the forest,
I shall resort to poison, fire, or water for the sake of death.
In this way, she entreated him in many ways regarding her departure.
The mighty-armed one did not consent to take her to the lonely forest.
Thus addressed, Maithilī was overcome with anxiety,
as if bathing the earth with the warm tears falling from her eyes.

As Vaidehī was thus reflecting and overcome with anger, the self-possessed Kakutstha sought to turn her back and consoled her in many ways. Being thus comforted by Rāma, Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, [replied].
On account of her dwelling in the forest, she spoke thus to her husband.
Deeply agitated, Sītā, out of both affection and pride, rebuked that broad-chested descendant of Raghu.
"What did my father Vaideha, the lord of Mithilā,
think when he obtained you as a son-in-law— a woman in the form of a man?
For this world, out of ignorance, will speak falsely regarding your strength."
There is no splendor greater than Rāma, who blazes like the sun;
why then are you despondent, and from what does your fear arise,
that you wish to abandon me, who am devoted to no other?
"O hero, know me to be devoted to Satyavanta, the son of Dyumatsena, and as one who has come under your own power, like Sāvitrī.
O sinless one, I shall not look upon any other than you, even in my thoughts."
"O Raghava, through you I would go forth like any other woman who brings disgrace upon her family.
But you, O Rama, wish to give me away to others— me, your own wife, who has lived with you since my youth and remains faithful— just as a stage-player might hand over his wife."
"You ought not to set out for the forest without taking me with you;
whether it be for asceticism, the wilderness, or even heaven, it shall be with you. Moreover, I shall experience no fatigue whatsoever on the path."
As I walked behind you, even upon the beds in the monasteries,
and on the path with you, the kuśa, kāśa, śara, and iṣīkā grasses, as well as the thorny trees, felt to my touch like cotton or deerskin.

O lover, the dust raised by the great winds that shall fall upon me, I consider it to be like the most precious sandalwood. When I, a dweller of the forest, shall rest upon the grassy swards at the edge of the woods.
What could be more pleasant than that, even on beds spread with woolen rugs?
Whatever leaves, roots, or fruit you give me yourself, whether it be little or much, it will be like the taste of nectar to me.
There, while enjoying the seasonal flowers and fruits, I shall not think of my mother, nor my father, nor my home;
and having gone there, you shall not see anything unpleasant.
On my account, you shall have no grief, nor shall I become a burden for you to bear. Knowing that with you there is heaven and without you there is hell, O Rāma, go with me in the highest joy.
If you do not lead me, who am thus undistracted, to the forest, I shall drink poison this very day; let me not fall into the power of my enemies.
For even afterwards, there would be no life for me in such sorrow.
O Lord, had you abandoned me at that very moment, death would have been better for me. For I cannot endure this grief even for a moment,
much less for fourteen years while suffering in misery.
Thus, tormented by grief, she lamented piteously at great length; exhausted, she embraced her husband tightly and cried out aloud.
Pierced by those many words as a female elephant is by poisoned arrows, she wept.
She released tears that had long been restrained, as a fire-drill releases fire;
from her eyes, water born of her anguish flowed like water from two lotuses.
Embracing her with both arms as she lay there unconscious and sorrowful,
Rāma then spoke these words to reassure her:
"O Queen, I do not desire even heaven itself at the cost of your suffering."
Indeed, I have no fear from any quarter, like the Self-Existent One himself.
O lady of auspicious countenance, without knowing your entire intention,
I do not find pleasure in dwelling in the forest, even though I am capable of providing protection.

"Since you were created by me to dwell in the forest together with me, O Maithilī, I cannot abandon you, just as a self-possessed man cannot abandon his reputation. Furthermore, O lady with thighs like an elephant's trunk, dharma has been practiced by the virtuous since ancient times."

And I shall follow him today, just as Suvarcalā follows the Sun. O lady of beautiful hips, this is indeed the dharma: obedience to one's father and mother; therefore, having transgressed his command, I have no desire to live.

"I wish to conduct myself exactly as my father, who stands upon the path of truth and righteousness, commands me; for that is the eternal dharma. Follow me, O timid one, and become my partner in the practice of dharma."
"Give jewels to the brahmins and food to the mendicants who are full of hope; hasten and do not delay.
Having understood that her departure was favorable to her husband's wishes, she [prepared herself].
Then the goddess, greatly delighted, immediately began to give.
Thereupon, the illustrious and wise lady, her heart full of joy and mindful of her husband’s words, prepared to bestow wealth and jewels upon those who uphold righteousness.
Then the immensely radiant Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, who stood before him, the heroic one who had been walking ahead, now standing with joined palms in supplication:
"O son of Sumitrā, if you go to that forest today along with me..."
Who will satisfy Kausalyā or the illustrious Sumitrā?
That lord of the earth, possessed of great splendor, who used to rain down all desires upon them like Parjanya upon the earth, has now been cast down by the snares of desire.
"For having obtained this kingdom as the daughter of King Aśvapati,
she will not act kindly toward her distressed co-wives.
Thus addressed by Rāma in gentle words, Lakṣmaṇa replied.
Then he, skilled in speech, replied to Rāma, who was himself an expert in discourse:
"O hero, by your very splendor, Bharata will honor Kausalyā and Sumitrā with devotion; of this there is no doubt."
The noble Kausalyā could support even a thousand people like me,
for she has received a thousand villages as her means of subsistence. Taking his bow along with arrows, he carried a spade and a basket.
"I shall go before you, showing you the way;
I will constantly bring for you roots and fruits, as well as other forest products that are the proper food for ascetics."
"But you, sir, shall take delight with Vaidehī upon the mountain ridges;
I shall do everything for you, whether you are awake or asleep.
Rāma, highly pleased by these words, replied to him:
"O Saumitri, take leave of all your friends.
And those two divine bows of terrible appearance, which the high-souled Varuna himself gave to King Janaka at his great sacrifice— "
The impenetrable divine armor, the two quivers with inexhaustible arrows,
and both the swords, bright as the sun and adorned with gold—
all this was respectfully deposited in the preceptor’s residence.
"Therefore, O Lakṣmaṇa, take up your weapon and return quickly.
Having addressed his friends and being resolved upon dwelling in the forest, he took leave of the elder of the Ikṣvākus and seized his excellent weapon.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, the tiger among kings, presented all those divine weapons— honored and adorned with garlands— to Rāma. The self-possessed Rāma spoke with affection to the approaching Lakṣmaṇa.
"O gentle Lakṣmaṇa, you have arrived at the very time I desired.
O scorcher of foes, I wish to bestow this wealth of mine upon the ascetic Brahmins along with you."
O best of the twice-born, those who dwell here with firm devotion toward their gurus—
bring them to me, as well as all my dependents,
and quickly bring here Suyajña, the noble son of Vasiṣṭha, the most eminent of the twice-born.
"I shall depart for the forest after having honored all the other learned twice-born ones. Then, having received his brother's most auspicious and pleasing command,
he went and quickly entered the residence of Suyajña.
Having saluted that brahmin who was staying in the fire-sanctuary, Lakṣmaṇa said,
"Friend, come and see the dwelling of him who performs such difficult deeds.
Then, having quickly performed the twilight devotions, he went with the son of Sumitrā.

He entered that delightful residence of Rāma, which was graced with prosperity. As Suyajña arrived, a knower of the Vedas, Rāghava, together with Sītā, approached him with palms joined in reverence, as one approaches a consecrated fire.
Kakutstha honored him with excellent ornaments made of gold— beautiful armlets,
earrings, gems with golden threads, as well as bracelets and bangles—
and many other various jewels.
Then Rāma, urged by Sītā, spoke to Suyajña:
"O gentle friend, Sītā now wishes to send a necklace, a golden chain, and a girdle for your wife."
Vaidehī also desires to place upon you that couch with its excellent coverlet, adorned with various jewels,
which my maternal uncle, the elephant named Śatruñjaya, gave to me.
"O bull among the twice-born, I give that to you along with a thousand elephants.
Thus addressed by Rāma, Suyajña accepted the gift and offered auspicious blessings upon Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā.
Then the sweet-spoken Rāma, being unperturbed, spoke these words to his beloved brother, the son of Sumitrā, just as Brahmā might speak to the Lord of the Thirty-three gods:
"Both Agastya and Kauśika are the foremost of Brahmins."

O Saumitri, having summoned him, honor him with jewels as one honors a crop with water. And there is the preceptor of the Taittirīyas, who is handsome, learned in the Vedas, and devotedly attends upon Kausalyā with blessings.
O Saumitri, provide him with a vehicle, female slaves,
and silken garments, until that twice-born man is satisfied;
for the noble Suta Citraratha has been his minister for a very long time.
"Delight him with highly precious jewels, garments, and wealth as well.
O Saumitri, provide a thousand oxen for drawing carts, two hundred auspicious bulls,
and a thousand cows for the sake of condiments."

Then that tiger among men, Lakṣmaṇa, himself gave that wealth to the foremost of the brahmins exactly as instructed, like the Giver of Wealth (Kubera). Then he spoke to his dependents who stood there, their voices choked with tears.
"Let much wealth be handed over for the maintenance of each of my dependents.
Let both the residence and the house of Lakṣmaṇa, as well as this house of mine,
be kept occupied by someone until my return."
Having spoken thus to all those distressed dependents, he said this to the treasurer: "Let the wealth be brought here.
Then his dependents brought forth all of his wealth.

Then that tiger among men, together with Lakṣmaṇa, caused that wealth to be distributed among the brahmins— the young, the old, and the destitute. There was a certain tawny-haired brahmin named Gārgya Trijaṭa.
No one stopped him until he reached the fifth enclosure.
Having approached the prince, Trijaṭa spoke these words:
"O illustrious prince, I am poor and have many sons."
"Always subsisting on gleaned grains in the forest, look after me," [Lakṣmaṇa said].
Then Rāma spoke to him with a touch of humor:
"Not even a single thousand cows has ever been bestowed by me."
"As far as you cast your staff, so far shall you go.
In great haste and agitation, he wrapped the garment around his waist, whirled it about, and,
impelled by speed, hurled the staff with all his might.
Then Rāma, consoling Gārgya, said to him:
"Indeed, you should not feel any anger; for this was merely a jest of mine.
Thereupon the great sage Trijaṭa, together with his wife, accepted the herd of cows and was filled with joy.
They pronounced blessings upon that great-souled one, which increase glory, strength, joy, and happiness. Having given much wealth to the brahmins along with Vaidehī,
the two Rāghavas departed with Sītā to see their father.
Then, once they were grasped, those two weapons— difficult to behold,
adorned with garlands, and decorated by Sītā— shone brilliantly.
Then [the people beheld] the palaces, the mansions, and the tops of the celestial chariots.
Having ascended, the illustrious people looked on with indifference;
for the streets were so crowded with many people that they could not be traversed,
and thus, having climbed the palaces, the wretched ones gazed upon Rāghava.
Seeing Rāma then on foot, his royal parasol discarded, the people,
their hearts overwhelmed by grief, uttered many kinds of words:
"He whom a great fourfold army used to follow as he traveled..."
Lakṣmaṇa followed that single man together with Sītā.
Though he was one who knew the taste of sovereignty and could grant the desires of those who long for them,
out of reverence for dharma, he did not wish to make his father's word false.
Sītā, whom even beings who travel through the sky could not see before, is today beheld by the people on the royal highway.
Sītā, who was accustomed to body-unguents and used red sandalwood paste—
The rain, both hot and cold, will quickly bring about his loss of color.
Surely today Daśaratha speaks under the influence of some spirit,
for a king ought not to banish a beloved son.
How could even a son devoid of virtues be sent into exile,
much less one by whose conduct alone this entire world has been conquered— whose nature is compassion, kindness, learning, good character, self-restraint, and tranquility?
These six qualities adorn Rāghava, the supreme among men.
Therefore, by his injury, the subjects are exceedingly tormented,
like aquatic creatures when the water dries up in the summer heat.
The entire world is afflicted by the suffering of this Lord of the World,
just as a tree laden with flowers and fruit is destroyed when its root is struck.
O Lakṣmaṇa, they— along with their wives and kinsmen— will swiftly [perish] like that.
We shall follow him as he goes, wherever Rāghava goes. Abandoning our gardens, fields, and homes,
we shall follow the righteous Rāma, sharing in his sorrow and joy as one.
Their treasures have been dug up, their courtyards are in ruins,
their wealth and grain have been seized, and they have been completely stripped of their essence;
covered in dust, they have been abandoned by the gods.
"Let Kaikeyī take possession of the dwellings abandoned by us.
Let the forest become a city for Rāghava as he departs;
and let the city, abandoned by us, become a forest."
"May all fanged beasts take to our abandoned caves, and may deer and birds abandon the mountain peaks they frequent.
Such were the various words uttered by many different people.

Rāma heard this, and having heard it, his mind was not shaken. Anticipating his noble lineage’s distress, he— though himself free from affliction and as if smiling— then went forth desiring to see his father and wishing to carry out his father’s command according to the prescribed rule.

Then, as the high-souled Rāma, the descendant of Ikṣvāku, was about to depart for the forest, he saw Sumantra looking distressed and stood still for a moment to have him inform his father. Yet, out of devotion to dharma, he had already resolved his mind upon entering the forest in accordance with his father’s command.
Seeing Sumantra, that descendant of Raghu said to him, "Announce my arrival to the king.
Sent by Rāma, the charioteer, his senses clouded with distress, quickly entered and beheld the king sighing deeply.
Having beheld Rāma, whose mind was deeply agitated and who was grieving for him alone, the highly wise charioteer approached with palms joined in reverence:
"O tiger among men, here is your son standing at the door."

Having given wealth to the Brahmins and to all his dependents, Rāma—whose prowess is truth—wishes to see you; may prosperity be yours. Having taken leave of all his friends, he now desires to behold you.
"O Lord of the World, behold him as he departs for the great forest,
endowed with all the virtues of a king like the sun with its rays;
he is truthful, righteous in soul, and like the ocean in depth."
Stainless as the sky, the lord of men replied to him:
"Sumantra, bring my wives— whosoever here belong to me—
for I wish to see Rāghava surrounded by all my wives."
Having passed through the inner apartments, he spoke these words to those women: "The noble king summons you; go there without delay.
Thus addressed by Sumantra at the king's command, all the women [prepared to depart].
Having received their lord’s command,
those seven hundred and fifty women with copper-hued eyes,
firm in their vows, surrounded Kausalyā and proceeded slowly toward that palace.
When his wives had arrived, the lord of the earth looked at them and said to the charioteer, "Sumantra, bring my son here. Then that charioteer took Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and the princess of Mithilā.
He went quickly toward the presence of the lord of the earth.
Seeing his son approaching from afar with palms joined in reverence, the king—
surrounded by the women and overcome with distress— rose swiftly from his seat.
Seeing Rāma, the lord of the people rushed toward him with speed;
failing to reach him, he fell to the ground, overcome by grief and unconscious.
Rāma and the great chariot-warrior Lakṣmaṇa quickly ran to his side.
Then the king was as if unconscious from his grief, overwhelmed by sorrow;
and in the royal palace, a cry of thousands of women suddenly arose, "Alas, alas, Rāma!", mingled with the sound of their ornaments.
Embracing him with their arms, both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, weeping, laid him down upon the couch together with Sītā. Then, after a moment, Rāma restored the lord of the earth to consciousness.
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke to him who was submerged in an ocean of grief:
"I take my leave of you, O Great King; you are the lord of us all.
Look upon me with favor as I set out for the Daṇḍaka forest."
Give leave to Lakṣmaṇa as well; Sītā follows me to the forest.
Though they are being restrained by many true arguments, neither of them desires to stay behind.
O bestower of honor, cast off your grief and grant permission to us all.

Beholding Rāghava waiting expectantly for the permission of the lord of the world— just as Prajāpati beholds his subjects— the king, looking at Lakṣmaṇa, myself, and Sītā, spoke thus to him regarding his dwelling in the forest.
"O Raghava, I have been deluded by Kaikeyī through the granting of boons;
therefore, seize me and you yourself become the king of Ayodhyā this very day.
Thus addressed by the king, Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma, [remained silent].
Making a gesture of salutation with joined palms, he who was skilled in speech replied to his father:
"O King, may you remain the lord of the earth for a thousand years;
as for me, I shall dwell in the forest—I have no need for falsehood on your part."
"For the sake of your welfare, your prosperity, and your return once more, my son, go now upon a path that is auspicious, free from agitation, and devoid of fear.
But for now, my son, do not go at all this very night."
"Beholding both your mother and me, dwell this night;
satisfied with all your desires, you shall accomplish your purpose tomorrow at the appointed time.
Then Rāma, having heard those words of his distressed father, [remained silent].
Together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa, he spoke these words in distress:
"Who will grant me tomorrow those virtues that I shall obtain today?
Therefore, I choose to depart from here rather than all my desires."
"This earth, along with its kingdom, its people, and its abundance of wealth and grain, has been relinquished by me; let it be given to Bharata.
Let your sorrow depart; do not be overwhelmed with tears."
For the invincible ocean, the lord of rivers, does not become agitated.
O bull among men, I do not desire the kingdom, nor happiness, nor even Maithilī; I desire only you in truth, and not untruth.
"The city, the kingdom, and the entire earth have been relinquished by me; let them be given to Bharata.
Obeying your command, I shall go to the forest to dwell there for a long time.
"Let Bharata take this earth, relinquished by me, with its mountain ranges, its cities, and its forests."
"O King, let him rule over the auspicious and well-bounded land; let that which was spoken by you stand as it is.

O Ruler of the Earth, my mind is not so intent upon great desires nor upon what is dear to myself as it is upon your command, which is approved by the wise. O sinless one, let your sorrow on my account depart."

Therefore, O sinless one, today I would not choose for you an undecaying kingdom, nor all objects of desire, nor happiness, nor Maithilī, nor even life itself, by joining you with untruth; let your vow remain true.
Thus, while eating fruits and roots in the forest, you shall behold mountains, rivers, and lakes.
"Having entered the forest filled with diverse trees, I shall become happy; may you find peace.
Then the descendant of Ikshvaku, distressed by his vow, sighed deeply with tears and spoke these words again and again to Sumantra.
"O charioteer, let an army consisting of the fourfold forces, fully equipped with jewels,
be quickly prepared for the purpose of escorting Rāghava. Let there also be beautiful courtesans and wealthy merchants."
Let them, well-arrayed, adorn the army of the prince. And those who depend upon him and those by whose valor he takes delight—
having given them various gifts, enjoin them also to this task.
Slaying deer and elephants, drinking wild honey,
and beholding various rivers, he will not remember the kingdom. Whatever storehouse of grain and whatever treasury of wealth belongs to me, [it shall follow him].
The two of them followed Rāma as he dwelt in the desolate forest;
performing sacrifices in holy places and bestowing abundant sacrificial fees,
he would dwell happily in the forest, meeting with the seers.
"And the mighty-armed Bharata shall protect Ayodhyā;
meanwhile, let the illustrious Rāma be propitiated with all his desires.
While the descendant of Kakutstha was speaking thus, fear came upon Kaikeyī.
Her face became parched and her voice was choked.
Despondent and terrified, Kaikeyī spoke these words:
"O virtuous one, the kingdom is now like wine whose essence has been drunk up and from which the people have departed."
"Bharata will not accept this utterly tasteless emptiness," King Daśaratha said to the large-eyed Kaikeyī as she spoke these most cruel words, having cast aside all shame.
"Why do you strike me, having yoked me to an ignoble burden?
Kaikeyī, her anger redoubled, said this to the king:
"In your own lineage, Sagara exiled his eldest son."
"This one known as Asamañja likewise deserves to go [into exile].
When he had spoken thus, King Daśaratha said, "Fie!
and all the people were ashamed; yet she did not understand that.
There, an elderly high minister named Siddhārtha by name— pure and highly esteemed by the king— spoke thus to Kaikeyī:
"Asamañja, while playing on the road, seized some children."
That evil-minded man took pleasure in throwing [the children] into the waters of the Sarayū.
Seeing him, all the citizens, filled with anger, said to the king:
"O increaser of the kingdom, choose either Asamañja alone or us."
Then the king asked them, "What is the cause of this fear?
And being thus questioned by the king, the subjects spoke these words:
"This man, his mind deranged, has been playing with our young sons."
By casting him into the Sarayū out of folly, he enjoys incomparable joy.
Having heard those words of the subjects, the lord of men abandoned that harmful son, desiring to do what was pleasing to them.
"In this way, the most righteous King Sagara did not abandon [the horse];
what evil deed has Rāma committed that he should be thus obstructed?
Having heard Siddhārtha’s words, the king spoke with a very weary voice.
With a voice stricken by grief, she said this to Kaikeyī:
"I shall follow Rāma today, renouncing the kingdom, happiness, and wealth;
together with the king and Bharata, may you enjoy the kingdom for a long time as you please."
Having heard the words of the high minister, Rāma, who was skilled in decorum, then addressed Daśaratha with humility:
"O King, for me, who has renounced all enjoyments and shall live on forest fare in the wilderness..."

What need has one who has renounced all attachments for an escort? For what use is a rope to one who, having given away the finest of elephants, sets his mind upon its girth, yet is about to abandon that supreme beast?
"Likewise, O best of virtuous men, O Lord of the World, what use have I for an army?
I renounce them all; let them bring me only bark garments. Go, and bring me both a spade and a basket."
"Thus shall I dwell in the forest for fourteen years.
Then Kaikeyī, shameless before the multitude of people, personally brought bark garments to Rāghava and said, "Put these on."
Having accepted those two bark garments from Kaikeyī, that tiger among men cast aside his fine cloth and donned the robes of a sage;
and Lakṣmaṇa likewise discarded his two beautiful garments right there.
In the presence of her father, she took the ascetic’s garment;
then Sītā, who was dressed in silk, seeing the bark-cloth intended for her own wearing, was as terrified as a doe beholding a snare.
Feeling ashamed and receiving him with a heavy heart,
she spoke thus to her husband, who resembled the king of the Gandharvas:
"How indeed do the sages dwelling in the forest fasten their bark garments?"
Having placed the bark garment around her neck and holding one end in her hand, Janaka’s daughter stood there, distressed and ashamed;
then Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma, quickly approached her.

He himself fastened the bark garment over Sītā’s silk dress. As she, who possessed a protector, put on the bark while appearing as if she were unprotected, all the people cried out, "Shame on you, Dasharatha!"
Sighing hotly, the descendant of Ikṣvāku said this to his wife:
"Kaikeyī, Sītā ought not to go clad in kusha grass and bark;
indeed, O wicked woman, this exile of Rāma is sufficient for you."
"What more can be gained from these wretched sins committed by you?
To his father, who was speaking thus and sitting with his head bowed, Rāma, having set out for the forest, spoke these words.
"O giver of boons, this righteous Kausalyā, my illustrious mother,
is aged and of noble character; she will not, O you who are censured by the gods,
look upon you when you have been separated from me and have fallen into an ocean of grief."
You ought to comfort her once more, for she has never before experienced such calamity.
You must provide for my mother, who is now pregnant with a child as great as Mahendra,
so that while I am dwelling in the forest, she does not— emaciated by grief— cast off her life and go to the abode of Yama.
Having heard Rāma's words and seeing him wearing the garb of a sage, the king, together with his wives, lost consciousness;
tormented by grief, he could not even look at that descendant of Raghu.
And beholding him, the king did not speak, being heavy-hearted;
for a moment that lord of the earth remained as if unconscious, and then, pained and reflecting only upon Rāma, the mighty-armed one lamented.
"I believe that in the past I must have caused many creatures to lose their young or even harmed them; therefore, this has come upon me.
Yet, as long as the time has not yet arrived, life does not depart from the body."
For me, who am being tormented by Kaikeyī, death does not exist—
since I behold before me my own son standing there, having cast off his two fine garments and clad himself in the dress of an ascetic, appearing like a blazing fire.
"Indeed, for the sake of this single Kaikeyī— who, striving for her own interest, has resorted to such deceit— these people are suffering.
Having spoken these words, his senses were overwhelmed by tears.

Having uttered the name "Rāma" only once, he was unable to speak further. But after a moment, having regained his senses, that lord of the earth, with eyes filled with tears, spoke these words to Sumantra: "O Sumantra, go quickly and bring my two sons, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, along with their wife, back here at once. ||| 7 || Hearing those words of his, Sumantra departed; but as he was about to leave, the king, overwhelmed by grief, cried out again, "Alas, Rāma! Having uttered the name "Rāma" only once, he was indeed unable to speak further. ||| 8 || But having regained consciousness after a moment, that lord of the earth, with eyes full of tears, spoke this to Sumantra: ||| 9 ||
"Having yoked the royal chariot with the best of horses, come here;
convey this highly fortunate one from this region to the land beyond.
Thus, I believe, is the fruit of the virtues of the virtuous said to be proclaimed."
Since this virtuous hero is being exiled to the forest by his father and mother,
Sumantra, swift in his prowess, having received the king’s command,
harnessed the chariot with its horses adorned and returned there.
Having joined his palms in reverence, the charioteer announced to the prince that the chariot, adorned with gold and yoked with excellent horses,
was ready; meanwhile, the king had quickly summoned the official occupied with the collection of wealth.
He who knew the proper place and time spoke with certainty and complete purity:
"Having calculated these years, quickly bring for Vaidehī costly garments and the finest ornaments."
Thus addressed by the lord of men, he went then to the treasury and,
having brought it all, quickly presented it to Sītā.
As she was about to depart for the forest, Vaidehī, who was herself well-born, [accepted] those well-fashioned [gifts].
She adorned her limbs with those various ornaments. Thus beautifully decorated, Vaidehī illuminated that palace like the radiance of the rising sun illuminates the sky at the time of dawn.
Embracing her with both arms and smelling the head of Maithilī— who was acting piteously— her mother-in-law spoke these words:
"In this entire world, unfaithful women are always honored by their lovers."
Women do not respect a husband who has fallen into misfortune.
Therefore, you must not disregard my son, though he has been exiled; let him be your deity, whether he be without wealth or possessed of wealth.
Having understood her words, which were consistent with righteousness and purpose, Sītā stood facing her mother-in-law and, with palms joined in reverence, spoke this:
"I shall do everything exactly as my noble lady instructs me."
"I know how one must conduct oneself toward a husband, and I have heard this from sacred tradition. Noble lady, you ought not to equate me with wicked women;
I am no more able to deviate from dharma than radiance is able to depart from the moon."
A lute without strings cannot be played; a chariot without wheels does not roll;
and even she who has a hundred sons does not thrive in happiness if she lacks a husband.
For a father gives only a limited amount, a mother gives a limited amount, and a son gives a limited amount.

Who would not honor a husband who is the giver of the immeasurable? Thus situated, O noble lady, I—who am preeminent and devoted to the higher and lower truths of dharma—how could I disregard him? For to women, the husband is indeed a deity.
Having heard Sītā’s heart-touching words, Kausalyā,
whose nature was pure, suddenly shed tears born of both sorrow and joy.
Approaching her with joined palms in the midst of her mothers, she paid her great respect.
Rāma, the supreme knower of dharma, spoke these words to his mother:
"O Mother, do not be sorrowful; look upon my father, for the end of this forest exile will surely come very soon."
"While you sleep, fifteen years will pass;
when that time is fully completed, you shall see me here, surrounded by my friends.
Having spoken these words to his mother, which were so purposeful and well-reasoned, he—
Indeed, he beheld three hundred and fifty mothers;
and the son of Daśaratha, seeing them likewise distressed,
spoke these words consistent with righteousness with palms joined in reverence.
"Whatever harsh thing I have done through living with you, or even out of ignorance, please forgive me for all that; I bid you all farewell.
Then there arose from them a great clamor, like the cry of female cranes.
While Rāghava was speaking thus to the wives of the lord of men,
the palace of Daśaratha, which formerly resounded like the roar of clouds with drums and tabors,
became filled with lamentation and wailing; fallen into calamity, it was overwhelmed with profound sorrow.
Then Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa, with palms joined in reverence, touched the king's feet and, being dejected, performed a circumambulation around him.
Having also taken leave of him, the knower of dharma, together with Sītā, [departed].
Overwhelmed by grief, Rāghava paid homage to his mother.
Immediately following his brother, Lakṣmaṇa also paid homage to Kausalyā,
and then he again grasped the feet of his own mother, Sumitrā.
As he was paying his respects, his mother, weeping yet desiring his welfare, smelled the head of the mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, and said to him:
"You have been sent away to dwell in the forest, even though you are so deeply devoted to your kinsmen."
"Do not be negligent toward Rāma, my son, as your brother departs.
Whether he is in distress or in prosperity, O sinless one, he is your refuge.
In this world, it is the duty of the virtuous that one should remain subject to the will of the eldest."
For this is the eternal and fitting conduct of this lineage:
charity, initiation for sacrifices, and the casting off of the body in battle.
Know Rāma to be Daśaratha, and know me to be the daughter of Janaka.
"Know that Ayodhyā is a wilderness; go, dear son, as you please.
Then Sumantra, humble and knowing the rules of propriety, addressed these words to the descendant of Kakutstha with palms joined in reverence, just as Mātali might address Indra.
"Mount the chariot— blessings upon you, O prince of great renown—
I shall swiftly convey you wherever Rāma tells me.
"For fourteen years must you dwell in the forest."
"Those [tasks] which you have been urged by the Queen must be undertaken.
Sītā, of beautiful limbs, having adorned herself, ascended that chariot which shone like the sun with a joyful heart.
Having likewise placed the various weapons, the two brothers' armor,
and that leather-covered quiver upon the seat of the chariot,
he saw that they had mounted with Sītā as the third and boldly urged the horses forward.
Sumantra yoked the highly esteemed horses, which were equal to the wind in speed;
and as Raghava departed for the great forest for a long time to come,
there occurred a fainting spell in the city, and the strength of the people failed them.
Then that city, filled with confusion and agitation, its elephants intoxicated and enraged, and echoing with the clatter of horses, became a great din.
Thereupon, the entire city, including children and the elderly, was deeply distressed.
Like one afflicted by heat rushing toward water, he ran straight toward Rāma.
Hanging from his sides and his back, all looking up at him with faces filled with tears, they spoke to him in great distress.
"O charioteer, restrain the reins of the horses; proceed very slowly.
I wish to behold the face of Rāma, which will soon become difficult for us to see.
Surely the heart of Rāma’s mother must be made of iron, beyond any doubt."
For when he, who resembles the offspring of a god, enters the forest, she does not falter;
for Vaidehī has accomplished her purpose, and devoted to dharma, she follows her husband like a shadow, never leaving him, just as the radiance of the sun never leaves Mount Meru.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, you have achieved your goal, for you shall serve your brother, who speaks ever kindly and resembles a god.
This indeed is a great accomplishment for you, and this is a magnificent prosperity."
"This is the path to heaven, since you follow him"—
speaking thus, they were unable to restrain the tears that welled up.
Then the king, surrounded by distressed women, his mind despondent, [departed].
He departed from his house, saying, "I shall see my beloved son," while the great sound of weeping women was heard before him,
like the cry of female elephants when a great bull elephant has been captured.
And his father, the illustrious King Kakutstha, then appeared dejected,
like the full moon eclipsed by Rahu at the proper time.
Then, a tumultuous roar arose behind Rama.
Seeing the king sinking down, deeply afflicted with grief, some people cried out, "O Rāma! while others wailed, "O Mother of Rāma!
as they lamented around the opulent inner apartments.
Looking back, Rāma beheld on the path his dejected father and his mother following him with troubled hearts;
bound by the noose of dharma, he did not look at them openly.
Seeing those two, who were worthy of vehicles and accustomed to comfort rather than suffering, walking on foot, he urged the charioteer, saying, "Go quickly!
For that tiger among men could not endure the sight of his father's distress.
And he was unable to endure his mother, like an elephant tormented by a goad, as Kausalyā followed that chariot, weeping and crying out, "O Rāma!
O Rāma! Alas, Sītā! O Lakṣmaṇa!"
At that time, he looked repeatedly at his mother, who was as if dancing;
"Stay! cried the king, while Rāghava shouted, "Go! Go!"—Sumantra’s mind was caught between them like a wheel.
"Even if you are reproached by the king, you shall say, 'I did not hear it';
this is the most wicked form of suffering for a long time," Rāma said to him.
Following Rāma's word and taking leave of those people, he departed.
Even as they were departing, the charioteer urged the horses on with speed.
The people turned back from the king after circumambulating Rāma;
yet, though they turned back in body, they did not turn back in mind, nor could they restrain the rush of their tears.
"One should not follow too far after one whom one wishes to see return," these were the words the ministers spoke to the great king Daśaratha.
With his limbs covered in sweat and his appearance dejected, he [accepted] their speech, which was endowed with every virtue.

Hearing this, the king, distressed, stood with his wife gazing at that son. As that tiger among men departed with palms joined in reverence, a great cry of lamentation arose from the women in the inner apartments.
Where indeed is that protector going— he who was the refuge and the resort for these people who are without a lord, weak, and wretched;
he who did not become angry even when accused, avoiding all causes for provocation?
Where is he going, who pacifies all those who are angry and shares their sorrow?
Where indeed is that great-souled one going, who behaves toward us just as he behaves toward his mother, Kausalyā, he of such great splendor?
Urged by the king, who was being tormented by Kaikeyī, where indeed does this protector of these people and of the world go to the forest? Alas,
the king has lost his senses regarding that which is so dear to the world of the living!
"Rāma, who is righteous and devoted to his vow of truth, shall depart for residence in the forest. Thus spoke all the queens, who, like cows deprived of their calves,
wept, afflicted by grief, and cried out loudly.

Hearing that terrible sound of distress within the inner apartments, the lord of the earth, tormented by grief for his son, became deeply distressed. The *agnihotra* sacrifices were no longer offered, and the sun vanished from sight.
The serpents disgorged mouthfuls of air, and the cows would not suckle their calves.
Triśaṅku, Lohitāṅga, Bṛhaspati, and Budha—
all these planets, having approached the moon, stood there in a terrible configuration.
The stars lost their radiance, the planets were stripped of their luster,
and the Viśākhā constellations shone in the sky accompanied by smoke.
Suddenly, all the people of the city fell into a state of despondency.
Whether eating or resting, no one set his mind to it;
the people on the royal road had their faces clouded with tears, and not a single person appeared joyful— everyone was overcome with grief.
The cool breeze does not blow, nor does the moon appear with its gentle aspect;
the sun does not warm the world, for the entire universe is in turmoil. Sons have no regard for their mothers, and likewise, husbands and brothers have no regard for one another.
Having abandoned everything, they all thought only of Rāma.
But those who were Rāma’s friends, their minds bewildered and overwhelmed by a burden of grief, did not leave their beds at that time.

Then Ayodhyā, deprived of that high-souled one, trembled violently like the earth with its mountains when shorn of Purandara, oppressed by a burden of fear; and it roared, along with its elephants, warriors, and throngs of horses.
As long as the form of his dust was visible as he departed, [the city remained in turmoil].
That best of the Ikṣvākus did not withdraw his eyes for as long as he beheld his beloved son, who was exceedingly righteous; indeed,
his longing to behold his son on the earth continued to increase.
When the king no longer saw even the dust raised by Rāma,
he fell to the surface of the earth, afflicted and despondent;
then the lady Kausalyā took hold of his right arm.
And Kaikeyī, who was fond of Bharata, followed at his left side. Then the king, endowed with prudence, righteousness, and humility, looked toward Kaikeyī and spoke to her, his senses distressed.
"O Kaikeyī, do not touch my limbs, you woman of evil conduct!
For I do not wish to see you; you are neither my wife nor my kinswoman.
As for those who depend upon you, I am not theirs, nor are they mine."

For I abandon you, who have abandoned dharma and are intent solely on your own selfish ends. I hereby revoke everything— the taking of your hand and the leading you around the fire— in both this world and the next.
"If Bharata were satisfied, he might give me this imperishable kingdom; let not that which was given for the sake of my father come back to me.
Then, having raised up that lord of men who was covered in dust, [he spoke].
Then Queen Kausalyā, emaciated by grief, turned back;
like one who has intentionally killed a Brahmin or touched fire with his hand, that righteous-souled man was consumed by remorse as he thought of his son as an ascetic.
Turning back again and again, as he sat upon the tracks of the chariot,
the king’s appearance did not shine brightly, like the sun eclipsed by Rāhu.
Afflicted with grief, he lamented, remembering his beloved son.
Realizing that his son had reached the edge of the city, he then said to him:
"The tracks of the foremost mounts carrying my son are visible on the road, yet that great-souled one is not seen."
Surely today he will have taken refuge at the foot of some tree, and having laid down a piece of wood or perhaps a stone, he will lie there;
and the miserable man, covered in dust, will rise from the earth.
Sighing like a bull elephant from a mountain spring,
forest-dwelling men will surely see Rāma— the long-armed lord of the world— rising and departing like one who is helpless.
"O Kaikeyī, may your desires be fulfilled; dwell in the kingdom as a widow, for I have no desire to live without that tiger among men.
Thus lamenting, the king was surrounded by a vast multitude of people.
Like one who has performed an expiatory bath after a misfortune, he entered that best of cities, which had its squares and the interiors of its houses empty, its marketplaces and shrines closed,
its great roads not crowded, and its people exhausted, weak, and afflicted by grief.
Beholding that entire city and thinking only of Rāma,
the king entered his palace lamenting, like the sun entering a cloud after its serpents have been carried away by Suparṇa from the unshakeable great lake.
"Let them lead me quickly to the house of Kausalyā, the mother of Rāma— a dwelling now bereft of Rāma, Vaidehī, and Lakṣmaṇa. As the king spoke thus, the doorkeepers led him away.
Then, having entered there and ascended to the chamber of Kausalyā, even as he lay upon the bed, his mind became agitated.
Seeing that, the valiant great king raised his arm and—
He cried out in a loud voice, "Alas, Raghava! You are abandoning me!
"O, those best of men shall surely live happily during that time who embrace Rama when they see him returned again."
"I do not see you, Kausalyā; please touch me with your hand.
My gaze, following after Rāma, does not turn back even now.
Seeing the king upon his bed thus lost in thought of that very Rāma, the queen [spoke].
Sitting down nearby, appearing even more distressed and sighing deeply, she lamented her bitter plight.
Then, seeing the king lying on his bed, overcome by grief,
Kausalyā, herself afflicted with sorrow for her son, spoke to the lord of the earth.
O tiger among men, having sown discord like a double-tongued serpent,
Kaikeyī will roam about like a female snake that has cast its skin;
for now that she has banished Rāma, that fortunate woman has attained her desire and is at ease.
"He will terrify me again, like a wicked snake in the house.
Then, O Rama, as you wander for alms in the city, it would be better to grant me the boon of dwelling in my house as a slave, even with my son.

Having caused Rāma to be cast down from his position at Kaikeyī’s will, the portion of the Rākṣasas was assigned [to him], just as a portion is offered by one who maintains the sacred fires on a festival day—
[Rāma] the hero, with the gait of a lordly elephant, mighty-armed, and bearing his bow.

"He has surely entered the forest with his wife and Lakṣmaṇa. What indeed will be the condition of those who have never experienced suffering in the forest, now abandoned by you at the command of Kaikeyī for their exile?"

Deprived of their wealth, these young men have been exiled at the very time they ought to be enjoying the fruits of their labor; how will those miserable ones survive, subsisting only on fruits and roots?
Would that this auspicious time for the end of my sorrow might now arrive.
"When shall I see Raghava here together with his brother and his wife?
Upon hearing that the two heroes have arrived, when will the glorious Ayodhya become filled with joyful people and garlanded with uplifted banners?"
When will the city, filled with joy, rejoice like the ocean on a full-moon day upon seeing those two tigers among men returned from the forest?
When will the mighty-armed hero enter the city of Ayodhyā?
Placing Sītā before him on the chariot, like a bull with its mate,
when will my two sons, the subduers of enemies, enter the royal highway while thousands of living beings scatter parched grain over them?

When will joyful maidens of noble birth, bestowing flowers and fruits, perform a circumambulation of the city? And when, mature in wisdom and in years, shall he who possesses the splendor of an immortal—
The knower of dharma will come to me, caressing me like a child three years old.
Without a doubt, O hero, I think that in the past, when I was cruel,
I must have cut off the breasts of nursing mothers while they were desiring to protect their young.

O tiger among men, I have been rendered like a cow deprived of her calf by a lion— though I am full of affection for my child— by Kaikeyī, who has forcibly taken away my young offspring, just as a cow is separated from her calf.
For you are endowed with every virtue and are proficient in all the scriptures.
Having but one son, I cannot endure to live without my son. Indeed, I perceive no capacity for life here for me who do not behold my beloved son, the mighty-armed and exceedingly powerful one.
"For this fire, arisen from grief for my son, consumes me;
it is like the divine sun, possessed of supreme radiance, scorching this earth with its rays during the summer heat.
Thus did Kausalyā, the best of women, lament.
Abiding in righteousness, Sumitrā spoke these righteous words:
