"O noble lady, that son of yours is endowed with excellent virtues and is the best of men;
what is the use of your lamenting or weeping so piteously?"
Noble lady, that son of yours who has departed, having renounced the kingdom, was a man of great strength and high soul; he acted rightly by serving his father, who was a speaker of truth,
in a manner practiced by the virtuous, which yields eternal fruit after death.

Rāma is established in dharma and is preeminent; he is never to be grieved for. Furthermore, the ever-virtuous Lakṣmaṇa always maintains the highest conduct toward him; that great-souled one is compassionate toward all beings, and this is his great gain.
Vaidehī, though accustomed to comfort, truly understands the hardships of dwelling in the forest and follows your righteous son;
he who is the lord that causes the banner of his fame to wave throughout the world.
Devoted to self-restraint and the vow of truth, what has your son not attained?
Clearly, having recognized Rāma’s purity and supreme magnanimity,
the sun ought not to scorch his body with its rays.
At all times, a pleasant breeze, free from excessive cold or heat, will blow forth from the forests to serve Raghava;
and at night, it will embrace the sinless one as he lies down, like a father.
The moon will gladden him by touching him with its cool rays. And Brahmā gave divine weapons to that one of great prowess when he saw the lord of the Dānavas, the son of Timidhvaja, slain in battle.
Together with the Earth, Vaidehī, and Śrī— that bull among men,
Rāma, shall soon be consecrated along with these three.
Beholding him as he departs, they shed tears born of sorrow.
"You will soon shed from your eyes the tears born of joy. Seeing your son together with his friends coming to offer his salutations,
you will quickly release tears of delight, like a rain-cloud in the monsoon season."
"Your son, the granter of boons, having quickly returned to Ayodhyā,
will press your feet with his soft and fleshy palms.
Having heard those words of Lakṣmaṇa’s mother, the wife of the lord of men, Rāma’s mother—
Immediately, grief perished from his body like an autumn cloud containing little water.
The devoted people followed the high-souled Rāma, whose prowess is truth, as he departed for his dwelling in the forest.
And even though the king and his circle of friends were forcibly turned back,
those who followed Rāma’s chariot did not turn back at all;
for the man of great renown was dear to the men whose home is Ayodhyā.
Endowed with all virtues, he was as beloved as the full moon.
Then, though being entreated by his own subjects, that descendant of Kakutstha,
making his father true to his word, departed for the forest.
Gazing with affectionate eyes as if drinking them in,
Rāma spoke with love to those subjects as if they were his own children:
"The joy and the great respect that the inhabitants of Ayodhyā have for me..."
"For my sake, let her be settled specifically with Bharata;
for he, of auspicious conduct and the increaser of Kaikeyī’s joy,
will duly perform what is pleasing and beneficial for you all."
"Though young in years, he is mature in wisdom; gentle yet endowed with the quality of prowess.
He shall be a worthy husband for you, a remover of fear.
For he is possessed of royal virtues and has been designated as the crown prince."
Moreover, you must carry out the command of your master as instructed by me;
and out of a desire to do what is pleasing to me, you must act in such a way that the Great King does not grieve when I have gone to dwell in the forest.
The more the son of Daśaratha remained steadfast in righteousness,
the more the subjects desired Rāma as their lord.
Together with the son of Sumitrā, Rāma was dejected and choked with tears.
As if binding the people with their virtues and drawing them back once more to their seat,
those twice-born ones— advanced in three ways by knowledge, age, and vigor,
their heads trembling from old age— spoke these words from afar.
"O swift and noble horses, carrying Rāma, turn back! You must not go; be well-disposed toward your master. Your master is to be carried *to* the forest from the city, not carried *away* from it."
Beholding those aged twice-born ones thus uttering their piteous lamentations, Rāma suddenly descended from his chariot; then,
accompanied by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, he proceeded on foot.
Rāma, devoted to the forest, walked with measured steps close by them;
yet Rāma, who cherished virtuous conduct and possessed eyes of compassion, could not bear to leave those twice-born ones on foot while he traveled by chariot.
Seeing Rāma departing, their minds filled with agitation and deeply distressed, the twice-born spoke these words to Rāma:
"All this Brahminhood follows you, who are devoted to the Brahmins."
"These fires, mounted upon the shoulders of the twice-born, follow after you;
behold these umbrellas of ours, arising from the Vājapeya sacrifice,
following behind like swans at the end of the rainy season."
"For you, who have not yet obtained the royal parasol and are scorched by the sun's rays,
we shall provide shade with our own Vājapeya umbrellas.
For our intellect, which constantly follows the Vedic mantras," [is thus directed].
For your sake, my child, she has been made to follow you into forest exile.
The Vedas, which are our supreme wealth, abide within our hearts;
and wives who are protected by their own virtuous conduct will remain even at home.
No further deliberation is required; your mind has already been well-set upon your course.
But if you have regard for dharma, what would it be to disregard dharma? We entreat you: turn back, O you whose hair is as white as a swan.
O you of restrained conduct, with their heads covered in the dust from prostrating upon the earth,
the many sacrifices of the twice-born who have gathered here depend for their completion upon your return, my child.
For all beings, both mobile and immobile, possess devotion;
therefore, show your devotion toward those devotees who are entreating you.
Unable to follow you because their roots have been uprooted and their momentum lost, they remain behind.
Tossed by the force of the wind, the trees seemed to cry out;
even the birds, rendered motionless and deprived of food, remaining fixed in their single spots upon the trees, implored him who is compassionate toward all beings.
While those twice-born ones were thus crying out to turn back,
Tamasā appeared there as if to restrain Rāghava.
Then Rāghava, having reached the lovely bank of the Tamasā, took his stand.
Gazing at Sītā, he spoke these words to the son of Sumitrā:
"O Saumitri, this first night of our departure for the forest has arrived;
may you be blessed. You ought not to feel anxious regarding our dwelling in the woods."
Behold the empty forests, which seem to weep on all sides as the deer and birds return to their respective dwellings;
today, however, the city of Ayodhyā, my father’s royal capital, [is likewise desolate].
Without a doubt, she will grieve for us who have departed along with our wives and husbands.
Indeed, the righteous Bharata will console my father and mother with words consistent with dharma, artha, and kāma.
Reflecting again and again upon the benevolence of Bharata,
O Lakṣmaṇa, I do not grieve for my father nor even for my mother.
O tiger among men, you have fulfilled your duty by following me.
For assistance must indeed be sought for the sake of protecting Vaidehī.
But, O Saumitri, I shall dwell this very night upon the waters alone;
for this pleases me, even though various forest resources are available.
Having spoken thus to the son of Sumitrā, Rāghava also said to Sumantra,
"O gentle one, remain vigilant regarding the horses.
Then Sumantra, having harnessed the horses, waited as the sun reached its setting.
Having provided them with abundant fodder, he stood close at hand.
When he saw that night had arrived, the charioteer, together with the son of Sumitrā, performed the auspicious evening prayers and prepared a bed for Rāma.
Having seen that bed made of tree leaves on the bank of the Tamasā,
Rāma, together with his wife and accompanied by the son of Sumitrā, lay down upon it.
Then, seeing his brother fast asleep with his wife, Lakṣmaṇa—

He recounted to the charioteer the various virtues of Rāma. While the son of Sumitrā remained awake throughout that night, speaking of Rāma’s virtues on the bank of the Tamasā, the sun rose for the charioteer.
Not far from the Tamasā river, whose banks were crowded with cowherds,
Rāma dwelt there that night together with his subjects. Then, having risen and observed those subjects, the one of great splendor [addressed them].
Rāma spoke to his brother Lakṣmaṇa, who was endowed with auspicious marks:
"O Saumitri, look now at those who, out of consideration for us, have become indifferent even toward their own homes; they are sleeping right now at the roots of trees, O Lakṣmaṇa."
"Just as these citizens are making this vow to turn us back,
they will even sacrifice their lives rather than abandon their resolve. Therefore, while they are still fast asleep, we must depart quickly."
"Having mounted the chariot, let us go upon a path free from fear.
Otherwise, the devoted inhabitants of the city of Ikṣvāku, taking refuge at the roots of trees, might not sleep again tonight out of affection for me."

"For the citizens must be liberated from suffering caused by their own actions by the princes; they must certainly not be joined with suffering by the princes themselves. Thus Lakṣmaṇa spoke to Rāma, who stood before him like Dharma personified.
"It pleases me, O highly wise one; let it be mounted quickly.
Then the charioteer, having swiftly yoked the chariot with those excellent horses, informed Rāma with palms joined in reverence.
To deceive the citizens, Rāma spoke these words to the charioteer:
"O charioteer, mounting the chariot, proceed facing north;
after traveling swiftly for a moment, turn the chariot back again."
"Act with such composure that the citizens do not recognize me," he said.
Having heard Rāma's words, the charioteer did exactly so; and having returned, he informed Rāma that the chariot was ready.
Mounting that chariot with his retinue, Rāghava crossed the swift-flowing river Tamasā, which was filled with turbulent eddies. Having crossed it,
the mighty-armed and illustrious prince reached a place that was auspicious and free from obstacles.
He set out upon the great road that is free from fear for those who perceive fear.
But when the night had turned to dawn, the citizens, deprived of Rāghava,
became motionless, their hearts stricken with grief and their spirits shattered.
Emaciated by tears born of grief and looking here and there, those sorrowful ones did not see even a glimpse of Rāma.
Then, having proceeded for a short while further along the path, they paused once more.
Overwhelmed by great despondency due to the loss of the path,
those high-minded men turned back from the chariot,
saying, "What is this? What shall we do, being struck down by fate?"
Then, with weary hearts, they all returned by the very same path they had come to the city of Ayodhyā, where the virtuous were filled with distress;
for the city-dwellers had turned back after following Rāma.
The hearts of those who were not self-controlled seemed to leap up;
having returned each to his own dwelling, surrounded by their sons and wives,
they all shed tears, their faces covered in weeping.
Neither did they rejoice nor did they celebrate; the merchants did not display their wares, nor did the goods look attractive, and the householders did not cook.
Seeing a loss, they did not welcome it, nor did they rejoice at the arrival of great wealth.

Having obtained her first-born son, the mother did not rejoice. And in every house, women, afflicted by grief, reproached their husbands who had returned home with words, as one would strike elephants with goads.
"What need have they for houses, what for wives, what for wealth, or even for sons and pleasures, who do not behold Rāghava?
In this world, Lakṣmaṇa alone, together with Sītā, is a virtuous man."
Those rivers, lotus ponds, and lakes that follow Kakutstha Rama as he serves him in the forest have performed meritorious deeds,
for into their pure waters Kakutstha will plunge and bathe.
Forests with lovely groves, rivers with vast marshlands, and mountains with their peaks shall all beautify the descendant of Kakutstha;
for whatever forest or mountain Rāma shall approach, it will be graced by him.
They will not be able to fail to honor him, as if he were a beloved guest who has arrived;
for even out of season, they bear many clusters of blossoms and carry choice flowers and fruits, with their crests of variegated blossoms.
Out of compassion, the mountains will show themselves to Rāma when he has arrived;
and displaying various and wonderful waterfalls upon their peaks, the trees will delight the descendant of Raghu.
Where Rāma is, there is no fear, nor is there any defeat;
for he is the brave, mighty-armed son of Daśaratha.
Before we are driven far away, let us follow Rāghava.
The shadow of the feet of such a great-souled lord is blissful; for he is the protector of these people, he is their refuge, and he is their ultimate resort.
We shall attend upon Sītā, while you attend upon Rāghava.
Thus the women of the city, afflicted by grief, spoke various words to their husbands:
"Rāghava will provide for your welfare and security in the forest; Sītā will provide for the welfare and security of these women."
Who indeed would find pleasure in this disagreeable dwelling, which is unpleasant, filled with longing, and has stolen away the heart?
If the kingdom were to fall to Kaikeyī, it would be unrighteous and like a state without a protector.
Indeed, we have no need for life, much less for sons or wealth.
Kaikeyī, that defiler of her family, who has abandoned both her son and her husband for the sake of power— whom else would she not cast aside?
"As long as Kaikeyī lives, we shall never dwell in the kingdom as her servants; by our very sons, we swear that we would rather die than live under her rule—
she who, devoid of compassion, has sent the son of the lord of kings into exile."
Who could live happily having obtained her, who is unrighteous and of wicked conduct?
For once Rāma has gone forth into exile, the lord of the earth will not survive;
and when Daśaratha is dead, it is evident that total ruin will follow immediately thereafter.
"Stirring up poison, drink it—you whose merit is exhausted and who are so ill-fated!
Follow Rāghava, or else go where you cannot hear [of him].
Rāma has been falsely exiled, along with his wife and Lakṣmaṇa."
"We have been delivered over to Bharata like cattle to a butcher.
Thus lamenting in the city, the women of the town cried out, deeply tormented as if at the approach of the fear of death.

In that way, the women were distressed on account of Rāma; when their son or brother had been exiled, they lamented piteously and wept, deprived of their senses, for he was indeed more than a son to them.
And Rāma, by means of that very remainder of the night, covered a great distance.

Remembering his father’s command, that tiger among men departed. As he was thus proceeding, the auspicious night passed away; having performed the propitious morning twilight rites, he entered the frontier territory.
Beholding those villages with their remote boundaries and the forests in full bloom, he passed through them swiftly, as if on arrows, with his excellent horses,
while listening to the voices of the men dwelling in the village settlements.
"Shame on King Daśaratha, who has fallen under the sway of passion!
Alas, today the cruel Kaikeyī— wicked, followed by evil, fierce, and one who has shattered all bounds of propriety— is engaged in a ruthless deed."
"She who exiles such a son of the king— one who is righteous,
highly wise, compassionate, and tireless— to dwell in the forest;
these are the words of the people living in the village settlements."
Hearing these words, the heroic lord of Kosala passed through the Kosala country.
Then, having crossed the river named Vedaśruti, which carries auspicious waters, he set out toward the direction inhabited by Agastya.

Having traveled for a very long time, he then crossed the Gomatī river, which flows toward the ocean, possesses cool waters, and has marshy banks frequented by cattle. And having crossed the Gomatī with his swift-moving horses, Rāghava—
He crossed the Syandikā river, which resounded with the cries of peacocks and swans.
There, Rāma showed Vaidehī the prosperous land, filled with kingdoms, which had been granted in ancient times by King Manu to Ikṣvāku.
Addressing that charioteer repeatedly with the words "O Sūta," the glorious bull among men, whose voice was like the cry of an intoxicated swan, spoke:
"When shall I return once more to the flowering forest on the banks of the Sarayū?"
"I shall go hunting together with my mother and father;
I do not desire hunting excessively, for this delight in the Sarayū forest is incomparable in the world and esteemed by the hosts of royal sages."
Addressing the charioteer with sweet words regarding various matters, that descendant of Ikṣvāku proceeded along the road, uttering these words.
Having traveled through the vast and beautiful Kosalas, the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa went on his way.
The mighty-armed one reached the city of Śṛṅgaverapura.
There Rāghava beheld the divine Gaṅgā, flowing through the three worlds, with its auspicious waters free of moss, holy and frequented by sages.
Resounding with the cries of swans and cranes, echoing with the calls of ruddy geese,
and frequented by porpoises, crocodiles, and serpents—
the great chariot-warrior gazed upon that river, filled with waves and swirling eddies.
He said to the charioteer Sumantra, "We shall stay right here today.
Not far from this river stands a very large ingudī tree, full of flowers and young shoots; let us stay right here, O charioteer."
Lakṣmaṇa and Sumantra said "So be it" to Rāghava,
and then they approached that iṅgudī tree with their horses.
Rāma, the joy of the Ikṣvākus, having arrived at that beautiful tree, [beheld it].
He descended from that chariot together with his wife and Lakṣmaṇa. Sumantra also, having descended and unyoked the excellent horses,
stood before Rāma at the foot of the tree with palms joined in reverence.
There, a king named Guha— a friend of Rāma who was his own equal, born of the Niṣāda caste, powerful, and renowned as a *sthapati*—
heard that Rāma, that tiger among men, had arrived in his domain.
Surrounded by his elders and accompanied by his ministers and kinsmen,
Rāma, together with the son of Sumitrā, approached Guha upon seeing the lord of the Niṣādas standing at a distance.

Embracing Rāghava in his distress, Guha said to him, "O Rāma, this place is just like Ayodhyā to you; what may I do for you? Then, having brought forth various kinds of excellent food and provisions...
He quickly brought forward the water of honor (arghya) and spoke these words:
"Welcome to you, O mighty-armed one! This entire earth is yours;
we are your servants and you are our lord. Please, rule over our kingdom."
To Guha, who was speaking thus— "Here are foods to be chewed, eaten, drunk, and licked, as well as excellent beds and fodder for your horses"— Rāghava replied.
"We have been honored and gladdened by you in every way. Having approached him on foot and having shown his affection, he spoke these words while pressing him with his virtuous arms: "Ram_2,44.16–17"
"By good fortune, Guha, I see you free from illness along with your kinsmen;
is all well with your kingdom, your friends, and your wealth? As for these things which have been prepared by you out of affection,"
I grant you all that; for I do not engage in the acceptance of gifts.
Know me to be an ascetic dwelling in the forest, devoted to dharma, wearing kusha grass, bark, and deerskin, and subsisting on fruits and roots. (Rāmāyaṇa 2.44.19–20)
"I have need only of fodder for the horses, and nothing else;
by this much alone shall I be well-honored by your lordship.
For these horses are dear to my father, King Daśaratha."
"By means of these well-prepared horses, I shall be honored," [he thought].
Guha then commanded the men right there, "Let fodder and grain for the horses be given quickly! (Rāmāyaṇa 2.44.22–23).
Then, having donned his upper garment of bark cloth and performed the evening twilight rites,
he himself took as food the water brought by Lakṣmaṇa.
After Lakṣmaṇa had washed the feet of him who was lying upon the ground, [he attended to him].
Then, approaching him who was with his wife, Guha stood nearby, taking refuge at the foot of a tree.
And Guha, along with the charioteer, keeping the son of Sumitrā in mind,
remained watchfully by Rāma’s side, bow in hand and vigilant.

Thus, as that wise and illustrious son of Daśaratha, the high-souled one who had never known suffering and was accustomed to comfort, lay there, that night passed for him at last after a long time. [Meanwhile,
Lakṣmaṇa remained awake out of sincere devotion for the sake of his brother.]
Guha, tormented by grief, spoke these words to Rāghava:
"O dear one, this comfortable bed has been prepared for your sake; rest well upon it, O prince, as you please."
"All these people are accustomed to hardships, while you are accustomed to comfort;
we shall stay awake through the night for the sake of guarding the descendant of Kakutstha.
For indeed, there is no one on earth dearer to me than Rāma."
I speak this truth to you, and I swear it by my very truthfulness:
through his grace, I hope for great fame in this world,
as well as the full attainment of dharma and the complete attainment of wealth.
Therefore, with bow in hand and accompanied by my kinsmen on all sides, I shall protect my dear friend Rāma as he lies sleeping with Sītā;
for nothing in this forest remains unknown to me as I constantly roam it.
"Indeed, we could withstand even a vast fourfold army.
To him, Lakṣmaṇa then replied: "O sinless one, while being protected by you who look only toward dharma, none of us here are afraid."
While the son of Daśaratha lies upon the ground together with Sītā, how can I find sleep, or life, or any pleasures?
He who could not be overcome in battle by all the gods and asuras combined.
Behold him lying comfortably upon the grass together with Sītā—
he who was obtained by means of counsel, asceticism, and various arduous efforts;
this son of Daśaratha is his very image in every characteristic.
Now that the king has gone forth into the religious life, he will not remain for long;
surely the earth will soon become a widow.
Having wailed with a great cry, the women have now ceased from their exhaustion.
"O father, I think the royal palace has fallen silent;
I do not expect that Kausalyā, the King, and likewise my own mother will all survive this night."
Indeed, my mother might even live on for the sake of looking after Śatrughna; but that grief which Kausalyā, the mother of a hero, shall suffer when she perishes, [is beyond measure].
She was once crowded with devoted people and brought forth the joy of pleasant sights.
"Afflicted by the king's calamity, that city will perish.
Having failed to achieve his desire again and again,
my father will perish without having installed Rāma in the kingdom."
When that time has arrived for all the funeral rites, the Siddhārthas will perform the consecration of their deceased father, the lord of the earth,
in a city with beautiful squares and well-laid-out main thoroughfares.
It was filled with mansions and palaces, adorned by the finest courtesans;
crowded with chariots, horses, and elephants; resounding with the music of trumpets;
complete with every auspicious thing; and teeming with happy and well-fed people.
They will roam happily through my father’s capital, which is filled with groves and gardens and abounds in social gatherings and festivals;
and may we also be well, together with him who is true to his promise.
"When this forest exile has ended, we shall enter Ayodhyā.
As the high-souled prince stood there lamenting, afflicted by grief, that night passed away.
For while the prince, who seeks the welfare of his subjects, was speaking the truth, Guha, out of deep affection,
shed tears, being oppressed by sorrow like an elephant afflicted by fever and suffering from pain. When the night had turned to dawn, the highly illustrious Pṛthuvṛkṣa—
Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, who was endowed with auspicious marks:
"This is the time for the rising of the sun; the blessed night has passed.
O dear one, that beautiful black bird, the cuckoo, is singing."
"The roar of peacocks calling in the forest can be heard;
let us cross the swift-flowing Jāhnavī, O gentle one, as it flows toward the ocean.
Having understood Rāma's words, the son of Sumitrā, the delighter of his friends, [prepared to act].
Having taken leave of Guha and the charioteer, he stood before his brother.
Then, having fastened their quivers and girded on their swords, the two Raghavas, armed with bows, proceeded with Sītā toward the Gaṅgā.
Approaching Rāma alone, who knows the dharma, with humility and palms joined in reverence, the charioteer said, "What shall I do?
To him, Rāma said, "Return"; for this much has been done for me.
"Abandoning the vehicle, we shall go to the great forest on foot. Seeing that he had been granted permission, the charioteer Sumantra, distressed,
spoke these words to that tiger among men, the descendant of Ikṣvāku.
No man in this world has ever surpassed this: that you, along with your brother and wife, must dwell in the forest like common folk.
I do not believe there is any fruit to be gained from celibacy or from the study of the Vedas.
O Raghava, even if calamity should befall you because of your gentleness and uprightness, dwelling in the forest with Vaidehi and your brother,
O hero, you will attain a destiny like that of one who conquers the three worlds.
"We are indeed ruined, O Rāma, for we have been deceived even by her;
we shall fall under the power of the wicked Kaikeyī and become partakers of sorrow.
Thus spoke Sumantra, the charioteer, at that time, words that were like his own heart.
Seeing that Rāma had gone far away, he, afflicted by grief, wept for a long time.
Then, when his tears had ceased and he had touched water and become pure,
Rāma spoke these sweet words to the charioteer again and again.
"I do not perceive any friend of the Ikṣvākus equal to you;
act in such a way that King Daśaratha does not grieve for me. For the lord of the world is aged and his mind is stricken with sorrow."
And being overwhelmed by the burden of desire, I therefore say this to you:
whatever that high-souled lord of the earth may command for the sake of pleasing Kaikeyī must be carried out without hesitation.
For it is for this purpose that lords of men govern kingdoms:
so that their minds meet with no obstruction in any of their undertakings. Therefore, let it be so arranged that the great king does not come to grief.
And do not distress him with grief, O Sumantra; act accordingly.

Having offered salutations, speak these words on my behalf to the aged and noble king, who has never known suffering and has conquered his senses: "Ram_2,46.19–20" [Note: The provided text contains two verse numbers, 19 and 20, which correspond to the two distinct sentences in the source.]
I do not grieve at all that we have been exiled from Ayodhyā, nor for the fact that Lakṣmaṇa and Maithilī and I shall dwell in the forest; rather,
I think again and again that when these fourteen years have passed, [we shall return].
"You shall soon see Lakṣmaṇa, myself, and Sītā returned.
Having spoken thus to the king, my mother, and the other queens together with Kaikeyī, O Sumantra, I addressed them again and again.
"Tell Kausalyā that you are well, and convey my salutations at her feet,
as well as those of Sītā and, by my command, those of Lakṣmaṇa.
And tell the Great King to summon Bharata here immediately."
"And when Bharata has arrived, he must be established in the position according to the king's will.
Once you have embraced Bharata and consecrated him as the crown prince,
the sorrow born of our suffering shall no longer overcome you."
And Bharata also should be told: "Just as you behave toward the king, so should you behave toward all your mothers without distinction;
and just as you treat Kaikeyī and Sumitrā without distinction."
In the same way, Queen Kausalyā, my mother especially, [was filled with grief].
Being turned back by Rāma, Sumantra, emaciated by sorrow,
heard all those words and spoke to the descendant of Kakutstha out of affection.
"Since I have spoken these words out of affection, without hesitation, and with devotion— not merely as a formal courtesy— you ought to forgive me.
For how indeed shall I, deprived of you, return to that city?"
"O father, as if agitated by grief for her son due to separation from you,
that city— even seeing my chariot with Sītā at that time— would surely shatter upon seeing the chariot without Rāma. (Rāmāyaṇa 2.46.31–32)
For the city will surely fall into despondency upon seeing this empty chariot,
its own army with only the charioteer remaining, like an army whose heroes have been slain in battle—
even though you dwell far away, it perceives you as standing before it in its mind.
Thinking of you today, the subjects have surely been deprived of food.
For the cry of distress uttered by the citizens at my departure would be increased a hundredfold upon seeing me standing on the chariot.
"What more shall I say to you, O Queen? 'This son of yours has been led by me to his maternal uncle's house;
do not grieve'—even such a word I would never speak, though it be untrue."
"How can I speak these words, though true, if they are so unpleasant?
For my excellent horses, who remain under my command and carry your kinsmen, how will they pull the chariot when it is deprived of you?"
"If you will indeed practice renunciation while I am entreating you,
I shall enter the fire along with my chariot the very moment I am abandoned by you here; for there will be many things in the forest that will create obstacles to your asceticism."
"O Raghava, I shall drive away those creatures in my chariot.
For your sake, I have not experienced the pleasure derived from driving a chariot;
I hope, however, for your sake to experience the pleasure derived from dwelling in the forest."
"Be gracious; I desire to be your close attendant in the forest.
I wish for that which you have spoken out of affection: become my husband's close attendant.
Dwelling in the forest, I shall perform service for you with my very head."
Whether it be Ayodhyā or the world of the gods, I shall abandon it in every way;
for without you, that capital city cannot be entered by me, just as the city of Mahendra cannot be entered by one of evil deeds.
And these horses as well, O hero, if they perform service for you while you dwell in the forest, shall attain the supreme goal;
for this is my heart's desire once our forest exile has come to an end.
"By means of this very chariot, I shall carry you back to the city again.
For fourteen years spent in the forest with you will pass like a single moment; otherwise, they would last for hundreds of years."
"O you who are affectionate toward your servants, you ought not to abandon me, your devoted servant, who stands firm in his duty while you yourself stand upon the path trodden by your lord's sons.
Thus did he, wretched and miserable, entreat him again and again in many ways.
But Rāma, compassionate toward his servants, spoke thus to Sumantra:
"I know your supreme devotion to me, O you who are devoted to your master;
now hear also the purpose for which I am sending you from here to the city."
Seeing that you had gone to the city, my younger mother Kaikeyī would have gained confidence; thus Rāma went to the forest,
for that queen was indeed well-pleased once I had departed for the forest.
One should not suspect a righteous king of being a liar.
This is my primary wish: that my younger mother may obtain the prosperous kingdom for her son, protected by Bharata.
"For my sake and for the sake of the king, go to the city with the chariot;
you have been instructed, so speak of those matters exactly as they are.
Having spoken these words to the charioteer and having consoled him again and again, [Rāma departed].
Rāma spoke these words, which were undaunted, purposeful, and full of reason:
"Having matted my hair, I shall depart; bring me the sap of the banyan tree.
Guha quickly brought that sap to the prince.
With that [grass], Rāma fashioned matted locks for both Lakṣmaṇa and himself.
Then those two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, dressed in bark garments and wearing circles of matted hair, shone like sages.
Then, having set out upon the path of the forest-dwellers (vaikhānasa), Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa, undertook his vow and spoke to his companion Guha:
"Be vigilant regarding the army, the treasury, the fort, and likewise the countryside."
"Guha, a kingdom is indeed considered most difficult to protect. Then, having granted him leave, the joy of the Ikṣvākus departed quickly and composedly, accompanied by his wife and Lakṣmaṇa.
Having seen a boat on the riverbank, that joy of the Ikṣvākus,
wishing to cross the swiftly flowing Gaṅgā, spoke this to Lakṣmaṇa:
"O tiger among men, climb slowly onto this boat that is waiting here."
Taking the high-minded Sītā upon his chest, he embraced her; then,
having heard his brother's command and complying with it all without opposition,
that self-controlled man first helped Maithilī onto the chariot and then ascended himself.
Then the radiant elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa himself ascended;
thereafter Guha, the lord of the Niṣādas, urged on his kinsmen.
Having given leave to Sumantra and to Guha along with his army, [Rāma departed].

Having boarded the boat, Rāma then urged the sailors forward. Then, propelled by them and steered by the helmsman, that boat, struck by the force of the beautiful oars, swiftly crossed over the water.
Having reached the middle of the Bhāgīrathī, the blameless Vaidehī, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words to the river:
"This is the son of the wise and great king Daśaratha."
O Gaṅgā, protected by you, let him fulfill this command;
having dwelt in the forest for a full fourteen years with his brother and me, he shall return once again.
Then, O blessed Goddess Gaṅgā, having returned safely, I shall worship you with great joy for the fulfillment of all my desires;
for you, O Goddess who flows through the three paths, behold the world of Brahmā.
And you are seen in this world as the wife of the King of the Ocean.
O Goddess, O beautiful one, I bow to you and praise you,
now that that tiger among men has returned safely with the kingdom regained.
"I shall bestow upon the Brahmins hundreds of thousands of cows, garments, and exquisite food, out of a desire to do what is pleasing to you," so spoke the blameless Sītā to the Gaṅgā.
The boat quickly reached the southern shore.
Having reached the shore and left the boat behind, that bull among men,
the scorcher of his foes, set forth together with his brother and Vaidehī.
Then the mighty-armed one said to the increaser of Sumitrā’s joy, “Go on ahead, O son of Sumitrā; let Sītā follow you.
I shall follow behind, protecting both you and Sītā.”

"Today Vaidehī shall indeed experience the suffering of dwelling in the forest. Having watched Rāma as he swiftly crossed to the further shore of the Gaṅgā, Sumantra, his vision failing due to the great distance of the road, wept in distress, a wretched man overcome with grief.
Having killed four great deer there— a boar, a rīṣya, a spotted deer, and a mahāruru—
and taking that sacrificial meat, the two of them, being hungry, went quickly at the proper time to a lordly tree for their dwelling.
Having reached that tree, they performed the evening twilight rites.
"Rāma is the best among those who bring delight," he said to Lakṣmaṇa.
"This is the first night spent outside the inhabited lands;
since it is without Sumantra, you should not feel anxious."
"From this night forward, O Lakṣmaṇa, we must remain vigilant and free from sloth, for the welfare and security of Sītā now depend upon us.
O son of Sumitrā, let us somehow pass this night."
"Let us settle upon the ground, having spread it with materials gathered by our own hands.
Having thus lain down upon the earth— though accustomed to a costly bed— Rāma addressed these auspicious words to the son of Sumitrā.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, it is certain that the great king sleeps in sorrow today;
Kaikeyī, having achieved her desire, must surely be gratified.
For that Queen Kaikeyī, for the sake of the kingdom, [has acted] toward the great king..."
Even upon seeing that Bharata has arrived, he might not lose his life;
yet, being helpless, aged, and separated from me,
what will that man of lustful soul do, having fallen under the power of Kaikeyī?
Beholding this calamity and the king’s mental derangement,
it is my opinion that desire alone is more powerful than both wealth and dharma.
For what man, even if he were ignorant, would abandon [his duty] for the sake of a woman?
"O Lakṣmaṇa, my father has a son who follows his own desires just as he did with me.
Alas, Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī, is truly happy along with his wife;
for alone, he shall enjoy the joyful land of Kosala like a sovereign ruler."
For he alone will become the sole head of the entire kingdom when our father has passed away in age and I have retired to the forest—
[he] who, abandoning both wealth and dharma, follows after desire.
Thus he falls into distress quickly, just like King Daśaratha.
O gentle one, I believe that Kaikeyī has arrived for the sake of Daśaratha’s end, my exile, and the kingdom of Bharata.
"May Kaikeyī, deluded by the intoxication of her own good fortune, not now oppress Kausalyā and Sumitrā on my account;
let not Queen Sumitrā dwell in sorrow because of me."
"Lakṣmaṇa, you must enter Ayodhyā from this very place at the proper time.
I alone shall go to the Daṇḍaka forest with Sītā;
for you will be the protector of the helpless Kausalyā."
For Kaikeyī is of base character; out of malice she would act unjustly, for she might even hand over my mother to Bharata, who knows what is right.
Surely, in some other birth, women must have been separated from their sons by her.
O Saumitri, that very thing has now come upon my mother as well.
For Kausalyā, whom I nourished for so long and raised with great hardship, has been separated from me at the very time she should have borne fruit; shame on me!
"O Saumitri, may no woman ever give birth to such a son as I, who bring endless sorrow to my mother.
O Lakṣmaṇa, I think that śārikā bird holds a love for me even greater than mine."
O Śuka, hear those words of hers:
"O subduer of enemies, what use is a son like me, who provides no assistance to my unfortunate mother as she grieves, and who merely bites the foot of the enemy?"
"For my mother Kausalyā is indeed of little fortune, for she lies deprived of me,
afflicted by supreme suffering, fallen into an ocean of grief.
For I alone, O Lakṣmaṇa, must traverse both Ayodhyā and the entire earth."

"Enraged, I could indeed overcome them with my arrows; yet, O sinless Lakṣmaṇa, valor is not the sole cause [of success]. Fearing unrighteousness and dreading the world beyond, I shall therefore not have myself consecrated today."
Having lamented this and many other piteous things in that solitary place,
Rāma sat silently at night with his face filled with tears.
When Rāma had finished his lamentation and ceased, he was like a fire whose flames have gone out.
Lakṣmaṇa consoled him, who was like a surging ocean, saying:
"O Rāma, best among warriors, now that you have departed, Ayodhyā will surely be lusterless today, like a night when the moon has vanished."
"O Rāma, this for which you are grieving is not appropriate;
you cause both Sītā and me alike to despair, O bull among men.
Neither Sītā nor I, O Raghava, can endure being separated from you."
"Even for a moment we shall live like two fish drawn out from the water;
for, O scorcher of enemies, without you I would not wish to see my father, nor Śatrughna, nor Sumitrā, nor even heaven itself."

Having heard these most excellent and abundant words of Lakṣmaṇa, Rāghava, the scorcher of foes, out of devotion to the forest life, undertook the practice of dharma for many years. Having spent that auspicious night under that great tree, they departed.
When the stainless sun had risen, they set out from that place;
plunging into the vast forest, they proceeded toward the region where the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā flows into the Yamunā.
Those illustrious ones traveled across various lands and delightful regions, beholding here and there places never seen before;
proceeding with safety, they observed the diverse trees along the way.
When the day had just ended, Rāma said to the son of Sumitrā:
"O Saumitri, look at the rising smoke near Prayāga;
I believe that the smoke-bannered fire of the Blessed One indicates that the sage is nearby."
"Surely we have reached the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā,
for the sound of water clashing against water is heard; likewise,
logs split by forest-dwellers are being carried along."
And here in the hermitage of Bharadvāja, these various trees are seen. Having traveled comfortably with their bows, as the sun was hanging low,
the two reached the dwelling of the sage at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
But Rāma, having reached the hermitage and frightening the deer and birds,
traveled for a short distance along the path and approached Bharadvāja.
Then, having arrived at the hermitage, the two of them were longing for a sight of the sage.
The two heroes, followed by Sītā, stood at a distance.
As soon as he saw the illustrious one who had performed his fire-sacrifice, Rāma, together with Saumitri and Sītā, saluted him with palms joined in reverence.
And the elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa announced himself to him, saying:
"O Blessed One, we two are the sons of Daśaratha, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa;
this auspicious Vaidehī, the daughter of Janaka, is my wife."
And this blameless woman has followed me to this desolate forest of asceticism.
When I was being exiled by my father, this beloved younger brother, the son of Sumitrā, firm in his vows, followed me to the very forest.
"O Blessed One, commissioned by our father, we shall enter the forest of asceticism;
there we shall practice dharma alone, subsisting on roots and fruits.
Having heard these words of the wise prince, [the sage replied:]
Then the righteous-souled sage brought forth a cow, water for the guest-offering (arghya), and water for washing the feet.
Seated amidst deer, birds, and sages on all sides,
the sage honored the arrived Rāma with a welcome and spoke to him.
Having accepted that worship and seeing him seated with Rāghava,
Bharadvāja then spoke these words consistent with dharma:
"O Kākutstha, it is indeed after a long time that I behold you arrived here."
"I have heard from you that this exile is without cause.
This secluded spot at the confluence of the two great rivers is holy and beautiful; may your lordship dwell here in comfort."
Thus addressed by Bharadvāja, Rāma,
the descendant of Raghu who is devoted to the welfare of all, replied with these auspicious words:
"O Blessed One, the people of the city and the countryside are near here."
"O Blessed One, people will come here as spectators to see both Vaidehī and me;
for this reason, I do not find pleasure in dwelling here. Look, O Blessed One, for an excellent site for a hermitage in a secluded place."
"Where Vaidehī, the daughter of Janaka who deserves happiness, finds delight.
Having heard these auspicious words of Raghava, the great sage Bharadvāja then spoke words that captured the very essence of the matter.
"Ten *krośas* from here, dear father, is a mountain where you shall dwell;
it is frequented by great seers, holy, and pleasant to behold from every side.
It is inhabited by langurs and frequented by monkeys and bears."
It is renowned as Citrakūṭa, resembling Mount Gandhamādana.
As soon as a man beholds the auspicious peaks of Citrakūṭa,
he attains well-being and does not set his mind upon evil.
"Many sages, having dwelt there for a hundred autumns,
ascended to heaven through their asceticism along with Kapālaśiras.
I consider that secluded dwelling to be a pleasant place for you to reside."
"Or rather, O Rāma, dwell here with me for a forest life.
Knowing the dharma, Bharadvāja welcomed his dear guest Rāma, along with his wife and his brother, honoring him with every object of desire.
As Rāma approached that great seer at Prayāga,
the holy night passed while he told him various stories;
when the night had turned to dawn, he drew near to Bharadvāja.
That tiger among men spoke to the sage of blazing splendor:
"O Blessed One, O you whose character is truth, we have spent this night here in your hermitage;
may your lordship grant us permission to dwell here."
When that night had dawned, Bharadvāja said this:
"Go to Citrakūṭa, which is provided with honey, roots, and fruits.
There, on all sides, were herds of elephants and herds of deer.
"You shall see them wandering at the edges of the forests, O Rāghava.

Having reached that auspicious mountain, which resounds with the cries of joyful lapwings and cuckoos and is made most delightful by many wild deer and rutting elephants, you should settle there in a hermitage."
Having stayed there for the night, those two princes, subduers of their enemies,
paid homage to the great seer and then departed toward that mountain.
Seeing them set out, the father followed after them like a father following his sons.
Then that great sage proceeded to speak these words:
"Having reached the Kālindī, a river of swift currents,
you must construct a raft there and cross over the river Aṃśumatī."
Then, having reached a great banyan tree with lush green foliage,
which has grown large alongside many other trees, is dark-hued, and frequented by perfected beings (siddhas)—
having gone from there for the distance of one krośa, you will see the Nīla forest.
O Rāma,
that path to Citrakūṭa, which I have traveled many times, is pleasant, gentle, and free from forest fires; it is lined with *palāśa* and *badarī* trees, as well as bamboo groves from the Yamunā.
Having thus pointed out the path, the great seer turned back. When the sage had departed, Rāma said to Lakṣmaṇa:
"O son of Sumitrā, we are truly meritorious, since the sage has shown us such compassion."
Having thus deliberated, those two wise tigers among men,
placing Sītā at their head, proceeded toward the river Kālindī.
Then they constructed a great raft by lashing together a multitude of logs.
Lakṣmaṇa, having cut it, fashioned a comfortable seat for Sītā.
There, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, helped his beloved— who was slightly bashful— to ascend the raft, which possessed an inconceivable splendor.

Then, by means of their raft, they crossed the swift-flowing Yamunā river, which was garlanded with waves and lined with many trees growing upon its banks. Having crossed over and abandoned the raft, they set out from the forest region of the Yamunā.
They approached a dark, cool banyan tree with green foliage.
Having joined her palms in reverence, Sītā circumambulated the lord of the forest, thinking, "May I behold Kausalyā and the illustrious Sumitrā."
Having gone from there for the distance of a *krośa*, the two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
killed many sacrificial deer and roamed in the forest of the Yamunā.
After they had sported in that auspicious forest, which resounded with flocks of peacocks and was filled with elephants and monkeys, they continued their journey.
Having approached the level bank of the river, they reached an agreeable dwelling, appearing undaunted.
Then, when the night had passed,
the joy of the Raghus gently awakened Lakṣmaṇa, who was sleeping nearby.
"O Saumitri, listen to the sweet warbling of the forest birds;
let us set forth, O scorcher of foes, for it is now the time to depart. Thus was Lakṣmaṇa, who had been asleep at the appointed hour, awakened by his brother.
They abandoned sleep, lethargy, and the exhaustion incurred on the road.
Then, having risen and touched the auspicious water of the river, they all set out upon the path to Citrakūṭa as directed by the sage.
Then, having set out at the proper time with the son of Sumitrā, Rāma spoke these words to Sītā, whose eyes were like lotus petals:
"O Vaidehī, look at all these flowering trees that seem as if they are ablaze on every side."
Behold the *kiṃśuka* trees at the end of winter, garlanded with their own blossoms.
Look at the flowering *bhallātaka* trees, untouched by men, bent down by their fruits and leaves; surely I shall be able to live upon them.
"Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, the honeycombs the size of *droṇas*, gathered by bees on every tree and hanging down!
There is a water-fowl crying out, and the peacock calls back to it."

Behold this Mount Citrakūṭa with its towering peaks, situated in a delightful forest region thick with carpets of flowers, frequented by herds of elephants, and resounded by the songs of flocks of birds.

Then, traveling on foot together with Sītā, the two of them reached the beautiful and enchanting Citrakūṭa mountain, which was filled with flocks of various birds. Having reached that mountain, they beheld it abounding in many kinds of winged creatures.
"O gentle one, let this be our dwelling for now; let us take our pleasure here.
Lakṣmaṇa, bring strong and excellent timber and build a residence, O gentle one; my mind is set on staying here."
Having heard those words of his, the son of Sumitrā, the subduer of enemies, gathered various trees and then constructed a leaf-hut;
then he spoke these words to him who was listening with one-pointed attention.
"Having brought the meat of a black antelope, we shall perform a sacrifice in the hall.
Then the powerful Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, having slain a pure black antelope,
cast it into the kindled fire.
Knowing that he was cooked, well-roasted, and drained of blood, Lakṣmaṇa then spoke to Rāghava, that tiger among men:
"This one has all its limbs complete; it is as if a black deer has been boiled."
"O god-like one, worship the deities, for you are skilled in such matters. Having bathed and become self-restrained, the virtuous Rāma, who was proficient in the chanting of prayers,
performed an excellent sacrificial offering (bali) that pacifies all evils.

They all gathered together and entered that delightful dwelling, roofed with tree leaves, well-constructed according to the site and sheltered from the wind, just as the hosts of gods enter the Sudharmā assembly hall;
it was filled with many various beasts and birds and possessed trees laden with clusters of diverse blossoms.

In that most excellent forest, resounding with the cries of predatory beasts, those who had conquered their senses dwelt in great happiness. Having reached the delightful Citrakūṭa and the river Mālyavatī with its beautiful bathing-places,
frequented by deer and birds, he rejoiced with gladness and cast off the sorrow caused by his exile from the city.
Having conversed for a long time with Sumantra while deeply afflicted by grief,
Guha returned to his own home once Rāma had reached the southern bank.
Then, having been granted leave, Sumantra harnessed the excellent horses.
Deeply distressed in mind, he proceeded toward the city of Ayodhyā itself;
beholding fragrant forests, rivers, lakes, villages, and towns, he passed through them swiftly.
Then, at the time of sunset on the third day, the charioteer,
having reached Ayodhyā, beheld it indeed devoid of joy;
seeing it as if empty and silent, he became exceedingly dejected in mind.
Struck by a surge of grief, Sumantra reflected:
"I hope that the city— along with its elephants, horses, people, and its sovereign— is not being consumed by the fire of sorrow born from the anguish of Rāma's departure."
Thus lost in thought, the charioteer entered in haste. Then,
as he approached Sumantra, hundreds and thousands of men rushed toward him, asking, "Where is Rāma?"
He told them: "Having taken leave of Raghava on the Ganges, I have returned, permitted by that righteous, high-souled one.
Upon learning that they had crossed over, the people, their faces filled with tears, [rejoiced].
Sighing, "Alas! Woe! they cried out, "O Rāma!
And he heard the words of those standing in groups:
"We are truly lost, we who do not behold Rāghava here."
"At charity-feasts, sacrifices, weddings, and great assemblies, we shall never again see the righteous Rāma in our midst.
What is beneficial for these people? What is dear to them? What brings them happiness?"
Thus the city was protected by Rāma as if by his own father.
And he heard the lamentations of the women, who were tormented by grief for Rāma, coming from the windows and the marketplaces.
With his face covered, Sumantra proceeded through the middle of the royal highway toward that very house where King Daśaratha was;
having quickly descended from the chariot, he entered the royal palace.
He passed through seven courtyards crowded with great throngs of people. Then, from the palaces here and there belonging to Daśaratha’s wives,
he heard their low-voiced lamentations, as they were tormented by grief for Rāma.
Having set out with Rāma and now returned here without him, what indeed will the charioteer say to the grieving Kausalyā?
And as I consider it, life itself is surely difficult to sustain in such a state; it is certainly not easy.
When her son had departed after being torn away from her, Kausalyā remained alive;
hearing those words of the king which were as true as reality,
she suddenly entered the palace, as if ablaze with grief.
Having entered the eighth courtyard, he beheld the king in a white chamber, dejected, afflicted, and consumed by grief for his son;
having approached that seated lord of men, he saluted him.
Sumantra reported Rāma’s words exactly as they had been spoken.
Having heard that, the king, his mind bewildered and tormented by grief for Rāma, fell to the ground in a swoon, remaining silent.
Then, when the lord of the earth had fainted and fallen to the ground, the inner apartments were thrown into turmoil; raising her arms,
Kausalyā, together with Sumitrā, wailed for her husband who lay prostrate on the earth.
Then he raised him up and spoke these words:
"O highly fortunate one, why do you not respond to this messenger of that performer of difficult deeds who has arrived here from his forest exile?"
"O Raghava, having committed this misconduct today, you feel ashamed; arise, may it be well with you—for there can be no assistance in grief.
O Lord, out of fear of whom you do not question Rama, the charioteer..."
"Kaikeyī is not here; speak with confidence.
Having spoken thus to the great king, Kausalyā, overwhelmed by grief and her voice choked with tears, suddenly fell prostrate upon the ground.

Seeing Kausalyā thus lamenting and fallen upon the ground, and beholding her husband as well, all those women wept aloud. Then, perceiving that cry arising from the inner apartments, both the old and the young men [were moved].

And all the women wept on every side; thus the city once again became filled with turmoil. When the king had recovered his composure and returned from his swoon, he then summoned the charioteer for the sake of news regarding Rāma.

The king beheld the aged charioteer standing before him, his limbs covered in dust, sighing deeply and lost in thought like an elephant in distress, aged, extremely tormented, and resembling a newly captured wild elephant.
With his face filled with tears, he spoke dejectedly like one in extreme distress:
"O charioteer, where indeed will that righteous-souled Raghava dwell, taking refuge at the foot of a tree? Having been accustomed to the highest luxury, what will he eat?"
How does the son of the protector of the earth lie upon the ground like one who is helpless?
How will that Rāma dwell, having taken refuge in the desolate forest, he whom foot-soldiers, chariots, and elephants once followed as he went?
Frequented by wild beasts and inhabited by black cobras—
how have the two princes arrived at this forest together with Vaidehī? O Sumantra, how have they come with Sītā, who is so delicate and wretched?
"How did the two princes descend from the chariot on foot?
O charioteer, you have indeed achieved your purpose, since you have seen my two sons entering the edge of the forest like the two Aśvins approaching Mount Mandara."
"What words did Rāma speak, and what did Lakṣmaṇa say?
O Sumantra, having reached the forest, what did Maithilī say? Tell us, O charioteer, where Rāma sat, where he slept, and what he ate."
Thus urged by the lord of men, the charioteer,
with a voice faltering and choked with tears, spoke to the king:
"O Great King, he spoke to me while strictly observing his duty."
Rāghava, having joined his palms in reverence and bowed his head low,
said: "O charioteer, by my word, pay homage with your head to the feet of that high-souled father of mine, who knows the self and is worthy of worship."
"O Sūta, you must announce my words to the entire inner court:
'May there be health for all without exception, and please offer salutations as is appropriate.
And to my mother Kausalyā, convey my inquiries after her welfare and my salutations."
"O Queen, protect the feet of the King as you would your own deity.
Bharata should be told of my welfare, and he should be addressed by my words:
'Treat all your mothers with due propriety and conduct yourself toward them according to what is right.'"
"And you must say to the mighty-armed joy of the Ikṣvāku dynasty:
'Established in the position of heir apparent, protect your father who remains established in the kingdom. Thus, O Great King, did the highly illustrious one speak to me.
Rāma, whose eyes were as copper-red as lotuses, shed profuse tears.
But Lakṣmaṇa, filled with great rage and sighing heavily, spoke these words: "By what offense has this prince been exiled?"
Whether Rāma was exiled because of the cause of greed or on account of the granting of a boon, in every respect a wrong has been committed; yet,
I perceive no just cause for the abandonment of Rāma.
"An undertaking begun without due reflection, contrary to reason through a lack of intelligence, will produce remorse for Rāghava's exile.
As for me, I do not perceive the status of 'father' in the Great King."
Rāghava is my brother, my husband, my kinsman, and my father. Having abandoned him who is beloved by all the world and devoted to the welfare of all the world—
how could all the world not be alienated by this deed of yours?
But Janaki, O Great King, sighing and distressed, stood there as if struck to the heart by a spirit, paralyzed and bewildered;
for that illustrious princess had never before experienced such calamity.
Weeping from that sorrow, she said nothing at all to me;
looking up at her husband with a parched face,
she suddenly shed tears upon seeing me departing.
In that very manner, Rāma stood with his face bathed in tears and his hands joined in reverence, supported by Lakṣmaṇa’s arm;
and likewise, the ascetic Sītā, weeping, gazed upon the royal chariot and me in the same way. But as I turned back, my horses would not proceed on the path.
Shedding hot tears as Rāma set out for the forest,
I then took my leave with joined palms from both princes and,
mounting the chariot, departed while bearing that sorrow.
I remained right there with Guha for many days,
hoping that Rāma might call for me again.
O Great King, in your realm, people are emaciated by the calamity that has befallen Rāma.
Even the trees, along with their flowers, sprouts, and buds, have withered;
living beings do not move about, and predatory beasts no longer roam.
Overwhelmed by grief for Rāma, that forest has become silent.
O lord of men, the lotus ponds have their lotus petals withered, their waters turbid, and their lotuses scorched; the fish and birds lie hidden within them.
Likewise, both the water-born flowers and the land-born blossoms have perished.
Today the fruits do not appear fragrant as they did before.
No one greets me as I enter Ayodhyā;
not seeing Rāma, the men sigh again and again.
Beholding the chariot arrived from their mansions, palaces, and towers, the women—emaciated by the sightlessness of Rāma—let out cries of "Alas!
Alas! with their long, clear eyes overflowing with a torrent of tears.
The women, clearly overcome by extreme distress, gaze at one another;
I do not perceive any distinction in their affliction, whether they belong to enemies, friends, or neutral persons.
O Great King, with its people joyless, its elephants and horses dejected,
its faces withered by cries of distress, and filled with the sound of sighs,
the city was devoid of joy, agonized by the exile of Rāma.
"Like Kausalyā deprived of her son, Ayodhyā appears to me," [the king thought].
Having heard the words of the charioteer, with a voice that was exceedingly dejected and choked with tears, the king spoke thus to the charioteer.
Prompted by Kaikeyī, who is of evil birth and disposition,
I did not deliberate with elders skilled in counsel,
nor with friends, nor with ministers, nor with the citizens.
"Out of delusion and for the sake of a woman, I have rashly committed this deed.
Surely, O charioteer, it was by the power of destiny that this great calamity has arrived by chance for the destruction of this lineage."
"O charioteer, if there is any merit whatsoever earned by me, let it bring Rāma to me at once; my life-breaths urge me forward.
Let my very command prevail and turn back the descendant of Raghu."
"I shall not be able to live for even a moment without Rāma.
Or else, since the mighty-armed one has gone far away,
place me upon the chariot yourself and show me to Rāma quickly."
Where is that elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, the great archer with well-formed teeth?
If I am to live, may I see him safely along with Sītā— him,
the red-eyed one, the mighty-armed, adorned with jeweled earrings.
"If I do not see Rāma, I shall go to the abode of Yama.
What indeed could be more painful than this, that I, having fallen into such a state, do not see Rāghava, the joy of the Ikṣvākus, here?"
"Alas Rāma! Alas Lakṣmaṇa! Alas, alas, Vaidehī, poor ascetic woman!
You do not know that I am dying of grief like one who is helpless.
O Queen, this ocean of sorrow is impossible for me to cross while I still live."
"It is a misfortune that today, though desiring to see Rāghava here along with Lakṣmaṇa, I do not find him"—

lamenting thus, the highly illustrious king suddenly fell upon his couch, swooning away. While the monarch was thus lamenting and had fallen unconscious, the sound for the sake of Rāma became twice as piteous.

Having heard his words, the queen, Rāma’s mother, was seized with fear once again. Then, trembling repeatedly as if possessed by a spirit, Kausalyā, appearing as if her life-force had departed from the earth, spoke to the charioteer.

"Lead me, O descendant of Kakutstha, to where Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa are; for without them, I cannot bear to live here even for a moment. Turn the chariot back quickly and take me to the Daṇḍaka forest as well."
"If I do not follow them, I shall go to the abode of Yama.

With a voice faltering and choked by a torrent of tears, the charioteer, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words to comfort the queen: 3-4. "If I do not follow them, I shall go to the abode of Yama. With a voice faltering and choked by a torrent of tears, the charioteer, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these words to comfort the queen:
Abandon grief, delusion, and the agitation born of sorrow; having shaken off all distress, Rāghava will dwell in the forest.
And Lakṣmaṇa, too, will attend upon Rāma’s feet in the forest.
The knower of dharma, having conquered his senses, attains the world beyond.
Even in the lonely forest, Sītā, having found her dwelling as if in a home,
feels no fear and finds confidence, for her mind is entirely entrusted to Rāma.
I do not perceive even the slightest trace of despondency in her;
Vaidehī appears to me as if she were accustomed to living in exile. She seems to me as though she were enjoying herself in the city gardens as she did before.
In that very same way, Sītā finds delight even in the lonely forests. Like a young girl, Sītā— whose face resembles the crescent moon—
finds joy in the desolate woods, for she is devoted to Rāma and her soul is entirely dependent upon him.
For her heart is fixed on him, and her life is dependent upon him;
even Ayodhyā would be like a forest to her if it were bereft of Rāma.
Along the way, Vaidehī asks about the villages and the cities.
Having observed the course of the rivers and various kinds of trees,
[he reflected that] due to the journey, the force of the wind, the agitation, and the heat of the sun,
the moon-like radiance of Vaidehī indeed does not appear.
The face of that generous Vaidehī, resembling a lotus and possessing a luster like the full moon, does not waver;
though devoid of red lac-dye, it possesses the hue of red lac-dye.
Even now, her feet possess the luster of lotus buds; that beautiful woman moves with a playful grace, as if accompanied by the tinkling of anklets.
Even at this moment, Vaidehī remains filled with passion for him, though she has laid aside her ornaments.

Whether seeing an elephant, a lion, or a tiger, she who has taken refuge in the forest feels no terror, for she rests in the arms of Rāma. You should not grieve for them, nor for yourself, nor even for the lord of men.
For this conduct shall endure forever in the world.
Having shaken off their grief with joyful hearts, firmly established on the path traversed by the great seers,
delighting in the forest and subsisting on wild fruits, they fulfill their father’s auspicious vow.
Nevertheless, though restrained by the charioteer who spoke so reasonably, the queen, emaciated by grief for her son, did not cease her lamentation, crying out, "O beloved! O my son! O Raghava!
while Rama, the best of those who delight others, had gone to the forest devoted to dharma.
Weeping and deeply distressed, Kausalyā spoke thus to her husband:
"O Raghava, although your great fame is celebrated throughout the three worlds, you are compassionate, generous, and sweet-spoken."
O best among the foremost of men, how will those two sons, along with Sītā—
though raised in comfort and now distressed— endure the hardships of the forest?
She is surely young, dark-complexioned, delicate, and accustomed to happiness.
How will Maithilī endure both heat and cold?
Having eaten auspicious food accompanied by soups and side dishes, how will the large-eyed Sītā subsist on a diet of wild grain?
Having heard the auspicious sound of singing and musical instruments, how will the blameless lady hear the unpleasant cries of flesh-eating lions?
Where indeed does that mighty-armed one sleep, he who resembles the banner of great Indra?
Resting his arm, which resembles a massive iron bar, the one of great strength [said]:
"When shall I see Rāma’s face— lotus-colored, with beautiful hair-ends, with breath like a lotus, and with eyes like lotuses?"
"Without a doubt, my heart is surely made of the essence of a diamond,
since it does not shatter into a thousand pieces even though I do not see him;
provided that Raghava returns again in the fifteenth year."
He would have to abandon both the kingdom and the treasury for Bharata to enjoy;
O lord of the people, why would the eldest and most excellent brother disregard the kingdom already enjoyed by his younger brother?
A tiger does not wish to eat food brought by another; in the very same way, that tiger among men will not accept what has been tasted by another.
The sacrificial oblation, clarified butter, the sacrificial cakes, the *kuśa* grass, and the sacrificial posts made of *khadira* wood—[all these are required for the rite].
These [sacrificial implements] do not perform their function again in the ritual;
for likewise, this kingdom, once seized, is like wine whose essence has been extracted,
which Rāma is unable to take pleasure in, resembling a sacrifice from which the Soma has vanished.
Rāghava will not tolerate such an insult, just as a powerful tiger cannot endure the touching of its tail;
he is one who possesses the strength of a lion, the eyes of a bull, and is a bull among men.
It is as if you have yourself slain your own son, like a water-born creature [slaying its offspring].
If the eternal dharma practiced by the twice-born and seen in the scriptures has been abandoned by you while exiling your son who is devoted to righteousness.
"O King, for a woman there is one refuge, her husband; the second is her son;
the third is her kinsmen; a fourth does not exist here in this world.
In that regard, you are no longer mine, and Rāma has taken to the forest."
"I do not wish to go to the forest, for I am utterly destroyed by you.
This kingdom, along with the realm, has been destroyed by you; likewise, my own self has been destroyed along with the ministers.
I am destroyed along with my sons, the citizens are destroyed, and both your son and your wife rejoice."
Hearing these words fraught with such harsh sounds, the king too fainted in his distress;
then that monarch fell into deep sorrow and again remembered his own past misdeeds.
Thus was the king addressed by Rāma’s mother, who was both enraged and grieving.

Having been addressed with harsh words, he reflected in his distress. As he was thus reflecting, there flashed before him a past misdeed which he had previously committed out of ignorance while shooting by sound alone.
Afflicted by that grief and by the grief for Rāma, the lord, the king, burning with these two sorrows, said to Kausalyā:
"I seek your favor, O Kausalyā; here I join my palms in supplication to you."

For you are indeed always affectionate and compassionate, even toward others. O Queen, for women who reflect upon their duty, a husband— whether he be virtuous or devoid of virtue— is a manifest deity.

"You, who are ever devoted to righteousness and have perceived the higher and lower truths of the world, ought not to speak unpleasant words— even though you are suffering— to one who is already deeply distressed.
Having heard those piteous words spoken by the dejected king, she [replied].
Kausalyā shed tears like a water-channel discharging fresh rainwater.

Weeping, she pressed her hands together in a lotus-like *añjali* upon her head and, trembling with agitation, spoke these words in hurried syllables: "I bow my head, weeping, with my palms joined like a lotus; out of distress, I speak these words in haste."
Be gracious; I entreat you with my head bowed, for I have fallen upon the ground before you.
I am a suppliant, O Lord; I am ruined, yet I must not be slain by you.
For she is no longer that woman who could be disregarded by one as wise and praiseworthy as you.
O hero, she who is propitiated by her husband gains both worlds.
O knower of dharma, I know what is right; I know you to be a speaker of truth.
Yet, afflicted as I am by grief for my son, I have said something quite improper.
Grief destroys fortitude; grief destroys sacred learning;
grief destroys everything—there is no enemy equal to grief. It is possible to endure a blow fallen from the hand of an enemy.
Even the slightest sorrow that has befallen me cannot be endured;
today, the fifth night of Rāma’s forest exile is counted by me—
who am struck with grief and robbed of joy— as if it were five years.
"For as she reflects upon him, this grief increases in her heart,
like the vast waters of the ocean swelling with force when it is not at rest.
Thus did Kausalyā speak these auspicious words.
The sun’s rays grew faint and the night set in.
Then, though comforted by the words of Queen Kausalyā, the king,
overcome by grief, fell under the power of sleep.
In a mere moment, King Daśaratha, his mind stricken with grief,
became like Indra himself due to the exile of Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, and he fell into deep reflection.
An affliction entered him, like darkness entering the sun, as if he were an asura.
On the sixth night after Rāma had departed for the forest,
King Daśaratha, at midnight, recollected the evil deed he had committed.
He spoke these words to Kausalyā, who was afflicted with grief for her son:
"O blessed lady, whatever a person performs— whether it be auspicious or inauspicious—
the doer surely reaps that very fruit born of his own action, O fortunate one."
He who does not understand the relative importance of matters, the fruit of actions undertaken, or their potential faults, is called a fool.
He is like one who cuts down a grove of mango trees and waters palāśa trees instead.
Seeing the flower and greedy for the fruit, he grieves when the time for the fruit arrives.
Having cut down the mango grove and watered the *palāśa* trees, I, being of wicked mind, have abandoned Rāma at the time of fruition and now grieve afterwards.
"O Kausalyā, because of the word 'shot' uttered by that archer prince— thinking 'the prince is a shooter by sound'— I committed this sin;
O Queen, this self-inflicted sorrow has now come upon me."
"Just as poison might be consumed here by a fool out of delusion, so too has this fruit consisting of the piercing of my reputation been swallowed by me unknowingly.
O Queen, you were yet unmarried when I became the crown prince."
Then the rainy season arrived, increasing passion and desire.
Having drawn up the juices of the earth and scorched the world with his rays,
the sun entered the formidable quarter frequented by the departed.
The heat vanished instantly, and glossy clouds were seen;
then all the frogs, deer, and peacocks rejoiced,
covered by the water that had fallen and was falling repeatedly.
He shone like a mountain by a lake filled with intoxicated deer;
during that most pleasant season, the archer, equipped with arrows and a chariot,
resolved to exercise himself and followed the Sarayū river.
At night, at a watering place, desiring to kill a buffalo, or an elephant that had come to the river,
or some other beast of prey, I— my senses unsubdued—
then heard in the darkness the sound of a water-jar being filled in the water.
Like one who cannot see the object of a sound, as if at the roar of an elephant,
I then drew forth a blazing arrow resembling a venomous serpent and released that sharp shaft, which was like a poisonous snake.
There, at dawn, the speech of the forest-dweller became manifest;
as he fell into the water, a human voice arose there, crying out, "Alas!
Alas!"—how could a weapon fall upon an ascetic such as me?
"I have come to this secluded river at night for water;
by whom have I been struck with an arrow, and what have I done to anyone? [Thus spoke he] regarding that seer who had laid down the rod of punishment, living in the forest on forest fare.
How indeed can the death of one such as I by the sword be ordained? For me, who bears a mass of matted hair and is clothed in bark and deerskin,
who would have any purpose in my killing, or what harm could I possibly have done to him?
No one would consider such a fruitless undertaking, fraught solely with calamity, to be right— just as one would not approve of violating the preceptor’s bed.
It is not for this destruction of my own life that I grieve so much.
I grieve for both my mother and father on my account. This aged couple has been supported by me for a long time; once I have met my death, what means of subsistence will they follow?
"My aged mother and father, and I myself—by whom have we all been struck down with a single arrow? By a mere child, one who has not disciplined his own self!
Hearing those piteous words from me, who am desirous of dharma, [the sages were moved].
The bow, together with the arrow, fell from the hands of the distressed man onto the ground.
Having arrived at that place, dejected in spirit and deeply troubled in mind, I saw the ascetic slain by the arrow on the bank of the Sarayū.
Gazing at me with his eyes, seeing me terrified and distressed in mind,
he spoke these cruel words as if wishing to consume me with his splendor:
"O King, what harm have I done to you while dwelling in the forest?"
"Since I was struck by you while seeking water for my father's sake,
two blind and aged people— my mother and my father— have indeed been slain by that single arrow which struck my vital organ."
"Those two, surely weak, blind, and parched with thirst, must now endure for a long time that painful craving born of hope while waiting for me.
Surely there is no connection between asceticism or sacred learning and the attainment of its fruit."
My father does not know that I am lying fallen upon the ground;
even if he did know, what could he do, being powerless and unable to move?
He is like one tree incapable of saving another tree that is being split asunder.
"O Raghava, go quickly and tell my father this for me:
let him not burn you with his anger, like a blazing fire consuming a forest.
O King, here is the path by which my father’s hermitage lies."
Go and appease him, lest he, in his anger, should curse you.
O King, extract the arrow from my vital wound;
it pierces me as a swift current of water erodes a soft, high riverbank.
"I am not a twice-born, O King; let there be no distress in your mind.
I was indeed born of a Śūdra woman by a Vaiśya father, O lord of the realm.
Thus he spoke with great difficulty, his vital organs pierced by arrows.
As he was bending over him, I pulled out that arrow. Having lamented piteously, his limbs drenched with water and his vital wound continuously breathing,
O blessed lady, I beheld him lying there upon the Sarayū and became deeply despondent.
Having committed that great sin out of ignorance, my senses were overwhelmed;
yet alone, I reflected with my intellect: "How indeed might this become a virtuous deed?
Then, taking that jar filled with excellent water, I departed.
Having reached that hermitage, I proceeded along the path as it had been described.
There I beheld his parents— feeble, blind, aged, and without a guide— like two birds with clipped wings.
Remaining motionless with that as their sole motive for conversation, they sat there, deprived of hope on my account, indifferent and like those who are helpless;
yet, hearing the sound of my footsteps, the sage spoke these words.
"Why do you delay, my son? Bring water quickly!
Because of this, dear child, your mother here is distressed while you were playing in the water; enter the hermitage at once."
"O son, whatever offense has been committed against you by your mother or by me, you,
my ascetic father, must not take it to heart.
You are the refuge for those without refuge, and you are the eye for those who are sightless."
"Our lives are entirely devoted to you, yet you do not say anything to us.
Seeing the sage with his speech indistinct, faltering, and lacking clear articulation, I spoke as if terrified by my own fear.
Restraining the power of my speech with mental effort and physical gestures, I declared to him the fear born of the calamity that had befallen my son:
"I am a Kṣatriya, Daśaratha; I am not the son of the Great-souled One."
"This suffering, born of my own karma, has been obtained as it is despised by the virtuous.
O Blessed One, with bow in hand, I came to the bank of the Sarayū desiring to kill some wild beast or an elephant that had come to a watering hole."
There, I heard the sound of a water-jar being filled in the water;
