thinking, "This is an elephant," I struck it with an arrow.
Then, having gone to the bank of the river, I saw [the creature] pierced in the heart by my shaft.
"The ascetic lay upon the ground, his body pierced and his life departed.
O Blessed One, having perceived a sound, I—desiring to kill an elephant—discharged an iron arrow into the water; by that means, your son was slain."
And with that arrow extracted, he remained right there, established in heaven,
lamenting and grieving for both of you who were blind:
"Your son was struck down by me suddenly through ignorance."
"Since things have come to this pass, may the Sage be gracious toward whatever remains for me.
Having heard those cruel words, the one of great splendor, emaciated by grief, sighed and spoke to me as I stood before him with palms joined in reverence.
O King, had you not yourself told me of this evil deed, your head would have instantly shattered into a hundred thousand pieces;
for the killing of one who has retired to the forest, especially by a Kshatriya, O King, [is a grave offense].
One who acts with prior knowledge could even cause the Wielder of the Thunderbolt to fall from his station;
but since this was done out of ignorance, you still live by him.
Otherwise, even today the lineage of the Raghavas would not exist—how then could you?
"O King, lead us to that place," he said to me,
"for today we wish to see our son for the last time—
his limbs smeared with blood and his deerskin garment scattered."
Lying unconscious upon the ground, fallen under the power of the King of Dharma; then,
having led those two who were deeply distressed to that place alone,
I allowed the sage and his wife to touch their son.
Having touched their son and reached him, those two ascetics collapsed upon his body; then his father spoke this to him:
"O righteous son, am I not dear to you? Look at your mother!"
"Why do you not embrace me, my son? Speak some tender words.
Whose sweet voice shall I hear in the latter part of the night—reciting the scriptures or, even better, something else?"
Who, having performed his twilight devotions, bathed, and offered oblations to the fire, will sit beside me as I am tormented by the fear and grief for my son and offer words of praise?
Who, having gathered roots, tubers, and fruits, will treat me like a beloved guest?
He will feed one who is incapable of work, unrestrained, and leaderless.
And how, O son, shall I support this blind, aged, and ascetic mother of yours— this wretched woman who yearns for her son?
"Stay, my son, do not go toward the abode of Yama;
tomorrow you shall go with me and your mother, united together.
For both of us are afflicted by grief, helpless, and miserable in the forest."
"Deprived of you, we shall go very quickly indeed to the abode of Yama.
Then, having seen the son of Vivasvat, I shall speak these words:
'May the King of Dharma forgive me; may he support these two parents.'"
"O son, you are sinless, though slain by one of evil deeds.
By that truth, go quickly to those worlds of those who fight with weapons—
the destination which heroes attain who do not retreat in battles."
But you, my son, being slain while facing the enemy, go to that supreme goal.
Go, my dear son, to that destination which Sagara, Śaibya, Dilīpa, Janamejaya, Nahuṣa, and Dhundhumāra have attained.

That destination which belongs to all the virtuous, that which is attained through Vedic study and austerity, and that which belongs to the giver of land, the maintainer of the sacred fires, and the one devoted to the vow of a single wife; that destination which belongs to those who bestow a thousand cows, and even to those who support their teachers.
"Go to that destination, my son, which is attained by those who have cast off their bodies;
for one born in this family never goes to an evil state.
Thus he lamented there piteously and repeatedly.
Then, together with his wife, he began to offer water for him;
but that son of a sage, by virtue of his own meritorious deeds, having assumed a divine form,
comforted his parents for a moment and spoke these words.
"I have attained this great station through service to you both, and you too shall soon come into my presence. Having spoken thus, he departed in a celestial, embodied chariot.

The son of the sage, having conquered his senses, swiftly ascended to heaven. Having quickly performed the water-libation for me along with his wife, that ascetic of great splendor spoke to me as I stood before him with palms joined in reverence.
"O King, kill me this very day; I feel no pain in death, since you have rendered me childless by striking my only son with an arrow.
For it was through your ignorance that my pure son was slain."
Therefore, I shall curse you with a most painful and exceedingly terrible affliction:
"O King, just as I am now experiencing this sorrow born of the loss of my son, so shall you bring about your own end through grief for your son."
Therefore, O blessed lady, come to me; for that noble man’s words have come true, that today, out of grief for my son, I shall give up my life.
If Rāma were to touch me even once today, or were to obtain me, [I would live].
"O Queen, what I have done toward Rāghava is not worthy of me.
I no longer see you with my eyes; my memory is failing me.
O Kausalyā, these messengers of Vaivasvata are hurrying me away."
But what could be more painful than this, that at the end of my life I do not see Rāma, the knower of dharma and whose prowess is truth?
Those who wear beautiful and auspicious earrings are not mere mortals; they are gods.
In the fifteenth year, they shall behold the face of Rāma once again—
his lotus-petal eyes, his beautiful brows, his fine teeth, and his lovely nose;
blessed are those who shall see Rāma’s face, which resembles the lord of the stars.
Fortunate are those who shall behold the face of my lord— fragrant like the autumn moon and like a blooming lotus—
when he has returned to Ayodhyā after completing his forest exile.
The happy ones shall behold Rāma, like the planet Venus appearing upon its path.
This grief born of my own self is destroying me, helpless and senseless, with such force as the current of a river erodes its bank.
"Alas, O mighty-armed Rāghava! Alas, O destroyer of my distress!
Thus King Daśaratha, grieving, reached the end of his life, speaking so piteously while tormented by the exile of his beloved son.
When midnight had passed, that man of noble vision, tormented by intense suffering, then gave up his life.
Then, when the night had ended, at dawn on the following day,
bards gathered around the king’s palace.
Then, women and eunuchs in great numbers, who were of pure conduct and skilled in attendance, approached as they had done before,
carrying water mixed with yellow sandalwood in golden jars.

Those skilled in the art of bathing brought the necessary items at the proper time and according to the prescribed rites; likewise, other women, many of whom were young maidens, brought auspicious unguents and various foods.
Then those women who were closest to the bed of the Lord of Kosala gathered together and attempted to awaken their husband;
trembling with fear, they were apprehensive regarding the king's life.
They trembled like blades of grass against a current;
and as they watched the king trembling, those women reached a certain conclusion regarding the evil they had suspected.
Then those beautiful women cried out piteously with loud voices,
like female elephants in the forest whose leader has been suddenly separated from his herd.
At the sound of their lamentation, her consciousness was suddenly restored.
Kausalyā and Sumitrā were both awakened from their sleep.
Having seen and touched the king, Kausalyā and Sumitrā cried out, "O Lord! and fell to the surface of the earth.
That daughter of the lord of Kosala, writhing upon the ground,
did not shine, her body covered in dust like a star fallen from the sky.
That place was filled with people who were agitated, bewildered, and deeply distressed.
Everywhere there was a tumultuous wailing from kinsmen afflicted by intense grief;
the palace of the god-like king, who had reached his end, suddenly became a place where joy had vanished and the sight was one of dejection and distress.
But having recognized that bull among kings, the illustrious one, as deceased, his wives, surrounded by him,
weeping piteously and deeply distressed, took hold of their arms and lamented like those who are helpless:
"He is like a fire extinguished, or like an ocean devoid of water."
Beholding the lord of the earth dwelling in heaven like the sun deprived of its radiance,
Kausalyā— her eyes filled with tears and emaciated by manifold grief—
clasped the king’s head and addressed Kaikeyī.
"O Kaikeyī, let your desire be fulfilled; enjoy the kingdom without any thorns, having abandoned the king with single-minded devotion, O cruel woman of wicked conduct!
Rāma has departed leaving me behind, and my husband has gone to heaven."
Like a caravan lost on a desolate path, I have no desire to live.
Abandoning that husband who is my own deity, what woman— other than Kaikeyī, who has cast aside all dharma— would wish to live?
A greedy man does not perceive his own faults, like one who eats a fruit unaware of its ripeness;
for the sake of Kaikeyī, who was like a hunchback, the lineage of the Raghavas has been destroyed by a king who,
though appointed to his duty, acted improperly by exiling Rāma.
Hearing that Rāma,
whose eyes are like lotus petals, has departed from here having lost his will to live,
along with Sītā, the daughter of the King of Videha and a woman of great ascetic merit, Janaka will suffer just as I do.
Unaccustomed to suffering, she will surely tremble with distress in the forest;
hearing the terrifying cries of beasts and birds at night, she will surely take refuge in Raghava in her fear.
"And he, being aged and having few sons, is already consumed by grief as he ponders for Vaidehī; will he not surely give up his life?
Then, she embraced that wretched woman who was thus lamenting.
The officials removed Kausalyā, who was afflicted by extreme grief.
Then the ministers, having laid the lord of the world upon a trough of oil,
performed all the subsequent rites as commanded for the king.
But the ministers, though all-knowing, were not able to perform the cremation of the king without his son; therefore, they protected the lord of the earth.
They laid that ruler of men upon a vat filled with oil.
"Alas, he is dead!"— realizing this, those women lamented.
Raising their arms in misery, with faces streaming from their eyes,
they wept and wailed piteously, consumed by grief.

Deprived of the high-souled king, the city of Ayodhyā did not shine, like a night without stars or a woman bereft of her husband; its people were overwhelmed with tears, and the women of the noble families cried out "Alas! Alas! in lamentation.
With its squares, houses, and interiors empty, the city did not shine as it had before.

Deprived of the Great-Souled One, the city appeared like the sky robbed of its luster without the sun, or like a night stripped of its host of stars; yet its streets and squares were not crowded with people whose throats were choked with tears.
Then, men and women gathered in groups, censuring the mother of Bharata;
they were distressed in that city following the death of the god-like king, and they found no peace.
When the night had passed and the sun had risen, then—
Having assembled, the twice-born who were counselors to the king went to the assembly hall:
Mārkaṇḍeya, Maudgalya, Vāmadeva, Kāśyapa,
Kātyāyana, Gautama, and the highly illustrious Jābāli.
These twice-born ones, together with their ministers, each uttered these words, facing toward Vasiṣṭha alone, the preeminent royal priest:
"The night has passed in sorrow, which to us was like a hundred years."
When this king had met his death through grief for his son,
the great monarch ascended to heaven; and Rāma took refuge in the forest,
while the radiant Lakṣmaṇa also departed together with Rāma.
"Let both Bharata and Śatrughna, the subduers of enemies, remain among the Kekayas in the delightful city of Rājagṛha, at their maternal grandfather’s residence.
Let some king of the Ikṣvākus be appointed here this very day."
For our kingdom would not fall into ruin if it were without a king.
In a land without a king, the rain-god Parjanya, garlanded with lightning and thundering loudly, does not pour down his divine waters upon the earth.
In a kingless land, a handful of seed is not sown;
in a kingless land, neither a son remains under the control of his father, nor does a wife remain under her husband's control.
In a kingless land there is no wealth, and in a kingless land there is no wife.
This is another great calamity: how can there be truth in a kingless state?
In a kingless land, men do not joyfully build assembly halls, delightful gardens, or sacred temples.
In a kingdom without a king, the twice-born who are devoted to sacrifice do not perform long sacrificial sessions (*sattra*);
nor do the self-controlled Brahmins of firm vows do so. In a kingdom without a king, there are no abundant actors and dancers.
Festivals and social gatherings that increase the prosperity of the kingdom flourish;
in a kingless land, litigants do not achieve their objectives, nor do those fond of storytelling find delight in tales through companions who love such stories.
In a kingdom without a king, men who are filled with desire do not go out to the forests on swift-moving vehicles together with their women.
In a kingdom without a king, even those who possess wealth are not well-protected.
Those who live by agriculture and cattle-rearing sleep with their doors wide open;
in a kingless land, merchants traveling great distances do not proceed safely on their journeys, even when they have accumulated much merit.
In a kingless land, the self-controlled sage does not wander alone, cultivating the self by means of the self, making his home wherever evening finds him;
for in a kingless land, the security of acquisition and preservation does not prevail.
Moreover, in a kingless state, an army cannot withstand its enemies in battle.
For as rivers without water, as a forest without grass,
or as cows without a cowherd, so is a kingdom without a king.
In a kingdom without a king, no one has anything as their own;
like fish, men constantly devour one another.
For those who have broken the bounds of propriety, who are atheists, and whose doubts are severed [by nihilism]...
Even they would be driven to evil deeds when oppressed by the king's punishment.
Alas, this world would be like darkness where nothing could be discerned, were there no king in the world to distinguish between the righteous and the unrighteous.
"Even while the Great King lives, we all do not transgress your word alone, just as the ocean does not overstep its shore.
Having observed that the king— who followed the conduct of the best of the twice-born— is gone, this kingdom has become a wilderness for us."
"Consecrate this prince, the son of Ikṣvāku, the generous one, as king here yourself!
Having heard those words of theirs, Vasiṣṭha replied with these words to all the hosts of friends and ministers, and to those brahmins.
Since that Bharata dwells happily in his maternal uncle’s family in the city of Rājagṛha, accompanied by his brother Śatrughna,
let swift messengers go there quickly on fleet horses.
"What should we consider doing in order to bring back our two heroic brothers?
Then they all spoke these words to Vasiṣṭha: "Let them go.
Having heard their speech, Vasiṣṭha spoke these words.
"Come, Siddhārtha, Vijaya, Jayanta, Aśoka, and Nandana;
listen, for I shall tell you all that must be done.
Having gone quickly to the city of Rājagṛha on swift-paced horses,"
"Free from sorrow, you must speak these words to Bharata by my command:
'The family priest and all the ministers inquire after your welfare;
depart with haste, for there is urgent business for you to attend to.'"
"Having gone to this abode of the Raghavas, do not tell him that Rama has gone into exile, nor that his father is dead.
[Give him] silken garments and excellent ornaments."
"Taking leave of the king and Bharata immediately, depart! Thus commanded by Vasiṣṭha, the messengers set out in great haste.
Having crossed the Gaṅgā at Hastināpura, they proceeded toward the west.
Having reached the Pāñcāla country through the center of Kurujāṅgala,
they swiftly crossed the divine Śaradaṇḍā river, which possessed clear waters, was frequented by various birds, and was crowded with people.
Having reached the divine Nikūla tree, which grants boons through truthful prayer,
and having approached and paid homage to it, they entered the city of Kuliṅgā;
then, having arrived at Abhikāla, they fell due to the overwhelming of their splendor.
They traveled through the midst of the Vāhlīkas and toward Mount Sudāmā,
beholding the footprint of Viṣṇu, as well as the Vipāśā and Śālmalī rivers;
those messengers, their mounts exhausted by the long journey along that remote road.
They reached Girivraja, the best of cities, swiftly and directly.
For the sake of their master’s pleasure, for the protection of the lineage, and for the preservation of their lord’s dynasty,
those messengers, free from malice, traveled with haste and arrived at that very city during the night.
On the very night those messengers entered that city,
Bharata also saw this unpleasant dream during that same night.
Having seen that unpleasant dream, he spent the rest of the night awake.
The son of the king of kings was deeply distressed.
Perceiving him to be suffering, his sweet-spoken friends, wishing to dispel his weariness, began conversations in the assembly hall.
Some played instruments for peace, while others danced; others performed plays and various kinds of comedies. Thus was that great-souled Bharata entertained by those friends who spoke so kindly.
Rāghava did not rejoice while they were making jokes and engaging in merriment.
His dear friend, surrounded by his companions and attended by his well-wishers, said to him: "Friend, why do you not join in the rejoicing?"
To his friend who was speaking thus, Bharata replied:
"Listen to the cause for which this dejection has come upon me.
In a dream, I beheld my father, soiled and with his hair disheveled."
I saw him falling from the mountain peak into a foul pool of cow dung;
and as he floated in that pool of cow dung, I saw him drinking oil with his cupped hands, laughing again and again.
Then, having eaten rice mixed with sesame seeds again and again, with his head hanging downward and his entire body anointed with oil, he immersed himself in oil alone.
Even in his dreams, he saw the ocean dried up and the moon fallen to the earth.
I saw the blazing fire suddenly extinguished;
I saw the earth split open and various trees withered;
and I saw the mountains shattered and enveloped in smoke.
Seated upon a black iron throne, dressed in black garments,
the righteous-souled king was hurried along while dark-brown women laughed at him; he was adorned with red garlands and unguents.
He set out toward the south in a chariot yoked with donkeys.
"This is what I have seen during this terrifying night:
either I, or Rāma, or King Lakṣmaṇa shall die."
Indeed, that man who travels in a dream by means of a vehicle yoked with donkeys will soon have the crest of smoke from his funeral pyre clearly seen;
for this reason I am dejected, and therefore I do not offer you my worship.
My throat seems to parch, my mind is not at ease,
and I feel as if I am loathing myself, yet I perceive no cause for it. For having observed this course of ill-omened dreams, so manifold in form and never before imagined, [I am filled with dread].
"Thinking of the king, whose appearance is inconceivable, that great fear does not leave my heart. While Bharata was speaking thus of his dream, those messengers, their mounts exhausted,
entered the beautiful city of Rājagṛha, which possessed an impassable moat.
Having met with the king and being honored by the prince,
they grasped the king's feet and spoke these words to Bharata:
"The family priest and all the ministers inquire after your welfare."
Depart in haste, for you have an urgent task to perform.
Here, O prince, are twenty crores belonging to your maternal uncle, the king,
as well as ten full crores more.
Having accepted all of that and having honored the messengers with gifts according to their desires, Bharata, who was deeply devoted to his circle of friends, said to them:
"Is my father, King Daśaratha, faring well?"
Is all well with Rāma and the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa?
And is the noble Kausalyā— the mother of the wise Rāma, who is devoted to dharma, knows dharma, perceives dharma, and is herself free from illness— also in good health?
I trust that Sumitrā, the mother of Lakṣmaṇa and of the heroic Śatrughna, is free from disease; for she is the middle queen,
who always seeks her own pleasure, is fierce, prone to anger, and considers herself wise.
"And is my mother Kaikeyī free from illness? What did she say?
Thus addressed by the high-souled Bharata, those messengers then spoke these humble words to Bharata.
"O tiger among men, those for whom you wish well are themselves virtuous.
Thus addressed, Bharata spoke to those messengers: "I must take leave of the Great King; the messengers are urging me to hurry."
Having spoken thus to those messengers, Bharata, the son of the king,
being urged by the messengers, addressed these words to his maternal grandfather:
"O King, urged by the messengers, I shall go into the presence of my father."
"I shall come again whenever you remember me.
When King Daśaratha had been addressed thus by Bharata, his maternal grandfather then smelled the head of the descendant of Raghu and spoke these auspicious words to him.
"Go, my son; I give you my permission. Kaikeyī has been blessed with a good son by you.
O scorcher of enemies, convey my welfare to your mother and your father, as well as to the family priest and those other best of the twice-born."
And those two great archers, the brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, O dear one—
having honored them, the King of Kekaya gave wealth to Bharata, including various excellent elephants, blankets, and skins.
Having honored him, the King of Kekaya bestowed wealth upon Kaikeyī’s son: two thousand gold neck-ornaments and sixteen hundred horses;
likewise, he assigned to him beloved ministers who were trustworthy and endowed with virtue.
Aśvapati quickly gave to Bharata followers;
his maternal uncle bestowed upon him wealth consisting of handsome Airāvatas and Aindraśiras elephants, as well as swift and well-trained mules.
He presented as gifts dogs raised within the inner apartments, possessing the prowess and strength of tigers, with large bodies, great fangs for weapons, and formidable forms; then,
having taken leave of his maternal grandfather and his uncle Yudhājit, he departed.
Mounting his chariot, Bharata set out accompanied by Śatrughna.
Having yoked more than a hundred chariots with wheel-rims adorned with jewels,
the servants followed the departing Bharata on camels, oxen, horses, and donkeys.

Protected by his army, the high-souled Bharata— having cast off all enemies— took Śatrughna and, accompanied by his maternal grandfather’s ministers who were equal to himself, departed from the palace like a perfected being departing from the world of Indra.
That valiant one, having set out from Rājagṛha facing the east, departed.
The illustrious joy of the Ikṣvākus crossed the river Śatadrū, which resounds, has distant shores, and possesses waves flowing toward the east;
having crossed that river at Elādhāna, he reached Aparaparpaṭa.
Having crossed the Śilāvahā river, which carries away rocks, and having passed through the Āgneya and Śalyakartana regions,
that truthful, pure, and glorious prince, looking about him, traversed great mountains toward the Caitraratha forest.
Having reached the Yamunā— swift-flowing, known as Kuliṅgā, resonant, and surrounded by mountains— he crossed it and then comforted his army. Having cooled their limbs, he reassured the weary horses.
Having bathed there and drunk, and taking water with him,
the prince set out for the great forest, which was seldom frequented;
like a noble man on a noble vehicle, he passed through it as the wind passes through the sky.

Passing through Toraṇa by way of the southern half, the son of Daśaratha reached Jambūprastha and proceeded to the delightful village of Varūtha. Having stayed there in that beautiful forest, he set out facing the east.
There is a garden where the *priyaka* trees grow for her who is departing; having reached those *priyaka* *sāla* trees and urged on his swift horses,
Bharata then took leave of the army and proceeded in haste.
Having stayed at Sarvatīrtha and having crossed the Uttānikā river as well as various other rivers with mountain-bred horses,
he reached Hastipṛṣṭhaka and passed beyond Kuṭikā.
And that tiger among men crossed the Kapivati at Lauhitya,
the Sthanumati at Ekaśāla, and the Gomati river at Vinata; and having then reached the Sāla forest in Kaliṅganagara.
Bharata arrived quickly, his mounts being utterly exhausted. Having swiftly traversed the forest at dawn during the night,
he beheld Ayodhyā, the city built by King Manu.
Having stayed on the road for seven nights, that tiger among men,
seeing Ayodhyā ahead of him, spoke to the charioteer from his chariot: "This glorious city, with its sacred gardens, does not appear joyful to me."
"O charioteer, Ayodhyā, with its pale soil, is visible from afar.
It is densely populated by performers of sacrifices, virtuous brahmins who have mastered the Vedas, and it is protected by the best of royal sages."

"In the past, a great and tumultuous clamor was heard everywhere in Ayodhyā from the men and women; today, I do not hear it. Indeed, in the evening, the gardens resound with men who have ceased their play."
"In former times, they shone as people ran about in every direction; today, abandoned by those seeking pleasure, they seem to weep for me.
O charioteer, that city appears to me as if it were a wilderness."
For here, these foremost of men are no longer seen going out or coming in by means of carriages, elephants, or horses, as they did in former times; moreover,
I perceive various undesirable and ominous portents.
"Because of these unpleasant omens, my mind is despondent.
With his mounts exhausted, he entered through the Vaijayanta gate;
having been asked for his victory by the gatekeepers who rose to meet him, he proceeded together with them.
But Rāghava, his heart distracted by many thoughts, honored that person standing at the gate and spoke there to the weary charioteer of Aśvapati:
"We have heard before what kind of omens occur at the time of the destruction of kings."
"O charioteer, I see all these signs here:
I see the people in the city, both men and women, dejected, their eyes filled with tears, miserable, lost in thought, emaciated, and full of longing."
Having spoken thus to the charioteer, Bharata, with a heavy heart,
beholding those ominous omens in Ayodhyā, proceeded toward the royal palace; he saw its crossroads, houses, and streets deserted, and its gate-panels and bolts reddened by dust.
Seeing the city, which once shone like the city of Indra, he became even more filled with sorrow as he beheld many things unpleasant to his mind that had never before existed in that city;
with his head bowed, dejected in spirit, and joyless, the high-souled one entered his father's residence.
Not seeing his father there in his father’s dwelling,
Bharata then went to see his mother in her own dwelling.
Seeing that her son had arrived after his long absence, Kaikeyī looked upon him.
Then, filled with joy, she flew up, leaving behind Lake Mānasa made of gold. Having entered his own home, which was now bereft of its splendor,
the righteous Bharata beheld it and grasped the auspicious feet of his mother.
Having smelled the head of that illustrious one, embraced him,
and placed Bharata upon his lap, he began to ask:
"How many nights have passed today since you departed from the house of your grandfather?"

"Is there no fatigue from the journey for you as you have come swiftly by chariot? Is your grandfather well, O Yudhājit, and is your maternal uncle well? My son, having been away from home, you ought to tell me everything regarding your welfare."
Thus questioned by Kaikeyī,
the lotus-eyed Bharata, the joy of the king, related everything to his mother:
"Today is the seventh night since I departed from the house of my grandfather."
My mother’s father is well, as are my maternal uncle Yudhājit and my other relatives.
The wealth and jewels that the king, the scorcher of his foes, gave me became a burden on the road; therefore, I have come ahead.
Urged by messengers carrying the king's command, I have come in haste;
my mother ought to tell me that which I wish to ask.
This golden couch of yours, intended for sleep, is empty.
Moreover, this people of Ikṣvāku does not appear joyful to me. The king is usually in his mother’s residence; I have come here wishing to see him, yet I do not see him today.
"I shall grasp my father's feet; tell me, as I ask you, mother, was he in the residence of my elder mother Kausalyā?
To him, Kaikeyī replied with words that were pleasant yet terrible and unpleasant:
"Deluded by greed for the kingdom, you, who know, have caused your father— who did not know [of his fate]— to go to that destination which is the destination of all living beings.
Having heard those words, the pure Bharata, who was noble by birth and devoted to dharma, [was overcome with grief].
Afflicted by the power of grief for his father, he suddenly fell to the ground.
Then, overwhelmed by sorrow and pained by the death of his father, the immensely energetic prince, his mind wandering and agitated, lamented.
"This bed of my father, which formerly shone so brilliantly,
does not shine today, now that it is bereft of that wise one.
Seeing him fallen upon the ground, distressed and resembling a god, [he spoke].
Having raised him up who was afflicted by grief, he spoke these words:
"Arise, arise! Why do you lie there, O prince of great renown?
For virtuous men like you, esteemed in the assembly, do not grieve."
Having wept for a long time and rolled upon the ground, he, overwhelmed by many sorrows, replied thus to his mother:
"The king will surely consecrate Rāma, or perhaps he will perform a sacrifice."
Thus, having made my resolve, I set out on my journey with a joyful heart.
But now this has turned out otherwise, and my mind is shattered,
for I do not see my father, who was ever devoted to my welfare and pleasure.
"Mother, by what illness has the king passed away before I arrived?
Blessed indeed are Rāma and all the others, who have personally performed the funeral rites for their father!
Surely the illustrious Great King did not know that I had arrived."
"O father, bowing down quickly, please smell my head!
Where is that hand of my father, whose actions are untiring, with its pleasant touch, which used to constantly wipe me clean when I was covered in dust?"
"Tell [him] quickly of me to that Rāma of unwearied deeds, who is my brother, father, and kinsman, and whose slave I am;
for to one who knows the noble Dharma, the eldest brother is indeed a father."
"I shall clasp his feet, for he is now my refuge.
"Noble lady, what did the king, my father of true valor, say? I wish to hear his final message to me."
Thus questioned, Kaikeyī spoke these words according to the truth:
"The great-souled king, the best among those who possess a goal, has gone to the other world while lamenting, 'O Rāma! Alas, Sītā! O Lakṣmaṇa!'"
Enveloped by the law of time like a great elephant bound by snares, your father uttered these final words:
"Men have achieved their purpose, for Rāma has returned together with Sītā."
"And they shall see the mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa returned again.
Hearing that, she despaired at the announcement of a second unpleasant thing;
with a dejected face, she questioned her mother once more.
"And where has that righteous soul, the increaser of Kausalyā’s joy, gone now, together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā?
Thus questioned, she began to relate the matter exactly as it had happened.
His mother simultaneously spoke these unpleasant words, yet out of a hope for what was pleasant:
"For that prince, my son, has gone to the great Daṇḍaka forest clad in bark garments, accompanied by Vaidehī and followed by Lakṣmaṇa."
Hearing that, Bharata was alarmed by suspicion concerning his brother’s conduct;
yet, out of pride in the greatness of his own lineage, he began to inquire:
"I hope that Rāma has not seized the wealth of any Brāhmaṇa?"
I hope that neither a wealthy man nor a poor man has been harmed by him through some sin;
I hope the prince does not covet another's wife—
for what reason has he been exiled to the Daṇḍaka forest like a killer of an embryo?
Then his fickle mother began to recount her own deed exactly as it happened, out of that very feminine nature:
"Rāma has not taken even the slightest bit of wealth belonging to any brahmin."
No one, whether wealthy or poor, has been harmed by him through sin; nor does Rāma even look upon the wives of others with his eyes.
But I, my son, having heard only of Rāma’s consecration...
Your father was entreated by you for the kingdom and for the exile of Rāma;
adhering to his own duty, your father did exactly that,
and Rāma, along with the son of Sumitrā and Sītā, was sent away.
Not seeing his beloved son, the highly illustrious protector of the earth, consumed by grief for his son, met his death.
O knower of dharma, you must now assume the kingship.
"For it was for your sake that I have done all this. "Therefore, my son, quickly, together with the foremost brahmins led by Vasiṣṭha who are learned in the ritual ordinances,
perform the funeral rites for the king of undaunted spirit and consecrate yourself upon the earth."
Having heard that his father had passed away and that his two brothers had been exiled,
Bharata, tormented by grief, spoke these words:
"What use have I for this kingdom, now that I am ruined and filled with sorrow?"
Now that I am deprived of my father and my brother who was like a father to me,
you have inflicted sorrow upon my sorrow, like applying salt to a wound,
by leaving the king in the state of the dead and turning Rāma into an ascetic.

"You have come like the Night of Doom for the destruction of our lineage; my father did not realize he was embracing a burning coal. Both Kausalyā and Sumitrā are now tormented by grief for their sons."
"It would indeed be difficult for them to remain alive if they were to find you, my mother;
surely even the noble one, whose soul is righteous and who knows how to behave toward elders, conducts himself toward you with the same supreme devotion as he does toward his own mother."
For my eldest mother, Kausalyā, who is far-sighted,
abides in righteousness toward you as if you were her own sister.
Her son, self-disciplined and clad in bark and rags—
Having sent him forth to dwell in the forest, how is it that you do not grieve, O sinful woman?
Having exiled the hero who perceives no evil, who is self-disciplined and illustrious, now clothed in bark garments— what possible reason can you see?
I believe that I have not been understood by you regarding Rāghava,
for you have brought about this great misfortune for the sake of the kingdom. Indeed,
I do not see those two tigers among men, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
By what power and influence am I able to protect the kingdom?
For the great king, that righteous soul of immense strength, always relied upon him as the mighty one, just as Mount Meru relies upon the forests of Meru.
"How then shall I, like a young ox encountering a yoke for the first time, bear this burden raised by one of great capacity, and with what strength?
Or perhaps I might possess the power through various means or the force of my intellect."
"I shall not fulfill your desire, you who are so greedy for your son;
I will bring back from the forest my brother, who is dear to his own people.
Having spoken thus, the high-souled Bharata tormented her with a multitude of unpleasant words.
Afflicted with grief, he roared again like a lion dwelling in a mountain cave. Having thus reproached his mother, Bharata,
then overcome by great anger, spoke these words once more.
Fall from the kingdom, Kaikeyī, you cruel woman of wicked conduct! Abandoned by righteousness, do not weep for me when I am dead.
What fault did the king or the exceedingly virtuous Rāma ever find in you?
"Since death and exile have come upon both of them equally because of you,
O Kaikeyī, you have incurred the sin of killing an embryo by destroying this lineage; go to hell and never share the same world as your husband."
For by you, through such a terrible deed, this sin has been committed;
having abandoned one who is dear to all the world, you have brought fear even upon me. Because of you, my father has passed away and Rāma has taken refuge in the forest.
And you have brought infamy upon me in the world of the living.
O cruel woman, enemy in the form of a mother, lustful for the kingdom, you of wicked conduct and slayer of your husband— I am not to be addressed by you.
Kausalyā, Sumitrā, and my other mothers have been overcome by great sorrow because of you, the defiler of the family;
you are not the daughter of the wise Dharmarāja Aśvapati.
It was there that you were born as a Rākṣasī, the destroyer of your father’s lineage,
because of whom the righteous Rāma, who is ever devoted to truth, was sent to the forest and your father passed away to heaven out of grief.
O you of sinful resolve, whatever primary sin you possess, let it fall upon me— who am deprived of my father,
abandoned by my brothers, and disliked by the whole world— and who have been separated from Kausalyā, who is devoted to righteousness.
Having done this, what world will you attain today, you who are destined for hell?
O cruel woman, do you not realize that Rāma— the eldest son born of Kausalyā, equal to his father— is surely dependent upon his kinsmen?
A son is born from the limbs and minor members of the body and is even born from the heart;
therefore, because of his dearness, he is more beloved to a mother than any other relative.
It is said that on another occasion, Surabhi, who knows the dharma and is honored by the gods, [spoke thus].
She saw her two sons being carried along the earth, deprived of their senses.
Seeing her two sons exhausted upon the ground at midday,
she wept from grief for her children, her eyes overwhelmed with tears.
As that high-souled king of the gods was passing below her,
subtle drops of fragrant scent fell upon her body.
Seeing that illustrious lady tormented by grief, the wielder of the thunderbolt [spoke].
With palms joined in reverence, Indra, the king of the gods, spoke these words in agitation:
"O you who desire the welfare of all, tell me: does some great danger not exist for us from somewhere? For what reason do you grieve? Speak."
Thus addressed by the wise king of the gods, the steadfast Surabhi, skilled in speech, then replied with these words:
"May all evil be averted; may no harm come to you from any quarter, O Lord of the Immortals."
"But I grieve for my two sons, who are submerged and situated in a perilous state.
O Lord of the Gods, seeing these two wretched oxen being dragged by the farmer, scorched by the heat of the sun's rays and tormented, I am filled with sorrow."
For those two, born from my own body, are now suffering and oppressed by their burden;
seeing them, I am consumed with grief, for there is nothing as dear as a son.
Even she, the wish-fulfilling cow who has thousands of sons, grieves for them.
How much more so, then, will Kausalyā fare without Rāma?
She is a virtuous woman who has but one son, and she has been made motherless by you;
therefore, you shall experience constant suffering both in this world and after death.
"For I shall undoubtedly perform this entire act of honoring for my brother and my father, as well as increasing our fame,
once I have brought back the highly resplendent son of Kausalyā."
"I myself shall enter the forest frequented by sages. Having spoken thus, like an elephant in the wild goaded by lances and hooks,
he fell to the ground in a rage, hissing like a serpent.
With bloodshot eyes, his garments disheveled, and all his ornaments cast aside, that scorcher of foes,
the prince, fell upon the ground like the banner of Indra at the end of a festival,
even as the high-souled Bharata continued to cry out in lamentation.
Recognizing the sound, Kausalyā said this to Sumitrā:
"Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī, who performs cruel deeds, has arrived;
I wish to see that far-sighted Bharata."
Having spoken thus to Sumitrā, she— pale and clad in soiled garments—
set out trembling and distraught toward where Bharata was.
And then Rāma’s younger brother, Śatrughna, accompanied him.
Bharata set out for the residence of Kausalyā. Then Śatrughna and Bharata, seeing the sorrowful Kausalyā fallen and unconscious with grief, embraced her.
Kausalyā, deeply afflicted by grief, replied thus to Bharata:
"Alas, this kingdom which you desired has been obtained by you without any thorns; yet it was secured by Kaikeyī through a swift and cruel deed."
Having sent my son away to dwell in the forest clad in bark garments,
what benefit does that cruel-looking Kaikeyī perceive in this?
Kaikeyī ought to dispatch me as well without delay.
"Where my son Hiraṇyanābha, who is of great renown, resides;
or else, accompanied by Sumitrā and placing the sacred fire in front of me, I myself shall set out happily for wherever Rāghava has gone."
Or rather, you ought to take me there yourself today,
where that tiger among men, my son, is performing austerities;
for this place of yours is vast and filled with wealth and grain.
"By her, a kingdom filled with elephants, horses, and chariots was surrendered.
To Kausalyā, who was thus lamenting and overwhelmed by many sorrows, Bharata then replied with his palms joined in reverence.
"Noble lady, why do you reproach me, who am innocent and unaware?
You know well my vast and steadfast affection for Rāghava;
may his mind never, at any time, be directed according to the dictates of the scriptures."
May he who has gone with the consent of that noble one—the best of the virtuous and true to his promise—fall into the service of the most wicked; may he urinate toward the sun;
may he strike a sleeping cow with his foot. May he who has gone with the consent of that noble one [suffer these fates]. (Rāmāyaṇa 2.69.14–15)

"Let that unrighteousness which belongs to the master who, having caused great works to be performed, leaves his servant without reward, belong instead to him with whose consent the noble one has gone—
[the master] who protects all beings like his own sons."
Therefore, let the sin of those who act with malice fall upon him by whose consent the noble one has departed;
and let that unrighteousness which belongs to a king who takes a sixth part as tribute yet fails to protect his subjects fall upon him by whose consent the noble one has departed.
Having promised the sacrificial fee to the ascetics at the session,
may the sin of those who misappropriate it fall upon him with whose consent the noble one has gone forth,
into a battle crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, and thick with weapons.
May he not practice the dharma of the virtuous, he by whose consent the noble one has departed!
May that evil-minded man destroy the scripture of subtle meaning which was diligently taught by the wise, he by whose consent the noble one has departed!
May that pitiless man, with whose approval the noble one has departed, eat milk-rice, sesame-rice, and goat's meat in vain; may he disregard his elders,
while surrounded by sons, wives, and servants in his own home.
"Let him alone eat delicacies, with whose approval the noble one has departed.
Let him incur that sin which is said to be incurred by the slaughter of the king's women, children, and the elderly,
as well as the sin incurred by the abandonment of dependents."
Whatever sin is conceived for one who sleeps during both twilights, that same sin shall belong to him with whose approval the Noble One has departed.
Whatever sin lies in one who sets fire to another, and whatever sin lies in one who violates the teacher’s bed— [all these shall belong to him].
May he incur that sin which lies in betraying a friend.
May he never perform service toward the gods, the ancestors, or likewise his own mother and father— he by whose consent the noble one has gone into exile.
"May he from whose consent the noble one has departed fall this very day from the world of the virtuous, from the fame of the virtuous, and likewise from deeds cherished by the virtuous—
may that prince leave Kausalyā bereft of both husband and son."
Even as he was thus offering consolation, he fell down, overcome by grief.
To Bharata, who was thus tormented by sorrow and uttering piteous oaths while unconscious of his surroundings, Kausalyā spoke these words.
"O son, this grief of mine arises all the more because you,
while swearing oaths, are threatening to take my life.
Fortunately, both you and Lakṣmaṇa have not wavered from dharma."
"My child, true to your promise as you are, you shall attain the worlds of the virtuous.
As that great-souled one was thus lamenting, afflicted by grief,
his mind became agitated due to delusion and the suppression of his sorrow.
As he lamented, unconscious, his intellect lost, fallen upon the ground and sighing long and deep again and again, that night passed for him in grief.
[To] that Bharata, the son of Kaikeyī, who was thus tormented by sorrow...
Vasiṣṭha, the best of speakers, the seer of excellent speech, said:
"Enough with grief; may prosperity be yours, O prince of great renown! Perform the final funeral rites for the lord of men, as the time has come."
Having heard the words of Vasiṣṭha, Bharata, who knew the dharma, regained his composure and caused all the funeral rites to be performed.
He had the body removed from the immersion in oil and laid upon the ground.
Having laid the lord of the earth upon an excellent bed adorned with various jewels— his face yellowish in hue as if he were fast asleep—
his son, deeply distressed, then lamented for Daśaratha.
"What have you resolved, O King, while I am away and have not yet returned, having banished Rāma, who knows the dharma, and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa?
Where will you go, Great King, after abandoning these grieving people?"

O King, now that you have departed for heaven and Rāma, whose deeds are effortless, has taken refuge in the forest, who will provide for the security and welfare of this city, which has been abandoned by that lion among men? O dear father, who will ensure your safety and well-being here?
"O King, the earth, widowed and deprived of you, does not shine;
to me, the city appears like a night when the moon has vanished. To Bharata, who was thus lamenting with a distressed mind—
The great seer Vasiṣṭha spoke these words once more:
"O mighty-armed one, let those funeral rites which must be performed for this lord of the people be carried out without distraction and without hesitation."
Saying "So be it," Bharata honored those words of Vasiṣṭha and urged all the sacrificial priests, family priests, and teachers in every way.
Those who had previously been stationed at the front of the king were now moved outside the fire-sanctuary.
They were carried according to the prescribed rites by officiating priests and sacrificial ministers.
Then, having placed the lifeless king upon a palanquin,
the attendants, their throats choked with tears and their minds distracted with grief, bore him away.
Scattering gold, fine gold, and various garments,
the people went before the king on the road;
likewise, they scattered sandalwood, aloe-wood resin, sal-tree resin, and padmaka wood.
Others, having brought devadāru wood, likewise constructed a funeral pyre.
Then, having offered various kinds of perfumes there, the officiating priests laid the lord of the earth upon the middle of the pyre.
Likewise, having offered oblations into the fire, his officiating priests recited prayers; and there, the chanters of the Sāman hymns sang the Sāmans according to the scriptures.
And his women, in palanquins and carriages, proceeded according to their rank.
Then, surrounded by the elders, they departed from the city;
and the sacrificial priests, as well as the women led by Kausalyā, tormented by grief, circumambulated the king, who had maintained the sacred fires, keeping him to their left.
There, the piteous cry of thousands of distressed women was heard, like the wailing of female curlews at that hour as they cried out again and again;
then, weeping helplessly and lamenting repeatedly, they fell silent.
The excellent women descended from their vehicles onto the bank of the Sarayū. Having performed the water-rites together with Bharata, the king’s wives, the ministers,
and the family priests entered the city with eyes overwhelmed by tears and spent ten days in sorrow upon the ground.
Then, when ten days had passed and he had performed his purificatory rites, the prince,
upon the arrival of the twelfth day, caused the śrāddha ceremonies to be performed.
He bestowed jewels, wealth, and abundant food upon the brahmins.
The king’s son gave to the Brahmins hundreds of goats and cows of many white hues,
as well as female and male servants, vehicles, and very large dwellings,
for the sake of his father's funeral rites.
Then, at the time of dawn on the thirteenth day,
the mighty-armed Bharata, overwhelmed with grief,
lamented with his throat choked by sobs as he arrived for the purpose of purification.
At the foot of the funeral pyre, deeply distressed, he spoke these words to his father:
"Father, now that my brother Rāghava, for whose sake I was entrusted to you,
has departed for the forest, I have been abandoned by you in this desolate place."
"O Father, O King, where have you gone, leaving behind that mother Kausalyā— she who, like a helpless woman, followed her son when he was exiled to the forest?
Having seen that circle of cremated bones, reddish with ashes..."
Sighing deeply at his father’s passing,
he was overcome with grief; seeing him weeping and dejected, he fell upon the surface of the earth, like the mechanical banner of Śakra when it has fallen and is being raised once more.
Then all his ministers rushed toward him, who was pure in his vows,
as they would toward Yayāti when he fell at the time of his end, like sages approaching a dying man;
and Śatrughna too, seeing Bharata overwhelmed with grief, [rushed forward].
Deprived of consciousness, he fell to the ground, remembering the protector of the earth;
like one insane and senseless, he lamented in great sorrow,
recalling again and again those various virtues of his father.
The fierce ocean of grief, originating from Mantharā and teeming with the crocodiles of Kaikeyī, unshakeable and consisting of the granting of boons, has submerged him—
you who are delicate, young, and always cherished by you.
"O father, where have you gone, leaving Bharata behind as he laments?
Surely you used to treat us all to choice foods, drinks, garments, and ornaments; who will do that for us today?"
Yet at the time of its rending, the earth did not split apart—
even though it was bereft of you, the high-souled king who knew the dharma,
now that our father has ascended to heaven and Rāma has taken refuge in the forest.
"What purpose is there in my life? I shall enter the fire.
Bereft of both my brother and my father, I will not enter the empty Ayodhyā protected by the Ikṣvākus; I shall enter the forest of asceticism."
Having heard their lamentation and observed that calamity,
all the followers became even more deeply distressed.
Then both Śatrughna and Bharata were despondent and exhausted.
They writhed upon the ground like two bulls with broken horns.
Then Vasiṣṭha, their father’s family priest, who was possessed of natural composure, raised Bharata up and spoke these words to him.
"Three pairs of opposites prevail among living beings without distinction; since these are unavoidable, one ought not to behave in such a manner.
Then Sumantra, having raised Śatrughna up and consoled him, spoke.
The knower of reality made them hear of the origin and dissolution of all beings. Those two tigers among men, illustrious and risen up,
shone like two separate banners of Indra, weathered by rain and sun.
Wiping away their tears, with reddened eyes and speaking piteously,
the ministers urged the two sons to hasten with the other rites;
meanwhile, Śatrughna, the younger brother of Lakṣmaṇa, desired to set out on his journey from this place.
He spoke these words to Bharata, who was tormented by grief:
"Rāma, who is the refuge of all beings in times of distress— how much more so for his own kin— is endowed with every virtue, yet he has been exiled to the forest by a woman."
Why does even that Lakṣmaṇa, who is powerful and endowed with heroism, not release Rāma after having himself subjected his father to restraint? Indeed,
he should have been restrained earlier, had he properly discerned between right and wrong policy.
"He who has mounted upon a wrong path, the king who has fallen under the power of a woman.
While Śatrughna, the younger brother of Lakṣmaṇa, was speaking thus at the eastern gate, a hunchbacked woman, adorned with all her ornaments, appeared.
Smeared with the essence of sandalwood and wearing royal garments,
she was like a female monkey bound by colorful ropes with various girdles;
seeing her, that gatekeeper then regarded her as a perpetrator of great evil.
Having seized the cruel hunchback, he presented her to Śatrughna, saying:
"She is that very woman for whose sake Rāma has gone to the forest and your father has cast off his body;
she is wicked and ruthless. Do with her as you see fit."
And Śatrughna, having understood those words, being deeply distressed and firm in his vows, spoke thus to all those who dwell in the inner apartments:
"Intense sorrow has been produced for my brothers as well as for my father."
"By this [act], may she reap the fruit of this cruel deed.
Having been addressed thus by him, the hunchback woman, surrounded by her circle of female companions,
was seized with force and made that house resound with her cries.
Then, all of her friends, becoming deeply distressed and perceiving that Śatrughna was enraged, fled in every direction.
And the entire circle of her friends took counsel together.
"Lest he, having thus advanced against us, should leave nothing remaining;
let us seek refuge with Kausalyā— she who is compassionate, generous, knower of dharma, and illustrious— for she shall be our certain resort."
With eyes copper-red from rage, Śatrughna, the scorcher of his enemies,
then dragged the wailing hunchback across the surface of the earth as Mantharā was being pulled here and there.
Various and manifold vessels were scattered across the earth;
strewn with those articles, the royal palace then shone even more brilliantly, like the autumnal sky.
That powerful bull among men, seizing Kaikeyī with forceful rage and rebuking her, spoke these harsh words.
By those painful and cruel words, Kaikeyī was deeply afflicted with grief.
Terrified by the fear of Śatrughna, she came to her son for refuge.
Seeing her, Bharata spoke thus to the enraged Śatrughna:
"Women are not to be slain by any living beings; let her be forgiven."
I would slay this wicked Kaikeyī of evil conduct,
were it not that the righteous Rāma would despise me as a matricide;
yet even if Rāghava learns that this hunchback has been killed, [he will not blame me].
"That righteous-souled one will certainly not speak to you or me.
Hearing these words of Bharata, Śatrughna, the younger brother of Lakṣmaṇa,
then turned back from his anger and released Mantharā.
At the feet of Kaikeyī, Mantharā fell prostrate;
sighing and afflicted by great sorrow, she lamented piteously.
And Bharata’s mother, seeing the hunchbacked woman whose consciousness was clouded by Śatrughna’s assault, [spoke].
He slowly comforted her, who was in a state of distress, looking about like a female curlew that has been caught.
Then, at the time of dawn on the fourteenth day,
those who were the king-makers assembled and spoke these words to Bharata.
Daśaratha, who was our most venerable elder, has gone to heaven after having sent away his eldest son Rāma and the mighty Lakṣmaṇa into exile;
O illustrious prince, do you become our king this very day.
"By acting thus, he does no wrong; for this kingdom is currently without a leader.
O Raghava, son of a king, having taken all these materials for the consecration, your kinsmen and the guilds of merchants await you."
"Accept this great kingdom of your father and grandfather, Bharata;
have yourself consecrated and protect us, O bull among men.
Having placed all the vessels for the consecration ceremony to the right, they spoke thus.
Bharata, firm in his vows, replied to all those people:
"In our lineage, sovereignty has always been the rightful lot of the eldest;
therefore, you who are wise men ought not to speak to me in this manner."
"For our elder brother Rāma shall indeed become the lord of the earth,
while I myself shall dwell in the forest for fourteen years.
Let a great army, possessing the immense strength of four divisions, be prepared."
"I shall bring my eldest brother Rāghava back from the forest. Taking all these preparations for the consecration with me,
I will go toward the forest for the sake of Rāma."
Having consecrated that tiger among men right there and placed him at my head,
I shall indeed bring back Rāma from the sacrifice like the sacrificial fire;
I will not allow this woman, who merely bears the name of mother, to have her desire fulfilled.
"I shall dwell in the difficult forest; Rāma shall become the king.
"Let the craftsmen prepare the road, smoothing out the uneven places, and let guards who are experts in traversing difficult terrain follow along the path."
To that prince who was speaking thus for the sake of Rāma, all the people replied with these most excellent and auspicious words:
"May the lotus-like Śrī attend you as you speak in this manner."
"O Prince, that you wish to give the earth to your eldest son—
having heard those unsurpassed words spoken in our hearing,
tears born of great joy fell from the eyes of the noble lady’s face toward him."

Having heard these words of yours, they—the ministers and the assembly—were delighted and their grief departed; the people devoted to the best of men [the King] prepared the road, and by your command, the guild of artisans was mobilized.
Then, those who were knowledgeable of the terrain and skilled in the work of measurement lines [surveyors] arrived.
Devoted to their respective tasks, there were brave men— diggers, engineers,
laborers, architects, and men skilled in mechanics; likewise, carpenters, road-makers, and woodcutters.
Well-diggers, plasterers, and bamboo-workers,
as well as those who were capable and onlookers, set out before him;
and that vast multitude of people proceeded toward that region with joy.
The great force shone like the ocean on a full-moon day.
Having taken their respective positions, those experts in the work of road-making set out ahead with various kinds of equipment.
Cutting down various trees, those people cleared the path of creepers, vines, shrubs, stumps, and even stones;
and in places where there were no trees, some planted new ones.
Some, here and there, were cutting with axes, chisels, and sickles;
others, powerful and even more mighty, were clearing away thickets of vīraṇa grass and difficult terrain from every side.
Others filled the wells with earth; some leveled the long chasms and low-lying areas on all sides;
they then bound what was to be bound and crushed what was to be crushed.
Then those men broke through various places that needed to be breached;
in a very short time, they created many canals of diverse forms, filled with abundant water, resembling the ocean itself.
He saw various kinds of wells adorned with railings; they had floors paved with plaster, were graced by flowering trees,
resounded with the cries of flocks of intoxicated birds, and were decorated with banners.
Sprinkled with sandalwood water and adorned with various flowers,
the road for the army shone greatly, resembling the path to heaven. Then, having been commanded, those authorized men applied themselves according to their orders.
In delightful regions abounding with many sweet fruits,
they further adorned that very place where the high-souled Bharata intended to encamp, making it as beautiful as an ornament with its own ornaments.
Under auspicious constellations and at favorable moments, those skilled in such matters established the residence for the high-souled Bharata;
it was surrounded by moats and possessed many mounds of earth.
There, the cities were adorned with gateways resembling Indra’s pillars, beautified by excellent main streets, joined by rows of palaces, enclosed by white-washed walls and ramparts,
all decorated with banners and featuring well-constructed great highways.
With their lofty mansions and turrets reaching as if into the sky, those dwellings shone like the city of Śakra.
And having reached the Ganges, with its various groves of trees, they settled there.
With its cool, pure water and teeming with great fish,
that royal road shone forth in due course; it was as beautiful as the stainless sky at night, adorned by the moon and the host of stars, and was constructed by skilled artisans.
Then, during the night of Nāndīmukhī, the bards and genealogists, skilled in the nuances of speech, praised Bharata with hymns filled with auspicious blessings.

at the proper time, dwell those wearing matted hair and deerskins, clothed in garments of bark.
But the sages, my dear, bathe in the river Mandākinī;
with arms raised high in accordance with their vows, they worship the sun.
O large-eyed one, these other sages here are firm in their ascetic observances.
With its peaks shaken by the wind, the mountain seemed to dance with the trees on all sides of the river as they shed their leaves and flowers;
does it have the waters of the Udā shining like jewels, and does it possess beautiful sandbanks?
Behold the river Mandākinī, crowded with perfected beings (siddhas). See the vast heaps of flowers shaken down by the wind;
see others floating amidst the waters.
O auspicious lady, those birds called rathāṅgas, possessing exceedingly sweet voices, are alighting upon them while uttering beautiful notes.
O beautiful one, behold Citrakūṭa and the Mandākinī!
I consider your sight even more superior to dwelling in the city.
Dwell with me, plunging into these waters which are perpetually agitated by the Siddhas, who are cleansed of all impurity and endowed with austerity, self-restraint, and tranquility.
"O Sītā, O beautiful lady, plunge into this Mandākinī like a female companion, submerging the lotuses and lilies.
Regard the wild beasts as the citizens and this mountain as Ayodhyā."
"O Vanitā, always regard this river as you do the Sarayū.
And since the righteous Lakṣmaṇa remains steadfast in my command,
and you, O Vaidehī, are so well-disposed, you both bring me great joy."
Performing ablutions at the three daily junctures and subsisting on honey, roots, and fruits,
I have no desire now for Ayodhyā nor for the kingdom, being with you.
For here is this lovely river, agitated by herds of elephants, its waters drunk by elephants, lions, and monkeys.
"There is no one who, beholding this place adorned with trees bearing flowers in full bloom, would not find his heart’s desire fulfilled.
Speaking such words, rich with many associations, regarding the river in the company of his beloved, Rāma—
the enhancer of the Raghu dynasty— wandered through the lovely Citrakūṭa, which possessed the luster of collyrium for the eyes.
Likewise, as Bharata approached while still at a distance,
both the dust of his army and its roar appeared, reaching up to the sky.
In that interval, those who were there became terrified by that great sound.
Afflicted and intoxicated, the leaders of the herds fled in all directions along with their followers.
Rāghava heard that sound arising from the army and beheld all those herd-leaders fleeing away.
Seeing them fleeing and hearing that sound, Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, who was possessed of radiant splendor:
"Ah, Lakṣmaṇa! Behold here how Sumitrā has truly borne a noble son in you!"
A tumultuous sound, deep as a terrifying thunderclap, is heard.
O Saumitri, you ought to find out whether it is a king or a royal official wandering the forest for the hunt, or some other wild beast.
"You ought to know all this according to its true nature before long.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, acting with haste, climbed a flowering *sāla* tree and,
surveying all the directions, gazed toward the eastern quarter.

Looking toward the north, he beheld a vast army crowded with chariots, horses, and elephants, and joined by disciplined foot soldiers. He saw that host, filled with horses and elephants, and adorned with chariots and banners.
He announced the army to Rāma and spoke these words:
"Let the noble one extinguish the fire, and let Sītā take refuge in the cave;
meanwhile, string your bow and prepare your arrows as well as your armor."
Rāma, that tiger among men, replied to Lakṣmaṇa:
"Look closely, O son of Sumitrā; whose army do you think this is?
Thus addressed by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa spoke these words.
"Enraged like a blazing fire wishing to consume that army,
Bharata— the son of Kaikeyī— is clearly approaching to slay us both, desiring the prosperous kingdom once he has obtained the consecration."
"Indeed, this most magnificent and glorious tree shines forth;
with its trunk rising high, it appears like the Kovidāra banner upon the chariot.
These swift-moving horses are mounting it according to their desire."
"Here these riders shine with great joy, mounted upon their elephants.
O hero, let us both take refuge on this mountain, holding our bows;
perhaps that one whose banner bears the kovidāra tree may come under our power in battle."
"Will I ever see Bharata, on whose account you, O Raghava, as well as Sita and I, have encountered such great calamity—
for his sake, O Raghava, you were deprived of your eternal kingdom?"
"O hero, this enemy Bharata has arrived; he must surely be slain by me.
O Raghava, I see no fault in the killing of Bharata, for no unrighteousness is prescribed in the abandonment of those who have previously done one harm."
"Once he has been slain, rule the entire earth.
Today, let Kaikeyī, who lusts after the kingdom, behold her son killed in battle by me— afflicted with extreme grief like a tree broken by an elephant."
"And I shall slay Kaikeyī, along with her attendants and her kinsmen;
today let the earth be cleansed of this great stain. O giver of honor, today I shall release this restrained anger and this indignity."
I shall set fire to the enemy armies like a conflagration in dry undergrowth.
Today, piercing the bodies of my enemies with sharpened arrows, I will drench this forest of Citrakūṭa in blood.
Let beasts of prey drag away the elephants, horses, and men slain by me, their hearts pierced by my arrows; thus,
in this great forest, I shall be free from my debt to my bow and my arrows.
"Having slain Bharata along with his army, I shall [attain my goal], of this there is no doubt.
But Rāma, having pacified the son of Sumitrā, Lakṣmaṇa, who was highly agitated and overwhelmed with rage,
then spoke these words.
"What need is there here for a bow, or a sword with its scabbard,
now that the great archer and highly wise Bharata has come in person?
Since Bharata desires to see us, the time for this has arrived."
"He would not do us even the slightest harm in his mind. Has Bharata ever done anything unpleasant to you before? Or what such fear do you have today that you suspect Bharata here?"
Indeed, Bharata must not be addressed with harshness or unpleasant words;
for I would be the one spoken to unpleasantly if anything disagreeable were done to Bharata.
How indeed could sons ever kill their father, even in any kind of calamity?

"O son of Sumitrā, even a brother might kill his own brother, who is dearer than life itself, if you speak these words for the sake of the kingdom. Upon seeing Bharata, I shall say to him: 'Let the kingdom be given to him.'"
"For if Bharata is addressed by me in truth, Lakṣmaṇa,
saying 'Give the kingdom to him,' he will surely say, 'So be it. Thus was he addressed by his brother, who is devoted to righteousness, while he himself remained intent on his welfare."
Lakṣmaṇa seemed to shrink into his own limbs out of shame.
Seeing Lakṣmaṇa thus abashed, Rāghava replied:
"I believe this mighty-armed one has come here to see us."
Reflecting upon his dwelling in the forest, he will surely take this Vaidehī, who has been accustomed to the utmost luxury, back home;
for here appear those two beautiful and noble-spirited brothers.
O hero, these two excellent steeds are swift as the force of the wind.
This very elephant of massive body, named Śatruñjaya, the aged mount of my wise father, trembles at the head of the army.
Having descended from that sal tree, Lakṣmaṇa, the conqueror in assembly, stood by Rāma’s side with his palms joined in reverence;
for Bharata had previously instructed him that there should be no crowding.
He established the army camp all around that mountain. That host of Ikṣvākus, crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, settled on the side of the mountain, covering one and a half yojanas.

Having placed the army at Citrakūṭa, Bharata—placing righteousness foremost, casting aside pride, and guided by the wise—led it forward for the sake of propitiating the joy of the Raghus; thus led, the host shone brightly.
Having encamped the army, the lord, the best among those who walk on foot, proceeded on foot himself.

He desired to approach that descendant of Kakutstha, who was devoted to his elders. Once the army had encamped according to its assigned quarters, Bharata, behaving with humility, spoke these words to his brother Śatrughna.
O gentle one, you ought to search this forest quickly on all sides with these groups of men and these hunters together,
until I see Rāma or the mighty Lakṣmaṇa.
"Or until I see the highly fortunate Vaidehī, I shall find no peace.
Until I behold my brother’s auspicious face, which resembles the moon and has eyes like lotus petals, I shall find no peace."
"As long as I do not bear upon my head the feet of my brother, which are endowed with the marks of royalty, there shall be no peace for me;
so long as he who is worthy of the kingdom does not stand established in the ancestral realm of his father and grandfather."
Drenched by the water of consecration, I shall find no peace.
Fortunate is Vaidehī, the daughter of Janaka, who has accomplished her purpose,
for she follows her husband across the earth bounded by the oceans.
Fortunate indeed is that mountain Citrakūṭa, which resembles the king of mountains,
for upon it dwells the descendant of Kakutstha like Kubera in the Nandana grove. This difficult forest, though inhabited by predatory beasts, has fulfilled its purpose.
"Where Rāma, the one of great splendor and the best among wielders of weapons,
resides. Having spoken thus, the highly energetic Bharata, that bull among men, entered the vast forest on foot.
That best of speakers passed through the midst of those groves of trees that had grown upon the mountain ridges with their tops in bloom;
he reached a flowering *sāla* tree on Mount Citrakūṭa.
He saw the raised banner of the fire that had been taken to Rāma’s hermitage.
Upon seeing it, the illustrious Bharata rejoiced with his kinsmen,
knowing that Rāma was there, like one who has reached the further shore of the ocean.
Having observed Rāma’s hermitage on Mount Citrakūṭa, frequented by holy men,
the high-souled one quickly withdrew his army and proceeded with Guha;
meanwhile, Bharata remained eager once the army had encamped.
He went to see his brother Śatrughna, pointing him out;
having instructed the sage Vasiṣṭha, "Bring my mothers here quickly," he who was devoted to his elders proceeded swiftly ahead.
Sumantra, moreover, followed close behind Śatrughna,
for his thirst to behold Rāma was just as great as Bharata’s. Then, as Bharata proceeded, he saw [the hermitage] situated within the dwelling of the ascetics.
The illustrious Bharata beheld his brother’s leaf-hut and the cottage; then, in front of that hall,
he saw logs of wood broken and flowers gathered.
And as he was traveling through that forest, the illustrious and mighty-armed Bharata then saw large heaps of dung made by deer and buffaloes for the sake of warmth against the cold.
And the bold one spoke to Śatrughna and all those ministers:
"I believe we have reached that region of which Bharadvāja spoke;
for I think the Mandākinī River is not far from here."
"These rags tied high must have been made into a trail of recognition by Lakṣmaṇa, who wished to travel at an improper hour;
and here are the marks of swift elephants with prominent tusks."
They wandered along the slopes of the mountain, roaring at one another.
That dense smoke of the fire, which the ascetics constantly desire to maintain in the forest, is now visible.
"Here, filled with joy, I shall behold that tiger among men, the noble Rāghava, who honors his elders like a great seer.
Then, after traveling for a short while toward Citrakūṭa, that descendant of Raghu—
Having reached the Mandākinī, he spoke these words to those people:
"O tiger among men, that lord of men sits upon the earth in the heroic posture (vīrāsana). Having found this desolate place, he laments, 'Fie on my birth and my life!'"
"Because of me, the Lord of the World, possessed of great splendor, has met with calamity;
Rāghava dwells in the forest, having renounced all desires.
Thus reviled by the people, he now seeks to propitiate them at his feet.
"I shall fall down before Rāma and Sītā again and again.
Lamenting thus in that forest, the son of Daśaratha beheld a great, holy, and delightful leaf-hut.
It was covered with many leaves of *sāla*, *tāla*, and *aśvakarṇa* trees;
it was spacious and strewn with soft *kuśa* grass like a sacrificial altar at a ritual, and it was filled with bows resembling Indra’s rainbow, capable of bearing great weight.
It was adorned with great, powerful arrows that struck down enemies and were backed with gold;
it shone with those terrible shafts, resembling the rays of the sun, contained within their quivers like the city of Bhogavatī adorned with serpents of blazing countenances.
She was resplendent with two great silver garments and two swords,
and further adorned with two shields variegated with golden spots;
she was also equipped with colorful finger-guards for the arms, decorated with gold.
Unassailable by hosts of enemies, like a lion’s den by wild beasts,
Bharata saw there in Rāma’s dwelling a vast, sacred altar sloping toward the northeast, glowing with a blazing fire.
After gazing for a moment, Bharata beheld his elder brother, Rāma, seated in the hermitage, wearing a mass of matted hair, clad in a black antelope skin and garments of bark.
He saw him bearing the black antelope skin and dressed in clothes of bark.
He beheld Rāma seated nearby, resembling a blazing fire—
lion-shouldered, mighty-armed, with eyes like lotuses,
the protector of the earth as far as the ocean, and a practitioner of righteousness.
Seeing the mighty-armed one seated upon the sacrificial ground strewn with darbha grass, like the eternal Brahmā himself, together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa,
the illustrious Bharata was overwhelmed by grief and delusion.

The righteous Bharata, son of Kaikeyī, rushed forward; and seeing him, he lamented in distress with a voice choked with tears, unable to maintain his composure, he spoke these words: *abhyadhāvata dharmātmā bharataḥ kaikayīsutaḥ / dṛṣṭvā ca vilalāpārto bāṣpasaṃdigdhayā girā / aśaknuvan dhārayituṃ dhairyād vacanam abravīt //* Ram_2,93.28-29*
He who was once fit to be attended upon by the subjects in assembly,
now sits here before me, his elder brother, attended only by wild animals; he,
the high-souled one who was formerly accustomed to being served with many thousands of garments.
He who formerly wore various colorful flowers here now wears this deer skin while practicing dharma;
how does that Rāghava endure this burden of matted hair?
He whose accumulation of merit was joined with sacrifices performed as prescribed now seeks that dharma which arises from the affliction of the body;
he whose limbs were once attended to with costly sandalwood paste [now endures this].
"How can this body of the noble one, now soiled with dust, be served?
Because of me, Rāma—who is worthy of happiness—has encountered this suffering. Shame on my life, cruel and despised by the world!"
Lamenting thus in distress, his lotus-like face covered in sweat,
the mighty prince Bharata, failing to reach Rāma’s feet, fell down weeping. Tormented by grief, the immensely powerful Prince Bharata collapsed.
Having spoken "Noble One" once, he was so overcome with grief that he did not say anything further.
With his throat choked by tears, and gazing at the illustrious Rāma, he could do nothing but cry out "Noble One! and was unable to speak beyond that.
Śatrughna also wept as he prostrated at the feet of Rāma; Rāma, in turn, embraced them both and shed tears.
Then, in the forest, the two princes were reunited with Sumantra and Guha.
Just as the sun and the moon in the sky [are accompanied] by Venus and Jupiter,
so too did those forest-dwellers, seeing all those kings— who resembled leaders of elephant herds— gathered there in that great forest, cast off their joy and shed tears.
Having smelled his head and embraced him, Rāma, the descendant of Raghu,
placed Bharata on his lap and, with a composed mind, questioned him:
"Where, my dear, was your father when you came to the forest?"
"Indeed, you ought not to have come to the forest while he is still alive. Alas! After a long time, I see Bharata arrived from afar;
yet his appearance is so ill-omened in this forest—why, my dear child, have you come to the woods?"

Is King Daśaratha well— he who is true to his promise, the performer of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices, and firm in his resolve for righteousness? Is that learned Brāhmaṇa well— he who is constant in dharma and possessed of great luster?
"O dear one, is our preceptor of the Ikṣvākus being honored as he deserves? O father, I trust Kausalyā and Sumitrā, the mother of progeny, are well;
and I trust the noble Queen Kaikeyī is also happy and rejoicing."
Is your family priest— a son of noble birth, endowed with discipline, learned, free from envy, observant, and honored by you— acting as such?
Is he devoted to the sacred fires, knowledgeable in the ritual injunctions, wise, and upright?
He always informs you at the proper time regarding what has been offered in sacrifice and what is yet to be offered.
My son, do you hold in high regard your preceptor Sudhanvan, who is endowed with excellence in archery and weaponry and is proficient in the science of statecraft?
"O dear one, have you appointed as ministers those who are equal to yourself, heroic, learned, self-controlled, of noble birth, and capable of discerning intentions?
