For counsel, O Raghava, is indeed the root of victory for kings."
Are you well-guarded by ministers who are mantra-holders and experts in the treatises? Do you yield to the power of sleep, or do you wake at the proper time;
and during the latter part of the night, do you contemplate the skillful means for achieving your goals?
I hope you do not deliberate on state affairs alone, nor with too many people; I hope that the counsel you have deliberated upon does not leak out and spread throughout the kingdom.
I hope that, having determined a matter of small cost but great profit, you act accordingly.
O Raghava, you begin your tasks swiftly and do not procrastinate.
Do kings know all their undertakings only after they have been completed or even when they have taken form, rather than while they are yet to be done?
I trust, my dear brother, that your secret counsel is not discovered by means of logic, nor by those who have not been told of it, whether by you or by your ministers;
and I trust you prefer a single wise man over a thousand fools.

For a wise man, in times of great difficulty regarding his welfare, can achieve a vast and supreme benefit. Even if a lord of the earth attends upon thousands or even tens of thousands of fools, there is no assistance to be found among them.
Even a single minister who is wise, brave, skillful,
and discerning can bring great prosperity to a king or a member of the royal family.
I trust that the foremost ministers are appointed only to high offices, and those of middling rank to middling ones?
And do you employ inferior servants in inferior tasks?
Do you appoint ministers who have passed the tests of integrity, who are pure, and who have served your father and grandfather, to the most excellent duties?
I hope that the officiating priests do not despise you as they would an outcast, nor women a man who accepts gifts from the fierce,
nor a physician skilled in means who is intent on corrupting his servants.
He who does not slay the brave man who desires power is himself slain.
Have you appointed as commander-in-chief one who is bold, brave, steadfast, wise, pure, of noble birth, loyal, and skillful?
And I trust that those leaders of yours who are powerful, skilled in battle,
of proven valor, and courageous, have been honored and respected by you;
and I trust that the food and wages for the army are provided as is appropriate.

"When the time has arrived, you give what is to be given and do not delay. For when the time for wages and rations passes, servants become angry with their master and turn hostile; that is remembered as a very great calamity."
I trust that all the noble sons of the family are devoted to you, especially the leaders;
I trust that, with focused minds, they would even sacrifice their lives for your sake.
I trust that the learned man from the countryside is skillful and eloquent.
O wise Bharata, you have appointed as your messenger one who speaks exactly as he is told.
Do you keep watch over the eighteen assemblies, your own five-and-twenty ministers,
and the three [councils], by means of three secret spies at each point?
O destroyer of enemies, do you always treat with no contempt those who have been expelled, those who have returned after being harmful, and those who are weak?
My dear son, do you not associate with Brahmins who are materialists?
For these fools, who imagine themselves wise, are skilled only in what is useless;
though the preeminent treatises on dharma exist, these dull-witted ones, having acquired a mere superficial understanding, propound what is meaningless.
O dear one, it was formerly inhabited by our ancestors— those heroes—
and is true to its name, with firm gates and crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots;
it is always filled with Brahmins, Kshatriyas, and Vaishyas devoted to their own duties.

Do you protect Ayodhyā, which is filled with thousands of noble men who have conquered their senses and possess great energy, which is crowded with palaces of various forms and throngs of physicians, and which is prosperous and flourishing?
Is it adorned with hundreds of shrines, crowded with well-settled people,
and graced by temples, water-stations, and ponds;
filled with joyful men and women, and beautified by social gatherings and festivals?

O Raghava, does that prosperous district dwell in happiness— a land with well-plowed boundaries, rich in cattle, free from violence, not dependent on rain for its water, delightful, and devoid of predatory beasts?
I hope all those who live by agriculture and cattle-rearing are dear to you;
for, my son, the world prospers in happiness when it relies upon the livelihood of *vārttā*.
And I trust that their maintenance is ensured through protection and the removal of obstacles.

For all those dwelling within his realm must be protected by the king in accordance with righteousness. Do you console the women, and are they well-protected? Do you refrain from placing undue trust in them, and do you never disclose secrets to them?
I trust the elephant grove is well-guarded; do you take pleasure in the elephants?
And do you regularly show them, adorned with ornaments, to the people every morning as the prince rises and rises upon the great highway?
I trust that all the fortresses are fully supplied with wealth, grain, weapons, water, and engines, as well as with artisans and archers;
I trust your income is vast and your expenditure is very small.
O Rāghava, I hope that your treasury does not go to unworthy recipients.
I trust that your expenditures are directed toward the gods, the ancestors, Brahmins, guests,
soldiers, and your circle of friends.
I hope that the noble one, pure of soul and innocent, is not being bound out of greed by those skilled in the scriptures, even though he has been accused of theft without being questioned;
for he was only seized, interrogated at the proper time, and found guilty with cause.
O bull among men, I hope that a thief is not released due to greed for wealth.
O Raghava, I hope that your learned ministers, when faced with the misfortunes of both the wealthy and the destitute, look upon their interests with impartiality.
O Raghava, the tears shed by those who have been falsely accused destroy the children and livestock of one who governs for the sake of his own pleasure.
O Raghava, do you perhaps [inquire after] the elderly, the young, and the foremost physicians?
Through these three— by gift, by mind, and by speech— you seek to prosper.
Do you pay homage to your gurus, the elders, the ascetics, the deities, guests, the sacred shrines, all those who have attained their goals, and the brahmins?
I hope that you do not obstruct dharma with wealth, nor wealth with dharma, nor both with the greed for pleasure or desire,
O best among victors; I hope you pursue wealth, dharma, and pleasure in harmony.

O knower of the proper time, do you serve all of them at the appropriate times, O Bharata? O highly wise one, do the Brahmins, who are experts in the meaning of all the scriptures, along with the people of the city and the countryside, wish you well?
Atheism, falsehood, anger, negligence, procrastination, not consulting those possessed of knowledge, laziness, and the fivefold indulgence;
as well as deliberating on matters of state alone, or consulting with those who do not understand the true purpose.

Do you avoid these fourteen faults of kings: failing to undertake what has been determined, failing to protect one's counsel, failing to employ auspicious rites, and rising from one's seat on all occasions?
"O Raghava, I hope you do not eat delicious food all by yourself;
I hope you share it with your friends who look forward to it.
Having heard Rama's words, Bharata replied.
"What will the duty of a king do for me, who am deprived of righteousness?
O bull among men, this eternal law has always been established among us:
O King, while the eldest son remains, a younger son cannot become the ruler."
"Go with me to prosperous Ayodhyā, O Rāghava,
and have yourself consecrated for the welfare of this lineage.
They call a king merely human, but in my estimation, he is a god."
They say that his conduct, which was consistent with righteousness and purpose, was superhuman. While I remained in Kekaya and you had retired to the forest,
the noble King, a performer of sacrifices esteemed by the virtuous, ascended to heaven.
"Arise, O tiger among men! Let the water-offering be made for our father;
Śatrughna here and I have already performed the libation.
For it is said, O Raghava, that what is given by a beloved son reaches the world of the ancestors."
"It becomes inexhaustible," they say, "and you are indeed dear to your father.
Hearing those piteous words spoken by Bharata concerning the death of his father, Raghava became senseless.
Having uttered those harsh words, the subduer of enemies,
Rāma, raised his arms like a tree with blossoming branches; and indeed, like a tree felled in the forest by an axe, he fell upon the earth.
For thus they saw Rāma, the lord of the earth, fallen upon the ground like an elephant exhausted by the collapse of a riverbank and fast asleep;
your brothers [saw] that great archer, emaciated on all sides by grief.
Weeping together with Vaidehī, they indeed sprinkled him with water. Having regained consciousness and shedding tears from his eyes,
that descendant of Kakutstha began to speak piteously at great length.
"What service indeed can I do for that high-souled one, born so ill-fated, who died through grief for me and was not even consecrated by me?
Oh, Bharata, you have achieved your purpose, O sinless one, since the king has been [honored] by you!"
And I have been honored by Śatrughna in all the funeral rites for the deceased. Yet,
even though my forest exile has ended, I do not venture to go to Ayodhyā, which is now leaderless, distracted, and deprived of the lord of men.
"O scorcher of enemies, now that my father has passed to the other world, who indeed will instruct me again when I have completed my forest exile in Ayodhyā?
Formerly, having observed my virtuous conduct, my father used to speak these words to me while consoling me."
"From where shall I hear those words so pleasing to the ear?
Having spoken thus to Bharata, Raghava, tormented by grief, approached his wife, whose face resembled the full moon, and said to her.
"Sītā, your father-in-law is dead; Lakṣmaṇa, you are deprived of your father;
Bharata announces that the lord of the earth has gone to heaven.
Having thus consoled the weeping daughter of Janaka, Rāma—
There, filled with grief, he spoke these sorrowful words to Lakṣmaṇa:
"Bring me the crushed pulp of the iṅgudī fruit and fetch a bark garment for an upper cloth;
I shall go to perform the water-libation for our high-souled father."
"Let Sītā go in front, and you follow beside her; I shall go behind, for this is the most dreadful path. Then his constant follower, the high-minded one who knew his own self, [spoke].
Gentle, self-controlled, and peaceful, and possessing firm devotion to Rāma,
Sumantra, together with those princes, comforted the descendant of Raghu and,
supporting him, helped him descend to the auspicious Mandākinī river.
Then those illustrious ones, having reached with great difficulty the beautiful river Mandākinī, which possesses excellent landing places and forests perpetually in bloom,
arrived at a auspicious, mud-free ford with its swift current.
They sprinkled water upon the king, saying, "May this come to pass.
Then the protector of the earth, raising his cupped hands filled with water and facing the southern direction, spoke these words while weeping.
"O tiger among kings, may this pure and inexhaustible water, given by me today, reach you who have gone to the world of the ancestors.
Then that descendant of Raghu, having ascended from the bank of the Mandākinī, [proceeded].
The radiant Rāma, together with his brothers, performed the funeral libations for his father.
Having placed oil-cake mixed with *iṅguda* and jujube fruits upon a bed of *darbha* grass, Rāma, afflicted by extreme sorrow and weeping, spoke these words: *(Rāmāyaṇa 2.95.29–30)*
"O Great King, eat this with pleasure—the very food that we ourselves eat; for whatever food a man eats, his deities eat that same food.
Then, by that very path, he ascended from the riverbank.
The tiger among men ascended the mountain with its beautiful peaks.
Then, having reached the door of the leaf-hut, the lord of the world took both Bharata and Lakṣmaṇa by their hands.
From the sound of those brothers weeping together with Vaidehī, an echo arose from the mountain like the roar of lions;
and perceiving that tumultuous noise, Bharata’s soldiers became terrified.
And they said, "Bharata must have certainly met with Rāma," for that was the great sound of those very people mourning their deceased father.
Then, abandoning their dwellings, they all moved toward the direction of the noise.
With focused minds, they rushed to their respective places;
some went on horses, others on elephants, and others on well-adorned chariots,
while other men, being delicate, went even on foot.
Desiring to see Rāma, who had been away but a short time as if he had been gone for a long time, all the people went suddenly to the hermitage;
they were in haste, longing to witness the reunion of the brothers.
They departed in various kinds of vehicles, crowded with hooves and wheel-rims.
That ground, struck by the many vehicles with their hooves and wheel-rims,
emitted a tumultuous sound like the sky at the gathering of clouds.
Terrified by him, the elephants, surrounded by their female companions,
fled from that forest to another, spreading their scent as they went.
Boars, deer, lions, buffaloes, bears, and monkeys likewise departed.
Tigers, gokarṇas, and gavayas, along with spotted deer, were terrified; likewise,
rathāṅgasāhvās, natyūhas, swans, kāraṇḍavas, plavas, as well as male cuckoos and krauñcas, fled bewildered in all directions.
Terrified by that sound, the sky was filled with birds and the earth was covered with men; both then shone forth [in their distress].
Then, beholding those men with eyes full of tears and deeply afflicted, he [Rāma]—

The knower of dharma embraced him as if he were his father and his mother. There, the prince embraced some men, while others saluted him; having approached them all, the son of the king then greeted his companions and kinsmen according to their rank.
Then, as those great-souled ones wept, their sound— resembling the resonance of a mṛdaṅga drum— was heard continuously, making the earth, the sky, the mountain caves, and all the directions resound.
Vasiṣṭha placed the wives of Daśaratha at the forefront.
Thirsting for the sight of Rāma, he proceeded to that place. And the wives of the king, walking slowly toward the Mandākinī, beheld there that bathing-place frequented by Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
With her face parched and filled with tears, the dejected Kausalyā spoke to Sumitrā and the other royal women:
"This is the plight of those who are now without a protector, though they themselves were performers of unblemished deeds."

Those who were previously the only ones to frequent the sacred bathing-places in the forest have now been deprived of their domain. O Saumitri, from here on, your son, ever unwearied, shall himself fetch water for the sake of my son.
On the ground, upon darbha grass with its tips pointing south, that large-eyed woman saw her father’s *iṅgudī* seed-cake placed there;
seeing it laid upon the earth by the distressed Rāma for his father, she looked on.
Queen Kausalyā said to all the wives of Daśaratha:
"Behold this, which has been given by Rāghava to his father, the high-souled Rāghava, the lord of the Ikṣvākus, according to the prescribed rites."
I do not consider this meal appropriate for that high-souled king, who is equal to a god and has already enjoyed every luxury; he who,
like the great Indra, was the lord who ruled the earth bounded by its four oceans.
How can that lord of the earth eat the oil-cake of the *iṅgudī* tree?
Nothing in this world appears more painful to me than this:
that the prosperous Rāma should have to offer the crushed pulp of the *iṅgudī* to his father.
"Seeing that my father was given only the pulp of *iṅgudī* seeds by Rāma,
why does my heart not shatter into a thousand pieces from grief?
Having thus consoled their distressed co-wife, those other wives then departed.
And in the hermitage, they beheld Rāma like an immortal fallen from heaven;
seeing Rāma deprived of all enjoyments, his mothers,
afflicted by grief, shed tears with loud lamentation.
Rising up, Rāma, that tiger among men who is true to his promise, grasped the auspicious feet of all those mothers with his hands,
which were pleasant to the touch and possessed soft fingers and palms.
The large-eyed women wiped the dust from the back of Rāma.
Then the son of Sumitrā, also seeing all those mothers, was deeply pained; immediately after Rāma, he greeted them slowly and with devotion.
Just as they had behaved toward Rāma, so did all the women behave toward Lakṣmaṇa, who was born of Daśaratha and possessed auspicious marks;
Sītā also, though distressed, touched their feet.
With her eyes filled with tears, she stood before her mothers-in-law;
then Kausalyā, distressed and wretched, like a mother embracing her daughter, embraced her who was emaciated by forest exile and spoke these words.
How has the daughter of the King of Videha, the daughter-in-law of Daśaratha, and the wife of Rāma, come to suffer such misery in the desolate forest?
She is like a lotus scorched by the sun, or a water-lily that has withered away.

"O Vaidehī, beholding your face— which is like gold obscured by dust or the moon eclipsed by clouds— the grief born from the friction-sticks of calamity burns intensely in my heart, consuming me as fire consumes its own source."
While his mother was thus speaking in her distress, that descendant of Raghu, the elder brother of Bharata, approached and grasped the feet of Vasiṣṭha,
the family priest who resembled fire, just as Indra, the lord of the immortals, grasps the feet of Bṛhaspati.
Taking the feet of him whose splendor was most abundant, Rāghava sat down together with him.
Then, along with his ministers, the leaders of the city, and the soldiers, as well as the people who were most deeply conversant with dharma, the righteous Bharata sat down beside his elder brother.
Then, having sat down and beheld Rāghava in the guise of an ascetic, blazing with splendor, the valiant Bharata joined his palms in reverence, like the disciplined Mahendra before Prajāpati.
"What words will Bharata now speak to Rāghava, after having bowed and honored him? he thought.
Thus, at that time, a truly supreme curiosity arose among those noble people.
Rāghava, firm in truth, the high-souled Lakṣmaṇa, and the righteous Bharata,
surrounded by their friends, shone like the three sacrificial fires accompanied by the officiating priests at a ritual.
Having consoled his brother, who was so devoted to his elders, Rāma, together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa, began to question him:
"I wish to hear this which has been spoken by you."
"Since you have come to this region wearing bark garments, matted hair, and an antelope skin—
for what reason have you entered this place, having abandoned your kingdom while bearing the black antelope skin and matted locks— you ought to tell me all of that."
Thus addressed by the high-souled descendant of Kakutstha, the son of Kaikeyī,
clasping his hands even more firmly, spoke these words:
"O Noble One, our father has departed, having performed an exceedingly difficult deed."
Afflicted by grief for his son, the mighty-armed one has gone to heaven. Urged by a woman— my mother Kaikeyī— he, O scorcher of foes, committed this most grievous sin that destroys his own fame.
"Without having obtained the fruit of sovereignty, my mother— now a widow, emaciated by grief— will fall into a most terrible hell.
You ought to show favor to me, who have become her slave."
Be consecrated this very day to the kingship, like Maghavan himself.
All these subjects and the widowed mothers have come into your presence; you ought to show them your favor.
O giver of honor, obtain the kingdom rightfully through dharma, endowed with that same succession; fulfill the desires of your well-wishers,
and let the entire earth cease to be widowed by having you as its lord.
Like an autumn night with the spotless moon, [may you be so with me].
Together with these ministers, I entreat you with my head bowed low; you ought to show favor to me, who am your brother, your pupil, and your servant.
"Therefore, O tiger among men, I cannot bring myself to transgress this entire circle of ministers, which is eternal, ancestral, and honored.
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed son of Kaikeyī shed tears.
Bharata again took Rāma’s feet with his head. Embracing his brother Bharata, who was sighing repeatedly like an elephant in rut, Rāma spoke these words to him.
"Noble by birth, endowed with courage, majestic, and firm in his vows—
how could a person such as you commit a sin for the sake of a kingdom?
O destroyer of enemies, I do not perceive even the slightest fault in you."
Nor should you, out of childishness, reproach your mother.
O knower of dharma, as much reverence as is shown toward a father who is honored by the world, so much, O best of those who uphold dharma, should be shown toward one's mother as well.
"O Raghava, having been told by my mother and father, who are both virtuous in character, 'Go to the forest,' how could I act otherwise?
You must receive the kingdom of Ayodhya, honored by the world."
"I must dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest, clothed in bark garments.
Having thus made this division in the presence of the world and having issued his command, the immensely radiant Great King Daśaratha departed for heaven.
And that righteous king, a man of authority and a teacher to the world, has assigned you your rightful portion; it is right for you to enjoy it.
O gentle one, having taken refuge in the Daṇḍaka forest, you shall remain there for fourteen years.
I shall enjoy the portion granted by my high-souled father;
for that which my father— honored in the world of men, high-souled, and like the lord of the gods— spoke to me,
that alone I consider to be for my supreme welfare, and not the imperishable status of sovereignty over all the worlds.
Then, as those lions among men remained surrounded by their circles of friends and continued to grieve, the night passed away in sorrow.
When the night had turned into a beautiful dawn, those brothers, surrounded by their friends, [arose].
Having offered oblations and performed their recitations at the Mandākinī, they approached Rāma.
Sitting there in silence, none of them said anything;
but Bharata, in the midst of his friends, addressed these words to Rāma.
"My mother has been appeased and this kingdom has been given to me;
therefore, I give it back to you alone—enjoy the kingdom free from all thorns.
Like a dam breached by a great torrent of water at the onset of the rains, [the king's resolve was shattered].
"This great portion of the kingdom is difficult for anyone other than you to govern.
O Lord of the Earth, just as a donkey cannot follow the pace of a horse, nor a bird the flight of Tārkṣya, I lack the power to follow your course."
O Rāma, life is truly well-lived for him who is constantly sustained by others; however, life is miserable for him who must depend upon others for his livelihood.
Just as a tree that has been planted and nurtured by a man [grows to provide shade and fruit], so too is the life of one who supports others.
A great tree with a high trunk is difficult to climb even for a short man;
yet when it has flowered but does not display fruit,
it does not experience that joy for which it was brought to such prominence.
This is the analogy, O mighty-armed one; you ought to understand its meaning:
for if you, our bull-like lord, do not govern us who are your servants. Let the guilds and the foremost men from all sides behold you, O great king.
Like the scorching sun, you, the subduer of enemies, are established in your sovereignty.
O descendant of Kakutstha, let the intoxicated elephants trumpet in your procession;
let the women of the inner apartments rejoice with composed minds.
Hearing those words of Bharata as he entreated Rama, the various people of the city thought, "Well said!
Seeing that illustrious man thus distressed and lamenting, they were deeply moved.
The self-possessed Rāma, having disciplined his soul, consoled Bharata:
"A man has no power over his own will; he is not his own master.
Fate drags him hither and thither."
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall; unions end in separation, and life ends in death.
Just as for ripe fruits there is no fear other than falling, so it is for all things.

Thus, for a man who is born, there is no fear other than death. Just as a house with strong pillars, having become old, collapses, so too do men collapse when they have fallen under the power of old age and death.
Days and nights pass for all living beings here, swiftly exhausting their lifespans like the rays of the sun [evaporate] water in the summer heat.
Grieve for yourself; why do you grieve for another?
The life of one who remains and of one who goes is constantly diminishing.
Death travels along with him; death sits down with him;
having traveled a very long path, he returns accompanied by death.
Wrinkles have appeared on his limbs and his hair has turned white;
when a man is worn out by old age, what indeed can he do to exert his power?
People rejoice when the sun has risen, and they rejoice when the sun has set.
Human beings do not perceive the exhaustion of their own life;
they rejoice upon seeing the arrival of each new season.
Yet, through the revolution of the seasons, there occurs the destruction of the life-force of living beings.
"Just as two pieces of wood might come together in the great ocean and, having met, drift apart after some time has passed;
even so it is with wives, sons, kinsmen, and wealth."
Having come together, they scatter; for their separation is certain. No living being here proceeds according to its own will;
therefore, there is no power in grieving for one who has passed away.
"Just as someone standing on the road might say to a caravan passing by,
'I too shall follow behind you,' so too is this the certain path traveled by our ancestors, our fathers and grandfathers."

How could one who has attained such a state grieve, for whom there is no transgression? As youth falls away like a flowing stream that cannot be turned back, one’s own self must be directed toward happiness; for it is taught that all subjects are sharers in the happiness of their sovereign.
Our father, the lord of the earth, was righteous in soul; having shaken off all sin through auspicious sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, he has gone to heaven,
owing to his proper maintenance of servants and his protection of his subjects.
And by taking wealth according to dharma, our father has gone to the third heaven;
having performed various sacrifices and obtained abundant enjoyments,
and having attained an excellent lifespan, that lord of the earth has gone to the celestial realm.
Having cast off his worn-out human body, our father has indeed attained divine prosperity that dwells in the world of Brahmā;
no wise person such as this ought to grieve for him.
One such as you, and one such as he, are both learned and highly intelligent. These various kinds of grief, as well as lamentation and weeping,
must indeed be avoided by a wise and steadfast man under all circumstances.
Be at ease and do not grieve; go and dwell in that city,
for you have been so commanded by your father, who is self-controlled, O best among the eloquent—
just as I too have been appointed by that very man of meritorious deeds.
Right there I shall carry out the command of my noble father;
it is not right for me to disregard his command, O subduer of enemies.
Therefore, you too must always honor it; he is indeed our kinsman and he is our father.
When Rāma had thus spoken and ceased his meaningful words,
the righteous Bharata addressed these wonderful and righteous words to him:
"O subduer of enemies, who indeed in this world could be such as you?"
Neither sorrow shall distress you, nor shall joy cause you excessive exultation.
You are esteemed by the elders, and you consult them regarding your doubts; whether dead or living, whether in non-existence or existence, you remain as you are.
Whoever should possess such an attainment of wisdom would not be distressed by anything;
having encountered such adversity, he ought not to despair. You, however, are equal to the immortals in courage, a great-souled man true to your promise.

O Raghava, you are all-knowing, all-seeing, and possessed of wisdom. One endowed with such virtues and skilled in the knowledge of both origin and dissolution as you are, ought not to encounter such utterly unbearable suffering.
Whatever evil my lowly mother committed out of affection for me while I was away—that which is so displeasing to me—may you be gracious toward me.
I am bound by the bond of dharma; therefore, I do not [acknowledge] this mother here.
"I shall punish with severe punishment that evil-doer who deserves it.
How could one born of Daśaratha, whose lineage and deeds are pure, knowing what is right, perform such a sinful and loathsome act?"
"My teacher, my active elder, my father, my deceased lord, and my kinsman— I must not revile him in the assembly, for he is a deity.
For who indeed would commit such a sinful deed, devoid of both dharma and worldly purpose?
O knower of dharma, one who knows dharma should act thus, desiring to do what is pleasing to his wife;
for there is an ancient scripture stating that "at the time of death, living beings become deluded," and by acting in this way toward the world, the king has made that scripture manifest.
"Whatever transgression my father has committed out of anger, delusion, or rashness in pursuit of a righteous goal, may you rectify it.
For a son who considers right what his father has transgressed is indeed a virtuous one."
In this world, that is considered offspring; otherwise, it is the opposite.
May you be his offspring; do not, O steadfast one, incur the reproach of the wise in this world by carrying out the evil deed committed by your father.
"Protect Kaikeyī, myself, our father, our friends, our kinsmen, and all the people of the city and the countryside—protect all of this through your power.
Where is the forest, and where is the duty of a Kṣatriya? Where are matted locks, and where is the protection [of the realm]?"
"You ought not to perform such a contradictory deed.
If you wish to practice a dharma born of hardship,
then endure hardship while protecting the four castes according to dharma."
"O knower of dharma, those who know the dharma say that among the four stages of life, the householder's stage is the most excellent; how then can you bear to abandon it?
For I am but a child to you in learning, in status, and by birth."
"How shall I protect the earth while you remain alive? Lacking both wisdom and virtue, a mere child and deprived of my position, I cannot endure to live without you."
O knower of dharma, rule this entire ancestral kingdom, free from thorns and undisturbed, according to your own duty together with your kinsmen.
O knower of dharma, let them consecrate you right here, along with your relatives.
"O you who are skilled in mantras, together with the officiating priests and Vasiṣṭha,
we have consecrated you with the sacred mantras; go now to Ayodhyā for its protection,
having swiftly conquered the worlds as Vāsava did with the Maruts."
Discharging the three debts, thoroughly consuming the ill-wishers,
and satisfying friends with their desires— you alone should instruct me in this matter.
O Noble One, let your friends today be joyful at your consecration.
Today, let your enemies flee terrified in the ten directions;
O bull among men, having wiped away the insults directed at me and my mother,
protect your venerable father today from this transgression.
"I entreat you with my head bowed; show compassion toward me and all my kinsmen, as Maheśvara does toward all living beings.
Or rather, having turned your back on this forest, depart from here."
"I shall go; I will go along with you as well.

Nevertheless, though Bharata, suffering in distress, sought to propitiate King Rāma with his head bowed low, the lord of the earth, steadfast in character and established in his father's command, did not at all set his mind on departing.
Beholding that wondrous steadfastness in Rāghava, the people simultaneously experienced joy and sorrow;

they were sorrowful because he was not going to Ayodhyā, yet they were joyful upon seeing his firm resolve. The sacrificial priests, the leaders of the merchant guilds, and the mothers, overwhelmed with tears, lost their senses.

As Bharata was speaking thus, they praised him, bowed to Rāma, and made their request together. Then the glorious elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa, highly honored in the midst of his kinsmen, replied to Bharata who was speaking in this manner.
"What you have spoken is indeed appropriate:
that a son was born to Kaikeyī from Daśaratha, the best of kings.
O brother, formerly our father, while marrying your mother..."
From his maternal grandfather, he heard of the unsurpassed bride-price for the kingdom;
O King, in the war between the gods and the asuras, the powerful lord, being highly pleased and gratified, granted a boon to your mother.
Then, having given her promise, your illustrious mother, that woman of excellent complexion, requested two boons from that best of men:
"O tiger among men, your kingdom for you, and likewise my exile."
And the king, being thus entreated by her, granted that boon.
O bull among men, I too have been enjoined here by my father to dwell in the forest for fourteen years as a result of that granting of a boon.
Thus, accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā, I have reached this uninhabited forest,
free from opposition and established in the truthful word of my father.
You too, likewise, [should remain] so as to make our father a speaker of truth.
O Indra among kings, he ought to perform the consecration immediately.
O Bharata, knower of dharma, release the lordly king from his debt for my sake; save your father and bring joy to your mother.
For it is heard, O dear one, that in ancient times a glorious śruti was sung by Gaya while he was performing a sacrifice for his ancestors at Gayā itself:
"Because a son delivers his father from the hell named Put, he is called 'putra'."
Therefore, he is called "putra" because he protects his ancestors, or because the son saves them. One should desire many sons who are virtuous and well-versed in sacred learning;
for among those who have gathered together, at least one might go to Gayā.
Thus all the royal sages are convinced, O delighter of the Raghus;
therefore, O best of men, O Lord, deliver your father from hell.
Go to Ayodhyā, Bharata, and win over the subjects.
"O hero, accompanied by Śatrughna and all the twice-born,
I too shall enter the Daṇḍaka forest without delay; O King, I shall go together with these two, Vaidehī and Lakṣmaṇa."

"O Bharata, you yourself become the king of men; I too shall be the king of the wild beasts. Go today to the excellent city with a joyful heart, and I, likewise joyful, shall enter the Daṇḍaka forest.
O Bharata, let the sun’s heat be cooled upon your head by the shade of my royal parasol."
I too shall happily take refuge in that most excellent shade of these forest trees.

O Bharata, you have Śatrughna of virtuous intellect as your companion, and the son of Sumitrā is known to me as my foremost friend; we four, the best of sons, shall attend upon the king who stands firm in truth—do not despair.
While comforting Bharata, Jābāli, the best of brahmins, spoke these words to Rāma, the knower of dharma, which were devoid of dharma:
"It is well, O Rāghava; let not your mind be thus set upon what is purposeless."
Just as with an ordinary man, so it is for the ascetic of noble intellect:
what man is a kinsman to whom, and what is obtainable by anyone from another?
For a living being is born alone, and alone indeed does he perish.
Therefore, O Rāma, that man who becomes attached to mother and father should be known as one who is like a madman; for no one truly belongs to anyone else.
Just as a man traveling to another village might stay somewhere along the way, so it is with human relations.
Having abandoned that dwelling, one should set out on the following day.
In this very way, O descendant of Kakutstha, father, mother, home, and wealth are merely a temporary lodging for humans; the wise do not become attached to them.
Having renounced his ancestral kingdom, that best of men does not deserve to follow a miserable, treacherous, and thorny wrong path.
Consecrate yourself in the prosperous city of Ayodhyā.
For the city, wearing a single braid of hair, awaits you;
O prince, enjoying costly royal pleasures, sport in Ayodhyā as Śakra does in Triviṣṭapa.
He is nothing to you, and you are nothing to him;
you are one king and he is another. Therefore, do what is being told to you. That king has gone to that place where he was destined to go.
This is the way of mortals, yet you are being needlessly distressed. I grieve for those who are devoted solely to wealth and dharma, and not for others;
for having encountered suffering in this world, they meet with destruction after death.
"The Aṣṭakā is for the ancestors as its deity"—thus the common folk have spread this [belief].
Behold the calamity regarding food: for what will the dead eat?
If what is eaten here by one person enters the body of another, [then why do people not eat the flesh of their own parents?]
One should perform a *śrāddha* for one who is traveling abroad; that [offering] shall not be mere food for the journey.
For these books composed by the wise are merely tools for persuasion through gifts:
"Sacrifice! Give! Undergo initiation! Practice austerities! Renounce! (Rāmāyaṇa 2.100.14–15).

"O Mahāmati, form the conviction that there is nothing beyond this; rely upon what is perceptible to the senses and turn your back on what is beyond them. Place before you the wisdom of the virtuous, which serves as a guide for all the world."
"Accept the kingdom, being entreated by Bharata.
Having heard these words of Jābāli, Rāma, the best among those whose souls are truth,
spoke with supreme reasoning and with unerring intelligence.

The words you have spoken here to me for the sake of doing what is pleasing, though they appear to be a duty, are actually a non-duty; though they seem wholesome, they are unwholesome. For a man who lacks self-restraint is possessed of sinful conduct.
One whose conduct and appearance are divided finds no honor among the virtuous.
Whether a man is of noble birth or base, whether he is a hero or merely proud of his manhood,
it is conduct alone that explains whether he is pure or impure.
But a non-noble man may appear like a noble one, being pure despite lacking true purity; he may possess auspicious marks though lacking them, and be of bad character while appearing as if virtuous.
I shall attain [this state] by abandoning what is auspicious, devoid as it is of the prescribed rules of action.
What conscious man, discerning between what ought and ought not to be done, would think much of me in this world as one of evil conduct and a defiler of society?
Whose way shall I follow, or by what conduct may I attain heaven, while I abide by this mode of life that fails my vow? Yet this entire world follows after the way of desire.
For as is the conduct of kings, so indeed is the conduct of their subjects. Truth and compassion are the eternal conduct of a king;
therefore, a kingdom has truth as its essence, and the world is established upon truth.
Both the seers and the gods indeed regard truth alone as supreme;
for in this world, the speaker of truth attains the highest state. Men tremble before a liar as they do before snakes.
In this world, truth is said to be the supreme dharma and the very root of heaven.
Truth alone is the sovereign in the world; Lakṣmī rests upon truth.
All things have their roots in truth; there is no state higher than truth.
"Gifts given, sacrifices performed, oblations offered, and austerities practiced—even the Vedas themselves are established upon truth; therefore, one should be devoted to truth.
One person protects the world, and another protects his family."

For one sinks alone into hell, while another alone is glorified in heaven. Why then should I, who have made a true promise and am bound by truth through my vow of truthfulness, not obey the command of my father?
"Neither out of greed, nor out of delusion, nor out of ignorance, nor possessed by darkness,
shall I break the bridge of truth, for I am my guru’s man of true promise.
For one who is untruthful in covenant, fickle, and of unstable mind— "
"We have heard that neither the gods nor the ancestors accept [offerings] from one who has turned his back on righteousness.
I myself perceive this truth as a duty inherent within my own self;
for the sake of that which is practiced by the virtuous, this burden is welcomed."
I shall indeed abandon the duty of a Kṣatriya, which is unrighteous though clothed in the guise of righteousness, practiced by the base, the cruel, the greedy, and those of sinful deeds;
for one commits sin with the body after having first resolved upon it with the mind.
One speaks falsehood with the tongue; thus, there are three kinds of sinful action.
For the earth, fame, glory, and fortune indeed seek out a man, and they follow him even when he dwells in heaven; therefore, one should devote oneself to truth alone.
For what you have told me after careful consideration, using such reasoned words— "Do this auspicious thing"— would indeed be most ignoble.
For how could I, having promised my father this forest-dwelling, [go back on my word]?
"I shall do as Bharata says, disregarding the word of my elder. Having made this firm vow in the presence of his elder,
the queen Kaikeyī then became joyful at heart.
Dwelling thus in the forest, pure and restricted in diet,
satisfying the ancestors and the gods with holy roots, flowers, and fruits,
I shall maintain my course through the world with my five faculties fully contented.
Free from deceit and full of faith, discerning what ought and ought not to be done,
one who has reached this land of action must perform whatever auspicious deed is required;
for fire, wind, and the moon are the sharers in the fruits of actions.
Having performed a hundred sacrifices, the king of the gods went to the third heaven;
and having undertaken fierce austerities, the great seers ascended to the celestial realm.
[Likewise, one should cultivate] truth, righteousness, valor, compassion for all beings, and pleasant speech.
The virtuous say that honoring the twice-born, the gods, and guests is the path to heaven.
Those who are devoted to dharma, who associate with holy men, who are radiant, preeminent in the virtue of generosity,
non-violent, and free from impurity— such eminent sages become worthy of worship in this world.
Perceiving that Rāma was enraged, Vasiṣṭha replied:
"Jābāli also knows the coming and going of this world;
desiring to turn you back, he spoke these words."
O Lord of the World, learn from me this origin of the world:
everything was once water alone, wherein the earth was fashioned;
from that, Brahmā, the self-existent, arose together with the gods.
Then, having become a boar, he lifted up the earth and created the entire world together with his sons who had perfected their souls;
Brahmā, born from space, is eternal, constant, and imperishable.
From him Marīci was born; Marīci’s son was Kaśyapa.
Vivasvat was born from Kaśyapa, and he is remembered as Vaivasvata Manu.
He was formerly a Prajāpati, and Ikṣvāku was the son of Manu.
Know that Ikṣvāku was the first king in Ayodhyā, to whom Manu gave this prosperous earth.
And the illustrious son of Ikṣvāku was renowned as Kukṣi.
Then, from Kukṣi, a heroic son named Vikukṣi was born.
From Vikukṣi was born the highly energetic and powerful son Bāṇa;
and from Bāṇa was born the long-armed and greatly illustrious Anaraṇya.
Under that best of virtuous men, the great king Anaraṇya, there was no lack of rain, nor was there famine, nor was there any thief whatsoever.
After Anaraṇya, the mighty-armed King Pṛthu indeed reigned.
From that great king Pṛthu was born Triśaṅku;
by virtue of his truthful speech, that hero ascended to heaven in his physical body.
To Triśaṅku was born a son of great fame, Dhundhumāra.
From Dhundhumāra was born the highly resplendent Yuvanāśva;
the illustrious Māndhātṛ became the son of Yuvanāśva;
and from Māndhātṛ was born the highly resplendent Susaṃdhi.
Susaṃdhi also had two sons, Dhruvasaṃdhi and the illustrious Prasenajit. From Dhruvasaṃdhi was born Bharata, the slayer of enemies;
and from the mighty-armed Bharata was born the one named Asita.
Against whom these rival kings arose as enemies—
the Haihayas, the Tālajaṅghas, the Śūras, and the Śaśabindus—
the king was driven into exile after having arrayed them all in battle.
And that sage took delight on that beautiful and excellent mountain;
it is heard that his two wives became pregnant.
There was a descendant of Bhṛgu named Cyavana who had taken refuge in the Himavat.
Having approached that seer, Kālindī paid him homage.
The brahmin addressed her, who desired a boon for the birth of a son;
then, having returned home, the queen gave birth to a son.
But his co-wife, desiring to destroy the fetus, gave him poison;
because he was born together with that very poison, he became known as Sagara.
He was the king named Sagara who caused the ocean to be dug.
Having performed a sacrifice at the auspicious juncture with great force, he terrified these creatures.
We have heard that Asamañja was the son of Sagara;
though still alive, he was cast out by his father for committing evil deeds.
The powerful Aṃśumān was the son of Asamañjas;
Dilīpa was the son of Aṃśumān, and Bhagīratha was the son of Dilīpa.
From Bhagīratha came Kakutstha, by whom the descendants are known as the Kākutsthas.
Kakutstha’s son was Raghu, from whom the lineage of Rāghavas derived its name.
Raghu’s son was the radiant Kalmāṣapāda, who grew up as a man-eater and became renowned on earth as Saudāsa.
The son of Kalmāṣapāda was the one renowned as Śaṅkhaṇa, who,
having encountered his prowess, perished along with his army.
The son of Śaṅkhaṇa was the heroic and illustrious Sudarśana.
The son of Sudarśana was Agnivarṇa; the son of Agnivarṇa was Śīghraga. Maru was the son of Śīghraga, and Praśuśruka was the son of Maru.
The son of Praśuśruka was Ambarīṣa, who possessed great luster.
Ambarīṣa’s son was Nahuṣa, whose valor was truth;
and Nahuṣa’s son was the supremely righteous Nābhāga.
Aja and Suvrata were both the sons of Nābhāga.
And the son of Aja was the righteous King Daśaratha;
you are his eldest heir, renowned by the name Rāma. Therefore, accept your own kingdom and look after the world, O King.

For among all the Ikṣvākus, the first-born becomes the king; the younger son is consecrated in the kingdom by the elder as the eldest. Therefore, you ought not today to abandon this eternal family dharma of the Raghavas.
"O you of great renown, govern the earth, rich in jewels and vast in kingdoms, just as your father did.
Then Vasiṣṭha, the royal priest, having thus addressed Rāma,
spoke again these further words endowed with righteousness.
For a man born here in this world, O Raghava, descendant of Kakutstha, there are three gurus: the teacher, the father, and the mother.
For it is the father, O bull among men, who procreates this person.
"The teacher bestows wisdom; therefore, he is called a guru.
O scorcher of foes, I am that teacher of your father and of you as well.
By acting upon my word, you shall not deviate from the path of the virtuous."
For these assemblies and guilds have gathered here; practicing righteousness among them, my dear son, you must not deviate from the path of the virtuous.
You ought not to act contrary to your aged mother, who is devoted to dharma.
But by doing her bidding, O Raghava, you shall not overstep the path of the virtuous. By complying with the request of Bharata as he entreats you,
O you whose prowess is truth and righteousness, you shall not overstep yourself.
Thus addressed so sweetly by his preceptor, Rāghava,
that bull among men, replied to Vasiṣṭha as he sat there:
"That which parents always perform for their son..."
But that which has been done for one by a mother and a father cannot easily be repaid—
by giving according to one's ability, by bathing, clothing, constant kind speech, and likewise by nurturing.
"For that King Daśaratha was my progenitor and father;
whatever has been commanded by me for him shall not be in vain.
Thus addressed by Rāma, Bharata immediately replied.
Extremely noble yet deeply distressed in mind, he said to the charioteer:
"O charioteer, quickly spread kusha grass for me upon this bare ground;
I shall sit here in fasting protest until my noble brother is appeased."
"Without food, without light, like a Brahmin who has lost his wealth,
I shall lie here before the hall until he returns.
But seeing Sumantra looking toward Rāma, he became dejected in spirit.
Having had the best of kusha grass prepared, he himself spread it upon the ground.
Then Rāma, the most excellent of royal sages and possessed of great splendor, said to him:
"Bharata, my dear son, what am I doing that you would sit down in opposition to me?"
For a Brahmin may indeed obstruct men here by lying on one side, but there is no rule for consecrated kings to sit in protest.
Arise, O tiger among men; abandon this cruel vow.
"O Raghava, go from here quickly to Ayodhyā, the best of cities.
But Bharata, while remaining seated, looked all around at the people of the city and the countryside and said, "Why do you not instruct our noble brother?"
The people of the city and the countryside said to that high-souled descendant of Kakutstha, "We recognize that Raghava speaks correctly;
for even this illustrious one stands firm in the word of his father."
"For this very reason, we are not able to turn you back directly.
Having understood their words, Rāma spoke these words:
"Understand thus the speech of your friends, who possess the eye of dharma."
"Having heard both of these, O Raghava, perceive them clearly; arise, O mighty-armed one, touch me and likewise touch water.
Then, having risen and touched water, Bharata spoke these words.
"Let my assembly, the ministers, and the guilds hear me:
I do not beg the kingdom from my father, nor do I instruct my mother;
I recognize the noble Raghava as one who knows the supreme dharma."
"If, however, you must necessarily dwell [there] and the word of our father must be fulfilled,
I alone shall dwell in the forest for fourteen years. At these truthful words of his brother, the righteous-souled one was struck with wonder.
Looking upon the people of the city and the countryside, Rāma said:
"Whatever was sold, pledged, or purchased by my father while he was alive cannot be annulled by me or by Bharata."
"I shall not incur the reproach of living in the forest;
what Kaikeyī said was right, and my father has done what is good.
I know Bharata to be patient and one who honors his elders."
"Everything here is auspicious for that great-souled one who is true to his promise.
Having returned from the forest with this brother of mine, who is devoted to righteousness, I shall once again become the supreme lord of the earth."
"For the king was indeed constrained by Kaikeyī, and I acted upon her word; by this deed, I have freed my father, that lord of the earth, from falsehood.
Thus he spoke to those two brothers of incomparable splendor, who caused his hair to stand on end.
Beholding that meeting, the assembled great seers were filled with wonder;
the invisible hosts of ṛṣis, siddhas,
and supreme ṛṣis praised those two high-souled brothers, the descendants of Kakutstha.
Blessed is he who has two sons such as these, knowers of dharma and possessing the prowess of dharma;
for having heard their conversation, we truly long for them both.
Then the hosts of sages, desiring the swift destruction of the ten-necked one, [spoke].
Gathering together, they spoke these words to Bharata, that tiger among kings:
"O you who are born of noble lineage, possessed of great wisdom, of great conduct, and of great fame—
if you have regard for your father, you must accept the word of Rāma."
"We desire that this Rāma be forever free from debt to his father;
for by discharging that debt, Daśaratha has gone to heaven.
Having spoken these words, the Gandharvas together with the great ṛṣis [departed].
And all those royal sages likewise departed for their respective destinations. Delighted by those auspicious words, the handsome Rāma, his face beaming with joy, paid honor to those seers.
But Bharata, his limbs failing him and his voice faltering, spoke these words again to Rāghava with palms joined in reverence,
reflecting upon the duties of kings and the continuity of family traditions.
O descendant of Kakutstha, you ought to grant my request and that of my mother.
For I am not able to protect this vast kingdom alone, nor to satisfy the citizens and the people of the provinces who are devoted to me.
For our kinsmen, warriors, friends, and well-wishers all look toward you alone, just as farmers await the rain-cloud;
O highly wise one, accept this kingdom and establish it.
"You are capable, O descendant of Kakutstha, in the protection of the world.
Having spoken thus, Bharata then fell at his brother's feet;
speaking so kindly, he earnestly entreated Rāma in this manner.
Placing his brother on his lap, Rāma himself spoke these words to him,
who was dark-complexioned, with eyes like lotus petals, and possessed a voice like that of a rutting swan:
"This understanding has come to you— both that which is innate and that which is acquired through discipline."
"My dear son, you are fully capable of protecting even the entire earth.
Consult with your ministers, friends, and wise counselors regarding all affairs, however great they may be, and then carry them out."

Lakṣmī might depart from the Moon, or the Himavat might abandon its snow, or the ocean might overstep its shore, but I shall not violate my father’s promise. Whether out of passion or greed, O dear one, this was done for you by your mother.
"You must not take that to heart; you should conduct yourself toward him as toward a mother.
To the son of Kausalyā who was speaking thus—whose splendor was like that of the sun and whose appearance was like the moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight—Bharata replied.
"O Noble One, please step into these gold-adorned sandals with your two feet;
for these shall provide for the welfare and security of all the world.
Having ascended them and then descended again, that tiger among men—
The one of great splendor gave them to the high-souled Bharata.
Having accepted those well-adorned sandals, the powerful Bharata, who knew what was right,
circumambulated Rāghava and placed them upon the head of his excellent elephant.

Then, having honored those people in due order, as well as his elders and the ministers and subjects, the enhancer of the Raghu dynasty dismissed his two younger brothers; he remained steadfast in his own duty, immovable like the Himalayas.
His mothers, their throats choked with tears, were indeed unable to address him because of their grief.
Having saluted all his mothers, Rāma entered his own cottage weeping.
Then, placing the sandals upon his head, Bharata,
filled with joy, ascended the chariot accompanied by Śatrughna.
Vasiṣṭha, Vāmadeva, Jābāli of firm vows,
and all the ministers honored for their counsel, proceeded ahead;
they then went toward the beautiful Mandākinī river, facing the east.
Performing circumambulations of the great mountain Citrakūṭa and beholding its thousands of various and delightful mineral veins,
Bharata then proceeded along its side with his army.
Then, not far from Citrakūṭa, the wise Bharata beheld the hermitage where the sage Bharadvāja had made his dwelling.
Having reached that hermitage of Bharadvāja, the intelligent one...
Having descended from the chariot, the delighter of his lineage paid homage at Bharata's feet. Then, filled with joy, Bharadvāja spoke these words to Bharata:
"My son, has your purpose been accomplished now that you have met with Rāma?"
Thus addressed by the wise Bharadvāja, Bharata,
who is devoted to righteousness, replied to Bharadvāja:
"Though entreated by my preceptor and by me, he of firm prowess..."
Rāghava, supremely delighted, spoke these words to Vasiṣṭha:
"I shall indeed fulfill that very promise made by my father in accordance with the truth;
for fourteen years is the duration of the vow my father gave me."
Thus addressed, the immensely wise Vasiṣṭha, skilled in speech, replied with these great words to Rāghava, who was himself eloquent:
"Joyfully bestow upon him these sandals adorned with gold."
"In Ayodhyā, O man of great wisdom,
which ensures your security and prosperity," thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, Rāghava stood facing the east and gave those sandals fashioned of gold to him for the sake of his kingdom.
"I have returned, permitted by the great-souled Rāma;
I am going back to Ayodhyā itself, taking with me the auspicious sandals.
Having heard these auspicious words of the high-souled Bharata, [the people were filled with joy].
The sage Bharadvāja uttered these most auspicious words:
"O tiger among men, best of those endowed with virtuous conduct, it is no wonder that nobility should reside in you, just as rainwater flows to the low ground."
"Your father, the mighty-armed Daśaratha, was immortal—
he who had such a son as you, a righteous soul devoted to dharma. To that high-souled sage who had spoken these words, he replied with palms joined in reverence.
Having clasped his feet, he began to take his leave;
then, after circumambulating Bharadvāja again and again,
the illustrious Bharata departed for Ayodhyā with his ministers.
With chariots, carts, horses, and elephants, that vast army of Bharata’s followers turned back once more.
Then they crossed the divine river Yamunā, which was garlanded with waves.

They all beheld once again that river Gaṅgā, with its auspicious waters. Having crossed that river filled with beautiful water, he entered the lovely city of Śṛṅgaverapura together with his kinsmen and his army.
From Śṛṅgaverapura, Bharata, tormented by grief, beheld Ayodhyā once more and spoke thus to his charioteer:
"O charioteer, look! Ayodhyā is devastated; it does not shine."
Devoid of splendor, joyless, dejected, and with its sounds silenced, [Ayodhyā lay desolate].
Then the illustrious lord Bharata, arriving in a chariot with a smooth and deep resonance, quickly entered Ayodhyā.
It was like a dark night, shrouded in gloom and devoid of light, where cats and owls roam, and men and elephants lie hidden;
it was like the beloved wife of the enemy of Rahu, blazing with radiant splendor.
She was like Rohiṇī afflicted by the risen planet Rāhu;
she was like a mountain stream emaciated, its waters slightly warm and agitated, its birds scorched by the heat, and its fish, large and small, and crocodiles lying dormant.
Like a smokeless flame rising from the sacrificial fire, golden-hued and sprinkled with oblations, that crest of fire has now reached its dissolution;
its armor shattered, its elephants, horses, chariots, and banners broken.
She was like an army in a great battle that has lost its heroes and fallen into distress;
she was like a wave of the ocean that had risen with foam and roar, only to become silent once the wind that stirred it had subsided.
Abandoned by all the sacrificial implements and the worthy officiating priests, she was like a sacrificial altar that has become silent once the time for the Soma-pressing has passed;
she stood distressed in the midst of the cow-pen, no longer grazing on fresh grass.
She was like a longing cow abandoned by her bull,
or like a fresh string of pearls deprived of its finest, most radiant, smooth, and blazing gems.
Suddenly shaken from her place as her merit was exhausted,
she was like a star fallen from the sky, its vast radiance withdrawn,
though still adorned with flowers and graced by intoxicated bees at the end of spring.
Like a forest creeper withered and scorched by the sparks of a raging wildfire; like the entire city with its thoroughfares bewildered, its markets and shops closed,
resembling the sky shrouded by clouds that conceal the moon and stars.
It was like an unadorned drinking hall in the sky where the revelers have been slain, covered with broken, excellent drinking bowls and overturned cups,
its ground torn up and uneven, strewn with shattered vessels.
It was like a water-station that had been used and broken, as if it had collapsed;
and like the great, extended bowstring of swift warriors, still joined with its loops, fallen to the ground severed by arrows from their weapons.
She was driven suddenly by that horseman, skilled in battle,
like a weak young mare abandoned with her gear laid down;
she entered the mass of clouds as the rainy season had set in deep.
Like the radiance of the sun obscured by dark clouds, so was [the path] hidden.
Then the illustrious Bharata, son of Daśaratha, standing upon his chariot,
spoke these words to the charioteer who was driving that excellent vehicle.
Why indeed is the sound of singing and musical instruments not heard today in Ayodhyā as it was before, deep and resonant? And why is the fragrance of wine and garlands so faint?
The fragrance of burning agallochum did not waft everywhere;
nor was there the sound of excellent vehicles, the gentle neighing of horses,
the trumpeting of elephants in rut, or the great roar of chariots.
Now that Rāma has been exiled, it is no longer heard in this city;
the great highways of Ayodhyā do not shine with young men of handsome attire walking with a stately gait as they come and go.
Thus lamenting in many ways, he entered his father’s residence,
which was bereft of that lord of men, like a cave devoid of its lion.
Then, having settled his mothers in Ayodhyā, he of firm vows—
Then Bharata, tormented by grief, spoke thus to his elders:
"I shall go to Nandigrāma; I bid you all farewell today.
There, in the absence of Rāghava, I shall endure all this sorrow."
"For the king has gone to heaven, and my elder is dwelling in the forest;
I await Rāma for the sake of the kingdom, for he is the illustrious king.
Having heard these auspicious words of the high-souled Bharata, [Vasiṣṭha spoke].
All the ministers and the family priest Vasiṣṭha said:
"O Bharata, the words you have spoken are worthy and praiseworthy; out of affection for your brother, they are truly suited to you alone."
Who among men would not approve of you, who are ever devoted to your kinsmen, who abide in brotherly affection, and who have entered upon the path of the noble?
Having heard the words of the ministers, which were as desired and pleasing, [Rama spoke].
He spoke these words to his charioteer: "Let my chariot be yoked.
With a joyful countenance, the illustrious prince, having offered salutations to all his mothers, ascended the chariot accompanied by Śatrughna.
Having quickly mounted the chariot, both Śatrughna and Bharata, filled with supreme joy and surrounded by ministers and family priests, set forth; meanwhile,
the elders and the twice-born led by Vasiṣṭha proceeded in front of them.
They all set out facing the east toward Nandigrāma;
and as Bharata departed, that army— crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots— and all the city-dwellers followed him, though they had not been summoned.
Standing upon his chariot, the righteous Bharata, who was devoted to his brother,
quickly proceeded to Nandigrāma, placing the sandals upon his head.
Then Bharata swiftly entered Nandigrāma.
Quickly descending from the chariot, he spoke these words to his elders:
"This kingdom has been given to me by my brother himself as a formal entrustment; and here are these gold-adorned sandals, which shall provide for its security and prosperity."
I shall protect this until the arrival of Raghava;
having quickly joined them once more to Raghava myself, I shall behold those two feet of Rama together with the sandals.
Then, having laid down my burden and met with Rāghava,
I shall hand over the kingdom to my elder and devote myself to the service of my guru. And having given these excellent sandals to Rāghava as a token of my abdication, I shall depart.
"If this kingdom and Ayodhyā are restored, I shall be cleansed of sin.
Once the descendant of Kakutstha is consecrated and the people are joyful and delighted, my pleasure and my fame would be four times greater than from the kingship itself."
Lamenting thus in distress, the highly illustrious Bharata,
sorrowful, ruled the kingdom from Nandigrāma together with his ministers;
that lord wore garments of bark and matted hair, assuming the garb of a sage.
Then the hero Bharata, accompanied by his army, dwelt in Nandigrāma;
longing for Rāma’s return, he was devoted to his brother,
obedient to his brother’s word, and intent on fulfilling his promise.

Then, having consecrated the sandals, Bharata dwelt in Nandigrāma at that time, offering all governance to the two sandals. While Bharata had departed, Rāma continued to dwell in the forest of asceticism.
He observed with agitation the anxiety of the ascetics;
he noticed that those who had taken refuge in Rāma and were devoted to him in the hermitage in front of Citrakūṭa were now filled with longing.
Pointing at Rāma with their eyes and knitted brows, they spoke apprehensively to one another and held private conversations in low voices. Observing their anxiety, Rāma became suspicious of himself.
Then, with palms joined in reverence, he spoke thus to the sage, the head of the community:
"O Blessed One, is there perhaps some change in my former conduct that is being observed, because of which these ascetics are undergoing such agitation?"
"Has any conduct of my younger brother Lakṣmaṇa been observed by the sages that was inconsistent with his own character due to negligence?
And has he remained devoted to serving you while attending to me?"
"Sītā does not behave in a manner befitting one accustomed to the life of a young woman. Then the seer, aged by years and worn out by asceticism,
spoke as if trembling to Rāma, who was supremely compassionate toward all beings.
O dear one, how could there be such a lapse on the part of Vaidehī, who is of virtuous nature and likewise devoted to what is good— especially toward ascetics?
This situation regarding the ascetics has arisen solely because of you.
Distressed by those demons, they spoke these words among themselves:
"A certain Rākṣasa named Khara, the younger brother of Rāvaṇa, has here uprooted all the ascetics dwelling in Janasthāna."
Arrogant, boastful of victory, cruel, a man-eater, haughty, and wicked— he does not tolerate you, my dear,
ever since you have been staying in this hermitage, father.
From that time forward, the rākṣasas began to harass the ascetics;
for they manifested themselves in various forms— loathsome, cruel, terrifying, deformed, and unpleasant to behold.
Having joined those ascetics with unworthy and impure things,
these ignoble men stand before others and quickly strike them down;
they do so by hiding themselves unobserved in various locations within the hermitages.
There, those small-minded ones take delight in destroying the ascetics;
they cast away the sacrificial ladles and vessels, douse the fires with water,
and trample the jars when the time for the oblation has arrived.
"O Rāma, those sages, wishing to abandon their hermitages which have been occupied by those evil-minded ones,
are now urging me to depart for another land before physical violence toward the ascetics occurs."
"For those wicked ones reveal themselves; we shall abandon this hermitage.
Not far from here is a forest with various and abundant roots and fruits;
I shall take refuge once more in that ancient hermitage along with my followers."
"O dear one, such harshness is improper even toward you;
go from here with us if your mind is so inclined,
for there is constant danger to him who is accompanied by his wife, O Raghava."
"Even though you are capable, staying here today is indeed painful for you," said the prince Rāma to that ascetic;
yet he was unable to restrain with further words the one who was so eager to depart.
Having greeted, taken leave of, and consoled Rāghava,

that leader of the community departed for his hermitage, leaving behind his kinsmen along with his family. Rāma, having seen off the host of sages from that place by following them a short distance and having saluted the sage who was the leader of the community, [returned].
Having been granted permission by them, who were filled with joy, and having received their instructions on his purpose, he returned to his own dwelling for a virtuous stay.
Yet that lordly Rāghava did not abandon the hermitage, even for a moment;
for the ascetics, who maintained the virtues practiced by the seers, constantly followed Rāghava.
But when the ascetics had departed, Rāghava reflected and, for many reasons, did not find dwelling there pleasing at that time:
"Here I saw Bharata, as well as my mothers and the citizens."
And that memory follows me constantly as I grieve for them; by the encampment of that great-souled one,
the ground was severely trampled by the excrement of horses and elephants.
Thinking, "Therefore, let us go elsewhere," Rāghava set out, accompanied by Vaidehī and Lakṣmaṇa.
Having reached the hermitage of Atri, the highly illustrious one paid his respects to him.
And the venerable Atri received him like a son;
having personally assigned all hospitality with great honor,
he comforted both the son of Sumitrā and the highly fortunate Sītā.
Having greeted his aged wife, who had arrived there and been duly honored,
he who knew the dharma and was devoted to the welfare of all beings comforted the highly fortunate ascetic Anasūyā, who lived according to righteousness.
"Accept Vaidehī," said the best of sages.
And he described that ascetic woman, a practitioner of dharma, to Rāma, saying:
"Ten years ago, when the world was scorched by a continuous drought..."
By her, roots and fruits were created and the Ganges was set in motion;
she was endowed with fierce asceticism and adorned by her religious observances.
By her, great penance was performed for ten thousand years.

O dear one, by means of her vows of freedom from malice, all obstacles have been removed. And she, who hastened for the sake of the gods' mission and made ten nights into a single night— she, O sinless one, has become like a mother to you.
"Let Vaidehī approach this illustrious woman, who is worthy of the homage of all beings, for she is aged and ever free from anger.
To that sage speaking thus, Rāghava replied, "So be it."
He spoke these excellent words to Sītā, who was well-versed in dharma:
"O princess, you have heard what has been uttered by this sage;
for the sake of your own welfare, go quickly to that ascetic woman."
"Go quickly to her who is known in the world by the name Anasūyā because of her deeds— that ascetic woman who is worthy of being approached.
Having heard these words of Rāghava, Sītā, desiring his welfare, [prepared to go].
The Maithilī approached that wife of Atri, who was knowledgeable in dharma,
who was frail, wrinkled, aged, with hair white from old age,
and whose limbs were constantly trembling like a plantain tree in a strong wind.
Then Sītā, composed and self-possessed, saluted the highly blessed Anasūyā, who was devoted to her husband, and announced her own name.
And having thus greeted that faultless ascetic woman, Vaidehī addressed her.
With palms joined in reverence and filled with joy, she inquired after her well-being.
Then, seeing the highly fortunate Sītā, who was devoted to righteousness, she spoke consolingly and cheerfully: "By good fortune, you remain steadfast in dharma."
"O Sītā, O proud lady, having abandoned your kinsmen, your pride, and your prosperity,
it is by good fortune that you follow Rāma, who is confined to the forest.
Whether he dwells in the city or the forest, whether he is virtuous or if he is wicked— "
For those women whose husband is dear to them, their worlds are of great prosperity.
Whether he be ill-behaved, driven by lust, or even destitute of wealth,
for women of noble nature, the husband is the supreme deity.
As I reflect upon it, O Vaidehī, I see no relative superior to this,
which is appropriate in every respect and like imperishable ascetic merit itself;
yet wicked women do not perceive the distinction between virtue and vice in this way.
O Maithilī, those women who have their hearts set on sensual desires and who wander about with their husbands as their masters,
incur infamy and a fall from dharma when they come under the sway of improper conduct— such indeed are those women.
"But women like you, endowed with virtues and having perceived the higher and lower worlds, shall roam in heaven just like those who have performed meritorious deeds.
Thus addressed by Anasūyā, whose mind was free from malice, Vaidehī—
Having honored her words, he began to speak softly:
"It is no wonder, noble lady, that you address me thus;
for this is also known to me, that for a woman, the husband is her preceptor."
"O noble lady, even if this man were my husband devoid of good conduct, he should nevertheless be served by me without hesitation;
how much more so since he is praiseworthy for his virtues, compassionate, and has conquered his senses?"
Steadfast in his affection, righteous in soul, devoted to his mother, and dear to his father—
the mighty Rāma conducts himself toward the other wives of the king in exactly the same manner as he does toward Kausalyā.

Even toward women seen but once, the hero, who is devoted to his king and knows the dharma, conducts himself like a mother, casting aside all pride. And as she was entering this desolate forest so full of fear, he acted thus.
For that which was settled by my mother-in-law remains fixed in my heart;
and those instructions I received from my mother long ago at the time of the giving of my hand, in the presence of the fire, have also been held fast by me.
All of that has been renewed by your words, O practitioner of dharma; for a woman, there is no austerity prescribed other than service to her husband.
Sāvitrī, having performed service to her husband, is glorified in heaven.
Likewise, you have gone to heaven through your service to your husband;
you are the most excellent of all women. And this Rohiṇī, the goddess among the stars in heaven, is not seen for even a moment without the Moon.
"Excellent women such as these, firm in their vows toward their husbands,
are honored in the world of the gods by virtue of their own meritorious deeds.
Then Anasūyā, having heard the words spoken by Sītā, was filled with joy.
Smelling her on the head, he spoke to the princess of Mithilā, gladdening her:
"Indeed, I possess great ascetic power acquired through various observances; relying upon that strength, O Sītā of pure vows, I offer you a boon."
"O Maithilī, your words are appropriate and fitting;
I am pleased. Tell me what I may do for you that is suitable;
say 'it is done,'" Sītā said to her who was endowed with the power of asceticism.
Thus addressed by her, she who knows the dharma became even more joyful;
"O Sītā, I shall indeed make your joy fruitful.
Here is this divine, excellent garland, clothing, and ornaments."
"And this precious body-unguent and ointment, O Vaidehī,
given by me— this shall adorn your limbs, Sītā; it is worthy of you, unblemished, and shall remain so forever."
"O daughter of Janaka, with my limbs anointed with divine unguents,
I shall grace my husband just as Śrī graces the imperishable Viṣṇu. She [then] took the garment, the unguent, the ornaments, and likewise the garlands.
Maithilī accepted that unsurpassed gift of affection. Having received that gift of affection, the illustrious and steadfast Sītā, with her hands joined in reverence, waited upon the ascetic woman.
Then Anasūyā, firm in her vows, approached Sītā as she sat nearby and began to ask about a certain pleasant story:
"It is said that you were won by this illustrious man at his svayaṃvara."
"O Sītā, this story concerning Rāghava has reached my ears.
O Maithilī, I wish to hear that story in detail; you ought to tell it to me fully, exactly as it was experienced."
Thus addressed by that practitioner of dharma, Sītā said,
"Listen," and then related this story:
"There was a heroic lord of Mithilā named Janaka, who was a knower of dharma."
Delighting in the duty of a Kṣatriya, he rules the earth with justice. While that king, plow in hand, was tilling the circle of his field,
it is said that I emerged, having pierced through the earth, as the daughter of that monarch.
Seeing me with my entire body covered in dust, King Janaka, intent on scattering handfuls of grain, was filled with wonder;
and being childless, he himself affectionately took me onto his lap.
Saying, "She is my daughter," he bestowed his affection upon me. And a voice, seemingly human, spoke from the sky:
"It is even so, O Lord of Men; by right, she is your daughter."
Then my father, the righteous lord of Mithilā, was filled with joy, O king,
having attained great prosperity through the acquisition of me;
and by that performer of meritorious deeds, I was given to his eldest queen as if she were his cherished desire.
I have been cherished by her with maternal affection and tenderness.
But seeing that my age has reached a point easily associated with union with a husband, my father fell into anxiety, distressed like a poor man who has lost his wealth.
In this world, the father of a maiden suffers humiliation from people who are his equals or even his inferiors,
even if he himself is equal to Śakra on earth. Perceiving that such an insult was not far off for himself, the king—

Like a man without a boat who has entered the ocean of thought, he could not reach the further shore. For, though reflecting upon it, that protector of the earth could find no husband for me— one born not from a womb, and one who was both worthy and suitable.
As that wise king was reflecting continuously, this thought arose in him: "I shall hold a svayaṃvara for my daughter.
Then, at his great sacrifice, he was visited by the high-souled Varuṇa.
Out of affection, he gave him an excellent bow and two quivers with inexhaustible arrows;
yet, due to its weight, even the lords of men were unable to bend it, even in their dreams, despite all their effort.
