Having obtained that bow, my father, who speaks the truth, first addressed the assembled kings and said: "That man who, having lifted this bow, makes it strung," ||| Ram_2,110.40 ||| "and [draws] the arrow from the notch to the tip, he shall win me as his wife. ||| Ram_2,110.41 ||| But no king was able to lift that bow, much less string it. ||| Ram_2,110.42 ||| Then, O Raghava, my father spoke to me, "O son, you must fulfill this vow. ||| Ram_2,110.43 ||| And so, having taken that bow, I lifted it with ease and made it strung. ||| Ram_2,110.44 ||| Then, having drawn the arrow from the notch to the tip, I released it toward the target. ||| Ram_2,110.45 ||| It pierced the target and entered the earth, like a snake entering its hole. ||| Ram_2,110.46 ||| Thereupon, all those kings were filled with wonder; they lowered their heads and stood silent. ||| Ram_2,110.47 ||| Then, having been invited by my father, I entered the city of Mithila, where I was honored by the people. ||| Ram_2,110.48 ||| Having married Sita, I lived there for twelve years, enjoying every pleasure. ||| Ram_2,110.49 ||| Then, O Rama, my father, the great king, departed for the forest to practice asceticism. ||| Ram_2,110.50 ||| He installed Bharata on the throne and consecrated me as the heir apparent. ||| Ram_2,110.51 ||| While I was ruling the kingdom righteously, the subjects were happy and free from fear. ||| Ram_2,110.52 ||| Then, O Rama, the aged king, having performed the funeral rites for his father, ruled the earth for ten thousand years. ||| Ram_2,110.53 ||| After he had passed away, I was consecrated by the citizens and the ministers as the king of the earth. ||| Ram_2,110.54 ||| I have ruled the kingdom for eleven thousand years, O Rama, and I am now old and feeble. ||| Ram_2,110.55 ||| Therefore, O Rama, please accept this kingdom, which has been enjoyed by your ancestors, along with its treasury and its army. ||| Ram_2,110.56 ||| O best of men, I am old and my life is at its end; I wish to depart for the forest to practice asceticism. ||| Ram_2,110.57 ||| O Rama, you are the protector of the world and the refuge of the people; therefore, protect the subjects as your own children. ||| Ram_2,110.58 ||| O Raghava, I have ruled the kingdom for many years; I am weary and desire to go to the forest. ||| Ram_2,110.59 ||| O Rama, I am old and my senses are failing; I wish to renounce this body and enter the forest. ||| Ram_2,110.60 ||| O Rama, you are the lord of the earth and the protector of the world; therefore, protect the subjects as your own children. ||| Ram_2,110.61 ||| O Raghava, I have ruled the kingdom for many years; I am weary and desire to go to the forest. ||| Ram_2,110.62 ||| O Rama, I am old and my senses are failing; I wish to renounce this body and enter the forest. ||| Ram_2,110.63 ||| O Rama, you are the lord of the earth and the protector of the world; therefore, protect the subjects as your own children. ||| Ram_2,110.64 ||| O Raghava, I have ruled the kingdom for many years; I am weary and desire to go to the forest. ||| Ram_2,110.65 ||| O Rama, I am old and my senses are failing; I wish to renounce this body and enter the forest. ||| Ram_2,110.66 ||| O Rama, you are the lord of the earth and the protector of the world; therefore, protect the subjects
"She shall become my daughter-in-law; of this there is no doubt.
Having seen that most excellent bow, which was like a mountain in its weight, the kings offered their salutations and departed, unable even to lift it.
After a very long time, this Raghava of great splendor,
Rama whose prowess is truth, has arrived together with his brother Lakshmana and Vishvamitra to witness the sacrifice.
But the righteous Viśvāmitra, who had been highly honored by my father,
spoke there to his father: "These two sons of Daśaratha, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, brothers, are desirous of seeing the bow."
Thus addressed by that brahmin, he brought forward the bow.
In the mere twinkling of an eye, that valiant one bent it, and having fixed the string, he suddenly drew it back with great strength.
As he was drawing it with full force, the bow broke in two in the middle;
its sound was terrifying, like that of a fallen thunderbolt.
Then, there, I [was presented] to Rāma by my father, who is true to his promise.
Raising up an excellent water vessel, she prepared to give it;
yet Raghava did not accept what was being offered at that time,
for he had not yet ascertained the will of his father, the lord and ruler of Ayodhya.
Then, having taken leave of my father-in-law, the aged King Daśaratha, I was given by my father to Rāma, who knows his own self;
and my younger sister, the virtuous and lovely Urmilā, [was given to Lakṣmaṇa].
My father himself gave me as a wife even to Lakṣmaṇa. Thus was I given to Rāma at that svayaṃvara; and by my devotion to dharma, I am devoted to my husband, the best among the valiant.
But Anasūyā, who knew the dharma, having heard that great tale,
embraced the princess of Mithilā with her arms and smelled the crown of her head, saying:
"What you have spoken is sweet, wonderful, and composed of distinct syllables and words."
I have heard all that occurred during the svayaṃvara. O sweet-spoken lady, I take great delight in your story;
the glorious sun has set, ushering in the auspicious night.
The sound of birds that were scattered about during the day for the sake of food is now heard at the time of twilight as they settle down for the sake of sleep;
and here are these sages, wet from their ritual ablutions, purifying themselves with fruits.
They move together, their bark garments drenched with water. When the sacrificial fires of the sages have been offered according to the prescribed rites,
smoke, reddish like the body of a pigeon, is seen rising up, stirred by the wind.
For the trees, though possessing few leaves, have become dense on all sides;
even in a distant place, they do not reveal the directions at all. The creatures that roam by night are moving about everywhere.
For these are indeed deer of the penance grove, lying down at the bathing places.
O Sītā, night has fully set in, adorned with the stars;
the moon, clothed in moonlight, is seen risen in the sky.
"Go, I give you leave; become an attendant of Rāma.
For I have been thoroughly gratified by your sweet conversation.
Moreover, O Maithilī, adorn yourself right before my eyes."
"O child, bring me joy, you who are adorned with divine ornaments. Having thus adorned herself, Sītā, resembling the daughter of a god,
bowed her head to her and went toward Rāma.
Thus Rāghava, the best among speakers, beheld Sītā adorned in that manner; he rejoiced at the ascetic woman’s gift of affection. Then Maithilī Sītā reported everything to Rāma.
The ascetic woman gave gifts of affection consisting of garments, ornaments,
and garlands; and Rāma and the great chariot-warrior Lakṣmaṇa became overjoyed upon seeing this hospitality toward Maithilī, which is very difficult for mortals to obtain.

Then, at the end of that auspicious night, the joy of the Raghus, whose face resembles the moon, dwelt there contentedly, honored by the ascetics and the perfected ones (siddhas). When that night had passed, he performed the consecration and offered oblations into the sacred fires.
Those two tigers among men took leave of the forest-dwelling ascetics.
Those forest-dwelling ascetics, practitioners of dharma, spoke to them concerning the movement through that forest, which was overrun by rākṣasas.
"This is the path of the great seers who gather fruits in the forest;
by this way, O Raghava, you are able to traverse the difficult woods.
Having been thus granted a blessing by those twice-born ascetics with palms joined in reverence, the scorcher of foes [departed].
Accompanied by his wife and Lakṣmaṇa, Rāghava entered the forest like the sun entering a circle of clouds.
Having entered the great Daṇḍaka forest,
the self-possessed and invincible Rāma beheld a circle of hermitages belonging to ascetics.
Encircled by a fence of kusha grass and endowed with Brahmanic splendor,
it was like the blazing and invincible solar disc in the sky;
it was a refuge for all beings, with its courtyards always well-swept.
It was constantly honored and attended by throngs of Apsarases;
it was adorned with spacious fire-sanctuaries, sacrificial ladles, vessels, deerskins, kusha grass, sacrificial fuel, water-pitchers, fruits, and roots.
It was surrounded by great forest trees, auspicious and laden with sweet fruit;
it was consecrated by offerings and oblations, holy, resounding with the chanting of the Vedas,
and strewn with wild flowers and a lotus pond filled with blossoms.

It was filled with ancient sages who subsisted on fruits and roots, were self-controlled, and wore garments of bark and black antelope skins; it was graced by holy supreme seers who shone like the sun and fire and were restricted in their diet.
Resembling the abode of Brahmā, resounding with the chanting of the Vedas,
and graced by highly fortunate Brahmins who were knowers of Brahman—
having seen that circle of ascetics' hermitages, the illustrious Rāghava [was filled with wonder].
Having strung his great bow, the one of great splendor approached them;
endowed with divine knowledge, those great seers, upon seeing Rāma and the illustrious Vaidehī, then approached them with joy.
Seeing him rising like the moon, those practitioners of dharma,
firm in their vows, welcomed him while pronouncing auspicious blessings;
they beheld his physical form, his stature, his splendor, his delicacy, and his elegant attire.
The forest-dwellers beheld them with expressions of wonder;
all those wanderers of the woods gazed at Vaidehī, Lakṣmaṇa, and Rāma with eyes that seemed as if they would not blink, seeing them as beings of great marvel.
Then those highly fortunate ones, devoted to the welfare of all beings,
settled the descendant of Raghu, their guest, within the leaf-hut according to the prescribed rites;
thereafter, those who resembled fire honored Rāma with due ceremony.
Those highly fortunate practitioners of dharma brought water for him;
having offered roots, flowers, wild fruits, and the hermitage to that great-souled one, those knowers of dharma then spoke with palms joined in reverence.
The protector of this people, a refuge for all, and one of great renown—
the king, wielder of the rod of punishment, the teacher, worthy of worship and honor—
is like a fourth part of Indra himself in protecting his subjects, O Raghava.
Therefore, the king, honored by the world, enjoys those excellent pleasures.
As inhabitants of your domain, we are to be protected by you;
whether you reside in the city or in the forest, you remain our king, O lord of men.
"O King, we have laid down our staffs; we have conquered anger and subdued our senses.
These ascetics, who are as dear as embryos, must be constantly protected by you.
Having spoken thus to Rāghava with fruits, roots, and wild flowers, [he offered them].
And with various other foods, they honored him along with Lakṣmaṇa.
Likewise, other perfected ascetics, who were like fire in their power and lived according to the righteous way, gratified the lord Rāma in the proper manner.
Then Rāma, having been hospitably received and having taken leave of all the sages, set out toward the forest at the rising of the sun;
it was a place teeming with various herds of deer and inhabited by tigers and wolves.

Accompanied by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma beheld the heart of the forest, where trees, creepers, and shrubs had been destroyed, where the reservoirs of water were difficult to discern, which was devoid of the warbling of birds, and resounded instead with the humming of swarms of crickets.
In the midst of that forest, which was filled with fierce wild beasts, the descendant of Kakutstha beheld a man-eater of great roar, resembling a mountain peak,
with deep-set eyes, a massive mouth, and a hideous, uneven belly.
He was loathsome, formidable, tall, deformed, and terrible to behold;
wearing a tiger skin wet with fat and smeared with blood,
he struck terror into all beings like Death himself with his mouth wide open.
Having impaled upon an iron stake three lions, four tigers, two wolves, ten spotted deer,
and the great head of an elephant smeared with fat and marrow,
he let out a loud roar.
Having seen Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā the princess of Mithilā,
he rushed toward them in a great rage, like Death the Destroyer toward living beings,
uttering a terrible roar that seemed to shake the earth.
Taking Vaidehī by the arm and stepping aside, he then said:
"Wearing matted hair and bark garments, yet bearing bows, arrows, and swords along with your wife, you two have entered the Daṇḍaka forest as if your lives were spent."
"How is it that you two ascetics dwell here together with a woman?
You are practitioners of unrighteousness, sinful ones; who are you two who defile the sages?
I am a Rākṣasa named Virādha, and this forest is my domain."
"I always wander about armed, devouring the flesh of sages.
This woman of beautiful limbs shall become my wife;
and I shall drink the blood of you two wicked ones in battle."
Hearing these bold and arrogant words spoken by that evil-minded Virādha, Janaka’s daughter Sītā trembled with agitation like a plantain tree in a gale.
Seeing the auspicious Sītā held in the embrace of Virādha, Rāghava,
his face parched, spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa:
"Behold, O gentle one, the daughter of King Janaka."
My wife, of virtuous conduct, who was brought into the lap of Virādha—
the illustrious princess who had been raised in extreme luxury— whatever is intended for us, whatever is dear to us, and whatever boon has been chosen; [all that shall be yours].
But for Kaikeyī, O Lakṣmaṇa, her purpose has been swiftly accomplished this very day—
she who, far-sighted for the sake of her son, was not satisfied with the kingdom,
and by whom I, who am well-disposed toward all beings, have been sent forth to the forest.
"Now at last, that middle mother of mine has had her desire fulfilled.
O Saumitri, there is nothing more painful for me than the touch of Vaidehi, nor even the destruction of my father or the seizure of our own kingdom."
While the descendant of Kakutstha was speaking thus, overwhelmed by tears and grief,
Lakṣmaṇa, enraged and hissing like a confined serpent, said:
"O you who are equal to Indra, you are the protector of all beings, yet you act like one who is without a protector."
"O descendant of Kakutstha, why do you grieve for me, your servant?
Today, when the Rākṣasa Virādha has been struck down by my arrow and is dead,
the earth shall drink his blood."
The anger that I felt toward Bharata because of his desire for the kingdom—
I shall release it upon Virādha, just as the wielder of the thunderbolt hurls his bolt at a mountain.
Let this great arrow, impelled by the force of my arm’s strength, fall upon his broad chest.
"May he take away my life from this body, and may I fall to the earth, reeling.
Then Virādha spoke these words again, filling the forest:
"Tell me who you are; where do you two intend to go?"
Then Rāma, endowed with great splendor, spoke to that Rakshasa of blazing countenance as he questioned him about his own Ikshvaku lineage:
"Know us to be two Kshatriyas, perfected in conduct, now dwelling in the forest."
"But we wish to know you: who are you that wanders through the Daṇḍaka forest?
Virādha replied to Rāma, whose prowess is truth:
"Ah, I shall tell you, O King; listen to me, O Rāghava."
"I am indeed the son of Jaya, and my mother is Śatahradā;
all the rākṣasas on earth call me Virādha.
Furthermore, through my ascetic penance, I have obtained [this power] born from the grace of Brahmā."

In this world, you shall be invulnerable to weapons, as well as incapable of being cut or pierced. Abandoning this woman, proceed quickly as you came without looking back; I will not take away your lives.
With eyes bloodshot with anger, Rāma replied thus to that evil-minded Rākṣasa Virādha of deformed appearance:
"O base one, shame on you! You are surely seeking your own destruction for the sake of a lowly purpose."
"Stay in the battle; you shall not escape from me alive!
Then Rāma, having strung his bow and very swiftly aimed well-sharpened arrows, struck down the rākṣasa.
With his bow strung with a bowstring, he released seven gold-feathered arrows of great velocity, which traveled like Garuḍa or the wind; those arrows,
adorned with peacock feathers, pierced the body of Virādha.
Stained with blood and resembling fire, they fell upon the earth.
Having let out a great roar and seizing his spear, which was like the banner of Indra,
he then shone like Death himself with his mouth wide open.
Rāma, the best among the wielders of weapons, severed that spear— which was like a thunderbolt and resembled a blazing fire in the sky— with two arrows;
then the son of Sumitrā broke the left arm of that fierce one.

Rāma, however, with great force, [struck] the right arm of that Rākṣasa. With his arm broken and filled with agitation, the Rākṣasa, resembling a cloud, fell swiftly to the earth like a mountain shattered by a thunderbolt.
Virādha spoke thus to Kakutstha, that bull among men:
"O dear one, you are known to me as Rāma, the noble son of Kausalyā;
so too are the highly fortunate Vaidehī and the greatly illustrious Lakṣmaṇa."
"Due to a curse, I have entered this terrible rakshasa body;
for I am a gandharva named Tumburu, cursed by Vaiśravaṇa.
And as I was propitiating him, that highly illustrious one said to me:"
"When Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, slays you in battle,
then, having returned to your natural state, you shall go to heaven.
Thus did King Vaiśravaṇa speak to him who was infatuated with Rambhā.
Not being attended by me, he spoke to me in great anger:
"By your grace, I have been released from a most dreadful curse; I shall go to my own home. May it be well with you, O scorcher of foes! (Rāmāyaṇa 3.3.21)
"O dear one, the righteous and powerful great seer Śarabhaṅga, who resembles the sun, dwells here at a distance of one and a half yojanas.
Go to him quickly; he will provide for your welfare."
"O Rāma, cast me into a pit and depart in safety;
this is the eternal law for Rākṣasas who have lost their lives: those who are placed in a pit attain eternal worlds."

Having spoken thus to the descendant of Kakutstha, the mighty Virādha, tormented by arrows, cast off his body and attained heaven. Raising him up— his throat released, his ears like spikes, and his voice loud— [Rāma departed].
He cast Virādha, who was screaming with a terrifying sound, into a pit.

Then, having slain the Rākṣasa, those two, whose variegated golden bows were [still] in their hands, took hold of Maithilī and wandered joyfully through the great forest like the sun and the moon stationed in the sky.
Having slain that Rākṣasa Virādha of terrible strength in the forest,
the valiant Rāma then embraced Sītā and comforted her; thereafter, he spoke to his brother Lakṣmaṇa, who was radiant with splendor.
"This forest is difficult and perilous, and we are not accustomed to dwelling in the woods;
let us go quickly to Śarabhaṅga, whose wealth is his asceticism.
Thus Rāghava proceeded to the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga.
Near that Śarabhaṅga, whose soul was purified by austerity and who possessed divine power, he beheld a great marvel:
one whose body was radiant, resembling the sun and the sacrificial fire.
He beheld the Lord of the Gods not touching the earth,
the deity adorned with radiant ornaments and wearing stainless garments,
being honored by many great-souled beings of a similar nature.
Not far from him, he beheld a chariot yoked with swift bay horses, moving through the intermediate space, resembling the young sun,
appearing like a mass of white clouds, and like the orb of the moon.
He saw a spotless umbrella adorned with variegated garlands, and two excellent chowries with golden handles, of great value,
held by two forest women and being fanned over his head.
Many Gandharvas, Amaras, Siddhas, and supreme ṛṣis praised the god stationed in the sky with the most excellent words.
Having seen Indra there, Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
"Those horses of Indra, the one invoked by many, which we have heard of from olden times—
those divine steeds that range through the atmosphere, these are surely those very ones. And these tigers among men who stand here around the chariot,"

Hundreds upon hundreds of youths, adorned with earrings and holding swords in their hands— O Saumitri, they all bear the appearance of twenty-five-year-olds, with necklaces blazing like fire upon their chests.
"Indeed, this is surely the eternal age of the gods, since these tigers among men appear so pleasing to behold.
O Lakṣmaṇa, stay here for a moment with Vaidehī."
"As soon as I recognize clearly who this radiant being is upon the chariot," having thus spoken to the son of Sumitrā,
"stay right here," the descendant of Kakutstha set out toward the hermitage of Śarabhaṅga.
Then, seeing Rāma approaching, the Lord of Śacī, having taken leave of Śarabhaṅga, spoke thus to the gods:
"Here comes that Rāma; let us wait until he addresses me."

"Wait until he has brought this to completion; only then should you see me. I shall see him soon when he has conquered and achieved his purpose, for he must perform a great task that is exceedingly difficult for others."
Having thus addressed and honored that ascetic, the Vajra-wielder,
the subduer of enemies, departed for heaven in his chariot yoked with tawny horses.
When the thousand-eyed one had departed, Rāghava, along with his retinue, remained there.
While he was seated performing the Agnihotra sacrifice, Śarabhaṅga approached him.
Having clasped his feet, Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa sat down with his permission; having been invited, they were granted lodging.
Then that Raghava asked about Śakra’s arrival,
and Śarabhaṅga related everything to the descendant of Raghu:
"O Rama, this granter of boons wishes to lead me to the world of Brahmā."
"Victory has been won through fierce asceticism, which is difficult for those of unrefined souls to attain.
O tiger among men, knowing that the world of Brahmā was not far away, I did not go there without first seeing you, my beloved guest."
Having met with you, O tiger among men, I shall go to the third heaven frequented by the gods; for I have won imperishable and auspicious worlds—
both those of Brahmā and those upon the vault of the sky— so please accept these from me.
Thus addressed by the seer Śarabhaṅga, Rāghava, that tiger among men and master of all scriptures, spoke these words:
"O great sage, I myself shall win all the worlds."
"I desire, however, that a dwelling be assigned for me here in this forest.
When he had been addressed thus by Rāghava, who was indeed equal in strength to Śakra,
the highly wise Śarabhaṅga spoke these words once more.
"Go to the ascetic Sutīkṣṇa in that pure and delightful forest region; he will provide you with a dwelling.
This is the path, O tiger among men; wait for me here for a moment, my dear."

"Until I cast off my limbs like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin. Then, having prepared the fire and offered oblations of clarified butter with sacred mantras, the highly effulgent Śarabhaṅga, a knower of the Vedas, entered the flames.
The fire consumed the body hair and the head hair of that great-souled one,
as well as his aged skin, bones, flesh, and blood;
and he became a youth resembling the blazing fire.
Having risen from that fire-altar, Śarabhaṅga shone with splendor;
transcending the worlds of the high-souled ṛṣis who maintain the sacred fires,
as well as those of the gods, he ascended to the world of Brahmā.
That bull among brahmins, a man of meritorious deeds, beheld the Grandfather (Brahmā) together with his attendants in that world;
and the Grandfather, seeing that twice-born one, rejoiced and said, "A most welcome greeting to you!
When Śarabhaṅga had attained heaven, the hosts of sages assembled there.
They approached Rāma, the descendant of Kakutstha, who was blazing with splendor—
Vaikhānasas, Vālakhilyas, Samprakṣālas, Marīcipas,
many Aśmakuṭṭas, and ascetics who subsist on leaves.
Some sages used their teeth as a mortar, while others remained constantly submerged in water; some subsisted on water alone, while others fed only on air;
some dwelt in the open air, and others slept upon the bare ground.

Likewise, there were those dwelling in upper chambers, self-restrained, and clad in wet garments; those constantly engaged in silent recitation and penance, as well as those practicing the "five-fire" austerity—
all of them endowed with Brahmanic splendor and firmly concentrated in yoga.
The ascetics at Śarabhaṅga’s hermitage approached Rāma;
having approached him, those hosts of sages, who were knowers of dharma, composed and supremely versed in righteousness, spoke to Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma.
You are the great chariot-warrior of this Ikṣvāku dynasty and of the entire earth;
you are the foremost and the protector, like Maghavan among the gods,
renowned throughout the three worlds for your glory and your prowess.
Devotion to your father, truthfulness, and abundant righteousness reside in you.
Having approached you, O high-souled one, who knows the dharma and loves righteousness, we shall speak out of our need; you ought to forgive us for that.
But great unrighteousness, my dear, would accrue to that lord of the earth who takes a sixth part as tribute yet does not protect [his subjects] like his own sons—
protecting them with his own life, as one would guard one's own vital breaths, and as one would cherish beloved sons.
O Rāma, he who is ever-yoked and always protects all those dwelling within his realm attains eternal fame lasting for many years;
having reached the station of Brahmā, he is honored there as well.
Whatever supreme dharma the sage, subsisting on roots and fruits, performs,
a fourth part of that belongs to the king who protects his subjects according to dharma. This great multitude of forest-dwellers consists primarily of brahmins.
"O Rāma, though you are our protector, we are being slaughtered mercilessly by the rākṣasas like those who have no protector.
Come, behold the bodies of many sages of purified souls, slain in various ways in the forest by the terrible rākṣasas."
A great slaughter is being carried out against those who dwell by the Pampā river and those whose homes are on Mount Citrakūṭa along the Mandākinī;
thus, we cannot endure this mistreatment of the ascetics.
While we were being subjected to terrible deeds by the Rākṣasas of fearsome actions in the forest,
we have now approached you, who are worthy of refuge, for protection.
O Rāma, protect us as we are being slaughtered by the night-stalkers!
Having heard this from the ascetics practicing austerities, the righteous-souled descendant of Kakutstha spoke thus to all those ascetics:
"It does not behove you to speak to me in this manner; I am one who must be commanded by the ascetics."
"I have come here by chance for the sake of accomplishing your purpose;
thus, this dwelling of mine in the forest will bear great fruit.
Desiring to slay my enemies in battle, I wish to destroy these Rākṣasas who afflict the ascetics."

Having granted a boon to those whose wealth is asceticism, that hero, whose soul was fixed on righteousness, and who was honored for his conduct by the ascetics along with Lakṣmaṇa, proceeded toward Sutīkṣṇa.
Rāma, the scorcher of enemies, however, remained together with his brother and Sītā.
He went with those twice-born brahmins to the hermitage of Sutīkṣṇa.
Having traveled a long distance and crossed many rivers of abundant water,
he beheld a vast mountain rising high like a great cloud.
Then those two Raghavas, the best of the Ikshvakus, entered that forest together with Sita— a forest constantly filled with various kinds of trees.
Having entered the formidable forest, which was filled with trees bearing many flowers and fruits, they proceeded.

In a secluded spot, he beheld an hermitage adorned with garlands of bark-cloth. There, Rāma approached Sutīkṣṇa according to custom— the aged ascetic seated there, bearing matted locks and covered in the dust of dirt— and addressed him.
"I am Rāma, O Blessed One; I have come to see you.
Therefore, address me, O Knower of Dharma, Great Sage of true prowess.
Then, having gazed upon the hero Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma...
Embracing him with both arms, he spoke these words:
"Welcome indeed to you, O hero, O Rama, best among the upholders of dharma! Now that this hermitage has been entered by you, it is as if it has found its protector."
"O illustrious hero, waiting for you alone, I did not ascend from this earth to the world of the gods after casting off my body.
I have heard that you were exiled from your kingdom and have taken up residence at Citrakūṭa."
"Kakutstha, the king of the gods, Śatakratu, has arrived here and declared that all the worlds have been won by my meritorious deeds—
those worlds frequented by celestial sages which were conquered by me through asceticism."
"By my grace, may you dwell here together with your wife and Lakṣmaṇa.
To that great seer of fierce austerities, radiant and truthful in speech,
the self-possessed Rāma replied, as Vāsava might to Brahmā.
"O great sage, I myself shall gather the worlds;
however, I desire a dwelling place designated for me here in this forest. You are skilled in all things and devoted to the welfare of all beings."
Thus it was told by the high-souled Gautama Śarabhaṅga.
Having been addressed in this way by Rāma, the great seer, world-renowned,
spoke these sweet words, overflowing with great joy.
"O Rāma, this very hermitage is virtuous; let it be enjoyed here, for it is frequented by hosts of sages and always provided with roots and fruits.
O highly illustrious one, having come to this hermitage, the herds of deer [have found peace]."
"Having wandered about and enticed him, they depart without fear from any quarter.
Hearing those words of the great seer, the steadfast elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa drew his bow with an arrow and spoke these words.
"O highly fortunate one, I would slay those assembled herds of deer with a sharp-edged arrow possessing the brilliance of a thunderbolt;
you would be deeply distressed by that— what could be more grievous than that?"
"I do not consider it appropriate to dwell in this hermitage for long.
Having spoken thus to the granter of boons, Rāma approached the evening twilight;
having performed the evening prayers, he took up residence there for the night.

Then, at the conclusion of the twilight prayers and observing that night had fallen, the high-souled Sutīkṣṇa himself, having honored them with great respect, gave those two bulls among men auspicious food fit for ascetics.
Rāma, however, along with the son of Sumitrā, was thus honored by Sutīkṣṇa.
Having passed the night there, he awoke at dawn.
Rising at the proper time, Rāghava, together with Sītā,
performed his ablutions with very cool water scented with the fragrance of lotuses.
Then, having duly worshipped the fire and the gods at dawn according to the rules, Vaidehī, Rāma, and Lakṣmaṇa— having purified their sins in that forest which was a refuge for ascetics—
beheld the rising sun.
Approaching Sutīkṣṇa, they spoke these gentle words:
"O Blessed One, we have dwelt happily, honored by you who are yourself worthy of honor.
We now take our leave; we shall depart, for the sages urge us to hasten."
"We hasten to see the entire circle of hermitages belonging to the sages of virtuous conduct who dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest;
we wish to be permitted to depart along with these bulls among munis."
By those who were constant in dharma, self-controlled through austerity, and shaven-headed like fires, [the hermitage was filled].
As long as the sun, whose heat is unbearable, did not yet shine intensely,
it was like a man of no lineage who has obtained wealth arrived by an improper path.
Having said, "We wish to depart for now," Rāghava, together with Sītā and the son of Sumitrā, paid homage at the feet of the sage.
Raising them up as they touched his feet, that bull among sages spoke.
Embracing him firmly with affection, he spoke these words:
"Go safely on your path, O Rāma, together with the son of Sumitrā and with this Sītā, who follows you like a shadow."
Behold, O hero, the delightful hermitage of these ascetics dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, whose souls are purified by austerity;
behold also the forests in full bloom, abounding in excellent fruits and roots.
The herds of deer were tranquil, as were the flocks of birds;
there were ponds and lakes with clear waters, scattered with *kāraṇḍava* ducks and clusters of blooming lotuses.
"You shall behold mountain cascades pleasing to the sight, and delightful forests resounding with the cries of peacocks.
Go, my child Saumitri; you too must go."
"And you must come back again to my hermitage once you have seen it.
Having been addressed thus, Kakutstha, together with Lakṣmaṇa, replied, "So be it," and after circumambulating the sage, he prepared to depart.
Then the large-eyed Sītā gave those two brothers two most excellent quivers and two bows, and thereafter she gave them two stainless swords.
Having fastened the auspicious quivers and taken up the resounding bows, they departed.
Having been permitted by Sutīkṣṇa, both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa set out from the hermitage to depart. As the joy of the Raghus was preparing to leave,
Vaidehī addressed these words to her husband in an affectionate voice.
This great Dharma is attained through a most subtle method, and it can be achieved here by one who has desisted from the calamities born of desire; for indeed,
there are only three such calamities born of desire in this world.
False speech is the worst of these; more grievous than that are both the pursuit of another's wife and cruelty without enmity.
O Raghava, false speech has never been yours, nor will it ever be.
Whence could there be such a longing for women that destroys the dharma of others?
O mighty-armed one, all of that can be borne by those who have conquered their senses;
and I know, O you of auspicious appearance, that your senses are under control.
This third thing, which is fierce— the senseless harming of the lives of others— has arisen for you through delusion; yet,
O hero, it was promised by you to those dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest.
For the sake of protecting the sages, there is the slaughter of the rākṣasas in battle;
it is for this reason that you have set out with your brother, bearing your bow and arrows, to the forest renowned as Daṇḍaka.
Therefore, seeing you set forth, my mind is overwhelmed with anxiety;
as I reflect upon your conduct, it occurs to me that what would truly be for your welfare and ultimate good is this:
O hero, your departure toward the Daṇḍaka forest does not please me.
I shall tell you the reason for this; listen to me as I speak.
For you, with bow and arrow in hand, having gone to the forest with your brother, might see all the forest-dwellers and discharge your arrows upon them.
In this world, for kṣatriyas, the bow and the fuel of the sacrificial fire,
when kept close at hand, greatly increase their splendor and strength.
Long ago, O mighty-armed one, it is said that there was a pure ascetic who was truthful in speech.
In a certain sacred forest where deer and birds took delight,
Indra, the lord of Śacī, arrived at that hermitage in the guise of a soldier with a sword in hand, intent on creating an obstacle to his asceticism.

In that hermitage, an excellent sword was deposited as a trust according to the rules of deposit, given to him while he remained engaged in meritorious asceticism. Having received that weapon, he became intent upon guarding the trust.
Wandering through the forest, he indeed protected his own security;
wherever he went to gather roots and fruits,
being intent on guarding the deposit, he never went without that sword.

Constantly carrying a weapon, that ascetic gradually made his own mind fierce, abandoning his resolve for austerity. Then, devoted to cruelty, he became intoxicated and was dragged away by unrighteousness.
Through association with that weapon, the sage went to hell.
Out of affection and great respect, I am merely reminding you; I am not instructing you.
Under no circumstances should that [weapon] ever be used by you while holding your bow.
O hero, it is not my desire to slay the Rākṣasas dwelling in Daṇḍaka without enmity, nor to slay people without offense;
yet for heroic Kṣatriyas who have restrained their souls in the forests, [this is the duty].
The purpose of the bow is only this: the protection of those who are distressed. Where is the weapon, and where is the forest? Where is the duty of a Kshatriya, and where is asceticism?
This [conflict] is inconsistent for us; rather, let the duty of the region be honored.
Then, O Noble One, a turbid intellect arises from the practice of weapons;
yet, having returned to Ayodhyā, you shall practice the dharma of the kṣatriyas.
Thus, there will be imperishable joy for my mother-in-law and father-in-law.
If indeed you were to renounce the kingdom and become a devoted sage,
then from dharma arises wealth, and from dharma arises happiness;
through dharma one obtains everything, for this world has dharma as its essence.

"By diligently emaciating themselves through various restraints, the wise attain dharma; happiness is not obtained through ease. O gentle one, always pure in mind, practice dharma in this forest of asceticism."
"For everything, even the three worlds, is known to you in its true essence.
These words were spoken by me out of a woman's fickleness; who indeed is capable of speaking on dharma to you?
Having deliberated with your intellect and with your younger brother, do what pleases you without delay."
Having heard these words uttered by Vaidehī out of devotion to her husband, Rāma, remaining firm in dharma, then replied to the princess of Mithilā:
"O Queen, you have spoken words that are beneficial and worthy of you, being so affectionate."
"O daughter of Janaka, knower of dharma, you who proclaim your noble lineage— what indeed shall I say, O Queen, since these very words were spoken by you yourself:
'The bow is to be wielded by Kshatriyas, so that the cry of distress may not arise'?"
And those sages of the Daṇḍaka forest,
firm in their vows and devoted to dharma, living on roots and fruits while dwelling in the woods, came to me themselves, O Sītā, and as seekers of refuge, they sought my protection.
Terrified by the Rākṣasas of cruel deeds, they find no happiness;
and though they are devoted at various times to diverse observances in the forest,
they are devoured by the fearsome Rākṣasas who subsist on human flesh.
"Being devoured by them, those sages dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, the best of the twice-born, said to me: 'Come to our aid!
Having heard these words as they fell from their mouths, I [acted].
Having performed service at his feet, he uttered these words:
"May you be gracious toward me, for this is a source of incomparable shame for me, that I have been approached by such Brahmins who are worthy of being honored."
"What shall I do? I asked in the presence of the twice-born. Then all those many Rākṣasas in the Daṇḍaka forest, who could assume any form at will, gathered together and uttered these words.
"We are greatly afflicted, O Rāma; you ought to protect us.
For when the time for the fire-oblation has arrived, and on the days of the lunar festivals, O sinless one, the irrepressible flesh-eating rākṣasas attack us."
For us ascetics and practitioners of austerity who have been oppressed by the Rākṣasas and are searching for a refuge, you are our supreme refuge.
Granted, by the power of our asceticism, we are capable of slaying the night-stalkers; yet [we seek your aid].
"O Raghava, we do not wish to break our asceticism, which has been accumulated over a long time. Constant in our penance and difficult to practice, it is beset by many obstacles;
therefore, even while being devoured by rakshasas, we do not utter a curse."
"Therefore, protect us who are being tormented by the rākṣasas dwelling in the Daṇḍaka forest, along with your brother; for we have you as our protector in the forest.
And having heard these words of mine, [he granted] full protection.
"O daughter of Janaka, this was promised by the sages in the Daṇḍaka forest.
Having heard it, I shall not be able to live while failing to fulfill my promise to the sages; for truth has always been dear to me."
"O Sītā, I would sooner abandon my life, or even you along with Lakṣmaṇa, than break a promise— especially one made to brahmins.
Therefore, I must certainly fulfill the protection of the seers."
O Vaidehī, this would have been done even if it had not been spoken; how much more so now that you have made a formal promise?
O Sītā, I am deeply gratified by these words spoken by you out of affection and friendship; for one who is not beloved does not offer such counsel.
"O beautiful one, this is worthy of you and befits your lineage.
Having spoken these words to his beloved Sītā, the princess of Mithilā, the high-souled Rāma,
armed with his bow, departed for the lovely penance groves along with Lakṣmaṇa.
Rāma went in front, Sītā of the slender waist in the middle,
and Lakṣmaṇa, bow in hand, followed behind. They beheld various mountain ridges and forests.
Accompanied by Sītā, they traveled along various delightful rivers,
as well as lakes filled with lotuses and frequented by water-birds, and the sandy banks of rivers where cranes and ruddy geese roamed.
They saw spotted deer in herds, horned buffaloes intoxicated with rut,
boars, and elephants— the enemies of trees.
Having traveled a long distance while the sun was hanging low, they reached their destination.
Together they beheld a delightful lake, a yojana in length,
crowded with lotuses and water-lilies, adorned by herds of elephants, and teeming with cranes, swans, kādamba ducks, and other aquatic birds.
In that delightful lake of clear waters,
the sound of singing and musical instruments was heard, yet no one at all could be seen.
Then, out of curiosity, Rāma and the great chariot-warrior Lakṣmaṇa [approached].
He began to question the sage named Dharmabhṛt:
"O great sage, having heard this most wonderful thing from all of us, a great curiosity has arisen; please tell us what this is."
Thus addressed by Rāghava, the righteous sage then began to relate the entire power of that lake:
"This is the pond named Pañcāpsaras, which possesses water at all times."
"O Rāma, it was created by the sage Māṇḍakarṇi through his ascetic power.
For that great sage Māṇḍakarṇi performed intense penance for ten thousand years, subsisting on air and dwelling within the water."
Then all the gods, led by Agni, being greatly distressed,
gathered together and spoke these words:
"This sage seeks the position of one of us."
Then, all the gods dispatched five principal Apsarases, whose splendor was like flashing lightning, to create an obstacle to his asceticism.
Thereupon, the sage— who had realized both the higher and the lower truths— was approached by those Apsarases.
He was brought under the power of passion for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods. And those five Apsarases became the wives of the sage;
for them, a hidden dwelling was constructed within this lake.

Right there, five Apsarases dwell at their pleasure, delighting the sage— who, through the power of his asceticism, has been restored to youth— with their charms. This sound of musical instruments belongs to them as they sport together.

"The enchanting sound of singing, mingled with the tinkling of ornaments, is heard. To these words of that noble-minded one, the highly illustrious Rāghava, together with his brother, replied, "It is wonderful!"
While he was speaking thus, Rāghava beheld the circle of the hermitage,
surrounded by kuśa grass and bark garments, and filled with various kinds of trees;
having entered it together with Vaidehī and Lakṣmaṇa.
Then, having dwelt most happily in that glorious circle of hermitages while being honored by the great seers, that descendant of Kakutstha visited the dwellings of those ascetics in succession.
That master of great weapons had previously dwelt in the presence of some for ten months, in others for one year,
in some for four months, and in others for five or six.
In other places he dwelt for more than a month, and in some for a month and a half;
thus Rāghava lived happily for three months and eight months in the hermitages of the sages as he resided there.
And as they lived in happiness and harmony, ten years passed by. Having wandered about, the illustrious Rāghava, who knows the dharma, returned once more with Sītā to the hermitage of Sutīkṣṇa.

Having arrived at that hermitage and being honored by the sages, Rāma, the subduer of enemies, dwelt there for some time as well. Then, while staying in the hermitage, he once approached that great sage with humility.
Sitting there, that descendant of Kakutstha spoke thus to Sutīkṣṇa:
"O Blessed One, I have constantly heard from those telling stories that the most excellent of sages, Agastya, dwells in this forest."
But because of the vastness of this forest, I do not know the location of that holy hermitage of the wise great seer; however,
by your favor, I shall go there with my younger brother and Sītā.
"I would go to the sage Agastya to pay him homage;
this great desire revolves within my heart,
that I might personally serve that best of sages."
Having heard these words of the righteous Rāma, the sage Sutīkṣṇa, being pleased, replied thus to the son of Daśaratha:
"I too was desirous of saying this very thing to you, along with Lakṣmaṇa."
"O Rāghava, go to Agastya together with Sītā.
"By good fortune, you yourself now speak to me regarding this matter;
I shall tell you, my child, where the great sage Agastya dwells."
"O dear one, go four yojanas from the hermitage;
to the south of that is the great and glorious hermitage of Agastya’s brother,
situated in a region of land mostly consisting of forest and adorned with groves of long pepper trees."
Abounding in many flowers and fruits, delightful, and resounded by the songs of various birds; there were various lotus ponds with clear, auspicious waters,
crowded with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks, and graced by ruddy geese.
Having stayed there for one night, O Rāma, you should depart at dawn toward the southern direction, along the edge of the forest tract;
having gone a distance of one yojana, you will reach the site of Agastya’s hermitage.
In that delightful forest region, thick with many trees, Vaidehī, Lakṣmaṇa, and you shall find delight;
for that forest region is indeed beautiful and crowded with many trees.
"O highly illustrious one, if you have made up your mind to see that great sage Agastya, then resolve today itself to go.
Having heard this from the sage, Rāma, together with his brother, paid his respects.
Accompanied by his younger brother and Sītā, he set out toward Agastya; along the way,
they beheld various beautiful forests, mountains resembling clouds,
lakes, and rivers, following the course of their journey.
Having traveled by that path pointed out by Sutīkṣṇa, he reached this place with ease and, filled with supreme joy, spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa:
"This must surely be the hermitage of that great-souled one."
The meritorious deeds of the sage Agastya’s brother are visible here;
for these thousands of trees in this forest, known to us along the path, are bowed down by the weight of their fruit and the weight of their flowers.
"And from this forest has come this scent of ripe pippalī fruits, wafted by the wind and suddenly giving rise to a pungent aroma.
And here and there, piles of wood are seen gathered together."
Mown darbha grass, possessing the luster of lapis lazuli, is seen along the path;
and rising from the fire situated in the hermitage, the crest of smoke is clearly visible, resembling the peak of a dark cloud in the midst of the forest.
And in secluded sacred fords, the twice-born, having performed their ablutions,
offer oblations of flowers with blossoms gathered by themselves.
O gentle one, such were the words of Sutīkṣṇa as I heard them.
"This must surely be the hermitage of Agastya’s brother;
it was here that this quarter, made secure by his brother of meritorious deeds, was established out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds after he had swiftly subdued Death."
It is said that once, there were two cruel and great asuras, the brothers Vātāpi and Ilvala, who lived together and were slayers of brahmins. Among them,
Ilvala assumed the form of a brahmin and spoke in refined Sanskrit.
Addressing the brahmins for the sake of the śrāddha rite,
that pitiless one [Kharadūṣaṇa] then had his brother, who was in the form of a ram and had been consecrated, fed to those twice-born men according to the ritual procedures prescribed for a śrāddha.
Then, after those brahmins had finished eating, Ilvala spoke with a loud voice, saying, "Vātāpi, come forth!
Hearing his brother's words, Vātāpi then roared like a ram.
Piercing through the bodies of the Brahmins again and again, he emerged;
in this manner, thousands of Brahmins were constantly destroyed in groups by those flesh-eaters who could assume any form at will.
Then, at the request of the gods, that great asura was indeed consumed by the great seer Agastya after he had partaken of him at a śrāddha ceremony.
Thereupon, having said, "It is prepared," and having offered water for washing the hands...

"Come out, brother! Ilvala addressed him. "How could I have the power to escape from that aged Rākṣasa,
your brother who took the form of a ram and has gone to the abode of Yama?
Then, having heard those words concerning the death of his brother, [Rāvaṇa spoke].
The night-stalker began to assault the sage out of anger;
he rushed toward that best of the twice-born, but was consumed and brought to his end by the sage’s blazing splendor, which was like fire, through its very gaze.
"This is the hermitage of that brother of yours, adorned with ponds and groves,
by whom this difficult deed was performed out of compassion for the brahmins.
While he was speaking thus with the son of Sumitrā, [the sun set].
The sun had set for Rāma, and the time of twilight arrived. Having performed the evening twilight devotions with his brother according to the prescribed rites,
he entered the hermitage grounds and paid homage to that sage.
Having been properly received by that sage, Rāghava dwelt for that single night after consuming roots and fruits. When that night had passed and the solar disc was clear, he arose.
Rāghava took leave of that brother of Agastya:
"I salute you, O Blessed One; I have spent the night happily.
I take my leave of you, for I am going to see your elder brother, your guru."
Told by him, "Go," the joy of the Raghus departed,
observing that forest along the path as it had been indicated,
[seeing] wild rice, jackfruit trees, palmyra palms, *timiśa* trees, *vañjula* reeds, and *dhava* trees.
There Rāma beheld hundreds of forest trees— ciribilvas, madhūkas, bilvas, and tindukas— all in bloom and entwined by creepers with flowering tips.
"Trampled by the trunks of elephants, adorned by monkeys,
and resounded by hundreds of flocks of intoxicated birds"—
then the lotus-eyed Rāma spoke to the one standing nearby.
Following behind the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, the enhancer of prosperity,
they saw the hermitage of the great seer of purified soul not far away— a place where the trees had glossy leaves and the deer and birds were peaceful.
Renowned in the world by his own deeds as Agastya,
his hermitage is seen there, which removes the fatigue of the weary;
its forests are filled with abundant smoke, and it is adorned with garlands of bark garments.
Where the herds of deer are tranquil and the place resounds with the songs of various birds;
where, desiring the welfare of the worlds, he who performed meritorious deeds forcibly subdued Death and made the southern quarter a sanctuary of refuge.
This is his hermitage, by whose power this southern quarter is merely looked upon in fear by the Rākṣasas and is not occupied by them;
ever since this direction was entered by that one of meritorious deeds.
From that time forward, the night-stalkers became free from enmity and were pacified.
Furthermore, this southern direction of the Blessed One became renowned throughout the three worlds as "Pradakṣiṇā," being unassailable by those of cruel deeds.
To block the path of the sun, that best of mountains, Vindhya, does not grow further, constantly observing his command;
this is the power of that long-lived one whose deeds are renowned in the world.
This is the glorious hermitage of Agastya, frequented by humble deer. This virtuous man, honored by the world and ever devoted to the welfare of the righteous,
will unite us with prosperity now that we have arrived here.
"O gentle one, O Lord, I shall propitiate that great sage Agastya here, and I shall dwell here for the remainder of my forest exile.
Here, the gods along with the Gandharvas, the Siddhas, and the supreme ṛṣis [dwell]."

They constantly attend upon Agastya, who is restrained in his diet. No liar, nor a cruel man, nor a rogue, nor a person of wicked intent, nor one who acts according to lust could live here; such is this sage.
Here dwell the gods, yakṣas, and nāgas, together with the birds,
restrained in their diet and seeking to realize the Dharma;
here the high-souled Siddhas reside in celestial chariots as radiant as the sun.

Having cast off their bodies, the supreme ṛṣis have ascended to heaven in new forms. Here, the gods, when propitiated by auspicious beings, bestow the state of a yakṣa, immortality, and various kingdoms.

"We have arrived at the hermitage, O son of Sumitrā; enter first and announce to the sage that I have arrived here along with Sītā. Having entered the hermitage, Lakṣmaṇa, the younger brother of Rāghava, [did as he was told].
Having approached a disciple of Agastya, he spoke these words:
"There is a king named Daśaratha; his eldest son, the mighty Rāma, has arrived with his wife Sītā to see the sage."
I am his younger brother, named Lakṣmaṇa, who is well-disposed, devoted, and loyal— if this has reached your ears.
We have entered this most formidable forest by the command of our father.
"We all wish to see the Blessed One; let it be announced.
Hearing those words of Lakṣmaṇa, the ascetic said, "So be it," and entered the fire-sanctuary to announce them.
Having entered, he spoke thus with palms joined in reverence to the best of sages, who was difficult to overcome due to his ascetic power, directly reporting the arrival of Rāma:
"These two sons of Daśaratha are Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa."
Having entered the hermitage together with our wife Sītā,
we two subduers of enemies have come to see you for the purpose of serving you;
you should now command us as to what must be done next.
Then, having heard from his disciple that Rāma had arrived along with Lakṣmaṇa and the highly fortunate Vaidehī, he spoke these words:
"By good fortune, Rāma has come today after a long time to see me."
For his arrival was indeed desired by me even in my mind.
Let Rama go, honored along with his wife and Lakshmana;
let him be ushered into my presence—why has he not been brought in?
Thus addressed by the great-souled sage who knows the Dharma, the disciple, having offered his salutations with palms joined in restraint, said, "So be it.
Then, departing in haste, the disciple spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
"Where is that Rāma? Let him come to see the sage; let him enter himself.
Then, having gone to the hermitage with his disciple Lakṣmaṇa, he showed the descendant of Kakutstha and Sītā, the daughter of Janaka.
Speaking these humble words, the disciple, conveying Agastya’s message, ushered him in according to custom, having honored him with great hospitality.
Then Rāma entered together with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa.
Beholding that hermitage filled with peaceful deer,
he saw there the abode of Brahmā, as well as the abodes of Agni, Viṣṇu, Mahendra, and Vivasvat.
The abode of Soma, the abode of Bhaga, and the abode of Kubera,
as well as the abode of Dhātṛ, the abode of Vidhātṛ, and likewise the abode of Vāyu—
thereupon the sage also emerged, surrounded by his disciples.
Seeing before him that sage of blazing splendor,
the heroic Rāma spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa, the increaser of prosperity:
"Lakṣmaṇa, here comes the venerable seer Agastya."
"I perceive this man to be a treasury of austerities by his very majesty.
Having spoken thus, the mighty-armed scorcher of foes, filled with supreme joy, grasped the feet of Agastya, who was radiant as the sun.

Having offered his salutations, the righteous Rāma stood with joined palms together with Sītā, the princess of Videha, and Lakṣmaṇa. And having received the descendant of Kakutstha, he honored him with a seat and water.
Having asked after his welfare, he said, "Please be seated.
Having offered oblations into the fire and presented the guest-offering (arghya),
he honored the guest and provided them with food according to the dharma of forest-dwellers.
Having first sat down, that bull among sages, who knew the dharma and was skilled in righteousness, spoke to Rāma, who was seated with palms joined in reverence:
"O descendant of Kakutstha, a practitioner of asceticism should indeed behave otherwise."
Like a false witness in the next world, one might have to eat one's own flesh.
You are a king who practices righteousness, a great chariot-warrior, worthy of worship and honor; you have arrived as a beloved guest.
Having spoken thus, and having honored Rāghava according to his desire with fruits, roots, flowers, and other offerings, he spoke once more:
"This is a great, divine bow, adorned with gold and diamonds."
O tiger among men, this Vaiṣṇava bow was fashioned by Viśvakarman.
This supreme arrow, given by Brahmā, is unfailing and radiant as the sun;
and these two quivers with inexhaustible shafts were granted to me by Mahendra.
Filled with sharpened arrows that are like blazing fires,
this sword, adorned with gold, has a great silver scabbard. O Rāma, having slain the great asuras in battle with this bow—
"In former times, Viṣṇu brought forth the radiant glory of the gods;
O giver of honor, take up that bow, those two quivers, the arrow, and the sword for the sake of victory, just as the wielder of the thunderbolt takes up the vajra."
Having spoken thus and having given all those excellent weapons to Rāma, the illustrious and highly energetic Agastya spoke again:
"O Rāma, I am pleased; may it be well with you! O Lakṣmaṇa, I am thoroughly satisfied."
Since you have come here with Sītā to pay me homage,
the exhaustion from the long journey surely oppresses you both with great fatigue;
it is evident that Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, is also feeling anxious.
For this delicate woman, though unaccustomed to hardships,
has reached the forest full of many evils, impelled by her love for her husband;
O Rāma, act in such a way that Sītā may find delight here.
"She has performed a difficult feat in following you into the forest.
For this, O delighter of the Raghus, is the nature of women since the beginning of creation:
they are devoted to one when he is in prosperity, but they abandon him when he is in adversity."
Women emulate the fickleness of lightning, the sharpness of weapons, and the swiftness of Garuḍa and the wind;
yet this wife of yours is free from these faults.
"Praiseworthy and worthy of renown is this place, just like the lady Arundhatī herself;
for here, O Rāma, subduer of foes, you shall dwell together with the son of Sumitrā and this daughter of Videha."
Thus addressed by the sage, Rāghava, with palms joined in reverence, spoke these humble words to the seer who blazed like fire:
"I am blessed; I am favored, O bull among sages, since you have come to me."
The Giver of Boons is well-pleased with the virtues of you, along with your brother and wife.
However, point out to me a region provided with water and abundant forests,
where I may establish a hermitage and dwell happily and contentedly.
Then, having heard Rāma's speech, the best of sages, that righteous and steadfast soul, reflected for a moment and spoke these most prudent words:
"Dear son, two yojanas from here there is a place abounding in roots, fruits, and water."
There is a glorious region, renowned as Pañcavaṭī, abounding in deer.
Having gone there and established a hermitage together with the son of Sumitrā, may you take your delight while faithfully observing the command of your father as it was spoken.
For this entire account is known to me in its entirety, O sinless one,
both through the power of my asceticism and through my affection for Daśaratha; moreover,
the desire residing in your heart has been perceived by me through my ascetic power.
"Having promised me that you would dwell here in this penance grove, I therefore say to you: go to Pañcavaṭī. For that region of the forest is delightful, and there Maithilī will find pleasure."
O Rāghava, that region is praiseworthy, not too far away,
and near the Godāvarī; there Maithilī will find delight,
for it abounds in plentiful roots and fruits and is filled with various flocks of birds.
O mighty-armed one, it is secluded, holy, and likewise delightful;
you, along with your wife, are capable of protecting it.
Furthermore, while dwelling there, Rāma will protect the ascetics.
"O hero, this great forest of Madhūka trees is visible;
one must go north of it to reach the Nyagrodha tree.
Then, having ascended the plateau not far from the mountain,"
"It is renowned as Pañcavaṭī, its forests perpetually in bloom. Having been addressed thus by Agastya, Rāma, together with the son of Sumitrā,
honored that truth-speaking ṛṣi and took his leave.
Having been granted leave by him and having performed obeisance at his feet, the two sons of the king,
accompanied by Sītā, departed from that hermitage for Pañcavaṭī;
they carried their bows and had quivers fastened to them, undaunted in the face of battle.
Following the path as instructed by the great seer, the two of them proceeded with concentrated minds toward Pañcavaṭī.
Then, while traveling toward Pañcavaṭī, the joy of the Raghus encountered along the way a vulture of massive body and terrifying prowess.
Seeing him staying in the forest, those two illustrious ones, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa,
thought him to be a rākṣasa bird and asked, "Who are you?
He, as if pleasing them with his sweet and gentle speech, [replied].
He said, "Child, know me to be a friend of your father.
Recognizing him as his father's friend, Rāghava honored him;
he then calmly inquired about his lineage and his name.
Having heard Rāma’s words, the twice-born sage described to him his own lineage and the origin of all beings,
beginning with those who were the lords of creatures (Prajāpatis) in ancient times, O mighty-armed one.
Listen, O Raghava, as I recount them all to you from the beginning:
Kardama was the first among them, followed by Vikṛta;
then Śeṣa, Saṃśraya, and the valiant Bahuputra.
Sthāṇu, Marīci, Atri, and the mighty Kratu;
Pulastya, Aṅgiras, Pracetas, and likewise Pulaha;
Dakṣa, Vivasvat, and another, Ariṣṭanemi, O Rāghava.
And the highly effulgent Kaśyapa was the last among them. O Rāma, we have heard that Prajāpati Dakṣa had sixty daughters, all illustrious and of great fame.
Kaśyapa accepted eight of those slender-waisted women: Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kālakā,
Tāmrā, Krodhavaśā, Manu, and Anala.
Then Kaśyapa, being pleased, spoke again to those maidens:
"O Aditi, Diti, and Danu, you shall give birth with intent minds, O Rāma, to sons who will be my equals and the lords of the three worlds."
And Kālakā, O mighty-armed one; as for the rest, they were dissatisfied.
From Aditi, O subduer of enemies, the thirty-three gods were born, O scorcher of foes:
the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the two Aśvins.
Diti, O dear one, gave birth to the illustrious sons known as the Daityas;
in former times, this earth with its forests and oceans belonged to them.
Danu, O subduer of enemies, gave birth to a son named Ashvagriva.
Tāmrā also gave birth to Naraka and Kālaka, as well as Kālikā;
she also bore Krauñcī, Bhāsī, Śyenī, Dhṛtarāṣṭrī, and Śukī—
these five daughters who are world-renowned.
Krauñcī gave birth to owls, and Bhāsī gave birth to the Bhāsas.
Śyenī gave birth to hawks and vultures of great brilliance,
while Dhṛtarāṣṭrī gave birth to swans and all kinds of Kalahaṃsa geese.
And that passionate woman also gave birth to the Cakravāka birds—blessings be upon you—and from Śukī was born Natā; from Natā, Vinatā was born as her daughter.
O Rāma, Krodhavaśā also gave birth to ten sons who were born of her own body.
Mṛgī, Mṛgamandā, Harī, and Bhadramadā; likewise Mātaṅgī, Śārdūlī, Śvetā, and Surabhī; as well as Surasā, who was endowed with every auspicious mark, and Kadrukā.
O best of men, all deer were the offspring of Mṛgī,
as were the bears, sṛmaras, and camaras born of Mṛgamandā.
Then Bhadramadā gave birth to a daughter named Irāvatī.
Airāvata, the great elephant and lord of the world, was her son. Haryā gave birth to offspring who were monkeys and ascetic forest-dwellers;
and Śārdūlī gave birth to sons who were both golāṅgūlas and tigers.
Furthermore, O bull among men, Mātaṅgī gave birth to elephants as her offspring;
and Śvetā gave birth to a son, the elephant of the quarter named Śvetākṣa.
Then, O Rāma, the goddess Surabhi gave birth to two daughters.
May you be blessed; Rohiṇī gave birth to the cows, and the illustrious Gandharvī gave birth to the horses.
O Rāma, Surasā gave birth to the Nāgas, and Kadrū to the Pannagas.
Manu begot human beings from the great-souled Kaśyapa—
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, O bull among men.
The Brāhmaṇas were born from his mouth, and likewise the Kṣatriyas from his chest.

"From his thighs the Vaiśyas were born, and from his feet the Śūdras," so says the Śruti. Analā also gave birth to all the trees that yield auspicious fruits; and Vinatā, the granddaughter of Śukī, as well as Kadrū, Surasā, and her sister [gave birth to their offspring].
Kadrū gave birth to a thousand earth-supporting nāgas, while Vinatā had two sons: Garuḍa and Aruṇa. From that Aruṇa I was born, and Sampāti is my elder brother.
"Know me as Jaṭāyu, the son of Śyenī, O subduer of enemies!
If you so desire, I shall become your companion during your stay;
moreover, my dear, I will protect Sītā once you have departed with Lakṣmaṇa."
Having honored Jaṭāyu and embraced him with joy, Rāghava bowed low;
for the self-possessed prince had heard from his father again and again that he was a friend to Jaṭāyu.
Having entrusted the Maithilī Sītā there to that exceedingly powerful bird, he departed along with him.
Desiring to consume his enemies like a fire consumes moths, he went to Pañcavaṭī together with Lakṣmaṇa.
Then, having reached Pañcavaṭī, which was filled with various beasts of prey and wild animals,
Rāma spoke to his brother Lakṣmaṇa, who was radiant with splendor.
"We have arrived at this very place as indicated by the great seer;
O gentle one, this is the region of Pañcavaṭī with its flowering groves. Let your gaze be cast everywhere in the forest, for you are indeed skilled in it."
"In which region would our hermitage be most agreeable?
O Lakṣmaṇa, let such a place be sought where Vaidehī, you, and I may find delight, and which is close to a body of water."
"A place where there is the beauty of forests as well as the beauty of waters,
and where sacrificial wood, flowers, kusha grass, and water are nearby.
Thus addressed by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa joined his palms in reverence.
In the presence of Sītā, he spoke these words to the descendant of Kakutstha:
"O Kākutstha, I am dependent on you; even though you remain for a hundred years, please tell me yourself to choose a delightful place."

Highly pleased by those words of Lakṣmaṇa, the immensely radiant Rāma reflected and chose a location endowed with every excellence. Having reached that delightful spot, he set about the work of establishing the hermitage.
Taking Saumitri by the hand, Rama said to him:
"This region is level and beautiful, covered with trees in full bloom;
O gentle one, you ought to establish a hermitage here in the proper manner."
Not far away, this beautiful lotus pond, adorned with lotuses that resemble the sun and possess fragrant scents, is visible;
it was described as such by the sage Agastya of purified soul.
This lovely Godāvarī is surrounded by trees in full bloom;
it is teeming with swans and kāraṇḍava ducks and graced by ruddy geese,
pressed upon by herds of deer neither too far nor too near.
O gentle one, lofty mountains resounding with the cries of peacocks, delightful, possessing many caves, and covered with blossoming trees, are visible;
they are adorned here and there with minerals of gold, silver, copper, and other ores.
The elephants appear as if they were latticed windows because of their supreme devotion.
[The mountain] is adorned with *sāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees, with *kharjūra*, *panasa*, and *āmra* trees, as well as with *nīvāra*, *timiśa*, and *puṃnāga* trees.
They were covered by various trees— mangoes, aśoka, tilaka, campaka, and ketaka— as well as flowering shrubs and creepers;
and by sandalwood, syandana, nīpa, jackfruit, and breadfruit trees.
"With Dhava, Aśvakarṇa, and Khadira trees, and with Śamī, Kiṃśuka, and Pāṭala trees—
this place is holy, this is pure, and it abounds in many deer and birds.
Here, O Saumitri, we shall dwell together with this bird."
Thus addressed by Rāma, the exceedingly powerful Lakṣmaṇa, slayer of enemy heroes,
soon constructed for his brother a vast leaf-hut made of compacted earth at that hermitage.
It was beautifully constructed with long bamboo poles as pillars;
having gone there, the glorious Lakṣmaṇa bathed in the river Godāvarī, gathered lotuses, and returned once more laden with fruit.
Then, having performed an offering of flowers and a ritual for peace according to the prescribed rites,
he showed that constructed hermitage to Rāma. Having seen that pleasant hermitage together with Sītā, he—
In the leaf-hut, Raghava experienced supreme joy.
"I am pleased with you, O Lord, for this great deed has been performed by you;
it is for this purpose that I have offered you my embrace,
O Lakṣmaṇa, who are discerning of intentions, grateful, and knower of dharma."
"Because of you as a son, my righteous father has not been preserved," Rāghava,
the enhancer of prosperity, said to Lakṣmaṇa; having spoken thus,
that self-controlled man dwelt happily in that region abounding in fruit.
For some time, that righteous-souled one dwelt there, attended by Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, like an immortal in the heavenly realm.
Yet, for that great-souled Rāghava, there was no happiness while he remained there.
When autumn had passed, the beloved winter season set in.
One morning, when the night had ended, that joy of the Raghus went to the beautiful Godāvarī river for the purpose of ritual ablution.
Bowing with a water-pot in his hand, the valiant brother Saumitri, following behind him together with Sita, spoke these words:
"O sweet-spoken one, that beloved time has now arrived which is dear to you."
By this, the auspicious year appears as if adorned;
the world is harsh with frost, the earth is garlanded with crops,
the waters are unfit for enjoyment, and the sacrificial fire is most beautiful.
Having worshipped the ancestral deities with offerings of the first-fruits of the harvest,

the virtuous people, having performed the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice at the proper time, were freed from all taint; their desires were abundant, and the cattle in the countryside yielded an abundance of milk.
Desirous of victory, the protectors of the earth wander about for the sake of military expeditions.
As the sun firmly serves the quarter inhabited by the God of Death,
the northern direction does not shine, like a woman whose forehead mark has been removed.

Naturally abounding in masses of snow and with the sun now far away, the mountain Himavat clearly lives up to its true name, "The Snowy One. At midday, it is pleasant to traverse and comfortable to the touch.
The days now possess a lovely sun, yet shadows and water have become wretched;
with gentle suns, accompanied by mist, sharp cold, and winds,
the days now shine upon empty forests devastated by frost.
Now the nights pass away, their cold having subsided, led by the month of Puṣya, reddened by frost,
and their duration increased as they move toward the end of winter. Their beauty has been transferred to the sun, while the orb of the moon is pale with frost.
Like a mirror blinded by breath, the moon does not shine;
the moonlight, soiled by frost on the full-moon night, does not gleam;
like Sītā darkened by the sun's heat, it is perceived but does not appear beautiful.
By its very nature cool to the touch, the western wind now blows, pierced by frost and doubly cold at this season;
the forests, covered in mist, are filled with barley and wheat.
They shine at the rising of the sun, with the cries of cranes and saras cranes;
the golden-hued rice stalks, hanging slightly low with their heads full of grain shaped like dates, look most beautiful.
With its rays approaching, veiled by frost and mist,
the sun, though risen high, appears like the moon;
its power is ungraspable in the forenoon, yet pleasant to the touch at midday.
The sunlight, slightly reddened and somewhat pale, shines upon the earth.
With its young rays resting upon it, the forest ground, where the grassy meadows are slightly moistened by the falling of dew, is beautiful.
Enveloped by the darkness of frost and shrouded in the gloom of mist,
the rows of forest trees, devoid of flowers, appear as if they are fast asleep;
their waters are covered with vapor, and the cranes can only be discerned by their cries.
The rivers now shine with banks whose sands are moistened by snow;
and because of the falling frost, the mildness of the sun,
and the cold, even the water situated upon mountain peaks is for the most part flavorful.
With leaves withered by age, their filaments and pericarps decayed, and reduced to mere stalks,
the lotus ponds, destroyed by the frost, no longer shine. Yet,
O tiger among men, at this very time, you are filled with sorrow.
The righteous-souled Bharata practices austerities in the city out of devotion to you;
having renounced his kingdom, his pride, and many various enjoyments,
that ascetic, restricted in diet, lies upon the cold ground.
He too, surely intent upon his ablutions at this very hour, goes regularly to the river Sarayū accompanied by his ministers;
he who has been raised in extreme luxury, being so delicate, must now be afflicted by the cold.

How is it that he, whose eyes are like lotus petals, who is dark-complexioned, glorious, large-statured, and pot-bellied; who knows the dharma, speaks the truth, is restrained by modesty, and has conquered his senses— how is it that he bathes in the Sarayū during the latter part of the night?
Speaking kindly and sweetly, long-armed subduer of enemies,
he has renounced various pleasures and has taken refuge in the noble one with his whole soul;
heaven has been won by your high-souled brother, Bharata.
"He who follows you in asceticism, even though you are staying in the forest"—
this well-known worldly proverb that "bipeds follow the mother's side rather than the father's" has been proven false by Bharata.
"How indeed can that mother Kaikeyī be so cruel in her vision, whose husband was Daśaratha and whose son was the virtuous Bharata?"—
thus did the righteous Lakṣmaṇa speak these words out of affection.
Unable to endure that disparagement of his mother, Rāghava said:
"O dear one, you must never, under any circumstances, speak ill of our middle mother.
Instead, speak only of Bharata, the lord of the Ikṣvākus."
"Though my mind is resolved and firm in its vow regarding residence in the forest,
it is made childish once again, tormented by affection for Bharata.
Lamenting thus, he reached the Godāvarī river there.
Kakutstha, together with his younger brother and Sītā, performed the consecration ceremony.
Then, having gratified the ancestors and the deities with water offerings, they,
with concentrated minds, praised the risen sun and the gods.
Having performed his consecration, Rāma shone with Sītā as his companion and Lakṣmaṇa,
like the blessed Lord Rudra accompanied by Nandin after having been consecrated along with the daughter of the mountain king. Thus,
Rāma, Sītā, and the son of Sumitrā were all consecrated.
Therefore, from the banks of the Godāvarī, they departed for their own hermitage.
Having reached that hermitage, Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa,
performed his morning rites and entered the leaf-hut.
Seated in the leaf-hut together with Sītā, the mighty-armed Rāma shone like the moon with the Citrā constellation;
and together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa, he engaged in various conversations.
Then, while Rāma was seated with his mind absorbed in conversation,
a certain rākṣasī arrived at that place by chance.
She was named Śūrpaṇakhā, the sister of the ten-necked rākṣasa.
Having approached Rāma, the sister beheld him who resembled a god;
he had the chest of a lion, mighty arms, and eyes like lotus petals;
he was delicate yet possessed of great strength, endowed with the auspicious marks of royalty.
Seeing Rāma, dark as a blue lotus and radiant like Kandarpa, who resembled Indra himself, the rākṣasī became infatuated with desire;
though she was ugly-faced, she gazed upon the handsome-faced Rāma, who had rounded hips and a large belly.
The wide-eyed woman looked upon the large-eyed one; she of the coarse hair gazed at him with beautiful locks.
She who was deformed beheld him of lovely form; she of the terrible voice listened to his sweet tone.
The aged and cruel woman gazed at the youth; she who spoke with deceitful words looked upon the upright one.
A Rākṣasī of evil conduct, who was unpleasant to behold, possessed by the passion of love (śarīraja), spoke to Rāma,
who was acting with righteousness and was accompanied by his wife, wearing matted hair in the guise of an ascetic and bearing a bow and arrows.
"How have you come to this region frequented by rākṣasas?
Thus addressed by the rākṣasī Śūrpaṇakhā, the scorcher of enemies,
out of his straightforward nature, began to relate everything.
There was a king named Daśaratha, whose prowess was equal to that of the gods;
I am his eldest son, known by people as Rāma.
This younger brother of mine is named Lakṣmaṇa, who is devoted to me.
"This is my wife, Vaidehī, renowned as Sītā.
Bound by the command of my father, the lord of men, and my mother,
and desiring righteousness for the sake of dharma, I have come here to dwell in the forest."
"But I wish to know you; tell me, who are you and to whom do you belong?
For what purpose have you come here? Speak the truth.
Hearing these words, the Rākṣasī, afflicted by passion, replied:
"Listen, Rāma, I shall speak these words to you according to the truth.
I am a Rākṣasī named Śūrpaṇakhā, capable of changing my form at will; I wander this forest alone, terrifying all beings."
My brother is the Rākṣasa named Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas;
and the exceedingly powerful Kumbhakarṇa is always in a deep sleep.
But Vibhīṣaṇa is righteous in soul and does not act like a Rākṣasa.
And the two brothers, Khara and Dūṣaṇa, are renowned for their prowess in battle.
O Rāma, having surpassed them all, I have come to you, the best of men, as my husband with my whole being, because of my first sight of you.
