"Be my husband for a long time; what will you do with Sītā?
She is deformed and misshapen; she is not a match for you.
Look at me—I alone am a wife suitable for you in beauty."
"This human woman— ugly, unchaste, hideous, and with a sunken belly— I shall devour her along with this brother of yours.
Then he [seized] mountain peaks and various forests.
"O beloved, wandering through the Daṇḍaka forest together with me, you shall behold [these sights].
Thus addressed, the descendant of Kakutstha, skilled in speech, smiled at the woman with intoxicating eyes and began to speak these words.
Then Rāma, with clear and gentle words and preceded by a smile, spoke to Śūrpaṇakhā, who was bound by the snares of passion:
"O lady, I am already married; this wife of mine is dear to me."
"For women such as you, the state of having a rival is exceedingly painful.
But this younger brother of mine, named Lakṣmaṇa, is virtuous, handsome, illustrious, heroic, and has not yet taken a wife."
"Never before married, seeking a wife, young, and handsome,
he shall be a husband worthy of this beauty of yours.
O large-eyed one, accept him as your husband and my brother."
"O lady of beautiful hips, you shall be without rivals, like the radiance of the sun upon Mount Meru.
Thus addressed by Rāma, the rākṣasī, deluded by passion,
suddenly dismissed Rāma and spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
"You, a woman of excellent complexion, are a fitting wife for this form of mine;
together with me, you shall wander happily through all the Daṇḍaka forests.
Thus addressed by the Rākṣasī, the son of Sumitrā, who was skilled in speech, replied.
Then, having smiled at Śūrpaṇakhī, Lakṣmaṇa spoke what was fitting:
"O lotus-complexioned one, how can you wish to become the wife of my servant? As such, O noble lady, I am dependent upon my brother."
"O large-eyed one, may you become the younger wife of this noble man whose purpose is fulfilled, you who have achieved your goal and possess joyful, stainless beauty.
As for this woman— deformed, unchaste, hideous, and with a sunken belly— "
"Having abandoned his aged wife, he will surely devote himself to you alone.
For what wise man, O woman of excellent complexion, would ever cast aside such supreme beauty to set his heart on mere mortals, O lady of noble form?"
Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, that Karālā, who had a sunken belly and was unskilled in discerning jest, took those words to be true;
she [then approached] Rāma, the scorcher of foes, as he sat within the leaf-hut.
Deluded by passion, she spoke thus to the invincible one in the presence of Sītā:
"Relying on this ugly, unchaste, hideous, emaciated, aged woman as your wife, you do not hold me in high regard."
"Today, while you look on, I shall devour this human woman; I will roam with you without a rival, as I please.
Having spoken thus to the fawn-eyed lady, she whose eyes were like glowing embers—
Highly incensed, she rushed toward him like a great meteor toward Rohiṇī. As she fell upon him like the noose of Death, the mighty Rāma seized her and, filled with wrath, then spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
"O son of Sumitrā, one should never engage in jesting with cruel and ignoble people; look, O gentle one, how Vaidehī somehow still lives!
[Look at] this woman who is deformed, unchaste, excessively intoxicated, and pot-bellied."
"O tiger among men, you ought to disfigure this ogress.
Thus addressed, the mighty Lakṣmaṇa, filled with rage while Rāma looked on,
drew his sword and cut off her ears and nose.
With her ears and nose cut off, the terrible Śūrpaṇakhā let out a discordant shriek and fled back toward the forest by the way she had come.
That hideous and most dreadful Rākṣasī was drenched in blood.
She uttered various roars like a rain-cloud in the monsoon;
streaming blood in many ways, she of the terrible appearance seized her arms and, roaring, entered the great forest.

Then, having been disfigured, she approached her brother Khara— who was possessed of fierce energy and surrounded by a host of Rākṣasas— in Janasthāna, and fell from the sky to the earth like a thunderbolt.
Then, seeing that Rāghava had arrived in the forest with his wife and Lakṣmaṇa, she fainted, overwhelmed by fear and delusion.
And drenched in blood, that sister related to Khara everything regarding her own disfigurement.
Seeing his sister fallen there, disfigured and drenched in blood, the Rākṣasa Khara, consumed by anger, questioned her.
Endowed with strength and prowess, able to go wherever you wish and assume any form at will, by whom have you been brought to this state, having become like Death itself?
[You who were once] among the gods, gandharvas, spirits, and the great-souled sages.
"Who is this man of such great prowess who has made you so deformed?
For I see no one in the world who could do me such an injury,
except for the thousand-eyed Mahendra, the subduer of Pāka."
Today, with my life-ending arrows, I shall take away my own life, like a crane drinking up milk mixed in water. When I have been slain in battle, my vital organs severed by arrows—
Whose blood, red and frothy, will the earth drink?
Whose bodies, once struck down by me in battle, will the birds of prey gather together and joyfully devour, tearing the flesh from them?
Neither the gods, nor the gandharvas, nor the piśācas, nor the rākṣasas are able to protect that wretched man, dragged away by me in this great battle.
Having gradually regained consciousness, you ought to tell me about him.
"By you, ill-behaved one, she was overcome through your prowess in the forest.
Hearing these words of her brother, who was especially enraged,
Śūrpaṇakhā then spoke these words with tears.
Young, endowed with beauty, delicate yet possessed of great strength,
with eyes as broad as lotus petals, they were clad in bark and black antelope skins;
resembling kings of the Gandharvas, they bore the marks of royalty.
Whether they be gods or men, I do not venture to conjecture who they are.
There, in their midst, I saw a woman of slender waist, youthful, endowed with beauty, and adorned with every ornament.
Through the combined efforts of both of them, I have been reduced to this state regarding that woman, so that I am left without a protector;
and I [shall suffer] for her who acts with crooked conduct and for those two who have been slain.
"I wish to drink blood with its froth at the head of the battle.
O father, let this first desire of mine be fulfilled by you:
that I may drink the blood of her and those two in combat."
While she was speaking thus, the enraged Khara commanded fourteen immensely powerful Rākṣasas who resembled Death itself:
"These two humans, though equipped with weapons and clad in bark and black antelope skins— "
"You two have entered the terrible Daṇḍaka forest together with that woman;
you ought to return after slaying her, for she is wicked.
And this sister of mine shall drink their blood."
"O Rākṣasas, go quickly and, having overwhelmed those two by your own prowess, fulfill this cherished desire of my sister; let it be accomplished at once.
Thus were those fourteen Rākṣasas commanded.
There they went together with her, like clouds driven by the wind.
Then the terrible Śūrpaṇakhā, having arrived at the hermitage of the descendant of Raghu,
informed the Rākṣasas of those two brothers along with Sītā.
They beheld the mighty Rāma seated in the leaf-hut together with Sītā, the princess of Videha, and Lakṣmaṇa.
Seeing them and that approaching Rākṣasī, the glorious descendant of Raghu—
Rāma spoke to his brother Lakṣmaṇa, who was radiant with splendor:
"O son of Sumitrā, remain for a moment close behind Sītā;
I shall slay those who have come here upon her trail."
Having heard these words of Rāma, who knows his own self,
Lakṣmaṇa honored Rāma’s speech, saying, "So be it.
Rāghava also [took up] his great bow, adorned with gold.
The righteous-souled one strung his bow and spoke to those rākṣasas:
"We two are the sons of Daśaratha, brothers Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa;
we have entered the difficult Daṇḍaka forest together with Sītā."
Why do you harm these two ascetics, who subsist on fruits and roots, are self-controlled, practitioners of dharma, and dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest?
It is to slay you, you evil-minded wrongdoers, in this great forest.
"By the command of the sages, I have arrived here equipped with my bow.
You should remain right here contentedly; you ought not to approach me. O night-stalkers, if you have any regard for your lives, turn back!"
Hearing those words of his, those fourteen Rākṣasas—
slayers of Brahmins, holding spears in their hands, fierce, with blood-red eyes and the corners of their eyes crimson with rage— spoke these words to Rāma, whose own eyes had red corners.
"Delighted by his harsh and sweet speech and having witnessed his prowess,
you have provoked the anger of our lord, the great-souled Khara.
You alone shall lose your life today, slain by us in battle."
For what power do you have, being alone, to stand before us many at the head of the battle, let alone to fight in combat?
[You would be struck] by these iron clubs, spears, and sharp-edged missiles hurled by our arms.
"You shall lose your life, your prowess, and the bow held in your hand.
Having spoken thus, those fourteen enraged Rākṣasas,
with weapons and swords raised, rushed toward Rāma.
They hurled those spears at Rāghava, who was difficult to conquer.
Kākutstha, with an equal number of fourteen arrows adorned with gold, cut all those spears to pieces.
Thereafter, the immensely radiant one, filled with supreme rage, took up fourteen iron arrows whetted on stone that were as bright as the sun;
having grasped his bow and drawn it back, he aimed at the rākṣasa targets.
Rāghava released arrows like Śatakratu releases thunderbolts. Those shafts, with golden feathers, blazing, and adorned with gold,
became equal in splendor to great meteors in the sky.
Having pierced the chests of the Rākṣasas with force, those arrows— smeared with blood and sounding like thunderbolts— then flew out and sank into the earth.
With their hearts shattered, they fell to the ground like trees cut at their roots.
They fell down, their limbs drenched in blood, disfigured and deprived of life.
Seeing them fallen upon the ground, the rākṣasī, overwhelmed with rage and terrified, again let out a terrible cry there.
Roaring a great cry, Śūrpaṇakhā, her blood somewhat dried, returned with speed to Khara; then, afflicted, she fell down once more like a sapless creeper.
Seeing the Rākṣasas struck down in battle, Śūrpaṇakhā then ran back;
that sister of Khara reported the entire slaughter of all those demons in its full detail.
Seeing Śūrpaṇakhā fallen once more, Khara was overcome with rage.
He spoke with a clear voice to her, who had come for a purpose that was not beneficial:
"I have now dispatched those blood-drinking Rākṣasa heroes for the sake of your welfare; why then do you weep again?"
They are devoted, loyal, and always well-disposed toward me;
even if they were to strike me, they should not be killed, for they would never disregard my word.
I wish to hear the reason why this is so.
"Alas, my lord! you cry out, writhing upon the ground like a serpent.
Why do you lament like one who is helpless when I, your protector, am present?
Arise, arise! Do not fear; cast off this despondency here.
Having been addressed in this way and consoled by Khara, the invincible one wiped her tearful eyes and spoke to her brother Khara:
"Those fourteen brave Rākṣasas were sent by you."
"Terrible ones, they sought to slay Rāghava along with Lakṣmaṇa for my sake.
But all of them, filled with indignation and bearing spears and axes in their hands, were slain in battle by Rāma with arrows that pierce the vital organs.
Seeing those mighty ones fallen upon the ground in an instant, and witnessing the great deed of Rāma, a profound terror came over me,
O night-stalker; thus I am afraid, agitated, and despondent.
Having seen fear on all sides, I have come to you for refuge once more.
Why do you not rescue me as I sink into this vast ocean of grief, inhabited by the crocodiles of despair and garlanded with the waves of terror?
And these flesh-eating Rākṣasas who have followed my path have been struck down upon the earth by Rāma with his sharpened arrows;
if you have compassion for me, and if you have compassion for those Rākṣasas as well.
"O night-stalker, if you have the power or the prowess, then destroy this thorn of the Rākṣasas who dwells in the Daṇḍaka forest— Rāma—
if you do not slay my enemy, Rāma, this very day."

And before your very eyes, I shall cast off my life, free from shame. By my own discernment, I perceive that you are not capable of standing before Rāma in battle, facing him with his bow in a great conflict.
"You are not a hero, though you fancy yourself one; your prowess is falsely attributed to you, since you cannot slay those two humans, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa.
Depart quickly from Janasthāna along with your kinsmen."
What kind of dwelling will there be for you here, who are devoid of courage and lacking in vigor?
For you shall quickly perish, being overwhelmed by the splendor of Rāma; indeed, that Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, is endowed with such majesty.
"And his brother is of great prowess, by whom I have been disfigured. Thus insulted by Śūrpaṇakhā, the heroic Khara then spoke these even harsher words in the midst of the rākṣasas.
This incomparable anger of mine, born from your insult, cannot be restrained, like the rising salt-water ocean. Because of his prowess, I do not count Rāma as a mere mortal whose life is spent.
"The self that has been slain by its own evil deeds shall today be released from life. Let these tears be restrained and this agitation be abandoned;
I shall lead Rāma, together with his brother, to the abode of Yama."
"O Rākṣasī, today you shall drink the warm, red blood of Rāma, whose life-force is failing as he lies upon the ground, slain by my axe.
Hearing these words falling from the mouth of Khara, she was filled with joy.
Out of foolishness, he praised his brother once again, the best of the Rākṣasas. Having been previously reviled by her and now praised once more,
Khara then spoke to his army commander named Dūṣaṇa.
There were fourteen thousand rākṣasas of terrible speed who never retreated in battles, following my will;
they were as dark as blue clouds, fierce, and performers of cruel deeds.
O gentle one, command all the efforts of those Rākṣasas who delight in harming the world, who are powerful and fierce in their splendor,
who possess the pride of tigers, who have gaping mouths and great energy,
and who are ever-exerting themselves.
"O gentle one, quickly bring my chariot, as well as bows,
variegated arrows, swords, and various sharp spears;
I wish to go forth ahead of the high-souled descendants of Pulastya."
"For the sake of slaying the ill-behaved Rāma, [I am ready]," said he who was skilled in battle.
To him as he was speaking thus, Dūṣaṇa then announced a great chariot, sun-bright in color, yoked with excellent dappled horses.
That golden wheel, shaped like the peak of Mount Meru,
adorned with refined gold, unobstructed, and having a pole made of lapis lazuli,
was marked with fish, flowers, trees, mountains, and golden suns and moons.
Surrounded by auspicious flocks of birds and stars,
and equipped with banners and swords, adorned with small bells and yoked to excellent horses, Khara ascended the chariot out of indignation.
Seeing him mounted on his chariot, the Rākṣasas of terrifying prowess stood surrounding him and the mighty Dūṣaṇa;
Kharas, however, [beheld] those great archers with their formidable shields, weapons, and banners.
"Drive [the chariot] forth! he said, seeing all the Rākṣasas standing upon the chariot.
Then that Rākṣasa army, with its terrible shields, weapons, and banners, marched out from Janasthāna with a great roar and immense speed.
With mallets, spears, spikes, and very sharp axes;
with swords, discuses, and shining lances held in their hands;
and with pikes, terrible iron clubs, and oversized bows.
With maces, swords, clubs, and thunderbolts of terrifying appearance held aloft,
fourteen thousand of the most formidable Rākṣasas, who followed the will of Khara, marched forth from Janasthāna.
Seeing those Rākṣasas of terrifying prowess rushing toward him,
Khara’s chariot also moved forward a little after them.
Then [he saw] those dappled horses adorned with refined gold.
Having understood Khara’s intention, the charioteer urged the horses forward.
Thus impelled, the chariot of Khara, the slayer of enemies,
swiftly filled the quarters and the intermediate directions with its sound.

But Khara, his fury intensified, with a harsh voice like the Destroyer himself hurrying for the sake of slaying his enemy, urged his charioteer once more, roaring like a mighty cloud raining down stones. That formidable and inauspicious army set forth, with blood for its water.
A tumultuous great cloud, the color of a donkey, rained down;
his swift horses, yoked to the chariot,
fell by chance upon a level, flower-strewn stretch of the royal road.
The halo surrounding the sun became dark blue at its edges with blood-red rims,
resembling a whirling circle of fire as it received the sun.
Then, he approached the raised standard with its golden staff.
Having descended, a massive and most dreadful vulture stood there;
and near Janasthāna, flesh-eating beasts and birds of harsh voices raised various discordant cries.
And in the blazing quarter of the sky, the terrible, loud-voiced jackals of the Yātudhānas uttered an inauspicious and fearsome cry;
they resembled mountains split asunder, their flowing streams of water having been dried up.
The formidable clouds made that sky devoid of space;
a terrible darkness arose, intense and hair-raising,
so that neither the cardinal nor the intermediate directions could be clearly distinguished.
At that time, apart from the hour of twilight, the sky shone with a hue like fresh blood;
fierce beasts and birds cried out facing Khara, while jackals,
portending constant ill in battle, howled with a terrifying appearance.
They roared toward Bala with mouths vomiting flames. A headless trunk (kabandha), resembling a massive iron club, was seen near the sun;
the great planet Svarbhānu seized the sun out of season.
The wind blew fiercely, the sun grew lusterless,
and stars with the brilliance of fireflies appeared even without night.
The lotus ponds, their flowers and mud dried up, had their fish and birds huddled together in fear.
At that moment, the trees were bereft of flowers and fruit;
dust, red as a cloud, was stirred up even without a wind;
and there, the sarika birds began to shriek with cries of "vīcī-kūcī."
Meteors, terrible to behold and accompanied by thunderous sounds, fell from the sky; and the earth, along with its mountains, forests, and groves,
trembled as the wise Khara stood upon his chariot and roared.
His left arm trembled and his voice became hoarse;
his vision, as he looked in every direction, became filled with tears;
a pain arose in his forehead, yet he did not turn back from his delusion.
Beholding those great portents that had arisen, causing the hair to stand on end,
Khara then spoke to all the Rākṣasas with a laugh:
"All these great portents that have arisen are terrible to behold."
Out of my own prowess, I do not regard myself as weak, like those who are feeble;
I could bring down even the stars from the vault of heaven with my sharp arrows,
and when enraged, I would subject even Death himself to the law of mortality.
I cannot return without having slain that Raghava, who is arrogant in his strength, and his brother Lakshmana with my sharp arrows;
let my sister’s desire be fulfilled once I have drunk their blood.
But for what reason has this reversal occurred for Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa?
Never before have I suffered defeat in battles;
this is evident to you all, and I do not speak a falsehood.
"Even the enraged King of the Gods, who rides upon the rutting Airāvata and holds the thunderbolt in his hand, I could slay in battle; how much more so those two mere humans?
Hearing that roar of the Rākṣasa, the great army [trembled].
She who was bound by the noose of death experienced incomparable joy;
and the high-souled rishis, gods, gandharvas, siddhas, and charanas gathered together, desiring to witness the battle.
Having gathered together, those performers of meritorious deeds said to one another:
"May there be well-being for cows and brahmins, and for those who are honored by the worlds.
May Rāghava be victorious in battle over the night-stalkers, the descendants of Pulastya."

"Just as one with a discus in hand [overcomes] all the foremost of the Asuras in battle," saying this and much more, the supreme seers beheld that army of those Rākṣasas whose lives had reached their end.
Then Khara, having emerged from the front of the army with speed on his chariot,
was seen; and seeing that Rākṣasa, other Rākṣasas also rushed forth—
Śyenagāmī, Pṛthugrīva, Yajñaśatru, and Vihangama.
Durjaya, Karavīrākṣa, Paruṣa, Kālakārmuka,
Meghamālī, Mahāmālī, Sarpāsya, and Rudhirāśana—
these twelve of great prowess set out on all sides toward Khara.
Mahākapāla, Sthūlākṣa, Pramāthin, and Triśiras—
these four leaders of the army followed behind Dūṣaṇa.
That most dreadful army of Rākṣasa heroes, possessing terrifying speed and eager for battle, [advanced].
Those two princes suddenly approached him like the moon and the sun approaching the planets.
When Khara, of fierce prowess, had departed for his hermitage,
Rāma, together with his brother, beheld those very same portents.
Seeing those most terrible portents that had arisen, which caused the hair to stand on end and were harmful to all creatures, he spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa:
"Behold these, O mighty-armed one, which carry away all living beings."
To avert these great portents that have arisen and all the rākṣasas,
these harsh clouds, reddish-brown like donkeys, are revolving in the sky, emitting blood-red streams and harsh sounds.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, all my arrows are smoking as they long for battle, and my gold-backed bows are twitching;
such is the way these forest-dwelling birds are crying out here."
"Great danger has come upon us, and there is doubt even for our lives.
A truly great battle will surely take place; of this there is no doubt.
This arm of mine, throbbing again and again, tells me so."
O hero, in our proximity, victory over the enemy and his defeat are certain;
for your face appears radiant and serene. Indeed, O Lakṣmaṇa, such is the sign of those who are prepared for battle.
Their faces become lusterless as their life-span comes to an end. A wise man who desires his own welfare and anticipates misfortune must take measures in advance to provide for it.
Therefore, taking Vaidehī with you, bow in hand and arrows ready,
take refuge in a mountain cave that is difficult of access and thick with trees;
for I do not wish for these words of yours to be disregarded by you.
"Bound by an oath upon my feet, go, my child, without delay.
Thus addressed by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, taking up his arrows and bow, took refuge in a secure cave along with Sītā.
When Lakṣmaṇa had entered the cave with Sītā, Rāma, saying "Alas, he has gone forth," donned his armor.
Adorned with that armor which resembled fire, he shone.
In the darkness, Rāma appeared like a smokeless fire that has flared up.
Raising his great bow and taking up his arrows, the valiant one stood there,
filling the quarters with the sounds of his bowstring.
Then the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Cāraṇas,
as well as the Guhyakas, spoke to one another in great terror:
"There are fourteen thousand Rākṣasas of fearsome deeds."
"And how will the battle proceed when Rāma is alone and righteous?
Then, an army of Yātudhānas appeared on all sides, with a deep resonance and formidable armor, weapons, and banners.
They let out lion-like roars and bellowed at one another,
repeatedly twanging their bows and yawning;
they raised a great clamor and beat upon kettledrums.
Their tumultuous noise filled that forest.
Terrified by that sound, the wild beasts roaming the woods fled silently to where they could not look back.
Then that army, possessing great speed and bearing various weapons, approached Rāma like a deep ocean; meanwhile,
Rāma, skilled in battle, cast his eyes in every direction.
He beheld that army of Khara, prepared and advancing toward the battle.
Drawing his formidable bow and drawing arrows from his quivers,
he summoned a fierce rage for the purpose of slaying all the rākṣasas.
Enraged and blazing like the fire at the end of an eon, he became difficult to behold;
seeing him possessed by such splendor, the forest deities trembled with fear.
At that time, the appearance of the enraged Rāma was seen.
Like the sacrifice of Dakṣa when it was prepared to be destroyed by the wielder of the Pināka bow,
Kharas, having arrived at the hermitage with his attendants, beheld Rāma— the slayer of enemies— who was enraged and had his bow drawn.
Seeing him, he raised his bow, which was endowed with excellent qualities and produced a harsh sound,
and urged the charioteer toward Rāma, saying, "Drive forward!
At Khara's command, the charioteer drove the horses.
Where the mighty-armed Rāma stood alone, shaking his bow,
all those night-stalkers and their ministers, seeing him rush forth, surrounded him while uttering a great roar.
Having entered into the midst of those Yātudhānas, Khara took his place like the red-limbed planet Mars risen in the center of the stars.
Then all the night-stalkers, enraged, [attacked] that one of the formidable bow.
They rained down various kinds of weapons upon the invincible Rāma;
in the battle, the rākṣasas, intent on their wrath, struck at Rāma with iron mallets, spears, lances, swords, and axes.
Resembling clouds, possessing great roars and immense strength,
those leaders of the Rākṣasas rushed toward Rāma, the descendant of Kakutstha, desiring to slay him in battle.
Those hosts of Rākṣasas discharged showers of arrows upon Rāma.
Like clouds raining upon the king of mountains with torrents of rain,
Rāghava was surrounded by those terrible hosts of rākṣasas,
just as Mahādeva is surrounded by his throngs of attendants on the auspicious lunar days.
That descendant of Raghu received those weapons released by the Yātudhānas with his own arrows, just as the ocean receives the torrents of rivers;
though his body was pierced by those terrible missiles, he did not flinch.
Like a great mountain struck by many blazing thunderbolts,
Rāma was pierced; with all his limbs smeared with blood,
that descendant of Raghu appeared like the sun enveloped by the clouds of twilight.
The gods, gandharvas, siddhas, and supreme ṛṣis were distressed,
seeing that single being then surrounded by many thousands.
Thereupon Rāma, filled with great rage, drew his bow into a circle.
Then Rāma effortlessly discharged in battle hundreds and thousands of sharp arrows— irresistible, unbearable, resembling the noose of Death,
fletched with heron feathers, and straight-flying.
Those arrows, released by Rāma with ease into the enemy armies,
took away the lives of the rākṣasas like nooses fashioned by Time.
Having pierced through those rākṣasa bodies, those arrows were drenched in blood.
Moving through the atmosphere, they shone with a brilliance equal to blazing fire.
From the circle of Rāma’s bow, there issued forth countless, exceedingly fierce arrows that snatched away the lives of the rākṣasas.
With those [arrows], they struck bows, the tops of banners, armor, and heads;
many thighs, resembling the trunks of elephants, along with their hand-ornaments.
Then, with hollow-pointed shafts, iron arrows, and sharp-tipped *vikarṇis*, [they struck].

Being pierced, the night-stalkers let out a terrifying cry of distress. Afflicted by Rāma with sharp arrows that pierce the vital organs, that army found no comfort, like a dry forest consumed by fire.
Some night-stalkers, heroic and possessed of terrible strength, being exceedingly enraged, hurled pikes, swords, and axes at Rāma;
but the mighty-armed Rāghava warded off those weapons with his arrows.
In that battle, he took away their lives and severed their necks.
And those night-rangers who remained there, dejected and tormented by arrows, fled toward Khara for protection.
Taking them all back once more and having comforted them, Dūṣaṇa,
enraged like Rudra at the end of time, rushed toward the descendant of Kakutstha. But they all turned back again, rendered fearless by their reliance on Dūṣaṇa.
Armed with *sāla* trees, *tāla* trees, and rocks, they rushed toward Rāma alone.
Then there occurred a wondrous, tumultuous, and hair-raising battle—
most terrible— between this Rāma and those Rākṣasas once more.
The righteous Rāghava received that great, life-destroying rain of trees and rocks with his sharp arrows; having warded it off,
he stood like a bull with its eyes closed.
Rāma was seized by a supreme rage for the purpose of slaying all the Rākṣasas.
Then, possessed by anger and as if blazing with splendor,
he covered the army, along with Dūṣaṇa, on all sides with his arrows.
Then the enraged general Dūṣaṇa, the harasser of his enemies,
seized a hair-raising iron club that resembled a mountain peak,
was encircled with golden bands, and was capable of crushing the armies of the gods.

In the battle, he seized that iron club, which resembled a great serpent, was strewn with sharp iron spikes, smeared with blood, possessed a touch like the thunderbolt, and was capable of shattering the gate-towers of enemies.
The night-stalker Dūṣaṇa, a doer of cruel deeds, rushed toward Rāma.
As Dūṣaṇa was charging at him, that descendant of Raghu severed his two arms, along with their ornaments, using two arrows.
Deprived of it, his massive body fell at the front of the battle like the severed iron bolt of Indra’s banner from its hand;
with his two hands scattered, Dūṣaṇa fell upon the earth.
Like a wise great elephant with its two shattered tusks, [he lay there].
Seeing Dūṣaṇa fallen upon the ground, slain in battle, all living beings honored the descendant of Kakutstha, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!"
In the meantime, three enraged leaders of the army—
Mahākapāla, Sthūlākṣa, and the exceedingly powerful Pramāthin— being bound by the noose of death, united and rushed toward Rāma.
Mahākapāla raised a massive spear,
Sthūlākṣa seized a sharp-edged lance (paṭṭiśa), and Pramāthin grasped a battle-axe;
seeing them rushing toward him, Rāghava [struck] them with sharp arrows.
He received those who approached him like guests with his sharp-pointed arrows. The joy of the Raghus severed the head of Mahākapāla and,
with countless floods of shafts, crushed Pramāthin.
He filled the eyes of Sthūlākṣa with sharp arrows;
struck down, he fell to the earth like a great tree with spreading branches. Then, with arrows resembling fire and adorned with gold and diamonds...
With his arrows, the radiant one left only the hindquarters of that army remaining.
Those gold-feathered shafts, like fires accompanied by smoke,
struck down those rākṣasas as thunderbolts strike great trees.
At the forefront of the battle, Rāma struck down a hundred Rākṣasas with a single barbed arrow (karṇin), and a thousand with a thousand;
by those arrows, their armor and ornaments were shattered, and their bows were cut to pieces.
Smeared with blood, the night-stalkers fell upon the earth. With those fallen in battle— hair disheveled and drenched in gore—
the entire ground was strewn like a great sacrificial altar covered with *kuśa* grass.
In an instant, that most terrible forest, its rākṣasas slain,
became like a hellish pit, mired in mud of flesh and blood;
there were fourteen thousand rākṣasas of fearsome deeds.
All were slain by Rāma alone, a mere human on foot.
Of that entire army, only the great chariot-warrior Khara remained,
along with the Rākṣasa Triśiras and Rāma, the slayer of enemies.
Then, beholding that army of formidable strength slain in the great battle by the more powerful Rāma,
Khara approached Rāma on his great chariot like Indra with his thunderbolt raised.
But as Khara was advancing toward Rāma, the commander of the host—
The Rākṣasa named Triśiras, having gathered together, spoke these words:
"O valiant one, employ me; turn back from this rashness! Behold the mighty-armed Rāma struck down in battle."
"I swear this truth to you; I touch my weapon as a pledge that I shall slay Rāma, who deserves to be killed by all the Rākṣasas.
Either I shall be his death in battle, or he shall be mine."
"Abandoning your enthusiasm for battle, be a witness for a moment.
Either, Rāma being slain, you shall go to Janasthāna filled with joy;
or, I being slain, you shall approach Rāma for combat."
Khara, having been propitiated by Triśiras out of a desire for death,
was granted permission with the words, "Go and fight," and he set out toward Rāghava.
And Triśiras, on a radiant chariot yoked with horses, [followed].
He rushed toward Rāma in battle like a three-peaked mountain;
discharging masses of streams of arrows like a great cloud,
he let out a roar resembling that of a drum soaked with water.
Seeing the three-headed Rākṣasa approaching, Rāghava received him with his bow,
brandishing sharp arrows.
That great and tumultuous battle between Rāma and Triśiras ensued.
The combat between those two exceedingly powerful warriors was like that between a lion and an elephant.
Then, struck on the forehead with three arrows by Triśiras,
the indignant and enraged Rāma spoke these words in a state of agitation.
"Aha! Such is the strength of this Rakshasa, a hero in valor, by whose arrows I have been wounded on the forehead as if by flowers. Now, accept my own arrows as well, released from the bowstring."
Having spoken thus, he, enraged and impetuous, struck fourteen arrows resembling venomous serpents into the chest of Triśiras;
with four more straight-jointed arrows, he struck his horses.
The radiant Rāma struck down his four horses with eight arrows; he felled the charioteer from the seat of the chariot with [another] arrow,
and cut down his lofty banner with a shaft.
Then, as the night-stalker leaped up from that destroyed chariot, Rāma pierced him in the heart with arrows; he became paralyzed.
And the one of immeasurable soul, filled with indignation, struck that Rākṣasa with his shafts.

With three hundred swift arrows, he struck off three heads. Oppressed by Rāma’s shafts, that night-stalker fell upon the earth vomiting blood, following after his own heads that had previously fallen.
Then the surviving Rākṣasas, broken and relying on Khara, fled and did not stay, like deer terrified by a tiger.
Seeing them fleeing, Khara, filled with rage, turned them back himself.
He rushed toward Rāma alone, just as Rāhu rushes toward the moon.
Seeing Dūṣaṇa slain in battle along with Triśiras,
and witnessing the prowess of Rāma, even Khara was struck with terror.
Seeing that the immensely powerful and invincible army of Rākṣasas had been slain by Rāma alone— Dūṣaṇa and Triśiras as well—
that Rākṣasa, observing his forces mostly destroyed, became despondent.
Khara assailed Rāma, just as Namuci once assailed Vāsava. Drawing his powerful bow, Khara loosed at Rāma blood-drinking iron arrows that were like enraged, venomous serpents.
Vibrating his bowstring repeatedly and displaying his mastery of weapons,
Khara, stationed upon his chariot, moved through various maneuvers in battle with his arrows;
that great car-warrior covered all the cardinal and intermediate directions with his shafts.
Seeing that immense bow, Rāma also filled it;
with his unbearable arrows, which were like sparks of fire,
he left no space in the sky, just as Parjanya fills it with showers of rain.
Due to those sharp arrows discharged by Khara and Rāma,
the sky became devoid of space, crowded on all sides with shafts;
shrouded by that net of arrows, the sun did not shine at all.
As the two of them fought together with a fury intent on killing one another,
he then struck Rāma in battle with hollow arrows, iron shafts, and sharp-pointed barbed arrows, like a great elephant being goaded with hooks.
All beings beheld that Rākṣasa standing upon his chariot, bow in hand, like Death himself with a noose in his grasp;
he was as valiant as a lion and possessed the majestic stride of a lion.

Upon seeing him, Rāma was not agitated, just as a lion is not disturbed by a small deer. Then, in his great chariot which shone like the sun, Khara encountered Rāma in battle, like a moth flying into a fire.
Then Khara, displaying his manual dexterity, severed the bow and arrow from the grip of the high-souled Rāma at the handle.
He then took up seven other arrows and aimed them at Rāma's armor.

Enraged in battle, he struck down those arrows which possessed a brilliance equal to Indra’s thunderbolt. Then that armor of Rāma, who was as radiant as the sun, fell to the ground, shattered by the well-jointed arrows discharged by Khara.
Pierced in all his limbs by those arrows, the enraged Rāghava shone in battle like a blazing, smokeless fire. Then Rāma, the destroyer of enemies, let out a deep roar.
He took up another great bow, strung with a cord, belonging to his enemy;
that very large Vaiṣṇava bow which had been bestowed as a boon by the great seer, he raised and rushed toward Khara.
Then, enraged in battle, Rāma severed Khara’s banner with gold-feathered arrows of straight joints;
that beautiful golden banner fell, shattered into many pieces.
The sun descended to the earth as if by the command of the gods.
Then the enraged Khara, who knew the vital spots, pierced Rāma in his limbs and heart with four arrows, like one striking an elephant with iron pikes.
Pierced by many arrows discharged from Khara’s bow, Rāma,
his limbs drenched in blood, became exceedingly enraged.
Grasping his bow in that supreme battle, he, the best among archers—
The supreme archer released six well-aimed arrows:
he struck him on the head with one shaft, then struck his two arms with two,
and struck his chest with three crescent-headed arrows.
Thereafter, the immensely powerful one, enraged and desiring to slay the Rākṣasa, discharged thirteen stone-sharpened iron arrows that resembled the sun;
with one he struck his yoke, and with four he struck the four horses.
And with the sixth arrow, he severed the head of Khara’s charioteer in battle;
with three more, the powerful one cut through the triple-pole, and with two, the mighty one destroyed the axle;
then, with the twelfth arrow, he shattered Khara’s bow along with the arrow fixed to it.
Having severed [the bow] with a shaft resembling a thunderbolt, Rāghava, laughing as it were,
pierced Khara in battle with his thirteenth arrow, like Indra himself.
With his bow broken, his chariot destroyed, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed, [Khara remained].
Then Khara, mace in hand, leaped down and stood upon the ground.

Having witnessed that feat of the great chariot-warrior Rāma, the gods and the great seers, gathered together and stationed at the forefront of their celestial vehicles, were filled with joy and, with palms joined in reverence, offered him their praise.
To Khara, who stood deprived of his chariot with mace in hand, the immensely radiant Rāma spoke these harsh words, yet with a gentle preface:
"While you remained within a vast army crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots..."
A most cruel deed has been committed, one loathed by all the world. A man who causes terror to living beings, who is ruthless and a doer of evil,
does not remain in power even if he were the lord of the three worlds.

O night-stalker, a person who performs an action contrary to the world is slain by everyone in an instant, like a fierce and wicked snake that has appeared. He who, out of greed or desire, commits sins and does not realize it—
One who has fallen from the path sees its end, just as a Brahmin woman [sees the end of her life] because of a water-pot.
O Rākṣasa, what fruit will you obtain by killing these highly fortunate ascetics who dwell in the Daṇḍaka forest practicing dharma?
Those who perform evil deeds— cruel and despised by the world— do not remain long in power once they have attained it, like trees whose roots are decayed.
The doer inevitably reaps the fruit of their sinful actions.

When the time has arrived, it becomes terrible, like seasonal flowers on a tree. O night-stalker, the fruit of evil deeds is obtained in this world before long, like the effects of poisoned food once it has been eaten.

"O night-stalker, I have been encountered by you, who practice terrible evil and desire what is unpleasant for the world, in order to take my life. For today, arrows adorned with gold shall be released at you by me."
They shall fall upon you like serpents bursting from an anthill. Those practitioners of dharma who were devoured by you in the Daṇḍaka forest—
you shall follow them today, slain in battle along with your army.
"Today let the supreme ṛṣis, who were previously tormented by you and now dwell in celestial chariots, behold you slain by my arrows as you lie in hell.
Strike as you wish, O lowest of your lineage; exert yourself!"
"Today I shall strike down your head like a palm fruit.
Thus addressed by Rāma, he, enraged and with eyes bloodshot,
replied to Rāma while laughing, though overwhelmed by fury.
Having slain the common rakshasas in battle, O son of Dasharatha,
why do you praise yourself when you are not worthy of praise?
For those bulls among men who are truly valiant or powerful—
"Proud of their own prowess, they say nothing at all.
But those common, undisciplined men who are the scum of the kshatriya caste in this world boast pointlessly, just as you, Rama, are boasting."
Proclaiming his lineage, what hero would utter praise of himself at the time of death when it has arrived, especially when there is no occasion for it?
In every way, you have demonstrated your own insignificance through this boasting.
Like a blazing fire of kusha grass with its glowing embers,
you do not see me standing here, wielder of the mace,
as unshakable as a mountain rich in minerals.
"With mace in hand, I am capable of taking your life in battle—
even that of all three worlds— like Death himself with noose in hand.
Although there is much more that could be said, I shall not speak it to you."
For if the sun were to set, there would then be an obstacle to the battle.
Fourteen thousand Rākṣasas have been slain by you;
today, in your destruction, I shall wipe away their tears.
Having spoken thus, the exceedingly enraged Khara, whose arms were like great ornaments, hurled that mace at Rāma like a blazing thunderbolt.
That great, flaming mace was released from Khara’s arm.

Having reduced the trees and shrubs to ashes, he approached its vicinity. As that flaming mace, resembling the noose of Death, came hurtling through the air, Rāma shattered it into many pieces with his arrows.
Shattered and pierced by arrows, it fell to the surface of the earth like a female serpent struck down by the power of mantras, spells, and herbs.
Having shattered that mace with his arrows, Rāghava, who is devoted to righteousness, [proceeded].
Smiling, he spoke these harsh and agitated words:
"O lowest of Rākṣasas, you have displayed all the strength you possess;
being far more devoid of power than I, you roar in vain."
This mace, shattered by Bāṇa, has fallen to the surface of the earth; it destroys the confidence of one as bold in speech as you.
This is the wiping away of tears for those who have perished, which was spoken by you.
"Even those words of yours, 'I shall do it for the Rākṣasas,' are false.
I shall take away the life-breaths of this base, vile-natured, and deceitful Rākṣasa, just as Garuḍa seized the nectar."
Today, with your throat severed and torn apart by my arrows, the earth shall drink your blood, adorned with bubbles of foam;
your entire body smeared with dust, your two arms fallen and cast aside.
You shall sleep embracing the earth as if it were a hard-to-attain woman. When you, the disgrace of the Rākṣasas, have fallen asleep with deep slumber,
these Daṇḍaka forests will become a refuge for those who are now without refuge.
O Rākṣasa, in Janasthāna, which has now become a place of slaughter by my arrows,
the sages will roam fearlessly throughout the forest; today, the female Rākṣasas, their kinsmen having been slain, will flee in all directions.
With faces wet with tears and wretched from fear,
O night-stalker who brings terror to others, today those wives of yours— who are born of noble families— will come to know the taste of grief, having such a husband as you.
"O you of cruel character, base-souled one, constant thorn in the side of the Brahmins! Because of you, the sages, filled with apprehension, cast their oblations into the fire.
To Raghava, who was speaking thus in the battle with such intense fury—
Khara, with a most harsh voice, rebuked him out of rage:
"You are indeed utterly arrogant, remaining fearless even in the face of dangers; for, being under the sway of death, you do not perceive what should and should not be said."
"For those men who do not know what ought and ought not to be done are ensnared by the noose of Time; they have cast aside their six senses.
Having spoken thus to Rāma, he then knit his brows.
The night-stalker saw a great sāl tree not far away;
looking all around for a weapon for the battle,
he tore it up upon catching sight of his own lips.
Lifting it up with his arms and roaring loudly, the one of great strength hurled it toward Rāma and cried out, "You are slain!
The majestic Rāma, having severed that oncoming weapon with a flood of arrows, [stood firm].
He summoned a fierce rage in order to slay Khara in battle. Then Rāma, covered in sweat and with the corners of his eyes red from anger,
pierced Khara in the encounter with a thousand arrows.
From the opening of his wound, much frothy blood flowed forth,
like a cascade of water streaming from a mountain spring;
thus was Khara rendered overwhelmed by Rāma’s arrows in the combat.
Intoxicated by the scent of blood, he rushed swiftly toward him.
As he charged forward, enraged and drenched in blood,
the skilled archer stepped back one pace at a time with quickened strides.
Then, for the sake of slaying Khara in battle, Rāma seized an arrow that resembled fire, like a second staff of Brahmā;
it had been given to him by the wise Maghavan, the king of the gods.
That righteous-souled one fixed it and released it toward Khara.
Released by Rāma with his bow raised, that great arrow, sounding like a thunderbolt, fell upon Khara’s chest.
He fell to the ground, scorched by the fire of the arrows,
like Andhaka in the Śveta forest utterly consumed by Rudra;
he was like Vṛtra struck by the thunderbolt, or Namuci by the foam.

Slain by Indra’s thunderbolt, the foolish Khara fell down dead. Then all the royal sages and supreme seers, having gathered together and honored Rāma with joy, spoke these words to him: *The foolish Khara, struck down by Indra’s thunderbolt, fell slain.* *Then all the royal sages and supreme seers, having assembled and honored Rāma with delight, spoke these words:* (Note: The provided text contains two distinct verses from the critical edition of the Rāmāyaṇa, 3.29.28 and 3.29.29, which have been translated as requested.)

For this purpose, the immensely radiant Mahendra, the subduer of Pāka and destroyer of cities, came to the holy hermitage of Śarabhaṅga. You were brought to this place by the great seers through a strategic means.
This task has been accomplished by you for the sake of slaying these cruel rākṣasas of evil deeds,
O son of Daśaratha; now the great sages shall practice their dharma in peace within the Daṇḍaka forest.
In the meantime, the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, having emerged from the mountain fastness with Sītā, entered his hermitage happily.
Then the victorious Rāma was honored by the great seers.
The hero entered the hermitage, having been greeted with salutations by Lakṣmaṇa.
Seeing him, the slayer of enemies who brings happiness to the great seers,
Vaidehī was overjoyed and embraced her husband.
Then Śūrpaṇakhā saw that fourteen thousand Rākṣasas of terrible deeds had been slain by Rāma alone, as well as Khara,
Dūṣaṇa, and Triśiras, all killed in battle.
Having seen this, she, who resembled a rain-cloud, let out a great roar.
Witnessing that deed of Rāma, which was so difficult for others to accomplish,
she departed, deeply agitated, toward Laṅkā, which was protected by Rāvaṇa.
She beheld Rāvaṇa of blazing splendor at the front of the palace,
seated with his ministers like Vāsava with the Maruts,
sitting upon a supreme golden throne that resembled the sun.
He stood upon a golden altar like a blazing fire,
a hero invincible in battle even to the gods, Gandharvas, spirits, and great-souled sages, appearing like Death with his mouth wide open.
He had scars made by the thunderbolt in the battles between the gods and asuras;
his chest bore calluses from being gored by the tips of Airāvata’s tusks;
he possessed twenty arms and ten necks, and his equipment was beautiful to behold.
The hero possessed a broad chest marked with the signs of royalty;
he resembled smooth lapis lazuli, wore earrings of refined gold, had beautiful arms, white teeth, a large face, and was like a mountain.
His limbs were struck hundreds of times by the falls of Viṣṇu’s discus in the battle of the gods, as well as by all the weapons of the deities;
yet he was the swift-acting one who could stir the unshakeable oceans.
He who hurls mountain peaks, the crusher of the gods,
the destroyer of righteousness, the violator of others' wives, the employer of all divine weapons, and the constant creator of obstacles to sacrifices.
Having gone to the city of Bhogavatī and defeated Vāsuki,
he conquered and carried off the beloved wife of Takṣaka;
and having gone to Mount Kailāsa, he overcame Naravāhana.
He who carried off his celestial chariot, the Puṣpaka,
which travels at will; he, the powerful one, who out of anger destroyed the divine Caitraratha grove, the Nalinī lake, the Nandana forest, and the gardens of the gods.
He who resembles a mountain peak, with his two arms, restrains the illustrious moon and sun as they rise, those scorchers of the foe;
he who, having performed austerities for ten thousand years in the great forest, [attained this power].
In ancient times, that steadfast one offered his own heads to Svayambhū;
he who granted immunity from fear in battle to gods, dānavas, gandharvas, piśācas, birds, and serpents— save for death at the hands of a human.
That one of great strength who seizes the sacred Soma, consecrated with mantras by the twice-born at the sacrifices, within the sacrificial sheds;
that cruel robber of completed sacrifices, the slayer of Brahmins, and the evildoer.
She beheld her cruel and mighty brother Rāvaṇa, who was harsh and pitiless, devoted to the harm of his subjects, and a source of terror to all beings and all the worlds.
To that illustrious lord of the Rākṣasas, the joy of the Paulastya clan, adorned with divine garments and ornaments and graced by celestial garlands, she—
faint with fear and delusion— showed him and spoke to him whose large eyes were blazing.
Having been disfigured by the high-souled one, Śūrpaṇakhā, who moves fearlessly, spoke these most cruel words.
Then Śūrpaṇakhā, distressed and enraged, addressed harsh words to Rāvaṇa, the one who makes the world cry out, in the midst of his ministers.
Addicted to sensual pleasures, acting according to your own whims and unrestrained,
you do not perceive the terrible danger that has arisen, even though it must be recognized. You are a lord of the earth who is attached to vulgar enjoyments and ruled by desire.
People do not hold a greedy man in high regard, just as living beings avoid the fire of a cremation ground.
That king who does not personally attend to his duties at the proper time perishes along with his kingdom and those very duties.
Men avoid from afar a ruler who acts improperly, who is difficult to behold, and who lacks self-control,
just as elephants avoid the mud of a river;
for those rulers who lack self-control do not protect their realm.

They do not shine forth through prosperity, just as mountains [do not appear] within the ocean. Having engaged in conflict with self-possessed gods, Gandharvas, and Dānavas, how will you, being fickle and lacking in secret spies, become a king?
O best among victors, those kings whose spies, treasuries, and methods of policy are not under their own control are equal to common people;
for it is because of these that lords of men perceive all matters even from afar.
Therefore, kings are called "long-sighted" because of their intelligence in employing spies;
yet I consider you to be one who lacks such spies, surrounded by common ministers,
since you do not perceive that Janasthāna has been destroyed by your own kinsmen.
Fourteen thousand Rākṣasas of fearsome deeds have been slain by Rāma alone, along with Khara and Dūṣaṇa;
safety has been granted to the sages, and the Daṇḍaka forest has been made secure.
Janasthāna has been laid waste by Rāma, whose actions are effortless;
yet you, O Rāvaṇa, greedy, heedless, and dependent on others,
do not perceive the danger that has arisen within your own domain.
All living beings flee from a king who is harsh, gives little in charity, is negligent, arrogant, and deceitful; likewise,
they abandon a man who is excessively proud, unapproachable, and self-conceited.
Even his own kinsmen will strike down a wrathful king in times of calamity.
He will not attend to his duties, nor will he fear danger;
soon cast out from his kingdom and rendered wretched, he will become equal to a blade of grass.
There may be need for dry wood, or even for clods of earth and dust;
but there can be no use for kings who have fallen from their station—
just like a garment that has been worn out, or a garland that has been crushed.
Thus, one who has fallen from his kingdom is rendered useless even if he is capable.
But that king who is vigilant, all-knowing, has conquered his senses, is grateful, and is virtuous by nature— he remains in power for a long time.
Even when asleep, he remains awake with the eye of policy;
that king, whose anger and favor are manifest, is honored by the people.
But you, O Rāvaṇa, are evil-minded and devoid of these virtues.

Since this great slaughter of the Rākṣasas was unknown to you through your spies, that scorner of others who is addicted to sensual pleasures, who does not understand the true nature of time and place,
and whose intellect is unfit for discerning virtues and faults, will soon perish now that his kingdom is ruined.

Having thus reflected with his intellect upon the faults of his own that she had proclaimed, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the night-stalkers— endowed as he was with wealth, pride, and power— pondered for a long time.
Then, to Śūrpaṇakhā, who was speaking harsh words in her anger, [he spoke].
Enraged in the midst of his ministers, Rāvaṇa questioned them:
"Who is this Rāma? What is his prowess, what is his appearance, and what is his valor?
And for what purpose has he entered the Daṇḍaka forest, which is so difficult to traverse?"
"And what was Rāma’s weapon, by which the rākṣasas were slain,
and Khara was killed in battle, as well as Dūṣaṇa and Triśiras?
Thus addressed by the lord of the rākṣasas, the rākṣasī was overcome with rage.
Then he began to describe Rāma according to tradition:
"The long-armed and large-eyed one, clad in bark and black antelope skin,
and possessing a beauty equal to Kandarpa— that is Rāma, the son of Daśaratha."
Drawing his bow, which resembled Indra’s rainbow, he who wore golden armlets discharged blazing iron arrows like highly venomous serpents; yet,
though possessed of great strength, one could not perceive him taking up those terrible shafts nor releasing them.
I do not see Rāma drawing his bow in battle;
rather, I see that army being slaughtered by showers of arrows,
like a fine crop struck down by Indra with a rain of stones.
Fourteen thousand rākṣasas of terrifying prowess,
along with Khara and Dūṣaṇa, were slain by his sharp arrows by that single foot-soldier in slightly more than half a muhūrta.
"Safety has been granted to the sages, and the Daṇḍaka forest has been rendered secure.
I alone have somehow been spared by the high-souled Rāma, who knows his own self and who, fearing the slaughter of a woman, showed me mercy."
And his brother, named Lakṣmaṇa, is possessed of great luster, equal to him in virtue and prowess; he is valiant, full of energy, devoted, and loyal.
He is indignant, invincible, a conqueror, courageous, wise, and strong.
She was Rāma’s right arm, his very life-breath moving outside of him.
And Rāma’s illustrious lawful wife, the daughter of Videha named Sītā, possessed large eyes, a beautiful form, and a slender waist.
Neither among goddesses, nor Gandharvas, nor Yakṣīs, nor Kinnarīs,
have I ever before seen a woman of such form upon this earth—
one whose wife Sītā might become, and whom she would joyfully embrace.
He would outlive everyone in all the worlds, even Indra himself.
She is virtuous, her form is praiseworthy, and she is peerless in beauty upon this earth; she is a wife suited to you, and you likewise are a husband suited to her.
"I have set out to bring that woman of broad hips and full, lofty breasts, with her beautiful face, to be your wife;
for today I shall see that Vaidehī, whose face resembles the full moon."
You shall become subject to the arrows of Manmatha.
If you have the desire for her as a wife,
let your right foot be swiftly raised here for the sake of victory.
O Lord of Rākṣasas, do what is pleasing to those Rākṣasas by slaying that cruel Rāma who dwells in the hermitage;
having struck him and the great chariot-warrior Lakṣmaṇa with sharpened arrows.
"Once you have slain the protector, you shall enjoy Sītā in happiness as is fitting.
O Lord of Rākṣasas, if this speech of mine pleases you,
O Rāghava, let my words be carried out without hesitation."
Having heard that the night-stalkers dwelling in Janasthāna have been slain by Rāma with straight-flying arrows,
and having learned that Khara and Dūṣaṇa have also been killed, you ought today to determine what must be done.
Then, having heard those hair-raising words of Śūrpaṇakhā...
Having dismissed his ministers and understood the matter at hand, he departed;
then, having investigated that business thoroughly and having deliberated upon the relative strength and weakness of its faults and virtues.
Having thus made a firm resolve within himself that "this is what must be done," he of steady intellect then went to the delightful carriage shed.
Having gone to the carriage shed, the lord of the Rākṣasas remained there in concealment.
"Urged the charioteer, saying, 'Let the chariot be yoked.
Thus addressed, the charioteer, swift in his movements, in an instant yoked that excellent chariot according to his master's desire."
Mounted upon a golden chariot that moved at will, adorned with jewels,
and yoked to donkeys with faces like Piśācas and decorated with golden ornaments,
that younger brother of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) traveled with a roar resembling the sound of clouds.
The glorious lord of the Rākṣasas went toward the ocean, the lord of rivers and streams.
That ten-faced one, adorned with white chowries and a white parasol,
resembled smooth lapis lazuli and was decorated with ornaments of refined gold.

Ten-faced and twenty-armed, with a magnificent retinue, the enemy of the gods and slayer of the lord of sages shone as he mounted his chariot that moves at will, like the king of mountains with ten peaks. The lord of the Rākṣasas was resplendent.
Like a cloud in the sky accompanied by lightning and cranes,
the valiant one gazed upon the coastal region of the ocean together with its mountains,
strewn with thousands of trees bearing various flowers and fruits.
It was surrounded on all sides by lotus ponds with cool, auspicious waters,
and by spacious hermitage grounds provided with sacrificial altars;
it was densely crowded with plantain and *āḍhakī* trees and adorned with coconut palms.
It was adorned with *sāla*, *tāla*, and *tamāla* trees in full bloom,
and graced by supreme ṛṣis who were extremely restrained in their diet,
as well as by thousands of *nāgas*, *suparṇas*, *gandharvas*, and *kiṃnaras*.
It was graced by those who had conquered their desires, by the Siddhas, and by the Cāraṇas;
it was filled with Ājyas, Vaikhānasas, Māṣas, Vālakhilyas, and Marīcipas,
and was surrounded by women of divine form adorned with celestial ornaments and garlands.
It was attended by thousands of Apsarases who were skilled in the arts of play and pleasure,
and it was graced with the splendor of glorious wives of the gods;
furthermore, it was frequented by hosts of Devas and Dānavas who subsist on nectar.
It was crowded with swans, cranes, and water-fowl, and resounded with the cries of cranes;
it was delightful with floors of vaidūrya stone, glossy with the splendor of the ocean,
and possessed vast white pavilions adorned with celestial garlands.

The younger brother of the Giver of Wealth beheld celestial chariots on all sides, graced with the sound of musical instruments and song; these vehicles, capable of moving at will, belonged to those who had conquered the worlds through their ascetic penance, and he also saw Gandharvas and Apsarases as they descended toward them.

He beheld thousands of groves of sandalwood trees, gentle and pleasing to the sense of smell, containing the essence of resin and their roots intact; he also saw forests and pleasure gardens of the finest agallochum.
There were also *takkola* fruits of noble quality, fragrant fruits,
blossoms of the *tamāla*, shrubs of black pepper,
and heaps of pearls drying upon the shore.
He saw heaps of conch shells as well as clusters of coral, mountains of gold and silver on every side,
delightful waterfalls, and clear lakes.
Beholding cities filled with wealth and grain, surrounded by jewels of women, and crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots;
[he beheld] that wind which was gentle and soft to the touch, blowing equally in every direction.
He beheld the marshy region of the King of Rivers, which resembled the third heaven;
there he saw a banyan tree, dark as a cloud, surrounded by sages,
whose branches extended for a hundred yojanas in every direction.
Taking an elephant and a massive tortoise for the sake of food, the mighty Garuḍa came to a branch;
by the weight of those two, that best of birds suddenly [broke] the branch.
Then the mighty Suparṇa shattered that tree thick with foliage.
There, the supreme ṛṣis— the Vaikhānasas, Māṣas, Vālakhilyas, Marīcipas, Ajas, and Dhūmras— were gathered together.

Out of compassion for them, the righteous-souled Garuḍa, having devoured that flesh, took up both those elephants and the tortoise and flew with speed, carrying that branch which was a hundred yojanas long. He traveled on one leg alone after consuming that meat.
Having struck down the Niṣāda territory with his branch and having liberated the great sages, that best of birds attained incomparable joy;
with that very joy, his prowess was doubled.
Having formed this resolve for the sake of bringing back the nectar of immortality,
the wise one then crushed the iron nets, broke through the excellent jewel-house well-guarded within the abode of Mahendra, and brought forth the nectar from there.
The younger brother of the Giver of Wealth beheld that banyan tree named Subhadra, frequented by hosts of great sages and marked with the sign of Suparṇa;
he reached it after crossing to the further shore of the ocean, the lord of rivers.
In a secluded, holy, and beautiful part of the forest, he beheld a hermitage.
There, he saw a Rākṣasa named Mārīca, wearing a black antelope skin and matted hair with bark garments, who was restricted in his diet.
Then Rāvaṇa, skilled in speech, having approached that Rākṣasa according to custom, spoke these words thereafter:
"O Mārīca, my dear, listen to the words I am speaking."
"I am afflicted, and for me in my affliction, you are indeed the supreme refuge.
You know Janasthāna, where my brother Khara dwells,
as well as the mighty-armed Dūṣaṇa and my sister Śūrpaṇakhā."
The immensely powerful three-headed Rākṣasa Piśitāśana,
and many other heroic night-stalkers who have attained their marks,
dwell there at my command and occupy that residence.
In the great forest, they oppressed the sages who practice righteousness—
fourteen thousand Rākṣasas of fearsome deeds, heroes who never miss their mark, and followers of Khara’s will.
But now, those mighty ones dwelling in Janasthāna have gathered together and are utterly dependent upon Rāma for their safety in battle;
by that Rāma, who has become filled with wrath at the front of the fray—
Without uttering a single harsh word, he discharged his bow with arrows;
fourteen thousand rākṣasas of fearsome deeds were slain by those sharp shafts, by a mere human on foot.
Khara was slain in battle and Dūṣaṇa was struck down;
having also killed Triśiras, the Daṇḍaka forest has been rendered free of fear.
Yet, driven out by his angry father along with his wife, my life is now at its end.
That Rama, a disgrace to the kṣatriyas, shall be the slayer of that army;
he is ill-behaved, harsh, cruel, foolish, greedy, and lacks self-control.
Having abandoned dharma, he is unrighteous in soul and devoted to the harm of all living beings.
By him who, out of enmity, relying solely on his strength in the forest,
disfigured my sister by cutting off her ears and nose—
that man’s wife, Sītā, who resembles the daughter of a god, [must be seized] from Janasthāna.
"I shall bring him back by my prowess; be my ally in this matter.
For with you as my companion standing at my side, O mighty one, and with my brothers, I do not fear all the gods in battle."
Therefore, O Rākṣasa, become my ally, for you are indeed capable in heroism, in battle, and in pride; truly, there is no one equal to you.
It is for this purpose that I have come into your presence, O night-stalker.
Listen to that task which must be performed to assist me according to my word:
becoming a golden deer, variegated with silver spots,
roam about in the hermitage of that Rāma in the presence of Sītā.
But having seen you in the form of a deer, Sītā will undoubtedly say to her husband and Lakṣmaṇa, "Let him be captured!
Then, when those two have departed and it is empty, [you may take] Sītā as you please.
"Unimpeded, I shall seize him as Rāhu seizes the light of the moon.
Afterwards, when Rāma has been emaciated by the abduction of his wife,
I shall strike him with confidence, my inner soul having achieved its purpose."
Having heard that account of Rāma from the high-souled Mārīca,
his mouth became parched and he was filled with terror.
Knowing the prowess of Rāma, he, with a terrified and dejected mind, addressed Rāvaṇa in the great forest.
With palms joined in reverence, he spoke these words— truthful, beneficial to him, and for his own welfare.
Having heard those words of the lord of the Rākṣasas, the highly wise Mārīca, who was skilled in speech, replied to the sovereign of the Rākṣasas.
"O King, men who always speak pleasant words are easy to find;
but one who speaks what is unpleasant yet beneficial, and one who listens to such words, are both rare.
Surely you do not realize that Rāma is possessed of great heroism and exalted virtues."
Fickle and acting improperly, [he has gone] toward him who is like Mahendra and Varuṇa.
O dear one, may it be well with all the rākṣasas on earth;
for if Rāma were enraged, he might rid the world of all rākṣasas.
"Could it be that the son of Janaka has not been born for the end of your life?
Could Sītā not be the cause of this great calamity?
Or could it be that, having obtained you as her lord, she has become unrestrained and given herself over to her desires?"
"Otherwise, the city of Laṅkā, along with you and the rākṣasas, would not perish.
For a king like you— one who acts according to his lust, is ill-behaved, and follows evil counsel— being of wicked mind, destroys himself, his kin, and his kingdom."
He was never abandoned by his father, nor was he ever lacking in propriety;
he was neither greedy nor ill-behaved, nor was he a disgrace to the kṣatriyas. He was not devoid of the virtues of dharma—he who increases the joy of Kausalyā.
For he was not harsh toward any living beings, but was devoted to the welfare of all;
seeing his father, who was truthful in speech, deceived by Kaikeyī,
the righteous-souled one resolved, "I shall do so," and then departed for the forest.
For the sake of pleasing Kaikeyī and for the benefit of his father Daśaratha,
Rāma abandoned both the kingdom and its enjoyments and entered the Daṇḍaka forest.
My dear son, Rāma is neither harsh, nor unlearned, nor one who has failed to conquer his senses.
"You have never heard a falsehood, nor indeed ought you to speak one.
Rāma is righteousness incarnate, virtuous, and one whose prowess is truth;
he is the king of the entire world, just as Vāsava is of the gods."
How do you wish to forcibly carry away Vaidehī, whom he protects by his own splendor— like the radiance of the sun—
[he who is] unassailable in battle, with arrows for its flames and bows and swords for its fuel?
You ought not to enter Rāma’s fire, which blazes suddenly;
he is a hero who wields the bow and arrows, whose mouth is wide open with his drawn bow, whose rays are his shafts, who is intolerant of enemies, and who destroys the armies of his foes.
O dear one, having renounced your kingdom, your happiness, and even your own cherished life, you ought not to approach Rāma’s end here.
For immeasurable indeed is the splendor of him to whom that daughter of Janaka belongs.

"You are not capable of carrying her off from the forest, for she relies upon Rāma's bow. Sītā, the slender-waisted one, is dearer to him than his own life; she is ever devoted to him, like the flame of a blazing fire."
O Lord of Rākṣasas, what is the use of making this futile effort?
If you are seen by him in battle, that will be the end of your life,
as well as your happiness and your kingdom, which are all so difficult to attain.
Having consulted with all his righteous ministers, who were led by Vibhīṣaṇa,
he reached his own decision after weighing the relative strength of the faults and virtues.
Having understood your own strength and that of Raghava in its true nature, and having determined what is indeed for your benefit, you ought to do what is appropriate.
However, I believe that an encounter with the son of the King of Kosala in battle is not suitable for you.
Furthermore, O Lord of the Night-rangers, hear these supreme words, which are both appropriate and fitting:
"Once, while wandering this earth by my own prowess, I possessed the strength of a thousand elephants and was like a mountain."
Resembling a dark blue cloud, wearing earrings of refined gold,
and armed with an iron club, I roamed the Daṇḍaka forest devouring the flesh of sages, striking terror into the world while wearing my diadem.
Then the great sage Viśvāmitra, whose soul was righteous, being terrified of me,
went in person to King Daśaratha and said this:
"May this Rāma, composed in mind, protect me during the time of the sacrificial rites."
"O Lord of Men, a terrible fear of Mārīca has arisen within me. When he had spoken thus, the righteous King Daśaratha then replied to the highly fortunate great sage Viśvāmitra.

"O best of sages, although this descendant of Raghu is less than sixteen years of age and untrained in weapons, my army, which shall go with me at my will, will slay your enemy exactly as you desire."
Thus addressed, the sage spoke again to the king:
"In this world, there is no strength other than Rāma that is sufficient for that Rākṣasa;
though he is but a child, he possesses great splendor and is capable of subduing him."
"I shall go taking Rāma with me; may you be well, O scorcher of foes.
Having spoken thus, the sage Viśvāmitra, taking the prince with him, departed for his own hermitage, filled with supreme joy.
Then, in the Daṇḍaka forest,
the glorious Rāma— still a youth with unmanifested secondary sexual characteristics, dark-complexioned and of auspicious eyes— stood consecrated for the sacrifice, stretching his wondrous bow.
Wearing a single garment, armed with a bow, and adorned with a golden garland and a topknot,
Rāma then appeared, beautifying the Daṇḍaka forest with his own radiant splendor, like the newly risen crescent moon.
Then, resembling a cloud and wearing earrings of refined gold, I— powerful and having received boons— approached that hermitage out of pride.
As soon as he saw me, I entered with my weapons suddenly raised.
But upon seeing me, he strung his bow without any agitation. Out of delusion, disregarding Raghava by thinking, "This is but a child," I rushed toward Viśvāmitra’s altar with great haste.
Then he released a sharp arrow, a destroyer of enemies;
struck by it and cast into the ocean a hundred yojanas away,
I was driven off by the force of Rāma’s shaft with my consciousness reeling.
I was then cast by him into the deep waters of the ocean; having regained consciousness after a long time, O dear one, I went toward the city of Laṅkā.
Thus was I released at that time, while your companions were struck down.
By Rāma, though he is a youth untrained in weapons yet unwearied in action— if you, despite being warned by me, engage in conflict with him,
you shall quickly meet with terrible calamity and perish.

To the Rākṣasas, who are experts in the arts of pleasure and play and who delight in social festivals, you will bring both distress and misfortune. [You shall see] that city, crowded with mansions and palaces and adorned with various jewels.

"You shall see the city of Laṅkā destroyed for the sake of Maithilī. Even those who do not commit sins themselves perish through association with the wicked due to the sins of others, just as fish in a serpent's pool."
Because of your transgression, you shall see the Rākṣasas— whose limbs are smeared with divine sandalwood paste and adorned with celestial ornaments— slain upon the ground;
some having had their wives carried off, others with their wives still by their side, they will flee in the ten directions.
"You shall see the night-stalkers who remain after the slaughter, left without refuge.
You will undoubtedly behold Laṅkā, its houses consumed by fire, enveloped in a net of arrows and surrounded by tongues of flame."
"O King, you have thousands of women as your wives;
be devoted to your own wife, O Rākṣasa, and protect your own lineage. [Preserve] your honor, your prosperity, your kingdom, and your own dear life."
If you wish to enjoy [this world] for long, do not act unfavorably toward Rāma.
If, despite being earnestly restrained by me, your friend, you should forcibly violate Sītā,
you shall go to the abode of Yama with your strength exhausted and your kinsmen, your life having been taken by Rāma’s arrow.
Thus was I somehow liberated from him in that battle;
now hear what happened next.
Although I had been treated in such a manner by the two Rākṣasas, I remained undaunted.
Accompanied by two deer-like forms, he entered the Daṇḍaka forest.
A great beast with a flaming tongue, a massive body, sharp horns, and great strength,
he roamed the Daṇḍaka wilderness devouring flesh.
O Rāvaṇa, wandering through Agnihotra sacrifices, sacred fords, and sacred trees,
I roamed about most terribly, assailing those ascetics;
having slain the practitioners of dharma in the Daṇḍaka forest.
Drinking their blood and likewise devouring their flesh,
I— cruel, a consumer of the sages' flesh, and intoxicated by blood— roamed the Daṇḍaka forest at that time, terrifying the forest-dwellers.
Then, while wandering through the Daṇḍaka forest as a destroyer of dharma, I encountered Rāma, who was devoted to the ascetic life and righteousness,
as well as the highly fortunate Vaidehī and the great chariot-warrior Lakṣmaṇa.
[He was] an ascetic, restricted in diet, devoted to the welfare of all beings.
Remembering our former enmity and thinking, "This is merely an ascetic," I disregarded the mighty Rāma who had gone to the forest.
Highly enraged, with sharp horns and the form of a deer, I rushed toward him—
desiring to kill him and remembering that previous blow, for I was lacking in wisdom.
By him, three sharp arrows, capable of destroying enemies, were released.
Having powerfully drawn his bow, those three arrows— resembling thunderbolts, most terrible, blood-drinking, swift as Garuda or the wind, and straight-jointed— all came together at once.
Knowing Rāma’s prowess, that deceitful one had previously perceived danger and escaped;
having been released from there, both those two Rākṣasas were slain.
Having somehow escaped Rāma’s arrow, he regained his life.
"Having renounced the world here, I am a disciplined ascetic, composed in mind.
Yet, in every tree I see Rāma, clad in bark and black antelope skin, holding his bow like Death himself with a noose in hand."
"O Rāvaṇa, terrified, I see even thousands of Rāmas;
this entire forest appears to me as being composed of Rāmas.
Indeed, O Lord of Rākṣasas, I see only Rāma everywhere, even in solitude."
Having seen Rāma in my dream, I wander about, deprived of my senses. O Rāvaṇa, names beginning with the letter 'R', as well as jewels and chariots, cause me great terror when I am frightened by Rāma.
"I know his power; it is not fitting for you to engage in battle with him.
Fight with Rāma in combat, or else grant him your pardon, O Rākṣasa. You should have no talk of Rāma if you wish to see me."
"If you do not accept these words spoken by me, who seeks the welfare of my kinsmen,
then today, along with your relatives, you shall lose your life in battle, slain by Rāma with his straight-flying arrows.
But Rāvaṇa did not find those words of Mārīca to be either appropriate or reasonable.

Though thus addressed, he did not accept it, like one desiring death refusing medicine. Driven by fate, the lord of the Rākṣasas spoke harsh and improper words to Mārīca, who had spoken what was beneficial and wholesome.
"O Mārīca, this speech which you address to me is indeed unreasonable; it is utterly fruitless, like seed sown in barren soil.
Yet, you shall not be able to dissuade me from battle with Rāma by means of your words."
Especially for a foolish man of evil character,
who— having abandoned his friends, his kingdom, as well as his mother and father—
departed for the forest all at once upon hearing the common words of a woman.
"O Mārīca, this is the firm resolve that dwells within my heart: I must, in your presence, forcibly abduct Sītā— who is dearer to him than his own life— from that slayer of Khara in battle."
It cannot be turned back even by the gods and asuras, including Indra himself.
Whether asked about a fault or a virtue, you alone ought to speak thus regarding the determination of this matter— whether it be its danger or the means to achieve it.
A wise minister who desires his own prosperity should, when questioned by the king, speak with palms joined in reverence words that are not contrary, but gentle, auspicious, and beneficial.
The lord of the earth should be addressed with courtesy;
however, O Mārīca, when beneficial words are spoken with condescension,
a king who deserves honor does not welcome them if they are devoid of respect.
Kings of immeasurable power assume five forms—
those of Agni, Indra, Soma, Yama, and Varuṇa—
and [manifest] heat, valor, gentleness, the power of punishment, and graciousness.
