Therefore, in all circumstances, kings are to be honored and revered;
yet you, failing to understand dharma, have resorted solely to delusion,
and out of wickedness, you speak such harsh words to me who have come as a guest.
"O Rākṣasa, I do not inquire into merits or faults, nor what is appropriate for myself; rather, you ought to provide assistance in this task of mine.
Become a golden deer, variegated with silver spots."
Having enticed Vaidehī, you may then depart as you wish.
But upon seeing you as a golden illusory deer, Maithilī will be filled with wonder and will quickly say to Rāma, "Bring this one here!"
Once the descendant of Kakutstha and Lakṣmaṇa have departed at their ease, I shall bring Vaidehī here, just as the thousand-eyed Indra brought Śacī.
Having accomplished this task, O Rākṣasa, go wherever you please.
"O Mārīca, you of noble vows, I shall give half of my kingdom to you.
Go, gentle one, upon an auspicious path for the success of this undertaking,
having obtained Sītā by deceiving Rāghava without a fight."
"I shall go toward Laṅkā with you once my task is accomplished.
You will certainly carry out this duty for me, even by force;
for one who stands in opposition to a king never prospers in happiness."
"Having encountered me, your life is in peril; for death is certain today for you who have opposed me.
Having reflected upon this with your intellect as it truly is, do whatever is beneficial in this situation accordingly.
Thus commanded like a king, the night-stalker [Rāvaṇa] spoke these contrary words.
Mārīca spoke these harsh words to the lord of the Rākṣasas:
"O night-stalker, by what evildoer has this destruction been advised for you, along with your sons, your kingdom, and your ministers?"

O King, O night-stalker, what evildoer does not rejoice in your happiness? By whom has this been taught to you as a means to the gateway of death? It is evident that your enemies are devoid of prowess.
They desire that you perish, held in check by one more powerful than yourself.
By what base person, speaking for his own ill, was this advised to you, O night-stalker, who wishes to see you destroyed by your own doing?
"O Rāvaṇa, indeed those ministers who do not restrain you in every way when you have mounted upon a wrong path deserve to be killed, yet they are not slain.
For a king who acts according to his lust and has taken to a wicked path is [ruined] by his ministers."
The virtuous must always restrain the wicked; you, however, are being restrained by those who should not restrain you.
O best among victors, O night-stalker, it is through the favor of their master that ministers obtain dharma, artha, kāma, and fame.
But in the opposite case, O Rāvaṇa, all that becomes useless;
other people suffer calamity due to the faults of their master.
For both righteousness and victory have their root in the king, O best among victors.
Therefore, O lord of men, the king must be protected in all circumstances.
A kingdom cannot be governed, O night-stalker, by one who is harsh,
nor by one who is hostile, nor by one who is undisciplined, O Rākṣasa.
Those ministers who possess harsh counsel are surely broken along with him,
just as chariots driven by a slow driver quickly perish in difficult terrain.
Many virtuous people in this world have remained steadfast in the practice of dharma.

O Rāvaṇa, ruined by the offenses of others, they have perished along with all their possessions. Protected by a hostile and cruel master, subjects do not prosper, just as sheep do not thrive when guarded by a jackal.
O Rāvaṇa, all these Rākṣasas will certainly perish,
for you have been their harsh king— evil-minded and one who has not conquered his senses. Thus,
this terrible calamity has befallen you by chance, like the falling of a palm fruit upon a crow.
What is auspicious here, that you shall perish along with your army?
Once I have been slain, that Rāma will kill you before long;
by this, I am fulfilled, since I die struck down by an enemy.
"Know that I am already slain by the mere sight of Rāma;
know yourself also to be slain, along with your kinsmen, for having abducted Sītā.
If I were to bring Sītā back from the hermitage together with me,"

Neither you exist, nor I, nor Laṅkā, nor the Rākṣasas. But though you were being restrained by me, who desires your welfare, you did not accept these words, O night-stalker. For men whose lives have ended and who are like the dead do not accept the beneficial advice offered by friends.
Having spoken these harsh words to Rāvaṇa, Mārīca, dejected out of fear of the lord of the night-rangers, then said, "Let us go.
And he was seen again by him, who bore a bow, arrows, and a sword.
My life has been destroyed by one like me with uplifted weapon;
yet, what can be done by me against you, O evil-minded one?
Here I go, my dear; may it be well with you, O night-stalker.
Delighted by those words, that Rākṣasa embraced him very closely and spoke these words:
"This speech of yours, full of valor, was spoken as if at my own command."
"Now you are Mārīca; previously you were another night-stalker.
Ascend quickly this sky-faring chariot adorned with jewels, which is yoked to donkeys with the faces of Piśācas, along with me."
Then Rāvaṇa and Mārīca, having mounted that chariot which was like a celestial vehicle, departed swiftly from that circle of hermitages,
beholding towns and forests along the way.
Having traversed all the mountains, rivers, kingdoms, and cities,
Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, together with Marīca, then reached the Daṇḍaka forest and beheld the hermitage of Rāghava.
Having descended from that chariot adorned with gold,
Rāvaṇa took Mārīca by the hand and spoke these words:
"This hermitage of Rāma is visible here, surrounded by plantain trees."
"O friend, quickly do that for the sake of which we have come.
Hearing Rāvaṇa's words, the Rākṣasa Mārīca then became a deer and roamed about at the entrance of Rāma’s hermitage.
With the tips of his horns adorned with the finest jewels, his face appearing white and black, his mouth like a red lotus and a blue water-lily, and his ears like blue lotuses;
with his neck slightly uplifted, his belly resembling a sapphire.
His flanks were like the *madhūka* flower, and his color resembled the filaments of a lotus;
his hooves were like lapis lazuli, his shanks were slender and well-proportioned,
and he was graced by a tail, the color of a rainbow, which rose upward.
With a captivating and lustrous complexion, adorned with various kinds of jewels,
the Rākṣasa in an instant became a most beautiful deer,
illuminating that lovely forest and the site of Rāma’s hermitage.
Having assumed a captivating and beautiful form, variegated with various minerals for the purpose of enticing Vaidehī, that Rākṣasa wandered about,
moving gracefully across the grassy meadows on all sides.
Variegated with hundreds of silver droplets and beautiful to behold,
he wandered about, breaking off and eating the tender shoots of the trees.
Having gone to the plantain groves and here and there among the karṇikāra trees, he roamed.
Moving slowly with the intent of being seen by Sītā,
that great deer, whose back was variegated like a lotus, shone brightly as he wandered at his ease near the vicinity of Rāma’s hermitage.
Having gone forth and returned again, that best of deer roamed about;
having gone with haste for a moment, he would turn back once more. He would play upon the ground and then sit down again.
Having reached the entrance of the hermitage, he goes toward the herds of deer;
followed by the herds of deer, that Rākṣasa, who had assumed the form of a deer, returns once again, longing for a sight of Sītā.
Beholding him, all the other deer that roam the forest flee in every direction, leaping away as he whirls in various circles.
Having approached and sniffed him, they scatter in the ten directions.
That Rākṣasa, though intent on killing wild deer, did not eat those forest animals even upon touching them, for the sake of concealing his true nature. At that very time, the beautiful-eyed Vaidehī—
Intent on gathering flowers, the intoxicating-eyed woman passed by the *karṇikāra*, *aśoka*, and *cūta* trees;
picking blossoms, the lovely-faced one wandered about.
That supreme woman, who was unaccustomed to dwelling in the forest, beheld that deer made of jewels, its limbs variegated with pearls and gems;
it indeed possessed beautiful teeth and lips, and its fine hair was like silver ore.
With eyes wide with wonder, she gazed affectionately at him.
And that illusory deer, beholding the beloved of Rāma,
wandered there, as if illuminating the forest.
Having seen that deer composed of various jewels, never before seen,
Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, was struck with the utmost wonder.
Beholding it while she was gathering flowers, the fair-hipped lady was filled with amazement.
Adorned with two sides having the color of gold and silver,
she— joyful, of faultless limbs, and possessing the hue of polished gold—
cried out to her husband and to Lakṣmaṇa, who was armed.
Summoned by her, the two tigers among men, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, while surveying that region with Vaidehī, then beheld a deer.
Seeing it, Lakṣmaṇa, filled with apprehension, spoke to Rāma.

"I consider this very deer to be the Rākṣasa Mārīca. While we were joyfully hunting in the forest, O Rāma, kings have been slain by him through this wicked artifice, for he can assume any form at will."
"O tiger among men, this illusory form of a deer was created by this master of illusion; it is radiant and resembles a city of the Gandharvas.
For such a deer, variegated with jewels, does not exist in reality, O Raghava."
"O Lord of the World, this on earth is surely an illusion; of this there is no doubt.
To the descendant of Kakutstha who was speaking thus, Sītā, her mind captivated by the deception, replied with a pure smile while appearing joyful.
"O noble son, this deer is so delightful that it captivates my mind.
Bring him here, O mighty-armed one; he shall serve for our sport. In this hermitage of ours, there are many other creatures of auspicious appearance."
Deer roam together, as do yaks and sṛmaras;
bears, herds of spotted deer, monkeys, and kinnaras likewise wander about, O mighty-armed one— beings of excellent form and great strength.
And never before, O King, has a deer such as this been seen by you, possessing such splendor, patience, and radiance as this best of deer;
its body is variegated with many colors and covered with spots like precious gems.
Illuminating the forest with composure, he shines like the moon.
Oh, what beauty! Oh, what splendor! And how magnificent is his perfection of voice! This wondrous and extraordinary deer seems to steal my very heart.
If your deer should be captured while still alive,
it will be a marvel that will produce astonishment for us once we have completed our forest exile and are established in the kingdom again.
"O Lord, this deer shall serve as an ornament for the inner apartments;
this divine form of a deer will cause wonder to Bharata, the noble son, to my mothers-in-law, and to me."
"O tiger among men, if this best of deer does not come into my grasp while alive, its beautiful hide will be mine;
for when this creature is slain, its skin is made of Jāmbūnada gold."
"I wish to attend upon him while he is seated on a cushion of young grass.
This fierce behavior, acting according to his own desires, is considered unbecoming of women;
yet, because of the nature of this being, it has produced wonder in me regarding his physical form."
At that sight— of the bull with golden hair, horns adorned with excellent jewels, possessing the hue of the rising sun and the splendor of the path of the stars—
even the mind of Rāghava was filled with wonder.
Having heard Sītā’s words and having seen that wonderful deer,
Rāghava, filled with joy, spoke these words to his brother Lakṣmaṇa:
"Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, this longing of Vaidehī directed toward the deer."
Indeed, because of his excellence of form, this deer shall not exist today—
not in the Nandana grove, nor in the retreat of Caitraratha;
how much less, O Saumitri, could there be any deer on earth equal to him?
And his beautiful, variegated lines of body hair, both growing upward and downward,
shine as they rest upon his deer-skin, adorned with golden spots.
Behold his blazing tongue, resembling a flame of fire, as he yawns.
With his tongue protruding from his mouth like lightning from a cloud,
whose mind would that handsome deer not captivate— he who has a face like emerald and sapphire, and a belly like a conch or a pearl?

Whose mind would not be struck with wonder upon seeing this divine form, radiant as Jāmbūnada gold and composed of various jewels? Even for the sake of meat, archers do not kill deer merely for the purpose of sport.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, kings kill [beasts] during the hunt in the great forest.
In the great forest, wealth is gathered through effort,
as well as various minerals consisting of gems, jewels, and gold."
O Lakṣmaṇa, that is the entire essence for men— a wealth that increases one's store and fulfills everything conceived by the mind— just as it was for Śukra,
by means of which a seeker of wealth proceeds without hesitation to accomplish his purpose.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, those learned in the science of statecraft and those seeking worldly prosperity have declared this to be the goal:
the slender-waisted Vaidehī shall sit together with me upon the supreme golden skin of this jewel among deer."
"Neither the kadalī, nor the priyakī, nor the praveṇī, nor the āvikī could be its equal in touch; this is my opinion.
And this glorious deer is the very same one who is divine and moves through the sky."
"Both these deer are divine— the deer of the stars and the deer of the earth.
Or, O Lakṣmaṇa, if what you tell me is true—
that this is the illusion of a Rākṣasa— then he must be slain by me."
For by this cruel and undisciplined Mārīca,
while he was previously wandering in the forest, many eminent sages were harmed; and by him, many lords of men were slain during the hunt.
The supreme archers have been slain; therefore, this deer must be killed.
Previously here, Vātāpi, having humiliated the ascetics, would kill the twice-born while staying within their bellies, like a fetus killing its mother, the female donkey.

Once, after a long time, he encountered the great sage Agastya, who was endowed with spiritual power, and he became the sage's food. And when the sage saw him desiring to assume his own form upon rising from that state, [he acted].
Smiling, the Blessed One then said this to Vātāpi:
"O Vātāpi, because you disregarded and insulted the best of the twice-born in the world of the living by means of your power, you have therefore reached old age."
Thus, O Lakṣmaṇa, that Rākṣasa shall not exist, like Vātāpi, who would dare to treat with contempt one such as I—ever devoted to dharma and having conquered his senses.
He shall be slain by me, just as Vātāpi was by Agastya; for I am his end.
"Stay here, gird yourself, and keep watch over Maithilī.
O descendant of Raghu, our duty depends upon her;
I shall either slay this deer or capture it."
"Come, Saumitri, I shall go quickly to bring back the deer;
look, Lakṣmaṇa, at Vaidehī, who has set her heart upon the deer's skin!
For today this deer will no longer exist, for its skin is the most precious thing."
"You must remain vigilant while staying at the hermitage with Sītā.
Lakṣmaṇa, I shall kill this spotted deer with a single arrow; having slain it and taken its hide, I will return quickly."

"O Lakṣmaṇa, having taken charge of Maithilī, remain vigilant at every moment, ever suspicious of danger from all sides, for the sake of the exceedingly powerful bird Jaṭāyu, who is possessed of great wisdom.
Having thus instructed his brother, the joy of the Raghus—
The one of great splendor fastened his sword, which had a hilt made of Jāmbūnada gold;
then, taking up his bow— which was bent at three points— and fastening his two quivers, he of fierce prowess departed.
Deceiving that lord of kings, he, observing the monarch rushing toward him,
became invisible out of fear and then appeared once more;
with sword girded and bow in hand, he fled toward where the deer had gone.
He saw him before him, shining as if with a radiant form;
with bow in hand in that great forest, he watched him running again and again, never once straying from the path of his arrow, yet appearing to lure him on.
Filled with apprehension and utterly bewildered, as if leaping into the sky, he was visible and then invisible in certain new regions,
like the autumnal orb of the moon veiled by scattered clouds.

In just a moment he was seen, and then again he appeared from afar; by this constant appearing and disappearing, he drew Rāghava toward him. Kākutstha became enraged, yet he was rendered helpless, bewildered by that [demon].
Then, having rested and being thoroughly fatigued, he stood taking shelter in the shade upon a grassy plot;
surrounded by wild deer, he was seen nearby.
Seeing him, the immensely radiant Rāma resolved to kill him.
Having fixed it upon his very firm bow and drawing it back with great force,
the powerful one aimed at that very deer and released a blazing, radiant weapon created by Brahmā, which was like a flaming serpent.
That supreme arrow, resembling a thunderbolt, having pierced right through the heart of Mārīca who was in the form of a deer,
fell down after springing up to the height of a palm tree, its victim afflicted by the shaft.
With his life ebbing away, Mārīca let out a terrifying roar upon the earth; as he was dying, he cast off that artificial body and,
perceiving that the time had come, produced a cry.
"Alas, Sītā! O Lakṣmaṇa!"—these words were exactly like those of Rāghava himself.
Indeed, pierced in his vital organs by that incomparable arrow, he cast off the form of the deer and assumed his own demonic form.
Then Mārīca, possessing a massive body, made that wheel as he was giving up his life.
Struck by the arrow, the Rākṣasa— adorned with variegated armlets, decorated with all kinds of ornaments, wearing a golden garland, and having great tusks— remained there.
Seeing that Rākṣasa of terrible appearance fallen upon the ground,
he went in his mind to Sītā, remembering the words of Lakṣmaṇa,
and cried out in a loud voice, "O Sītā! O Lakṣmaṇa!"
"That Rākṣasa has died; what will become of Sītā?
And what state will the mighty-armed Lakṣmaṇa reach?"—thinking thus, the righteous-souled Rāma's hair stood on end with joy.
Then, having killed that rakshasa in the form of a deer and having heard its cry, a sharp fear born of despair entered Rama; meanwhile,
Raghava, having slain another spotted deer, took its meat.
Then, hurrying toward Janasthāna, he set out. Recognizing that distressed cry in the forest as resembling her husband's voice,
Sītā said to Lakṣmaṇa, "Go and find Rāghava."
Indeed, my life does not remain in its place, nor does my heart stay still,
for I have heard the intense cry of one who is most afflicted and wailing.
You ought to rescue your brother as he is lamenting in the forest.
"Run quickly to that brother of yours who seeks refuge,
having fallen into the power of the Rākṣasas like a bull among lions.
Though addressed thus, he did not go, yet he understood his brother's command.
Then, filled with anger, the daughter of Janaka said to him there:
"O son of Sumitrā, though you appear to be a friend, you are like an enemy to your brother,
since you do not come to his aid in this state."
"Do you wish for Rāma to perish on my account, Lakṣmaṇa?
I consider this calamity to be pleasing to you; you have no affection for your brother, which is why you remain so confident even while not seeing that one of great splendor."
"For what indeed should be done by me here, standing in this place, while he has fallen into such uncertainty, since you, the foremost one, have come here?"—
thus spoke Vaidehī, overwhelmed with tears and grief.
Lakṣmaṇa spoke to the terrified Sītā, who was like a doe:
"O Queen, among gods, humans, Gandharvas, birds, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, Kinnaras, and animals— " (Rāmāyaṇa 3.43.9–10).
"O beautiful one, among even the most terrible Dānavas, there is no one who could fight against Rāma, who is like Vāsava himself, in battle.
Rāma is invincible in combat; you ought not to speak thus."
I cannot bear to leave you in this forest without Rāghava;
for his power is irresistible, even by the forces of the strongest,
or by the three worlds joined together, including their lords and the gods.
"May your heart be at peace; let this distress be abandoned.
Your husband will soon return after having slain that foremost of deer.
That was clearly not his voice, nor was it the voice of any deity.
That illusion of that Rākṣasa is like a city of the Gandharvas.
O Vaidehī, you have been placed as a trust with me by the high-souled Rāma; O lady of beautiful limbs, I do not venture to abandon you here.
"O auspicious lady, we have incurred enmity with these night-stalkers, O Queen, on account of the slaughter of Khara and the destruction of Janasthāna.
Thus do the Rākṣasas utter their words in the great forest according to their nature."
"O Vaidehī, you ought not to think thus of one who delights in violence.
Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, she, enraged and with eyes bloodshot,
spoke these harsh words to the truth-speaking Lakṣmaṇa.
"O ignoble one, devoid of compassion, cruel defiler of your lineage! I believe you are dear to him, which is why you speak these words.
It is not surprising, O Lakṣmaṇa, that such wickedness should be found in enemies."
Among those like you, who are cruel and always move in disguise,
you are most wicked; you follow Rāma alone into the forest alone, either hidden for my sake or employed by Bharata.
How could I, having taken as my husband Rāma—who is dark as a blue lotus and has eyes like lotuses—desire an ordinary man?
O Saumitri, in your very presence I shall give up my life; of this there is no doubt.
"I cannot live on this earth for even a moment without Rāma.
When Sītā had spoken these harsh words that caused his hair to stand on end,
Lakṣmaṇa, who had conquered his senses, replied to Sītā with palms joined in reverence.
"I do not venture to give a reply, for you are a deity to me; yet it is no wonder that my words are unseemly toward women, O Maithilī,
for such is the nature of women seen throughout these worlds."
Women are by nature fickle, impulsive, sharp-tongued, and divisive.
Let all these forest-dwellers, acting as witnesses, hear my words:
I have been addressed with harsh speech by you, though I spoke only what was just.
"Fie on you! Woe to you today for perishing, since out of your womanly nature and wicked disposition you thus suspect me, even though I am established in the command of my elder.
I shall go where the descendant of Kakutstha is; may it be well with you, O fair-faced one."
"O large-eyed one, may all the forest deities protect you!
For terrible omens appear before me;
yet, having returned, I shall see you once again together with Rāma."
Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, Janaka’s daughter, weeping and overwhelmed with tears, then replied with these piercing words:
"O Lakṣmaṇa, without Rāma, I shall enter the Godāvarī."
I shall either bind myself fast or cast my own body from a precipice;
I shall drink fierce poison or enter the fire.
Yet, I will not touch even with my foot any man other than Raghava.
Having thus reproached Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā, overcome with grief,
weeping out of sorrow, struck her belly with both hands.
Seeing her, the large-eyed daughter of Sumitrā, distressed in appearance, dejected, and weeping, [Lakṣmaṇa...]
Sītā comforted him but said nothing at all to her husband’s brother.
Then Lakṣmaṇa, having saluted Sītā with joined palms and bowing slightly while looking back repeatedly at the princess of Mithilā, the self-possessed one departed for the presence of Rāma.
But having been addressed harshly by her, Rāghava’s younger brother became enraged;
longing intensely for Rāma, he set out almost immediately.
Then Daśagrīva, finding an opportunity, quickly took his stand in the interval.
Assuming the form of a wandering mendicant, he approached Vaidehī;
clad in smooth saffron robes, with a topknot, carrying an umbrella and sandals,
and having hung a beautiful staff and water-pot over his left shoulder.
In the guise of a wandering mendicant, he approached Vaidehī in the forest; the exceedingly powerful one found her there, deprived of her two brothers,
like the great darkness of nightfall overtaking the twilight when it is bereft of both the sun and the moon.
Then that exceedingly cruel being beheld the illustrious princess, the young girl, like the star Rohiṇī separated from the Moon by a malignant planet.
And the trees growing in Janasthāna [beheld] that fierce evildoer.
Having observed him, they did not tremble, nor did the wind blow;
and seeing him with his blood-red eyes looking about, the swift-flowing river Godāvarī began to flow sluggishly out of fear.
Seeking an opportunity against Rāma, the ten-necked Rāvaṇa approached Vaidehī in the guise of a mendicant during that interval—
this unrighteous one, appearing in a righteous form, to her who was grieving for her husband.
He approached Vaidehī like Saturn approaching the star Citrā; that wicked man, disguised in a handsome form like a well concealed by grass,
stood gazing at Vaidehī, the illustrious wife of Rāma.
He saw her, auspicious, with beautiful teeth and lips, her face like the full moon,
sitting in a leaf-hut, overwhelmed by tears and grief—
her eyes like lotus petals, clothed in yellow silk.
The evil-minded night-stalker approached Vaidehī;
possessed by the arrows of the god of love and uttering the sounds of Vedic chanting,
the lord of the Rākṣasas spoke these humble words in that secluded place.
Rāvaṇa praised her, who was radiant with her body like the supreme splendor of the three worlds deprived of the lotus, saying:
"Who are you, O lady with the luster of gold, dressed in yellow silk?"
Bearing a beautiful garland of lotuses like a female lotus (padminī),
O lady of auspicious countenance, are you Hrī, Śrī, Kīrti, the auspicious Lakṣmī, or a celestial nymph (apsaras)?
Or are you Bhūti, O lady of excellent hips, or Rati wandering at will?
Your teeth are even, pointed, smooth, and white;
your eyes are large and clear, with red corners and black pupils.
Your hips are broad and full, and your thighs resemble the trunks of elephants.

These two breasts of yours are well-developed, rounded, closely set, and full; with their plump and elevated nipples, they are lovely and resemble smooth palm fruits. Adorned with exquisite jewel ornaments, they are truly beautiful.
O lady of lovely smiles, lovely teeth, and lovely eyes, O playful one,
you steal my heart, Rāma, as a riverbank is swept away by the water.
You have a waist measured by the span of a hand, beautiful hair, and firm breasts.
She is neither a goddess, nor a Gandharva woman, nor a Yakṣī, nor a Kiṃnarī.
Never before have I seen a woman of such form upon this earth; her dwelling here in the wilderness maddens my heart.
"Go back, may prosperity be yours; you ought not to dwell here.
This is the abode of terrible Rākṣasas who can assume any form at will. [There are] magnificent palaces and delightful city groves."
These excellent, fragrant, and worthy things are fit to be used by you.
O beautiful one with dark eyes, I consider excellent garlands, excellent drink, excellent garments, and an excellent husband to be most fitting for you.
Who are you among the Rudras, the Maruts, or the Vasus, O lady of radiant smiles? O beautiful one, you appear to me to be a goddess.
Neither Gandharvas, nor gods, nor Kinnaras come here.
"This is the dwelling place of Rākṣasas; how indeed have you come here?
Here dwell monkeys, lions, leopards, tigers, deer, bears, hyenas, and herons; how is it that you do not fear them?"

"How is it that you alone do not fear in this great forest those terrible and swift elephants filled with rut? Who are you, whose are you, from where have you come, and for what purpose are you in the Daṇḍaka forest, O lady of lovely countenance?"
"You wander alone, O auspicious lady, through these terrible regions inhabited by rākṣasas.
Thus was Vaidehī addressed by the evil-minded Rāvaṇa, who had approached her disguised in the form of a brahmin upon seeing her.
Maithilī honored him with every hospitality due to a guest.
Having first offered a seat and invited him with water for his feet, she then said to that gentle-looking man, "It is ready."

Seeing him approaching in the guise of a twice-born, carrying a vessel and saffron powder, Maithilī—perceiving that he could not be driven away because of his skillful means—invited him as one would a Brahmin who had arrived unbidden:
"O Brahmin, here is a grass mat; please sit at your pleasure, and accept this water for washing the feet."
"And let this excellent forest-grown produce, prepared for you, be enjoyed here without distraction.
Having observed Maithilī, the queen of the king, speaking with such full assurance as she was being thus invited,
Rāvaṇa laughed and set his mind upon her abduction for the sake of his own destruction.
Then, waiting for her well-attired husband who had gone hunting, and looking about for him along with Lakṣmaṇa, she beheld that great green forest, but neither Rāma nor Lakṣmaṇa.
At that time, Vaidehī was questioned by Rāvaṇa, who desired to carry her away.
In the guise of a wandering mendicant, he praised himself by his own account.
Thinking, "He is both a brahmin and a guest; if not addressed, he might indeed curse me," Sītā reflected for a moment and then spoke these words.
"I am the daughter of the high-souled Janaka of Mithilā;
my name is Sītā, and I am the wife of Rāma—blessings be upon you, O best of the twice-born. I have lived for one year in the residence of the descendant of Raghu."
Enjoying human pleasures and having all her desires fulfilled,
she then, after a year had passed, agreed with the assembled royal ministers to consecrate my husband Rāma.
While the preparations for Raghava’s consecration were being made,
my noble mother-in-law named Kaikeyi asked her husband for a boon. Having accepted it from her father-in-law through my own good deed, she [now demands it].
She requested two things from her husband, that best of kings who was true to his word: my own exile and the consecration of Bharata as heir apparent.
"Today I shall not eat, nor shall I sleep, nor shall I ever drink again."
"This is the end of my life if Rāma is consecrated. To Kaikeyī, who was speaking thus, my father-in-law— that bestower of honor— petitioned with meaningful requests, yet she did not grant his plea.
My husband is of great splendor, twenty-five years of age,
renowned in the world as Rāma; he is virtuous, truthful, pure,
large-eyed, long-armed, and devoted to the welfare of all beings.
When Rāma had approached his father for the consecration,
Kaikeyī quickly spoke these words to my husband:
"O Raghava, listen to this which has been commanded by your father."
"This kingdom must be given to Bharata, free from all thorns.
You, however, must dwell for fourteen years in the forest; go forth, O descendant of Kakutstha, and deliver your father from falsehood."
"So be it," Rāma said to Kaikeyī, free from all fear;
my husband, firm in his vows, acted according to her word. He would give but not receive, and he would speak the truth and never a falsehood.
"O Brahmin, this is the firm and unsurpassed vow of Rāma.
His half-brother, the valiant Lakṣmaṇa— a tiger among men and slayer of enemies— is his companion in battle."
That brother of mine named Lakṣmaṇa, a practitioner of dharma firm in his vows,
followed me as I went forth into exile, bow in hand. Thus,
we three have been deprived of our kingdom on account of Kaikeyī.
"O best of the twice-born, let us roam through this deep forest by our own power.
Take heart for a moment; it is possible for you to stay here, for my husband will return bringing abundant forest produce."
"Therefore, O twice-born one, tell me truly your name, your lineage, and your family; and for what purpose do you wander alone in the Daṇḍaka forest?
While Sītā, the wife of Rāma, was speaking thus, the one of great strength—
Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, gave this sharp reply:
"O Sītā, I am that Rāvaṇa by name, the sovereign of the hosts of Rākṣasas, by whom the worlds— including the gods, asuras, and pannagas— have been terrified."
But seeing you, O blameless one, with your golden complexion and clad in silk, I find no pleasure in my own wives,
despite having brought many excellent women here and there from various places.
"Blessings to you; from all of them, become my chief queen.
My great city named Laṅkā is situated in the midst of the ocean, surrounded by the sea and established upon the summit of a mountain."
There, O Sītā, you shall wander with me through the forests,
and you will have no longing for this forest life, O beautiful lady.
Five thousand female attendants, adorned with every ornament, [shall be yours].
"O Sītā, they shall serve you if you become my wife.
Thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, the daughter of Janaka, whose limbs were faultless, replied in anger, showing no respect for that Rākṣasa.
I am devoted to Rāma, who is as unshakable as a great mountain, like Mahendra himself, and as imperturbable as the great ocean;
he is long-armed, broad-chested, and moves with the prowess of a lion.
I am devoted to Rāma, who is like a lion, resembling a lion; I am devoted to Rāma, the hero with a face like the full moon, the prince who has conquered his senses;
I am devoted to the long-armed Rāma of vast renown.
But you, a jackal, desire me here, a lioness who is difficult to attain;
I cannot be touched by you, just as the radiance of the sun cannot be grasped.
O man of little merit, you surely see many golden trees.
O Rāvaṇa, you who desire the beloved wife of Rāghava wish to take a fang from the mouth of a hungry, swift-moving lion— the enemy of deer—
or from the mouth of a venomous serpent.
You wish to carry away Mandara, the best of mountains, with your hand;
having drunk the Kālakūṭa poison, you wish to depart in safety.
You wipe away a needle with your eye and lick a razor with your tongue.
You wish to win the beloved wife of Rāghava;
you wish to cross the ocean with a stone tied around your neck;
and you wish to seize both the sun and the moon with your bare hands.
He who desires to violate Rāma’s beloved wife is like one who,
seeing a blazing fire, wishes to seize it with his garment—
he who desires to abduct Rāma’s wife, who is of virtuous conduct.
You desire to walk upon the tips of iron-tipped spears,
you who wish to obtain Rāma’s wife, who is his equal. The difference between a lion and a jackal in the forest is the same as the difference between a mountain stream and the ocean.
The difference between the finest wine and sour gruel is the same as the difference between you and the son of Daśaratha;
the difference between gold and lead, between sandalwood water and mud,
and between an elephant and a wildcat in the forest— that is the difference between the son of Daśaratha and you.
The difference between you and the son of Daśaratha is like the difference between a crow and a Vainateya, between a water-fowl and a peacock, or even between a crane and a vulture in the forest;
for while Rāma— possessing a splendor equal to that of the thousand-eyed Indra— stands with bow and arrow in hand.
"Even though I have been carried off by you, I shall not undergo old age, just as a diamond swallowed by a fly [remains unchanged].
Having spoken these words so clearly to that night-stalker with an uncorrupted heart,
she— slender as a plantain tree shaken by the wind— became distressed, her limbs trembling.
Observing Sītā trembling, Rāvaṇa, whose power was equal to Death itself,
announced his lineage, strength, name, and deeds for the purpose of instilling fear.
While Sītā was speaking thus, he became enraged and spoke harsh words.
Knitting his brows upon his forehead, Rāvaṇa replied:
"O lady of excellent complexion, I am the half-brother of Vaiśravaṇa;
my name is Rāvaṇa, the ten-headed and powerful one—blessings be upon you."
Before whom the gods, along with the Gandharvas, Piśācas, birds, and serpents,
always flee in terror like living beings fleeing from death;
by whom his half-brother Vaiśravaṇa was driven away for a certain reason.
Having encountered him in combat, he was overcome by anger and defeated through valor;
afflicted by fear of me, that man-vehicled one abandoned his own prosperous abode and now dwells upon Kailāsa, the best of mountains.

O auspicious Maithilī, as soon as he beholds my face when I am filled with rage, that beautiful celestial chariot named Puṣpaka— which travels at will and was won by my prowess— shall carry me through the sky.
The gods, led by Śakra, flee in terror;
where I stand, the wind blows with apprehension,
and both the sun of fierce rays and the moon become dim for fear.
Wherever I stay or move about, the trees have motionless leaves and the rivers have still waters.
On the far shore of the ocean is my auspicious city named Laṅkā.
It was filled with terrible Rākṣasas like Indra’s Amarāvatī;
the beautiful city was encircled by a white wall, adorned with golden courtyards and gateways made of lapis lazuli.
Crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots, resounding with the music of trumpets,
and adorned with gardens filled with trees that bear the fruits of all desires—
there, O Princess Sītā, you shall dwell together with me.
O wise lady, you shall not remember human women;
O woman of excellent complexion, while enjoying both human and divine pleasures,
you shall not remember Rāma, a mere mortal whose life has come to an end.

What is the use of that Rama, whose kingdom has been lost and whose mind is distracted, whom King Dasharatha— having set aside his beloved son— dispatched to the forest as the eldest son of weak prowess?
"O large-eyed lady,
you must not reject this lord of all the rākṣasas, who has come here of his own accord out of desire and is pierced by the arrows of Love, merely because he is an ascetic performing penance."
"Having rejected me, O timid one, you shall suffer remorse,
just as Urvaśī did after striking Purūravas with her foot.
Thus addressed, Vaidehī became enraged, her eyes bloodshot with anger.
In private, he spoke these harsh words to the lord of the Rākṣasas:
"How is it that, having claimed Vaiśravaṇa— the god honored by all beings—
as your brother, you wish to commit such an evil deed?"
O Rāvaṇa, all these Rākṣasas will surely perish,
for you have become their harsh king— evil-minded and one whose senses are unsubdued.
Having abducted Śacī, the wife of Indra, it is impossible for him to continue living.

But having abducted me, the wife of Rāma, there is no life for you. One might live long after violating Śacī, who possesses incomparable beauty, from the hand of the wielder of the thunderbolt; but having violated one such as I, O Rākṣasa, there is no escape for you, even if you have drunk the nectar of immortality.
Having heard Sītā’s words, the powerful Ten-necked one struck his hands together and assumed a truly massive form;
he then spoke these words once more to the princess of Mithilā with great intensity.
I believe that through my unimpaired hearing, my vigor and prowess are such that,
standing in the sky, I could lift up the earth with my two arms;
I could drink up the ocean, and standing in battle, I could slay Death himself.
"I could stop the sun with my sharp arrows and indeed split the surface of the earth; O madwoman, behold me, your husband, who can assume any form at will and grant all desires.
To Rāvaṇa, who had spoken thus, [she replied] in a voice as radiant as fire:
The eyes of the enraged one became red at the corners like those of a monkey;
instantly abandoning his gentle mendicant form, that Rāvaṇa,
the younger brother of Vaiśravaṇa, assumed his own form, which resembled the appearance of Death itself.
With bloodshot eyes, glorious, wearing earrings of refined gold,
ten-faced, and armed with a bow and arrows, that night-stalker became [Rāvaṇa] in an instant;
he cast off that disguise of a wandering mendicant, revealing his massive body.
Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, resumed his own form;
with eyes bloodshot from rage and possessing the splendor of a mass of clouds,
he stood there wearing red garments, gazing upon Maithilī, that jewel among women.
Rāvaṇa spoke to that Maithilī, who had dark-ended hair and was adorned with garments and ornaments like the radiance of the sun:
"If you desire a husband renowned throughout the three worlds..."
Take refuge in me, O lady of beautiful hips; I am a husband worthy of you.
Devote yourself to me for a long time; I am a praiseworthy and beloved husband to you, and I shall never do anything that is displeasing to you, my dear.
"Abandon this human sentiment and direct your devotion toward me!
O foolish woman who fancies herself wise, for what virtues are you so infatuated with Rāma— he who has been fallen from his kingdom, whose purpose is unfulfilled, and whose life is limited?"
"Having abandoned his kingdom along with his friends and kinsmen at the word of a woman,
that evil-minded man dwells in this forest haunted by beasts of prey.
Having spoken these words to Maithilī, who was worthy of affection and spoke so sweetly, [he departed].
Rāvaṇa seized Sītā, as Budha seizes Rohiṇī in the sky; with his left hand he grasped the lotus-eyed woman by her hair,
and with his right hand he took hold of her thighs.
Seeing him, who resembled a mountain peak, possessed sharp fangs and mighty arms,
and appeared like Death itself, the forest deities fled, afflicted by fear.
And that divine, illusory chariot was yoked with donkeys and made a harsh sound.
Then Rāvaṇa’s great chariot, with its golden limbs, came into view. Then, having threatened Vaidehī with harsh words in a loud voice, he took her onto his lap and placed her upon the chariot.

Seized by Rāvaṇa, the illustrious Sītā, afflicted with grief, cried out "Rāma! for Rāma was far away in the forest. Afflicted by passion, he seized her against her will, as one might seize the wife of a serpent king.

Then Rāvaṇa, seizing her as she writhed, flew up into the air. As she was being carried away through the sky by the lord of the rākṣasas, she cried out loudly like one intoxicated, her mind bewildered and distressed.
"Alas, Lakṣmaṇa, O mighty-armed one, you who delight the heart of your elder!
You do not know that I am being carried away by a Rākṣasa who can assume any form at will,
you who renounce life, happiness, and wealth for the sake of dharma!"
O Raghava, you do not see me being carried away by unrighteousness!
Surely, O scorcher of foes, you are the disciplinarian of the undisciplined;
why then do you not punish such a sinner as Ravana?

"Is it not seen that the fruit of an ill-performed action appears immediately? In this matter, time also acts as a contributing factor, just as it does for the ripening of crops. He performed this deed with his consciousness impaired by time."
"May you meet with a terrible calamity at the hands of Rāma, one that shall bring an end to your life!
Alas! Now Kaikeyī, together with her kinsmen, has achieved her desire; for I, the lawful wife of this illustrious man who loves righteousness, am being carried away."
I bid farewell to Janasthāna and the flowering Karṇikāra trees;
quickly announce to Rāma that Rāvaṇa is carrying away Sītā.
I pay homage to the peaked Mālyavān and Mount Prasravaṇa.
"Quickly report to Rāma that Rāvaṇa is carrying away Sītā!
I bow to the river Godāvarī, resounded by flocks of swans and cranes;
quickly report to Rāma that Rāvaṇa is carrying away Sītā!"
And the deities who dwell in this forest of various trees—to them I offer my salutations; tell my husband that I have been carried away.
And whatever other creatures reside here as well, [I salute them].
"I seek refuge with all of you, even with the multitudes of beasts and birds.
Proclaim that Sītā, who is dearer to her husband than his own life, has been carried off by Rāvaṇa while she was helpless."
"Having learned of me there as well, the mighty-armed and exceedingly powerful one will exert his prowess and bring me back, even though I have been seized by Vaivasvata.
O Jaṭāyu, tell Rāma exactly how my abduction occurred."
"And all of that must be related to Lakṣmaṇa in its entirety.
Then Jaṭāyu heard that sound while he was fast asleep;
he quickly looked about and beheld Rāvaṇa and Vaidehī.
Then that best of birds, resembling a mountain peak, with a sharp beak,
majestic and perched upon a great tree, uttered these auspicious words:
"O Ten-necked One, you who stand firm in the ancient dharma and take refuge in truth," Ram_3.48.2.
"I am the mighty king of vultures, known by the name Jaṭāyu.
Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, is like Mahendra and Varuṇa; he is the king of the entire world and is ever intent on the welfare of all beings."
She is the illustrious and noble-limbed Dharmapatnī (lawful wife) of that Lord of the World, named Sītā, whom you desire to abduct here.
How could a king established in dharma touch the wife of another?
O one of great strength, the king's wives must be protected with special care;
turn your mind away from this base intent to violate another's wife.
A wise man should not practice that which another would censure him for.

Just as one's own, so too must the wives of others be protected from improper scrutiny. O descendant of Pulastya, whether it concerns wealth or pleasure, the learned determine what has not been explicitly stated in the scriptures by following the conduct of kings.
The king is both righteousness and pleasure, and the supreme treasury of all things;
for whether it be merit or sin, everything proceeds with the king as its root.
O best of Rākṣasas, how can you be so fickle and of such evil nature?
Having attained sovereign power, he is like a sinner who has obtained a celestial chariot. One's inherent nature of desire cannot be wiped away;
for nobility does not dwell long in the abode of those with wicked souls.
Whether in the forest or in the city, since that righteous and mighty Rāma does not commit any offense against you, how can you offend him?
Even if Khara, who was in Janasthāna, acted on account of Śūrpaṇakhā—
He has already been overstepped and slain by Rāma of unwearied deeds.
Tell me here, according to the truth, what transgression was committed by Rāma,
the lord of the world, against whom you have gone after abducting his wife?
Release Vaidehī quickly, lest she consume you with her terrible gaze,
which is like the fire itself, just as Indra’s thunderbolt consumed Vṛtra.
You do not realize that you have bound a venomous serpent at the hem of your garment.
And you do not see the noose of Time fastened around your neck.
O gentle one, that burden should be borne which does not exhaust a man;
that food should be consumed which is digested without causing illness.

"O Rāvaṇa, what action would one perform that results neither in dharma, nor fame, nor renown on earth, but only in the exhaustion of the body— especially for me, who have lived for sixty thousand years? (Rāmāyaṇa 3.48.18)
While you rule the ancestral kingdom of your father and grandfather in accordance with dharma,
I am old; yet you are young, equipped with bow, chariot, armor, and arrows— nevertheless, even taking Vaidehī with you, you shall not return in safety.

"You are not able to carry off Vaidehī by force while I look on, any more than one can alter the eternal Vedic revelation through arguments joined with logic. If you are a hero, fight; stay for a moment, Rāvaṇa!"
"You shall lie slain upon the ground, just as Khara did before;
though you have repeatedly struck down Daityas and Dānavas in battle,
Rāma, dressed in bark garments, will slay you in combat before long."
"What indeed can I do, now that the two princes have gone far away?
You shall perish quickly, O base one; you will undoubtedly be terrified of them.
For while I am alive, you shall not carry off this auspicious lady."
Sītā, whose eyes are like lotus petals, the beloved queen of Rāma—
surely I must perform what is pleasing to that great-souled one,
even at the cost of my own life, as well as to Rāma and Daśaratha.
Stay, stay, O ten-necked one! Wait a moment, Rāvaṇa;
I shall provide you with the hospitality of battle according to my strength, O night-stalker, and I shall cause you to fall from your excellent chariot like a fruit from its stalk.
When Jaṭāyu spoke thus to Rāvaṇa according to what was right,
all twenty of the enraged demon's eyes blazed like fire;
his eyes were bloodshot with anger, and he wore earrings of refined gold.
The intolerant lord of the Rākṣasas rushed toward the lord of birds.
A tumultuous clash occurred between the two of them in that great forest,
like that between two clouds driven by the wind in the sky.
Then that battle between the vulture and the rākṣasa became a marvel,
like the clash between two great winged mountains, Mālyavat and [Gandhamādana], both covered with garlands.
Then, with nālīkas, nārācas, and sharp-pointed vikarṇis—
The mighty one showered the king of vultures with most terrible shafts.
Jaṭāyu, the lord of winged chariots, received those nets of arrows— the weapons of Rāvaṇa— in the encounter.
Then that one of great strength, the best of birds, made many wounds upon his body with his two sharp-clawed feet.
Thereupon, out of anger, the Ten-necked One seized ten arrows.

Desiring to crush his enemy, he [discharged] those terrible arrows resembling the rod of Death. With those sharp, fierce, straight-flying, and whetted stone-tipped shafts released from a full draw, that one of great prowess pierced the vulture.
Beholding Jānakī with tearful eyes upon the chariot of the Rākṣasa,
he disregarded those arrows and rushed toward the Rākṣasa.
Then, his bow, adorned with pearls and gems, along with its arrow, [was severed].
With his two feet, the lord of birds, possessed of great splendor, shattered [Rāvaṇa’s shield];
and with his two wings, that lord of birds of great splendor shook off Rāvaṇa’s blazing shield, which was like fire.
In that battle, the powerful one struck down those divine donkeys, which had golden breastplates, faces like Piśācas, and were endowed with great speed;
they possessed excellent triple-pole chariot-frames, moved at will, and blazed like the flames of fire.
He shattered the great chariot, its body adorned with jewels and gold,
as well as the parasol resembling the full moon along with the fans.
With his bow broken, deprived of his chariot, his horses slain, and his charioteer killed, he remained there.
Taking Vaidehī on his lap, Rāvaṇa fell to the ground.
Seeing Rāvaṇa fallen upon the earth, his vehicle shattered, all living beings honored the king of vultures, crying out, "Excellent! Excellent!"
Seeing that leader of the birds exhausted by old age,
Rāvaṇa, filled with joy, took hold of the daughter of Mithilā and flew up once more as he carried her on his lap while departing.
The king of vultures, Jaṭāyu, springing up, spoke these words:
"O Rāvaṇa of small intellect, you who seize this wife of Rāma— whose arrows have the touch of a thunderbolt— are surely acting for the destruction of the Rākṣasas."
Together with your friends, kinsmen, ministers, army, and retinue,
you drink this poison as if you were thirsty for water— unwise men who do not foresee the consequences of their actions.
They will perish very quickly, just as you shall perish. Bound by the noose of Time, where can you go to escape it? You are like a sea creature that has seized a baited hook for its own destruction.
For the two Raghavas, the descendants of Kakutstha, are never to be overcome; O Rāvaṇa, they will not forgive either your assault upon them or this violation of the hermitage,
for the deed you have committed is cowardly and condemned by the world.
"This is the path practiced by thieves; it is not frequented by heroes.
Fight, if you are a hero! Stay for a moment, O Rāvaṇa;
you shall lie slain upon the ground just as your brother Khara did."
At the time of death, whatever unrighteous action a man undertakes leads to his own destruction; you have undertaken such an action. For what man indeed would perform an act that results in sin?
"Even the Lord, the self-born Sovereign of the World, would do so.
Having spoken these auspicious words, the powerful Jaṭāyu fell violently upon the back of that ten-necked Rākṣasa.
Seizing him with his sharp claws, he tore at him on all sides,
just as an elephant-rider, having mounted a rogue elephant, might tear at it;
pressing his claws against its back, he tore at its snout.
And he, whose weapons were his claws, wings, and beak, tore out his hair.
Thus being tormented repeatedly by the king of vultures,
that Rākṣasa trembled, his lips quivering with indignation.
Embracing Vaidehī with his left arm, Rāvaṇa,
overcome with grief and frantic with rage, struck Jaṭāyu with his palm.
But Jaṭāyu, the lord of birds, leaping over him, struck that ruler of the Khara-demons with his beak.
Then that subduer of enemies severed his ten left arms.
Thereupon, the valiant Ten-necked one, filled with rage, released Sītā and crushed the king of vultures with his fists and feet.
Then, for a moment, a battle took place between those two of incomparable prowess—
the chief of the Rākṣasas and the foremost of birds—
while Rāvaṇa was striving for the sake of Rāma.
Raising his sword, he sliced off its wings, feet, and flanks.
With its wings severed by the Rākṣasa of terrible deeds,
the vulture fell to the earth, slain and with but little life remaining.
Seeing Jaṭāyu fallen upon the ground, drenched in blood,
Vaidehī ran toward him in her grief as if toward her own kinsman—
him who resembled a dark blue cloud, possessed a most pale and broad chest, and was endowed with noble valor.

The lord of Laṅkā beheld Jaṭāyu upon the earth, like a forest fire extinguished. Then Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, whose face shone with the luster of the moon, wept as she once again embraced that bird who had been struck down to the ground and crushed by the force of Rāvaṇa.
The lord of the rākṣasas saw that vulture with its life nearly spent, quivering on the ground and fallen near the hermitage of Rāghava.
But she, whose face was like the lord of the stars, beheld him by Rāvaṇa.
Deeply distressed, she lamented for the slain king of vultures:
"The knowledge of omens, the science of marks, and the observation of birds and their cries necessarily manifest for men amidst both happiness and sorrow."
"Surely you do not realize, O Rāma, the great calamity that has befallen you;
surely the beasts and birds are fleeing for my sake, O descendant of Kakutstha!
Save me today, O Kākutstha, Lakṣmaṇa!"—thus cried the beautiful woman.
Terrified, she cried out as if in the presence of those who could hear her;
then Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, rushed toward Vaidehī, who was lamenting like one without a protector, her garlands and ornaments disarrayed.
As she was winding around like a creeper, embracing the great trees, the lord of the Rākṣasas cried out many times, "Release me! Release me!
while she, separated from Rāma in the forest, was crying out, "Rāma! Rāma!"
Resembling the God of Death himself, he seized Vaidehī by her hair to end her life.
When Vaidehī was thus assaulted, the entire world, including all that is mobile and immobile, became lawless and enveloped in blinding darkness.
Having seen Sītā seized and distressed with his divine eye,
the illustrious Grandfather declared, "The task is accomplished.
All those supreme ṛṣis were both overjoyed and pained.
Seeing Sītā thus violated, the inhabitants of the Daṇḍaka forest cried out, "O Rāma! O Rāma! and "O Lakṣmaṇa!
Then Rāvaṇa, the lord of the Rākṣasas, took her and flew into the sky as she wept, crying "Rāma! Rāma! and "Lakṣmaṇa!"
With all her limbs adorned with glowing ornaments and wearing yellow silk garments, the princess shone like a flash of lightning from the clouds;
and by her uplifted yellow garment, Rāvaṇa was likewise illuminated.
The mountain shone even more intensely, as if ablaze with fire. Upon Rāvaṇa, those most auspicious copper-hued and fragrant lotus petals belonging to Vaidehī were scattered.
Her silken garment, tossed up into the sky and glowing with the luster of gold,
shone like a copper-hued cloud in the sunlight due to the redness of the sun. Her stainless face, held in Rāvaṇa’s embrace, appeared in the sky.
Without Rāma, she did not shine, like a lotus without its stalk;
her face, with its beautiful forehead and lovely hair-tips, unblemished and radiant as the interior of a lotus, appeared like the moon risen after piercing through a dark cloud.
Adorned with white, perfectly pure, and radiant teeth;
its weeping wiped away, it was as pleasing to behold as the moon,
possessing a beautiful nose and lovely copper-hued lips, shining like gold in the sky.
That auspicious speech of hers, though shaken by the lord of the rākṣasas,
did not shine in his presence without Rāma, like the moon risen during the day.
Maithilī, who was golden-hued, [stood before] the lord of the rākṣasas, whose limbs were dark blue.
The golden girdle shone as if it were resting upon a blue gem;
Janaka’s daughter, fair as a lotus and radiant as gold, adorned with ornaments of refined metal, shone as she entered Rāvaṇa like lightning entering a cloud.
At the sound of Vaidehī’s ornaments, the lord of the rākṣasas became like a pure, dark rain-cloud accompanied by thunder;
and a shower of flowers fell from her head in every direction.
As Sītā was being carried away,
that shower of flowers fell upon the surface of the earth; yet, shaken by the force of Rāvaṇa, it returned once more toward the Ten-necked one from all sides.
A stream of flowers fell upon the younger brother of Vaiśravaṇa,
like a pure garland of stars upon Mount Meru, the highest of mountains. From Vaidehī’s feet, an anklet adorned with jewels had fallen.
Resembling a circle of lightning and possessing a sweet voice, she descended.
Vaidehī, with her limbs as red as tree-sprouts, illuminated the dark-bodied lord of the rākṣasas, just as a golden girth-belt adorns an elephant.
Entering the sky, the younger brother of Vaiśravaṇa seized Sītā, who was blazing with her own radiance like a great meteor in the heavens;
her ornaments, glowing like fire, fell upon the surface of the earth.
Resounding, they were scattered like stars exhausted from the sky.
The necklace, possessing the luster of the lord of stars, slipped from the space between Vaidehī’s breasts; falling down, it shone like the Gaṅgā descending from the heavens.
Struck by the violent winds and filled with flocks of various birds,
the trees, their tops shaken, seemed to cry out, "Do not fear! The lotus ponds, their lotuses destroyed and their fish and aquatic creatures terrified, lay desolate.
As if grieving for Maithilī, who was like a friend whose spirit had departed,
lions, tigers, deer, and birds then rushed together from all sides and pursued her in their rage, following the shadow of Sītā.
With waterfalls for their tearful faces and mountain peaks for their upraised arms,
the mountains seemed to cry out as Sītā was being carried away.
And seeing Vaidehī being abducted, the sun became despondent.
The glorious lunar orb, its circle now pale, had its radiance utterly destroyed.
Where Rāvaṇa carries off Vaidehī, the wife of Rāma, there is no dharma; how can there be truth, uprightness, or compassion?
Thus all the creatures lamented in groups;
with terrified hearts and dejected faces, the young fawns wept,
casting their eyes upward again and again, their vision blurred by the falling of tears.
And the forest deities had their limbs trembling violently.
Seeing Sītā crying out piteously, fallen into such a state of suffering,
and calling out to Lakṣmaṇa and Rāma with her sweet voice—
Gazing repeatedly at the surface of the earth, the ten-necked one carried away that high-minded Vaidehī— her locks of hair disheveled and her forehead mark rubbed away— for his own destruction.
Then Maithilī, that woman of beautiful teeth and pure smiles, separated from her kinsmen and not seeing either Rāghava or Lakṣmaṇa, her face turned pale and oppressed by a burden of fear,
beheld him as he was leaping into the sky— Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka.
Afflicted with grief, extremely agitated, and beset by great fear,
Sītā— her eyes copper-red with anger and weeping— spoke these words piteously as she was being carried away to the terrifying-eyed lord of the Rākṣasas.
O base Rāvaṇa, you feel no shame for this deed, you who, having known me to be separated from my husband, steal me away and flee!
Surely it was by you alone, O evil-souled coward, desiring to abduct me, that [this was done].
"My husband has been carried away by you through illusion in the form of a deer;
for even he who was prepared to rescue me has been struck down.
Indeed, O lowest of Rākṣasas, your supreme prowess is truly displayed."

"Having indeed proclaimed your name in battle, there is no one here who has been conquered by you. O base man, how are you not ashamed to have committed such a despicable deed— the abduction of another's wife in his absence?"
Men in the worlds will speak of this contemptible,
cruel, and most unrighteous deed of yours, you who pride yourself on your heroism: "Fie on your valor and your strength, as described by you at that time!"
"Shame on such conduct of yours, which brings reproach upon your lineage in this world!
What can possibly be done since you flee with such speed?
Stay but for a moment; you shall not return alive."
For once those two sons of the king have come within the range of your sight, you will not be able to remain alive for even a moment, even with your army;
you are not capable of enduring the touch of their arrows in any way whatsoever.

"O Rāvaṇa, do what is beneficial for yourself and release me at once; for my husband, enraged by this assault upon me, will surely come with his brother. Just as a bird avoids the touch of a fire blazing in the forest, so must you avoid me.
"If you do not release me, you shall bring about your own destruction.
That resolve by which you desire to carry me off by force, O base one, will prove to be fruitless."
For, not seeing my husband who resembles a god, I, fallen under the power of my enemies, cannot endure to sustain my life for long.
Surely you do not perceive what is for your own welfare or what is beneficial for yourself.
Just as a mortal at the time of death resorts to perverse actions, so too for all who are about to die, that which is wholesome is no longer pleasing. Indeed,
I see you as if already caught in the noose of Time around your neck.
And since you do not fear this place of terror, O Ten-faced One,
it is clear that you perceive these trees as being made of gold.
[How much less would you fear] the terrible Vaitaraṇī river, which carries a torrent of blood?
And you shall see, O Rāvaṇa, the terrifying forest of sword-leaves;
and you will behold the sharp Śālmali tree, covered with iron thorns and bearing flowers of molten gold with petals of the finest vaidūrya gem.

For having committed such a falsehood against that great-souled one, O pitiless Rāvaṇa, you will not be able to endure it for long, like a man who has drunk poison and is bound by the irresistible noose of Time.
Where have you gone that you shall find peace, having deprived my high-souled husband—
who, in the space of a mere moment in battle, slew fourteen thousand Rākṣasas— of his brother?
"How could that heroic Rāghava, powerful and skilled in all weapons,
not slay you with his sharp arrows— you who have abducted his beloved wife?
These and other harsh words did Vaidehī address to Rāvaṇa as she remained in his embrace.
Overcome by fear and grief, she lamented piteously.
As the beautiful woman was thus deeply afflicted, speaking much and wailing piteously as before,
the sinful one carried off the young princess— who was writhing and trembling all over— while she was still struggling.
While being carried away, Vaidehī, seeing no protector anywhere,
beheld five bull-like monkeys stationed upon a mountain peak.
In their midst, the large-eyed lady saw a garment of silk with the luster of gold.
Maithilī cast off her upper garment and her beautiful ornaments, thinking, "Lest they should reveal me to Rāma. She discarded the cloth and threw it along with the jewelry into their midst.
But due to his agitation, the ten-necked Rāvaṇa did not perceive that deed.
Then those bulls among monkeys, with their tawny eyes like those who do not blink, beheld Sītā as she was crying out, her large eyes wide.
Having passed beyond the Pampā lake, the Lord of the Rākṣasas, taking the weeping Maithilī with him, went toward the city of Laṅkā;
greatly delighted, Rāvaṇa carried her away, even though she was his own death.
Carrying the sharp-fanged, highly venomous female serpent upon his lap,
he swiftly traversed through the sky over forests, rivers, mountains, and lakes, like an arrow released from a bow.
Having reached the inexhaustible ocean, the abode of Varuṇa and the refuge of rivers, which is the dwelling place of whales and sea-monsters, he crossed over it; there,
out of agitation, its waves were tossed about and its fish and great serpents were obstructed.
While Vaidehī was being carried away, the ocean, the abode of Varuṇa, became agitated;
and then the Cāraṇas dwelling in the sky uttered these words, while the Siddhas then declared: "This is the end for the Ten-necked One."
Taking Sītā, who was writhing, in his arms, Rāvaṇa entered the city of Laṅkā, which was his own death personified.
Having reached the city of Laṅkā with its well-laid-out great highways, he entered.
He entered his own inner apartments, which were filled with many well-trained courtesans.
There, Rāvaṇa placed Sītā— her dark-cornered eyes cast down, overwhelmed by grief and delusion— just as Maya once deposited the illusory Asurī Māyā.
And the ten-necked one spoke to the Piśācīs of terrible appearance:
"So that no man or woman may see Sītā without permission,
[provide] pearls, gems, gold, garments, and ornaments."
Whatever she may desire, that alone should be given to her according to my will.
And as for whoever shall speak any unpleasant word to Vaidehī,
whether out of ignorance or knowledge, life shall not be dear to them.
Having spoken thus to those rākṣasīs, the powerful lord of the rākṣasas emerged from that inner apartment and, reflecting on what ought to be done,
beheld eight rākṣasas of great prowess who were eaters of flesh.
Seeing them, the one of great prowess, deluded by the granting of the boon,
praised them for their strength and valor and spoke these words:
"Armed with various weapons, go quickly from here with all haste."
Janasthāna, formerly the abode of Khara, has become a place of slaughter.
Having cast fear far away and relying on your manly strength, stay there in Janasthāna, now empty and devoid of Rākṣasas.
Indeed, that very great force which I had stationed in Janasthāna has been slain in battle by Rāma’s arrows, along with Dūṣaṇa and Khara;
therefore, an unprecedented rage rises within me, overcoming my fortitude.
A very great and most terrible enmity has arisen toward Rāma;
I wish to exact that enmity from my enemy,
for I shall find no sleep until I have slain the foe in battle.
But now, having slain that Rāma— the slayer of Khara and Dūṣaṇa— I shall obtain peace, just as a pauper obtains wealth.
While you were dwelling in Janasthāna, you took refuge with Rāma.
"His movements must be observed in truth as to what he does;
all the night-stalkers must proceed with vigilance,
and constant effort must be made toward the slaying of Rāghava."
"For I have known your strength many times on the front lines of battle;

therefore, you have been appointed by me to this Janasthāna. Then those eight Rākṣasas, having approached with these pleasing and highly significant words and having paid homage to Rāvaṇa, [departed].
Leaving Laṅkā together, they set out for Janasthāna, remaining invisible to sight.
Then, having obtained Sītā and seized Maithilī, Rāvaṇa was exceedingly delighted;
that Rākṣasa, through delusion, became joyful and entered into a supreme enmity with Rāma.
Having dispatched eight terrible and mighty Rākṣasas, Rāvaṇa,
due to the confusion of his intellect, considered himself to have accomplished his purpose;
he brooded over Vaidehī, pierced by the arrows of desire.
Hurrying to see Sītā, he entered the beautiful palace.
Having entered that residence, Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas,
beheld Sītā in the midst of the rākṣasīs, wholly devoted to her grief.
With her face filled with tears, miserable and oppressed by a heavy burden of grief,
she was like a boat sinking in the ocean, overwhelmed by the force of the winds;
she was like a doe strayed from the herd, surrounded by dogs.
Approaching her as she sat dejected with her face cast downward, the night-stalker,
the lord of the Rākṣasas, forcibly showed that wretched woman, who was helpless and overcome by grief, his palace which resembled the abode of the gods.
It was crowded with mansions and palaces, frequented by thousands of women,
inhabited by various flocks of birds, and endowed with diverse jewels;
it was likewise adorned with gold, refined gold, crystal, and silver.
With pillars variegated with diamonds and lapis lazuli that were enchanting to the sight,
he ascended together with her the wonderful golden staircase, which featured archways of refined gold and resounded with the beat of divine drums.
The windows were made of ivory and silver, lovely to behold, and the rows of palaces there were covered with golden lattices;
furthermore, the floor areas everywhere were variegated with lime and jewels.
The Ten-necked one showed Maithilī his own palace;
Rāvaṇa showed Sītā, who was devoted to her grief, long ponds and lotus-pools covered with various kinds of flowers.
Having shown Vaidehī that entire, most excellent palace,
the evil-minded Rāvaṇa spoke these words to the daughter of Janaka:
"There are ten crores of Rākṣasas, and another twenty-two crores besides."
"Excluding those who are aged and those who are children,
O Sītā, I am the lord of all those night-stalkers of fearsome deeds;
a thousand of them attend to my every purpose."

"This entire system of my kingdom is established in you; so too is my life, O large-eyed one. You are dearer to me than my own vital breaths. As for that collection of many thousands of women whom I have taken as my wives—"
"You are their sovereign, Sītā; become my wife, my beloved.
Enough of this other resolve of yours—accept my words. Deign to show favor to me, who am tormented by love."
This Laṅkā, extending for a hundred yojanas and surrounded by the ocean,
cannot be overcome even by the gods and asuras led by Indra;
neither among the gods, nor the yakṣas, nor the gandharvas, nor the ṛṣis [is there anyone capable of it].
"I do not see anyone in the worlds who could be equal to my prowess.
What will you do with Rama— a mere human of little luster, fallen from his kingdom, wretched, a mere ascetic, and whose life is spent?"
"O Sītā, devote yourself to me alone; I am a husband worthy of you.
For youth, O timid one, is transient; take your pleasure here with me.
Do not set your mind on seeing Rāghava, O lady of the beautiful countenance."
O Sītā, even by means of one's desires, it is impossible for him to come here; for the wind of great velocity cannot be bound with ropes in the sky,
nor can the pure flame of a blazing fire be grasped.
O beautiful one, among all the three worlds, I do not see anyone who could carry you away by force while you are protected by my arms. Rule over this vast kingdom in Laṅkā.
Drenched by the water of consecration and satisfied, do you delight me. Whatever evil deed was done in the past, it has been removed by your dwelling in the forest;
now, receive here the fruit of that righteous merit which you have performed.
"O Maithilī, here are all kinds of garlands of divine fragrance and the finest ornaments; enjoy them with me.
O lady of beautiful hips, this is the Puṣpaka chariot belonging to my brother Vaiśravaṇa."
That celestial chariot is delightful and moves with the speed of thought;
there, O Sītā, sport with me as you please.
Your face is like a lotus, stainless and beautiful to behold.
"O lady of beautiful hips, O lovely-faced one, he does not shine when afflicted by grief;
enough of this shame, Vaidehī, regarding the transgression of dharma on your part.
This is the flow of divine destiny ordained by the seers, that he shall come to you."
"I have pressed these tender feet with my heads;
grant me your favor quickly. I am your submissive slave.
These words were not spoken in vain by me, who am now wasting away."
"Nor indeed would Rāvaṇa ever bow his head before any woman," having spoken thus to Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, the ten-necked one,
fallen under the power of Death, thought, "She is mine."
Thus addressed, Vaidehī, though emaciated by grief, spoke fearlessly to Rāvaṇa after placing a blade of grass between them:
"There was a king named Daśaratha, who was like an immovable bridge of dharma."
He whose son is that Rāghava, known for his fidelity to truth;
he named Rāma, whose soul is righteousness, renowned throughout the three worlds,
long-armed and large-eyed— he is my husband and my deity.
Born in the lineage of the Ikṣvākus, with shoulders like a lion’s and great splendor, he who,
together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa, shall take away your life—
if I had been seen by him while being forcibly violated by you.

"You shall lie slain in battle, just as Khara was in Janasthāna. All these rākṣasas of whom you spoke— terrible in form and possessed of great strength— are rendered powerless against Rāghava, like serpents before Suparṇa."
Those gold-adorned arrows, released from his bowstring,
will shatter your body like waves against the bank of the Ganges,
O Rāvaṇa, even if you are incapable of being slain by either Asuras or Suras.
"Having provoked such great enmity, you shall not escape him while you yet live.
That mighty Rāghava will be the end of your remaining life;
like a sacrificial animal bound to a post, your life is now difficult to preserve."
O Rākṣasa, if that Rāma were to behold you with an eye blazing with wrath, you would be consumed this very day and meet your immediate destruction.
He is one who could bring down the moon from the sky to the earth or utterly destroy it.
He might even dry up the ocean and here he shall liberate Sītā.
Your life is spent, your fortune is gone, your strength is lost, and your senses have failed;
because of you, Laṅkā shall be joined with widowhood.
"This evil deed of yours shall not result in happiness,
since I have been led from the forest by you away from my husband, who is without a rival.
For that husband of mine is endowed with divine power and possesses great splendor."
Fearless and relying on his valor, he dwells in the Daṇḍaka forest.
In battle, with a rain of arrows, he will strip from your limbs your pride, strength, heroism, and such arrogance.
When the destruction of beings is seen, impelled by time,
then men, fallen under the power of time, become negligent in their duties.
O lowest of Rākṣasas, that very time has now arrived for you, having assailed me.
For the sake of slaying ourselves, the Rākṣasas, and the women of the inner apartments, [Rāma spoke:
"The sacrificial altar, situated in the midst of the sacrifice, adorned with ladles and vessels, and consecrated by the mantras of the twice-born, cannot be desecrated by a Caṇḍāla."
"This body is insentient; bind it or cause it to be slain.
O Rākṣasa, this body is not to be protected by me, nor even my life;
for I shall not allow myself to bring reproach upon the earth."
Having spoken these very harsh words out of anger, Vaidehī Maithilī said nothing more to Rāvaṇa there.
Having heard Sītā’s harsh speech, which caused the hair to stand on end—
Then he spoke these words, intended to inspire fear, to Sītā:
"Listen to my words, O Maithilī, O beautiful woman; if you do not yield to me within these twelve months, O lady of lovely smiles."
"Then, for the sake of your morning meal, the cooks shall cut you into pieces.
Having spoken these harsh words, Rāvaṇa, the terror of his enemies,
being enraged, then addressed these words to the rākṣasīs.
"Quickly, you hideous Rākṣasīs of terrible appearance, who feed on flesh and blood, must humble her pride!
At his very word, those hideous ones of terrible appearance—
Having joined their palms in reverence, they stood surrounding Maithilī.
Then Rāvaṇa, of terrible appearance, spoke to them,
shaking the earth as it were with the forceful stamping of his feet.
"Let Maithilī be led into the middle of the Aśoka grove;
there she must be guarded by you in secret, surrounded on all sides.
There, Maithilī is to be treated with both terrible threats and repeated conciliations."
"Bring her all under your control, like a wild female elephant! Thus commanded by Rāvaṇa, those rākṣasīs took Maithilī and went to the Aśoka grove.
It was filled with trees bearing all desired fruits and various flowers and fruits,
and it was frequented by birds that were intoxicated at all times;
yet Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka, her limbs overwhelmed with grief, [beheld it].
Having fallen under the power of the rākṣasīs like a doe among tigresses,
Maithilī found no peace there; being excessively threatened by those with misshapen eyes,
she remembered her beloved husband and her brother-in-law, and, overwhelmed by fear and grief, she lost her composure.
Having slain the Rākṣasa Mārīca, who was wandering in the form of a deer and could assume any shape at will, Rāma quickly turned back on his path as he hastened,
desiring to see the princess of Mithilā.
Then a jackal, emitting a cruel cry, howled behind him. Recognizing that terrible, hair-raising sound of the jackal, he became apprehensive and reflected upon it.
"Alas, I consider this inauspicious; it sounds like the howling of a jackal.
May it be well with Vaidehī, even if it means she is being devoured by the Rākṣasas. But Mārīca, having recognized and perceived my voice, [replied].
If Lakṣmaṇa should hear that cry uttered by the one in the form of a deer,
that son of Sumitrā, having heard the voice and left Maithilī there,
will quickly come here to my presence, sent by her.
Surely the destruction of Sītā was desired by the Rākṣasas acting in concert; for Mārīca,
having become a golden deer, drew me away from the hermitage,
and once he had led me far off, the Rākṣasa was struck down by my arrow.

"Alas Lakṣmaṇa! I am slain!"—these were the words he uttered. Even if all be well with those two who are now separated from me in the forest, I have indeed incurred the enmity of the Rākṣasas on account of Janasthāna.
"And many terrible omens are seen today.
Thinking thus, Rāma, having heard the cry of the jackal and [reflecting] upon his own abduction by the Rākṣasa in the form of a deer, [was filled with anxiety].

Rāghava, filled with apprehension, arrived at Janasthāna. As he approached, dejected in mind and distressed, the beasts and birds gathered around that high-souled one; they kept him to their left and let out terrible cries.
Having seen those most terrible omens, Rāghava then beheld Lakṣmaṇa approaching, his radiance departed.
Then, not far away, Lakṣmaṇa met with Rāma.
Despondent himself, he was despondent toward him; sorrowful himself, he was sorrowful for his brother who shared in his grief.
