Then the elder brother reproached Lakṣmaṇa, who had arrived there, for having abandoned Sītā in the lonely forest frequented by Rākṣasas.
And taking Lakṣmaṇa by his left hand, the joy of the Raghus spoke these harsh words, which were yet sweet in their ultimate consequence, like one who was afflicted:
"Alas, Lakṣmaṇa! You have done a despicable thing, in that you have abandoned her."
"O gentle one, you have come here wondering whether Sītā might be safe;
however, O hero, I have no doubt that the daughter of Janaka has either perished or been devoured by the forest-dwelling Rākṣasas."
"O Lakṣmaṇa, since these inauspicious omens appear so frequently to me, let us ensure that we recover Sītā in her entirety.
For this demon, appearing in the form of a deer, has lured me far away."
Having somehow been struck down with great effort, that Rākṣasa was on the very point of death.
"My mind is dejected and joyless here, and my left eye throbs;
without a doubt, O Lakṣmaṇa, Sītā is no more—either she has been abducted, or she is dead, or she lies upon the path."
Seeing Lakṣmaṇa distressed in the empty forest, the righteous son of Daśaratha questioned him, for he had arrived without Vaidehī,
she who had followed him when he set out for the Daṇḍaka forest.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, where is that Vaidehī, leaving whom you have come here?
Where is that slender-waisted Vaidehī, my companion in sorrow, as I wander through the Daṇḍaka forest, fallen from my kingdom and wretched?"
O hero, without whom I cannot bear to live for even a moment—
where is that Sītā, my companion in life, who resembles the daughter of a god? O Lakṣmaṇa, whether it be lordship over the immortals or even over the earth, [what is the use] without her?
Without that daughter of Janaka, who possesses the luster of refined gold, I would not desire to live.
O gentle one, does Vaidehī still live, she who is dearer to me than my own life? And will my exile not prove to have been in vain?
O son of Sumitrā, when I am dead on account of Sītā and you have departed, will that Kaikeyī finally have her desire fulfilled and be happy, while I,
the wretched woman whose son has died, am left with the kingdom and my purpose accomplished through my sons?
"Kausalyā will attend to you, gentle friend; I hope she does not [attend to] Kaikeyī.
If Vaidehī still lives, I shall go back to the hermitage;
if she, who was so virtuous in conduct, has passed away, I shall give up my life, Lakṣmaṇa."
"If Vaidehī does not speak to me again when I have reached the hermitage, O Lakṣmaṇa, I shall perish— Sītā being so full of smiles.
Tell me, Lakṣmaṇa, whether Vaidehī lives or not."
While you were negligent, that poor ascetic woman may have been devoured by the rākṣasas.
Delicate, young, and never before having seen suffering, Vaidehī is clearly grieving and distressed in mind due to her separation from me.
In every way, fear has been instilled in you as well by that crooked and evil-minded Rākṣasa as he cried out "Lakṣmaṇa! loudly;
and I suspect that voice, so similar to mine, was heard by Vaidehī.
Sent by her in her terror, you have come quickly to see me.
But in every way, a grievous wrong has been committed by abandoning Sītā in the forest;
you have given the cruel rākṣasas the opportunity for retaliation.
Afflicted by that harsh blow, those flesh-eating Rākṣasas will undoubtedly have killed Sītā with their terrible weapons; alas,
O destroyer of enemies, I am utterly submerged in calamity.
"But what shall I do now? I fear that such a thing must be endured.
While reflecting thus upon Sītā, the lady of noble form, Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, returned to Janasthāna with great haste.
Reproaching his younger brother, who appeared distressed by hunger, fatigue, and thirst,
sighing deeply with a parched mouth and despondent, the hero reached their dwelling and, finding it empty,
entered his own hermitage and wandered through various places of recreation.
Thinking, "This is that very place," he stood upon the dwelling ground with his hair standing on end and became deeply distressed.
Then, as Saumitri returned from the hermitage along the way, Rāma, the joy of the Raghus, afflicted by grief, questioned him once more.

He said to him: "Lakṣmaṇa, why have you come here having abandoned Maithilī, she who was left by me in the forest because of her trust in you? As soon as I saw that you had arrived, [I realized] you had left Maithilī behind."
My mind is truly distressed as I suspect some great calamity;
O Lakṣmaṇa, having seen you from afar on the path, separated from Sītā, my left eye, my arm, and my heart are throbbing.
Thus addressed, Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā who bears auspicious marks,
overcome once more by sorrow, spoke to the grieving Rāma:
"I did not come here of my own free will after abandoning her."
Urged on by her with harsh words, I have come here into your presence. That cry of Maithilī—"O Sītā! O Lakṣmaṇa! Save me!"—which was uttered as if by my noble brother, has reached my ears.

Maithilī was thus addressed with these words, which were full of confidence in you:
"I do not see any Rākṣasa who could bring him fear; be at ease, for this has been spoken by no one else."
"How could a noble one like you utter such a reproachable and base word as 'Save me,' O Sītā, when he is capable of saving even the thirty gods?
For what reason, and by whom, was my brother made to adopt this tone?"
"Lakṣmaṇa, save me!"—this cry was uttered in a discordant voice.
You should not feel distress, which is the lot of wretched women; enough of resorting to such dejection, be composed and free from anxiety.
"And there is no man in the three worlds, whether already born or yet to be born, who could defeat Raghava in battle.
Thus addressed, Vaidehi’s mind was utterly bewildered.
Shedding tears, she spoke these harsh words to me:
"An exceedingly wicked intent has been placed by you within me;
even if your brother is destroyed, you shall not obtain me."
It is only by a secret agreement that you follow Rāma,
for you do not come to his aid even as he cries out most piteously;
you follow him for my sake, acting like a hidden enemy.
"Seeking an opportunity against Rāghava, you do not approach him in such a manner.
Thus addressed by Vaidehī, he became agitated, his eyes turning red;
with his lips quivering in rage, he departed from the hermitage.
To Saumitri, who was speaking thus, Rāma— overwhelmed by grief—
said: "O gentle one, it was a misdeed that you have come without her,
even though you know me to be capable of warding off the rākṣasas."
"By these words of anger from Maithilī, you have been dismissed.
Indeed, I am not at all pleased that you have departed after abandoning Maithilī,
having returned here only after hearing harsh words from an angry woman."
In every respect, you have been deprived of Sītā because, having fallen under the sway of anger when urged by her, you did not carry out my command.
For that Rākṣasa now lies slain by my arrow.
"By him, in the form of a deer, I was lured away from the hermitage.
Having drawn his bow and fixed an arrow, he struck me with that playful shaft;
then, casting off his deer body, that Rākṣasa wearing armlets appeared with a distressed voice."
Stricken by arrows and speaking with a pained voice that reached even to my distant ears,
she uttered those most cruel words because of which you have come here, abandoning Maithilī:
"As he was returning in great haste, his left eye began to throb."
Rāma trembled, faltered, and a shudder arose within him.
Perceiving those inauspicious omens again and again,
he nevertheless declared, "Is Sītā well?"
Then, longing for the sight of Sītā, he went in haste;
seeing the dwelling empty, his mind became distressed. The joy of the Raghus wandered about as if with great speed, casting his gaze all around.
Having looked all around at the locations of the various huts here and there,
he then beheld the leaf-hut devoid of Sītā,
stripped of its splendor like a lotus pond withered in the winter.
With its trees appearing as if weeping, its flowers withered and its birds and deer despondent, the forest was bereft of splendor, devastated, and abandoned by its presiding deities;
its deerskins and kusha grass were scattered about, and its cushions and mats were strewn in disorder.
Seeing the site of the empty hut, he lamented again and again:
"She must have been carried off, or dead, or lost; perhaps she has been devoured, or the timid one is hiding, or has fled into the forest."
She had gone either to gather flowers or fruits,
or perhaps she had gone to a lotus pond or to a river for water; yet,
though he searched diligently, he did not find his beloved in the forest.
With eyes reddened by grief, he appeared as if mad with sorrow;
running from tree to tree, from mountain to mountain, and from river to river,
Rāma lamented, submerged in an ocean of the mud of grief.
"O Kadamba tree, have you seen that beloved who is so fond of the kadamba? If you know her, tell me of Sītā,
whose face is beautiful, who resembles tender sprouts, and who is clothed in yellow silk."
"O Bilva tree, tell me if you have seen her whose breasts are like bilva fruits;
or else, O Arjuna tree, tell me if that beloved, the daughter of Janaka who is so dear to Arjuna— that timid girl— still lives or not."
"This *kakubha* tree knows clearly that Maithilī, whose thighs are like the trunk of a *kakubha*, for this lord of the forest shines forth, rich with creepers, shoots, and flowers,
and is celebrated by the humming of bees."
"Clearly this *tilaka* tree knows the one who loves the *tilaka*,
for I am afflicted by grief; O Aśoka, dispeller of sorrow, quickly make me one whose name is 'Aśoka' (sorrowless) by the sight of my beloved."
O Tāla tree, if you have seen her whose breasts are like ripe tāla fruits—
tell me of that woman of beautiful limbs, if you have any compassion for me.
O Jambu tree, if Sītā, who possesses the luster of refined gold, has been seen by you...
If you know my beloved, tell me without hesitation.
Or else, O deer, if you know Maithilī— that fawn-eyed,
lovely woman with the glance of a deer— she might be together with the other does.
O elephant, if she whose thighs are like an elephant's trunk has been seen by you, I believe she must be known to you; tell me, O noble elephant!
O tiger, if that beloved with a face like the moon has been seen by you—
"O Maithilī, speak to me with confidence; you have no cause for fear.
Why do you run away, my dear? Surely you have been seen, O lotus-eyed one; why do you not answer me after hiding yourself behind a tree?"
"Stop, stop, O lady of excellent hips! You have no compassion for me;
you are not naturally prone to excessive laughter, so why do you disregard me?
O woman of beautiful complexion, you are revealed by your yellow silk garment."
"I saw her even as she was running; stay, if you have any affection for me!
Surely she, the sweetly smiling one, has not been harmed, for she would never have neglected me had I fallen into such distress."
"Clearly that young girl, separated from me, has been devoured by flesh-eating rākṣasas after they divided all her limbs;
surely that face with its beautiful teeth and lips has lost its luster."
For that auspicious neck of my beloved, possessing the luster of a campaka flower and adorned with a necklace,
has surely been devoured as she lamented;
and those two arms of hers, tender as young shoots, must have been cast about.
Deprived of me, the young woman, with her trembling hands and her armlets and ornaments, was indeed devoured by the Rākṣasa for his meal;
she who had many kinsmen was left behind like one abandoned by a caravan.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, O mighty-armed one, do you see my beloved anywhere?
"O dear one, where have you gone, O blessed lady? O Sītā! Thus lamenting again and again, Rāma ran from forest to forest.
In some places he wanders with speed, in others he staggers by force; intent on searching for his beloved, he appears in some places like one intoxicated.
He traverses forests, rivers, mountains, and mountain cascades.
He wandered through the forests with speed, remaining unsteady in his course.
Having thus traveled through that vast and great forest and searched everywhere for Maithilī, he—
his hope still unfulfilled— again exerted the utmost effort in the search for his beloved.
Seeing the hermitage empty, Rāma, the son of Daśaratha,
saw that the leaf-hut was deserted and the seats were overturned;
not seeing Vaidehī there, he looked about in every direction.
Raising his beautiful arms and crying out, Rāma said:
"O Lakṣmaṇa, where is Vaidehī? To what region has she gone from here?
By whom has she been carried away, O son of Sumitrā, or by whom has my beloved been devoured?"
"O Sītā, if you wish to mock me by hiding behind a tree, enough of your jesting today; come to me, for I am deeply distressed.
O Sītā, those trusting young deer with whom you used to play—"
"O gentle one, these wretched men are meditating with eyes clouded by tears;
surely my father, the great king, will see me dead in the next world from the great grief born of Sītā’s abduction."

"How is it that, having promised me a pledge, you were pressed by me and yet have come here to my presence without fulfilling that time? You are one who acts according to desire, ignoble, and indeed a speaker of falsehood."
"In the world beyond, my father will clearly say to you, 'Fie on you!'—
for having abandoned me here, helpless, tormented by grief, wretched, and with my hopes shattered, you have acted like a man who has forsaken his own crooked reputation."
"Where are you going, O lady of beautiful hips, having abandoned me, O slender-waisted one?
Bereft of you, I shall give up my own life.
Thus did Rāma lament, longing for the sight of Sītā.
Afflicted by extreme sorrow, Raghava did not see the daughter of Janaka;
failing to find Sita, the son of Dasharatha was like an elephant sinking in a vast expanse of mud.
Out of a desire for his welfare, Lakṣmaṇa spoke at length to Rāma:
"Do not despair, O mighty-armed one; exert yourself together with me.
For this forest, O hero, is adorned with many caves."
Wandering through the groves of Priya trees and intoxicated by the forest, that Maithilī may have entered the woods, or perhaps a lotus pond in full bloom,
or even reached a river frequented by fish and *vañjula* reeds.
Or perhaps she may be hiding somewhere in the forest, wishing to terrify us,
O bull among men, desiring to test you and me; therefore, O illustrious one,
let us both exert ourselves immediately in searching for her.

"Let us search the entire forest where that daughter of Janaka may be, O descendant of Kakutstha; if you so think, do not set your mind on grief. Thus addressed by Lakshmana out of affection, he became composed.
Together with the son of Sumitrā, Rāma began to search;
those two sons of Daśaratha searched through the forests, the mountains, the rivers, and the lakes, searching everywhere for Sītā.
Searching the ridges, caves, and peaks of that mountain in their entirety, they did not find her at all.

"Lakṣmaṇa, son of Sumitrā, I do not see Vaidehī here on this auspicious mountain. Then, tormented by grief while wandering through the Daṇḍaka forest, Lakṣmaṇa spoke these words to his brother of radiant splendor.
"O one of great wisdom, you shall recover Maithilī, the daughter of Janaka,
just as the mighty-armed Viṣṇu recovered this earth after binding Bali.
Thus addressed by the heroic Lakṣmaṇa, that descendant of Raghu—
With his mind struck by grief, he spoke in a piteous voice:
"O highly wise one, the entire forest has been thoroughly searched, as have the lotus ponds with their blooming lotuses; and here is this mountain, abounding in caves and waterfalls."
"For I do not see Vaidehī, who is dearer to me than my own life.
Thus lamenting, Rāma— emaciated by the abduction of Sītā,
miserable, and overwhelmed by grief— became distraught for a moment.
With all his limbs trembling, his intellect gone, and deprived of consciousness,
he was overcome with despondency and dejection;
sighing long and hot breaths many times, the lotus-eyed Rāma remained thus.

"Alas, my beloved! he cried out many times, his voice choked with tears. Then Lakṣmaṇa, the knower of dharma, who was dear to his kinsman, consoled him in many ways, being humble and joining his palms in reverence.
But disregarding those words falling from the lips of Lakṣmaṇa,
and not seeing his beloved Sītā, he cried out again and again.
Distraught, he spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa in a piteous voice:
"Lakṣmaṇa, go quickly to the Godāvarī river and find out whether Sītā has gone there to fetch lotuses. Thus addressed by Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa once again—
He of swift prowess went to the beautiful river Godāvarī.
Having searched that river, which was filled with bathing places, Lakṣmaṇa said to Rāma: "I do not see her at the fords; though I call out, she does not hear me."
"To what region has Vaidehī, the destroyer of suffering, gone?
For I do not know, O Rāma, where that slender-waisted woman is.
Having heard Lakṣmaṇa’s words, he was dejected, overwhelmed by grief and delusion.
Rāma himself approached the river Godāvarī.
Having reached it, Rāma asked, "Where is Sītā?
even though all beings knew she had been carried off by the lord of the Rākṣasas, who deserved to be slain.
The river Godāvarī did not report her to Rāma in that manner;
then, urged by the spirits to report his beloved to him,
she, though questioned by the grieving Rāma, did not speak of Sītā.
Reflecting upon that form and the deeds of the evil-minded Rāvaṇa, the river, out of fear, did not reveal Vaidehī to him; thus,
she was rendered hopeless by the river regarding the sight of Sītā.
Rama, emaciated by the failure to find Sita, spoke to the son of Sumitra:
"O Lakshmana, what unpleasant words shall I say when I meet Janaka and the mother of Vaidehi, being without her?"
Where indeed has that Vaidehī gone— she who dispelled all my grief when I was deprived of my kingdom, living on forest fare in the woods,
and now seeing no princess and being destitute of the support of my kinsmen?
I think that the nights will be long for me as I remain awake,
if indeed Sītā is not found. I shall wander throughout the Godāvarī, Janasthāna, and this Prasravaṇa mountain, searching everywhere.
As the two brothers were conversing with one another in this manner,
they both beheld a trail of flowers fallen upon the earth.
Seeing that shower of flowers fallen upon the ground, Rāma—
The hero, himself distressed, spoke these sorrowful words to the distressed Lakṣmaṇa:
"I recognize these very flowers here, Lakṣmaṇa;
they were gathered by me in the forest and given to Vaidehī."
Having spoken thus to Lakṣmaṇa, that bull among men, the mighty-armed one,
being enraged, addressed the mountain like a lion to a small deer:
"O Mountain, show me Sītā, who is golden-hued and radiant as gold."
Until I have destroyed all your peaks,
you shall be consumed by the fire of my arrows and reduced to ashes;
forever unfit for habitation, stripped of grass, trees, and sprouts.
"Or else, O Lakṣmaṇa, I shall dry up this river today if she does not tell me of Sītā, whose face resembles the moon.
Thus spoke the enraged Rāma, as if wishing to consume everything with his very eyes.
He saw upon the ground the large footprint of the Rākṣasa that had emerged;
having observed the tracks of Sītā and the Rākṣasa,
Rāma, his heart agitated, spoke to his beloved brother.
"Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, the shattered golden drops from Vaidehī’s ornaments,
O Saumitri, as well as her various garlands,
now covered with colorful drops of blood resembling molten gold."
"Behold, O Saumitri, how the surface of the earth is covered on all sides!
I think, Lakṣmaṇa, that Vaidehī must have been torn apart, divided, or devoured by the Rākṣasas who can assume any form at will."
O son of Sumitrā, it was on account of Vaidehī that a terrible battle took place here between those two Rākṣasas as they disputed over her.
And this [necklace], studded with pearls and gems and adorned with refined gold—
O gentle one, whose great bow has fallen broken upon the earth?
Whose golden armor, resembling the rising sun and inlaid with beads of lapis lazuli,
lies shattered and fallen on the ground?
"O gentle one, whose is this celestial umbrella with its hundred ribs, adorned with divine garlands, now fallen to the ground with its staff broken?
And what of these donkeys with faces like Piśācas, wearing golden breastplates?"
Whose were those of terrifying form and massive body slain in battle? Whose was that resplendent battle-standard, resembling a blazing fire, now cast away and broken; and whose was that war-chariot?
Whose are these arrows, resembling chariot axles and adorned with gold, scattered here by one of terrible deeds?
Behold this enmity of mine, increased a hundredfold, which shall bring an end to his life.
O gentle one, by those Rākṣasas of most cruel hearts who can assume any form at will,
the ascetic Sītā has surely been abducted, killed, or devoured;
for dharma does not protect Sītā as she is being carried away in the great forest.
For even if Vaidehī has been devoured or carried away, O Lakṣmaṇa,
who in this world, O gentle one, would be able to do what is pleasing to me, even if they were the lords of the worlds,
heroic, compassionate, and the creator of all?
Out of ignorance, O Lakṣmaṇa, all beings might despise me;
the lords of the thirty gods surely think that I am devoid of prowess, though I am gentle, devoted to the welfare of the world, self-controlled, and compassionate.
"Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, how even a virtue has become a fault upon reaching me!
This very day, for the destruction of all the Rākṣasas,
I have risen like a great sun that has withdrawn the moonlight."
Neither Yakṣas, nor Gandharvas, nor Piśācas, nor Rākṣasas, nor Kiṃnaras, nor humans shall find peace, O Lakṣmaṇa;
behold, O Lakṣmaṇa, the sky is filled with my missiles and arrows.
"Today I shall indeed make the three worlds devoid of movement for those who roam therein;
with the hosts of planets obstructed,
the moon veiled, and the brilliance of fire, wind, and the sun completely extinguished."
With the mountain peaks pulverized, the reservoirs of water drying up,
the trees, creepers, and shrubs destroyed, and the ocean itself devastated—
the lords will not restore that Sītā to me in safety.
At this very moment, O son of Sumitrā, all beings shall behold my prowess; nor shall they leap into the sky, O Lakṣmaṇa,
because it will be rendered without interval by the nets of arrows released from the string of my bow.
"O Lakṣmaṇa, behold today this world, afflicted by my iron arrows, its deer and birds destroyed and bewildered, thrown into turmoil and stripped of all order;
[behold] the world of living beings with my irresistible arrows drawn back to the ear."
For the sake of Maithilī, I shall rid the world of Piśācas and Rākṣasas.
Today the gods shall behold the power of my arrows, released in fury and traveling far, as they are propelled by my wrath.
Neither gods, nor Daityas, nor Piśācas,
nor Rākṣasas shall remain when the three worlds have been destroyed by my wrath;
even those worlds belonging to the gods, Dānavas, Yakṣas, and Rākṣasas shall cease to exist.
They shall fall in many ways, cut to pieces by floods of arrows;
today, with my shafts, I shall make these worlds lawless,
just as old age, death, time, and destiny do.
O Lakṣmaṇa, just as my [commands] are never thwarted among all beings,
so too am I undoubtedly not to be restrained when joined with anger today,
if they do not point out the blameless Sītā of Mithilā, who possesses beautiful teeth, to me as before.
"I shall overturn the world— including its gods, gandharvas, humans, and serpents, as well as its mountains.
Thus tormented by the abduction of Sītā, Rāma was emaciated and intent on the destruction of the worlds, like the fire of universal dissolution (saṃvartaka).

Seeing Rāma looking at his strung bow, sighing again and again, and desiring to kill him like the enraged Rudra wishing to slay the sacrificial beast at Dakṣa’s sacrifice— seeing Rāma thus provoked, whom he had never seen before in such a state, Lakṣmaṇa...
With palms joined in reverence and a parched mouth, he spoke these words:
"Having formerly been gentle, self-controlled, and devoted to the welfare of all beings,
you ought not to abandon your true nature by falling under the sway of anger."
Fortune resides in the moon, radiance in the sun, motion in the wind, and forbearance in the earth;
all these qualities are eternally present in you, as is unsurpassed glory.
Yet, I do not know whose shattered war-chariot this is.

For what reason, or for whose sake, is he equipped with weapons and his retinue? O prince, why is this region— where a most terrible battle has taken place— marked by hoofprints and wheel-ruts, and drenched with drops of blood?
"But this destruction, O best of speakers, belongs to one alone, not to two;
for I do not see the footprint of a great army here.
You ought not to destroy the worlds for the sake of a single person."
For kings who rule with just punishment, being mild and tranquil, are indeed lords of the earth.
O Raghava, you have always been the refuge and the supreme goal for all beings; who indeed would consider the loss of your wife to be right?
O King, the rivers, the oceans, the mountains, the gods, the gandharvas,
and the dānavas are not capable of doing you harm, just as virtuous men cannot offend one who is consecrated for a sacrifice;
therefore, you ought to search for him by whom Sītā was abducted.
With me as my companion, bow in hand, and accompanied by these supreme sages,
we shall search the ocean, the mountains, the forests,
various formidable caves, and the mountain lotus-lakes.
With concentrated minds, we shall search through the worlds of the gods and the gandharvas until we find the one who has carried away your wife;
for if the lords of the thirty gods do not restore your wife to you through peaceful means, [we shall act otherwise].
"O Lord of Kosala, you shall perform what is appropriate for the occasion thereafter. O Indra among men, if you do not win Sītā through virtue, conciliation, humility, and diplomacy,
then destroy her with floods of gold-tufted arrows resembling the thunderbolt of great Indra."

Then, after a moment, Lakṣmaṇa, the son of Sumitrā, comforted him as he was thus tormented by grief, lamenting like one who is helpless, overwhelmed by great delusion, utterly dejected, and unconscious.
Pressing his feet, he addressed Rāma:
"O Rāma, by means of great austerity and great deeds,
King Daśaratha obtained you, just as the immortals obtained the nectar of immortality."
Bound by your very virtues, the lord of the earth has attained divinity through separation from you, just as was heard regarding Bharata,
O descendant of Kakutstha; if you cannot endure this sorrow that has been met.
Who else, being ordinary and of little strength, could endure this? For if you, in your distress, were to consume the worlds with your splendor,
O tiger among men, where indeed would the afflicted subjects find relief?

This is indeed the very nature of the world: Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, attained the same world as Śakra, yet misfortune touched him as well. And so too was the great seer Vasiṣṭha, who was our father’s domestic priest.
In a single day, a hundred sons were born to him, and likewise they were slain again.
O you who are true to your word, even this very earth— the mother of the world and the goddess honored by all beings— is seen to tremble.
And these two, the sun and the moon— the eyes of the worlds, upon whom everything is established— those two of great power have undergone an eclipse,
O bull among men; even the greatest beings and the gods [are affected].
"O tiger among men, all embodied beings cannot escape destiny; even among the gods, beginning with Śakra, both right conduct and misconduct are heard of. You ought not to be distressed."
O sinless hero, even though Vaidehī has been lost or even abducted, you ought not to grieve like any other common man;
for those like you, who constantly perceive the truth, do not grieve.
"Even in the midst of great hardships, Rāma’s countenance remains free from despondency.
O best of men, reflect upon this with your intellect according to the truth;
for those endowed with wisdom and great insight discern between the auspicious and the inauspicious through their intelligence."
For actions whose merits and defects are unseen and which remain unperformed,
their desired fruit does not come to pass without the performance of those acts. Indeed,
O hero, you yourself have previously instructed me many times in this very way.
For who indeed could instruct you, even Bṛhaspati himself in person? O man of great wisdom, your intellect is difficult even for the gods to follow;
I shall awaken your knowledge, which has been lulled to sleep by grief.
O bull among the Ikṣvākus, having observed your own divine, human, and personal prowess, strive for the destruction of your enemies.
O bull among men, what is the use to you of destroying everyone else?
"But you ought to recognize that very same evil enemy and uproot him. As soon as these well-spoken words were uttered by Lakṣmaṇa,
Rāghava, who grasps the essence, accepted that most profound truth.
Restraining his own surging anger and steadying himself, the mighty-armed Rāma took up his wonderful bow and said to Lakṣmaṇa:
"What shall we do, dear child? Or where shall we go, Lakṣmaṇa?"
"Reflect on what means I might use to see Sītā.
To Rāma, who was thus afflicted by intense anguish, Lakṣmaṇa said:
"It is fitting that you search right here in Janasthāna."
It is strewn with many rākṣasas and filled with various trees and creepers; here there are mountain fastnesses, waterfalls, and caves,
as well as various formidable caverns teeming with diverse herds of wild animals.
The abodes of the kinnaras and the palaces of the gandharvas—
these you ought to search together with me, being diligent; for high-souled ones like you, O bull among men, are endowed with wisdom.
"They do not tremble in calamities, like mountains before the force of the wind.
Having been told this, Rāma, together with Lakṣmaṇa, wandered through that entire forest;
enraged, Rāma fixed a terrible, razor-sharp arrow upon his bow.
Then he beheld the illustrious Jaṭāyus, the best of the twice-born, fallen upon the ground like a mountain peak, drenched in blood;
seeing him who resembled a mountain summit, Rāma spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.
"By him Vaidehī Sītā has been devoured; of this there is no doubt.
This is clearly a Rākṣasa wandering the forest in the form of a vulture;
having eaten the large-eyed Sītā, he sits at his ease."
"I shall slay him with these terrible, straight-flying arrows with flaming tips," Rāma said, and having fixed a razor-sharp arrow to his bow, he rushed toward the vulture,
as if making the earth bounded by the oceans tremble with his rage.
Vomiting blood mixed with foam, the bird addressed Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, in a most piteous voice:
"O long-lived one, that medicinal herb which you seek in the great forest— "
That queen was my very life, and both have been taken away by Rāvaṇa.
O Rāghava, separated from you and Lakṣmaṇa, I saw the queen being carried off by the powerful Rāvaṇa.
I have come to the rescue of Sītā, and Rāvaṇa, his chariot and parasol shattered by me in battle, has been cast down upon the surface of the earth.
This is his broken bow; this is his quiver.
O Rāma, this is that battle-chariot of his which was shattered in combat;
while I was exhausted, Rāvaṇa cut off my wings with his sword and,
seizing Sītā, the princess of Videha, soared into the sky.
"You ought not to kill me, who was previously struck down by a *rākṣasa*.
Having learned from him this beloved story concerning Sītā, Rāma embraced the king of the vultures and wept along with Lakṣmaṇa.
Seeing him somehow sighing alone on that difficult, narrow path, the sorrowful Rāma spoke these words to the son of Sumitrā:
"We have been fallen from our kingdom, we dwell in the forest, Sītā is lost, and the brahmin has been killed."
Such is this misfortune of mine that it could even consume fire itself.
Even if I were to cross the great ocean today while it is at its full tide,
that lord of rivers would surely dry up through my ill fortune.
"There is no one more unfortunate in this world of moving and unmoving beings than I, by whom this great snare of calamity has been encountered.
This king of vultures, advanced in years, is my father’s friend."
"Lying slain upon the ground through the reversal of my fortune," having spoken thus many times, Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa,
touched Jaṭāyu, demonstrating his paternal affection.
Embracing that king of vultures, whose wings were severed and who was drenched in blood, Rāma uttered the words, "Where is Maithilī, my life-breath? and collapsed upon the ground.
Then Rāma beheld that vulture fallen on the earth, struck down by a terrible force.
He spoke these words to Saumitri, who was endowed with many friends: "Surely this bird, while striving for my sake,
has been slain by a Rākṣasa in battle and is now giving up its life, which is so difficult to relinquish."
"O Lakṣmaṇa, this vital breath still exists within his body; yet, deprived of his voice, he gazes upon us in distress.
O Jaṭāyu, if you are able to speak again..."
Tell me of Sītā—blessings be upon you—and tell me of your own death.
For what reason did Rāvaṇa carry off Sītā? What offense have I committed against him, that my beloved was seen and abducted by Rāvaṇa?
O best of the twice-born, how was that heart-stealing face, which resembled the moon, at that time? And what were the words spoken by Sītā then?
What was the prowess, what was the form, and what were the deeds of that Rākṣasa?
"And where is his dwelling, my dear? Tell me as I ask you.
Then, looking up at Rāma who was thus lamenting, Jaṭāyu, his soul distressed, spoke these words to him with a very feeble voice.
She was carried off through the sky by Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas,
who employed a vast illusion filled with wind and storm clouds;
O father, that night-stalker cut off my wings while I was exhausted.
Taking Vaidehī Sītā, he set out facing the south.
"My life-breaths are failing, O Rāghava, and my vision is spinning;
I see trees with golden trunks and hair made of uśīra grass."
In the very moment that Rāvaṇa departed taking Sītā,
the owner of lost wealth quickly recovers it;
O Kākutstha, that moment was named Vinda, and he did not perceive it.
Like a fish seizing a hook, he will surely perish instantly. You need not feel any anxiety regarding Janaka’s daughter;
having slain that Rākṣasa in battle, you shall soon take your pleasure with Vaidehī.
As the vulture, who was not deluded, spoke back to Rāma,
blood flowed from his mouth as he was dying over the meat.
He was the son of Viśravas and the actual brother of Vaiśravaṇa.
Having spoken thus, the lord of birds gave up his life, which is so difficult to obtain.
As Rāma, with palms joined in reverence, cried out, "Speak!
Speak!", the vital breaths of the vulture abandoned the body and ascended into the sky.
Then, having laid his head upon the ground, stretched out his feet,
and cast his body aside, he fell to the surface of the earth.
Beholding that vulture, with copper-colored eyes, lifeless and resembling a mountain, [he was moved].
Distressed by many sorrows, Rāma spoke to the son of Sumitrā:
"While dwelling happily for many years in the abode of the Rākṣasas,
this bird has roamed here throughout the Daṇḍaka forest."
"He who has lived for many years and has endured for a long time now lies slain today; indeed, Time is difficult to overcome.
Behold, Lakṣmaṇa, this vulture, my benefactor, has been killed."
Indeed, he did not abandon Sītā even when assailed by the more powerful Rāvaṇa;
for my sake, this lord of birds relinquished his great ancestral kingdom of the vultures and gave up his life.
"O Saumitri, virtuous practitioners of dharma who are brave and worthy of refuge are indeed seen everywhere, even among those born as animals.
My grief, O gentle one, does not weigh upon me so heavily because of the abduction of Sita."
O scorcher of enemies, just as the destruction of the vulture occurred for my sake,
so too is this lord of birds worthy of worship and honor by me, just as the illustrious and highly renowned King Daśaratha was.
"O Saumitri, bring wood; I shall kindle a fire.
I wish to cremate the king of vultures who has met his death on my account. I shall place the lord of the world of birds upon the funeral pyre."
"O Saumitri, I shall cremate this man who has been slain by a fierce Rakshasa—
him who has attained the destination of those devoted to sacrifice, the destination of those who maintain the sacred fires,
the destination of those who never retreat in battle, and the destination of those who bestow land."
"Permitted by me, go to the unsurpassed worlds, O great-souled king of vultures; having been consecrated by me, depart.
Having spoken thus, he placed the lord of birds upon the blazing funeral pyre.
The righteous Rāma burned with grief, as if for his own kinsman.
Then the valiant Rāma, accompanied by the son of Sumitrā, having gone into the forest and killed large deer, spread them out over that twice-born man.
Having extracted the flesh of a rohita fish and formed it into a patty, the highly illustrious Rāma gave it to the bird on a lovely green meadow—
just that which the twice-born describe as belonging to a deceased mortal.
Rāma then quickly chanted that prayer for his ascent to heaven.
Then, having gone to the river Godāvarī, both sons of the best of men offered water oblations to that king of vultures.
Having performed that glorious and most difficult deed, the king of vultures was struck down in battle;
then, having been consecrated by one who was like a great seer, he attained his own auspicious and meritorious destination.
Having thus offered the water libations for him, the two Raghavas then set forth.

Searching for Sītā in the forest, the two descendants of Ikṣvāku proceeded toward the western direction. Having gone toward that southern quarter, bearing their arrows, bows, and swords, the two princes reached a path that had not been previously traversed.
Enveloped by many shrubs, trees, and creepers,
it was surrounded on all sides, impenetrable, dense, and terrible to behold;
yet, having moved swiftly past it, he took his course toward the southern direction.

Those two of great strength passed through that most formidable great forest. Then, having traveled three krośas beyond Janasthāna, those two Raghavas of immense luster entered the dense Krauñca forest.
Resembling various thick clouds, appearing as if joyful on all sides,
and filled with flocks of beasts and birds along with auspicious flowers of many colors,
those two searched that forest, desiring to see Vaidehī.
As they remained here and there, emaciated by the abduction of Sītā,
the highly energetic Lakṣmaṇa— endowed with courage, virtuous, and pure—
spoke these words with joined palms to his brother of blazing splendor.
"My arm trembles violently and my mind is as if agitated;
moreover, I perceive for the most part many inauspicious omens.
Therefore, O noble one, prepare yourself and carry out this beneficial advice."
Indeed, these omens portend immediate agitation for me alone.
This most dreadful bird named Vañculaka is crying out as if announcing our victory in battle.
As they were thus searching through that entire forest with such vigor,
a great sound arose as if shattering the woods,
like a dense thicket being violently enveloped by a mighty wind.

The sound of that forest arose as if filling the very heavens. Seeking the source of that sound, Rāma, together with his younger brother, beheld in the thicket a Rākṣasa of immense body and broad chest.
Then they both approached that which stood before them:
a massive, headless, and neckless trunk with a mouth in its belly,
towering like a great mountain, covered with sharp, bristling hairs.
Resembling a dark blue cloud, fierce, and sounding like the thundering of clouds,
he possessed a single, terrible eye on his chest— tawny, large, wide, and long, with rapid vision.
He was endowed with great tusks and was licking his massive mouth,
devouring most terrible bears, lions, deer, and elephants;
he was distorting both his formidable arms, each a yojana in length.
Seizing various bears, flocks of birds, and deer with his two hands—
dragging them in and pulling them away—
he stood blocking the path of the two brothers who had approached him.
Then, having passed beyond that, at the distance of a krośa, they beheld a massive, dreadful, and terrifying headless trunk (kabandha), enveloped by its own arms.
That long-armed being stretched out its two vast arms to an extreme length.
He seized both Raghava brothers together, overpowering them by force—
those two brothers of mighty arms, armed with swords and firm bows, possessed of fierce energy and great strength, who had fallen helpless as they were being dragged away.
The mighty-armed Kabandha, the best of the Dānavas, said to them:
"Who are you two, with shoulders like bulls, bearing great swords and bows,
who have reached this terrible region and presented yourselves as my prey?"

"Tell me, what is your business here, and for what purpose have you two come to this region? You stand here like two bulls with sharp horns, equipped with arrows, bows, and swords, while I remain oppressed by hunger."
"Once I have reached his mouth, life will be difficult for me to regain again.
Having heard those words of the evil-minded Kabandha,
Rāma, with a parched face, spoke to Lakṣmaṇa.

"O Lakṣmaṇa, having encountered hardship after hardship and reached this terrible calamity that threatens the end of life, yet failing to find my beloved, one perceives the immense power of Time over all beings, O you whose valor is truth."
"O tiger among men, O Lakṣmaṇa, behold both you and me deluded by calamities; there is no burden too heavy for destiny among all living beings.
Even those who are heroic, powerful, and skilled in weapons on the field of battle—"
"Overcome by time, they perish like bridges of sand.
Speaking thus, the son of Daśaratha— possessing firm truth and valor, great fame, and majesty—
beholding the son of Sumitrā of exalted prowess, then reaffirmed his own steady resolve within himself.
Seeing the two brothers, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, standing there with their arms encircled as nooses, Kabandha spoke these words:
"O bulls among Kṣatriyas, why do you stand still upon seeing me, who am tormented by hunger?"
"Commanded by fate for the sake of food, we have lost our senses.
Hearing those words, which were timely and beneficial, Lakṣmaṇa— though overcome with distress— spoke, having resolved upon a course of action.
"Before that lowest of Rākṣasas can quickly seize both you and me,
let us therefore swiftly sever his two heavy arms with our swords.
Then those two Rāghavas, who knew the proper place and time, [struck] him with their very swords.
Greatly delighted, they both seized his arms at the shoulders. Then Rāma, with his sword, swiftly severed the right arm, while the hero Lakṣmaṇa effortlessly cut off the left.
With his arms severed, that mighty-armed one fell with a great roar,
making the sky, the earth, and all the directions resound like a rain-cloud.
Seeing his two arms cut off, he was drenched in a flood of blood.
Distressed, the Dānava asked those two heroes, "Who are you?
While he was speaking thus, the mighty Lakṣmaṇa, endowed with auspicious marks, described the descendant of Kakutstha to Kabandha.
"This is the heir of Ikṣvāku, known to people by the name Rāma;
know me to be his younger brother, Lakṣmaṇa.
While he, who possesses the splendor of a god, dwells in this lonely forest..."
"Our wife was carried off by a *rākṣasa*, and it was for her sake that we came here seeking her.
But who are you, and for what purpose do you writhe in the forest like a headless trunk (*kabandha*), with your legs broken and your mouth blazing upon your chest?"
Thus addressed by Lakṣmaṇa, Kabandha, remembering those words of Indra, spoke these words in reply with great joy:
"Welcome to you both, O tigers among men; by good fortune do I behold you."

"By good fortune, O tigers among men, these two arm-bonds have been severed by you both. Now listen as I relate to you in truth, O tiger among men, how this deformed appearance was acquired by me through my own lack of discipline."
"O mighty-armed Rāma, in former times my form was inconceivable and renowned throughout the three worlds, possessing great strength and prowess,
like the bodies of Soma, Śakra, and the Sun."
Having assumed this great form that strikes terror into the world, O Rāma, I then and there terrified the sages dwelling in the forest.
Thereupon, the great seer named Sthūlaśiras was provoked to anger by me.
While gathering various forest fruits, I was overpowered by him in this form. Upon seeing me, he spoke thus, pronouncing a terrible curse:
"Let this very form of yours remain as it is—cruel and contemptible."
When I asked him, "How might there be an end to this curse? he, being provoked to anger, spoke these words regarding the curse he had cast:
"When Rāma, having severed your two arms, burns you in the lonely forest."
Then you shall regain your own vast and auspicious form. Know, O Lakṣmaṇa, that this son of Danu, resplendent with beauty,
has thus assumed this form on the field of battle due to the wrath of Indra.
"For I gratified the Grandfather with fierce asceticism, and he granted me long life; thereafter, delusion took hold of me:
'I have obtained long life; what can Śakra do to me?'"
Having thus resolved my mind, I assailed Śakra in battle;
by the hundred-jointed thunderbolt released from his arm,
both his thighs and his head were driven back into his body.
Though entreated by me, he sent my father to the abode of Yama,
saying to me, "Let the word of the Grandfather be true. How could he, with his thighs, head, and face shattered, have been capable [of acting otherwise], even while fasting?
"Struck by the thunderbolt, one cannot live even for a very long time.
Thus addressed by me, Śakra gave me two arms a yojana in length and fashioned a mouth with sharp fangs upon my belly.
Thus, drawing in the forest-dwellers—lions, elephants, deer, and tigers—with my two long arms, I devour them on all sides.
But Indra said to me: "When Rāma arrives with Lakṣmaṇa..."
"When your arms are severed in battle, then you shall go to heaven.
You are that very Rāma; may prosperity be yours, O Rāghava. I cannot be slain by anyone else"—this was spoken by the great seer according to the truth.
"For I shall provide counsel with my intellect, O bull among men,
and I shall point out a friend to you both once you have been consecrated by the fire.
Thus addressed by that Danu, the righteous Raghava—
He spoke these words while Lakṣmaṇa listened:
"My illustrious wife Sītā was carried off by Rāvaṇa when I had departed from Janasthāna at my ease with my brother."
I know only the name of that Rākṣasa, but not his form;
we do not know his dwelling place nor his power, as we wander about thus, afflicted by grief and without a protector.
"Let him act with compassion and remain intent on doing us a favor.
O hero, having gathered dry logs broken by elephants, we shall eat you when you have been placed in a great pit prepared at the proper time."
"Therefore, tell us of Sītā—by whom she was taken or where;
perform this great service for us if you know the truth.
Thus addressed by Rāma with these unsurpassed words, Danu spoke.
Skilled in speech, he spoke even to Rāghava, the speaker himself:
"I possess no divine knowledge, nor do I know Maithilī.
Once I am burnt and have resumed my own form, I shall tell you who it is that will know her."
"O Lord, as long as I am not consumed by fire, I do not have the power to discern that immensely powerful Rākṣasa by whom your Sītā was abducted,
O Rāghava; for my great supernatural knowledge has been lost due to the fault of a curse."

"I have obtained this form, censured by the world, through my own actions. However, O Rāma, before the sun with its weary horses sets, cast me into a pit and burn me according to the prescribed rites."
"O descendant of Raghu, I have been burned by you according to justice;
O hero, I shall tell you of that Rākṣasa who will recognize him.
Friendship should be formed with him, O Rāghava, for he follows a righteous course."
Delighted, he of swift prowess will provide you assistance;
for there is nothing in the three worlds unknown to him, O Raghava,
as he has formerly traversed all the worlds for various reasons.
When the two heroes had been thus addressed by Kabandha, those lords of men reached a mountain cleft and set fire to it.
Lakṣmaṇa, moreover, [threw] great flaming torches on all sides.
She set the funeral pyre ablaze, and it flared up on all sides. As the great body of Kabandha— resembling a mass of ghee—
was being cooked by its own fat, the fire burned it only slowly.
Having quickly shaken off the funeral pyre, like a smokeless fire rising up,
the one of great strength, wearing two stainless garments and a celestial garland,
emerged with speed from the pyre, radiant and clad in spotless raiment.
Greatly rejoiced and adorned with ornaments on every limb, he quickly leapt up,
standing upon a radiant, glory-bestowing celestial chariot drawn by swans;
endowed with great splendor, he illuminated the ten directions with his brilliance.
Having ascended into the air, Kabandha spoke these words to Rāma:
"Listen, O Rāghava, to the truth of how you shall regain Sītā. Rāma, there are six expedients in this world by which everything is deliberated."
Polished by the edge of a blade, a gem is used for its tenth part;
yet you, O Rāma, along with Lakṣmaṇa, have been diminished by that tenth part,
on account of which you have suffered this calamity— the violation of your wife.
Therefore, O best of friends, you must certainly act as a friend toward him;
for even upon reflection, I do not see how you can achieve success without doing so.
Listen, Rāma, I shall tell you: there is a monkey named Sugrīva.
Banished by his angry brother Vālin, the son of Śakra,
that self-controlled hero dwells on Ṛṣyamūka, the best of mountains, which is beautified by the vicinity of Lake Pampā, together with four other monkeys.
"O Raghava, go from here this very day and quickly make him your friend;
having approached him with no malice while the fire blazes,
you must not treat Sugriva, the lord of monkeys, with contempt."
He is grateful, able to assume any form at will, seeking companionship, and full of vigor.
For you two are capable today of accomplishing the task he desires to perform;
whether his purpose has already been achieved or not, he will carry out your business.
That son of Ṛkṣarajas, the legitimate son of Bhāskara who had committed an offense against Vālin, wanders apprehensively around Lake Pampā;
he has quickly set aside his weapons and is staying at the monkey's dwelling on Mount Ṛṣyamūka.
O Raghava, by means of truth, make an ally of this forest-dweller.
For that elephant among monkeys, through his skill, thoroughly knows all the haunts in this world of those who feed on human flesh.
"O Raghava, subduer of enemies, there is indeed nothing in this world that remains unknown to him as long as the thousand-rayed sun shines.
He knows the vast rivers, the mountains, the mountain fastnesses, and the caves."
Having searched together with the monkeys, he will find your wife;
and Raghava will dispatch monkeys of massive form to scour the directions for that Sita, who is grieving due to her separation from you.

That foremost of monkeys, having slain the rakshasas, will restore your blameless beloved to you— whether she is found upon the peak of Mount Meru or dwelling even in the depths of the netherworld. Having thus shown the way for the recovery of Sita, he presented himself before Rama.
Knowing the meaning, Kabandha spoke these words again:
"O Rāma, this is the auspicious path where these beautiful, flowering trees shine, situated toward the western direction."
Jambū, priyāla, and panasa trees; plakṣa, nyagrodha, and tinduka trees;
aśvattha, karṇikāra, and mango trees, as well as other plants—having climbed them, or having forcibly felled them to the ground.
Eating fruits that are like nectar, you two shall proceed;
wandering through excellent regions from mountain to mountain and forest to forest,
O heroes, you will then reach the lotus-lake named Pampā.
O Rāghava, it was free from gravel, without steep descents, with level landing-stairs and no moss; it possessed newly formed sandbanks and was adorned with lotuses and water-lilies.
There, O Rāghava, were swans, ducks, cranes, and ospreys.
The beautiful-voiced birds dwelling in the waters of the Pampā warble melodiously;
they are not alarmed upon seeing men, for they are unacquainted with slaughter.
You two shall devour those auspicious birds, fat as lumps of ghee.
O Rāghava, O Rāma, there at Pampā you shall kill with your arrows those excellent fish— rohitas, vakratuṇḍas, and nalas—
which are skinless, scaleless, roasted on iron spits, fleshy, and possessed of a single spine.
Endowed with devotion for you, Lakṣmaṇa will provide it.
As you eat your fill of fish, there is the auspicious water of the Pampā, fragrant as a lotus, cool and pleasant, and free from all harm.
Then, having extracted that unblemished [root], which resembles silver or crystal,
Lakṣmaṇa will cause him to drink it using a lotus leaf.
[He will likewise bring] large wild boars dwelling in mountain caves and roaming the forest.

O best of men, wandering at evening, O Rāma, you will see on Lake Pampā bulls endowed with beautiful forms, like those who have turned back from their greed for water and are bellowing, wearing garlands upon the trees.
And upon seeing the cool waters of the Pampā, you shall cast off your grief,
O Rāghava, as you behold there the *tilaka* trees covered with blossoms, the *naktamālaka* trees, and the blooming blue lotuses and red lotuses.
"No man there was to offer those garlands;
rather, the disciples of Mataṅga, sages of profound concentration, were present there.
They, oppressed by the weight of their burden as they gathered forest produce for their teacher,"

Those drops of sweat that quickly fell from their bodies to the earth became garlands for the sages through the power of their asceticism; O Raghava, those things born from the drops of sweat do not perish.
Even today, O descendant of Kakutstha, their female attendant, a long-lived female ascetic named Śabarī, is seen right there; she remains ever established in dharma and is honored by all beings.
But as for you, who are eternally established in dharma and revered by all creatures—
"Having seen you, O Rāma, who resemble a god, he will go to the heavenly realm.
Then, O Rāma, descendant of Kakutstha, having reached the western shore of the Pampā, you will behold that incomparable and secret hermitage site."
The Nāgas were unable to attack that hermitage or that grove due to the ordinance of the seer Mataṅga;
it was like the Nandana garden, resembling the forest of the gods.
O Rāma, you shall take delight and find peace amidst the various birds that crowd there.
To the east of Pampā stands Mount Ṛṣyamūka, its trees in full bloom;
it is known as Suduḥkhārohaṇa (Difficult to Ascend) and is guarded by young serpents.
This vast mountain was fashioned by Brahmā himself in ancient times.
O Rāma, whatever wealth a man lying upon the summit of that mountain obtains in a dream, he acquires it upon waking.
But one of wicked conduct or evil deeds does not escape him;
right there, the Rākṣasas seize him while he sleeps and strike him down.
Even from that place, the great roar of young serpents is heard.
O Rāma, as those who dwell in the Mataṅga forest sport in Lake Pampā,
the mighty elephants, dark as clouds and full of speed, having come together and then scattered apart, roam about drenched with streams of blood.
Having drunk there that pure, cool, and inexhaustible water, those forest-dwellers, filled with awe, turned back and plunged into the forests.
O Rāma, a great cave belonging to that mountain shines forth.
O descendant of Kakutstha, its entrance is covered by a stone slab, and entry into it is difficult.
At the eastern gate of that cave, there is a large lake of cool water,
delightful with its many roots and fruits, and surrounded by various trees.
Sugrīva dwells there with four other monkeys; sometimes he stays upon the summit of that mountain.
Having thus instructed both Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, Kabandha—
Wearing a garland and radiant with the luster of the sun, the valiant one shone in the sky.
As he stood there in the air, the illustrious Kabandha, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa spoke these words from nearby as they were setting out: "Go on your way."
"You must go for the sake of accomplishing your purpose," he said to them;
then, having granted them leave, Kabandha departed, well-pleased.
Having resumed his true form, Kabandha was enveloped in splendor, his body resembling the sun.
Pointing this out and looking toward Rāma while remaining in the sky, he then said, "Form an alliance with him.
Taking the western direction as their guide, those two sons of the best of men set out upon that path through the forest which Kabandha had shown them to Pampā.
Beholding upon the mountains many trees laden with fruit as sweet as honey, Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa proceeded to see Sugrīva.
Having made their dwelling upon the mountain ridge, those two descendants of Raghu remained there.
The two descendants of Raghu approached the western shore of the Pampā.
Having reached the western bank of the lotus-lake Pampā,
they then beheld there the beautiful hermitage of Śabarī.
Having reached that hermitage, which was surrounded by many trees and exceedingly beautiful, the two of them beheld it and approached Śabarī.
Seeing them, the perfected one (Siddhā) then rose with palms joined in reverence.
She grasped the feet of Rāma and of the wise Lakṣmaṇa.
Then Rāma spoke to that female ascetic of rigid vows:
"I hope your obstacles have been overcome; I hope your asceticism prospers."
O lady rich in asceticism, is your anger restrained and is your food regulated?
Have you attained your religious observances, and is there peace in your mind? O sweet-spoken one, has your service to your elders borne fruit?
Questioned by Rāma, that aged Śabarī— a perfected woman esteemed by the Siddhas— having presented herself before Rāma, related her story:
"When you arrived at Citrakūṭa, [the gods came] in celestial chariots of incomparable splendor."
From here they have ascended to heaven, whom I have served.
And I was told by those illustrious great seers, who know the dharma:
"Rāma will come to this most holy hermitage of yours."
That guest, accompanied by the son of Sumitrā, must be received by you;
and upon seeing him, you shall go to the excellent, imperishable worlds.
O bull among men, various forest provisions have been gathered by me.
"O tiger among men, for your sake [I have brought] that which grows on the banks of the Pampā.
Thus addressed by Śabarī, the righteous Rāghava said this to Śabarī: "I know her to be one who is eternally excluded from no dharma."
"From Danu, you have heard in truth of the power of that high-souled one; now, if you so deem it right, I wish to see it for myself.
Having heard these words issuing from the mouth of Rāma, [Vasiṣṭha replied: "So be it."
Śabarī showed both of them that great forest:
"Behold, O descendant of Raghu, this forest renowned as Mataṅgavana, which resembles a dense mass of clouds and is teeming with beasts and birds."
O one of great luster, here my gurus, whose souls were cultivated,
performed oblations at this sacred ford, consecrated with mantras according to the rites.
This is the sacrificial altar (vedi) facing west, where they were well-honored by me.
They offer flowers as an oblation with hands trembling from exhaustion.
O best of the Raghus, behold how even today, by the power of their asceticism,
those altars of incomparable splendor illuminate all directions with their radiance.
Unable to proceed, exhausted by the fatigue of their fasts, they thought, "Behold the seven seas gathered here together.
Having performed their ablutions, they hung their bark garments upon the trees here.
Even today, O descendant of Raghu, those spots have not dried up.
This entire forest has been seen by you, and what was to be heard has been heard;
therefore, permitted by you, I wish to cast off this body.
"I wish to go into the presence of those sages of purified souls, whose hermitage I shall serve as an attendant.
Having heard these most righteous words, Rāghava, together with Lakṣmaṇa, [consented].
"Go," he said with a joyful countenance, granting her permission.
Having been thus permitted by Rāma, she offered herself as an oblation into the fire;
resembling a blazing flame, she departed for heaven itself.
By means of her own meditative concentration, Śabarī went to that holy place where those great seers of virtuous soul dwell;
for when Śabarī had departed for heaven by virtue of her own deeds, [the mountain peak became empty].
Rāghava reflected together with his brother Lakṣmaṇa.
Having reflected, the righteous Rāghava spoke to Lakṣmaṇa, who was single-mindedly intent on his welfare, regarding the power of those great-souled ones.
"O gentle one, this hermitage of those who have perfected their souls has been seen; it is full of many wonders, where deer and tigers dwell in confidence and which is frequented by various birds.
And here, O Lakṣmaṇa, are the seven oceans at these sacred fords."
Having performed the ritual ablution according to the rules, the ancestors have also been gratified with libations.
That which was inauspicious has vanished and prosperity has arrived;
therefore, O Lakṣmaṇa, my mind is now filled with joy.
"For in your heart, O tiger among men, auspiciousness shall manifest;
therefore come, let us go to that lovely Pampā,
where Mount Ṛśyamūka appears not far away."
In that place dwells the righteous Sugrīva, the son of Aṃśumat, who,
constantly terrified by the fear of Vālin, resides together with four other monkeys.
"I am in haste to see Sugrīva, that bull among monkeys; for, O gentle one, the search for Sītā depends entirely upon him.
To Rāma, who was speaking thus, the son of Sumitrā replied as follows:
"Let us go there quickly; my mind also hastens there.
Then, having departed from that hermitage, the lord of the people, the subduer of foes, went to Lake Pampā together with Lakṣmaṇa.

Beholding that great forest on all sides, abounding in flowers and vast trees, resounding with the cries of koyaṣṭis, arjunakas, śatapattras, and kīcakas, as well as various other birds, he gazed upon it.
Beholding various trees and diverse lakes, Rāma, tormented by desire, proceeded toward a great lake. Having reached that place from afar, Rāma beheld the river flowing with water.
They entered the lake named Mataṅgasarasa;
and Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, overcome with grief,
entered the Pampā lotus pond, which was covered with lotuses.
It was filled with *tilaka*, *aśoka*, *puṃnāga*, *bakula*,
and *uddālaka* trees, crowded with lovely groves, its waters pressed down by lotuses,
rich in water as clear as crystal, and strewn with smooth sands.
Crowded with fish and tortoises, adorned with trees standing upon its banks,
entwined by creepers as if by companions,
and frequented by kinnaras, uragas, gandharvas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas.
It was filled with various trees and creepers, a beautiful reservoir of cool water; it appeared copper-colored with *saugandhika* lotuses, white with clusters of water-lilies (*kumuda*),
and blue with blossoming blue lotuses, like a multi-colored rug.
Having seen that Lake Pampā, which abounded in red and blue lotuses, was filled with fragrant lilies,
possessed groves of blossoming mango trees, and resounded with the cries of peacocks,
Rāma, together with the son of Sumitrā, gazed upon it.
And the spirited son of Daśaratha lamented out of longing for her,
[seeing] the *tilaka*, *bījapūra*, and *vaṭa* trees, as well as white trees in bloom,
*karavīra* flowers, and beautifully blossomed *puṃnāga* trees.
It was graced like a young woman by clusters of *mālatī* and *kundaka* flowers, as well as by *bhaṇḍīra*, *nicula*,
*aśoka*, *saptaparṇa*, *ketaka*, and *atimuktaka* trees,
and by various other kinds of trees.
On its bank stands the mountain previously mentioned, adorned with minerals and known as Ṛśyamūka, its forests filled with variegated blossoms;
there dwells the son of that high-souled one named Ṛkṣarajas, a monkey.
"The one of great prowess who occupies that place is the renowned Sugrīva.
"O bull among men, go to Sugrīva, the lord of monkeys," he spoke these words again to Lakṣmaṇa, whose valor is truth.

Then, having traveled by degrees along that great path which extended for a long distance while surveying the forest, he beheld Lake Pampā, whose woodlands were beautiful to behold and crowded with many kinds of birds.
